samples. The continuous training and retraining 
of analytical skills are also important elements of personnel comp etence. The laboratory 
shall maintain an up -to-date record of the competence and training of each employee 
involved in sample analysis. The purpose of this is to prove that every member of the staff 
has been adequately trained and is competent to perform sample analysis. In order to ensure

6. Chain of Custody 
If the laboratory wishes to prove that it has reliable results, it must ensure that th e chain of 
custody procedure has been strictly followed. Chain of custody is used in most chemical 
sampling and analysis situations to maintain the integrity of the results of sample analysis 
by providing docume ntation of the coding, control, transfer , and analysis of samples. The 
chain of custody procedure starts with sample collection and continues through the 
destruction of the sample. Chain of custody is described in Section 4, Chapter III. 
7. Summary 
If a laboratory wishes to ensure outside bodies, e.g., customers, that it can produce valid and 
reliable results, it must follow a written quality system procedure and must have documented 
data from every step of the analysis process. The l aboratory must show tha t the s

can produce valid and 
reliable results, it must follow a written quality system procedure and must have documented 
data from every step of the analysis process. The l aboratory must show tha t the sample 
analysis is done with functioning and tested equipment and by trained and qualified 
personnel. Chain of custody is one of the key elements of the sample analysis. The laboratory 
must be able to demonstrate that the principles of the chain of c ustody have been followed 
throughout the analysis process and that there is no possibility of cross -contamination or a 
mix-up of the samples.

2. Method validation 
Method validation is confirmation by examination and the provision of objective evidence 
that analytical requirements are fulfilled. Analytical results are often used to make important 
decisions. Method validation demonstrate s that a method is fit for purpose. It is also an 
important requirement according to ISO/IEC 17025. 
A method needs to be validated when one or more of the following applies: 
1. New method. 
2. Established method revised to incorporate improvements or extended to a new 
problem; or, comparison of two methods. 
3. The quality control of a method is changing with time. 
4. Established method is used in different laboratories or with different equipment. 
Prior to validation, the operator must ensure that the equipment is within the performance 
specification and adequately calibrated . In addition, apparatus required for validation 
(e.g. balances, pipettes) must be calibrated.

validation are set by the authorities or a client, their guidelines must be followed. Otherwise, 
the laboratory can define the validation requirements based on their operational requirements.

External calibration. 
External calibration is based on the signal intensity (area or height) of the analytes compared 
to the signal intensity in the calibration standard solutions without matrix or internal 
standard. External calibration is simple to perform, and it can be applied to many type s of 
methods. It is recommended that the same sample matrix is employed for both analytes and 
calibration standards (i.e. matrix-matched calibration). If the slopes of the curves are similar, 
it can be assumed that no significant matrix suppression is evident.

If blank sample matrix is unavailable, or if the matrix is very complex, samples may be

Internal standards. 
Internal standards compensate random errors in sample preparation and analysis. 
Internal standards must behave similarly in sample preparation, but the analysis result must 
be distinguishable from the analyte. Ideally , the isotopes of the analytes (e.g. 2H, 13C, 15N) 
may be used as internal standards as their physicochemical properties are the same compared

internal standards, however 6 mass units are preferable. Moreover, the fragmentation effect 
(lose label) and exchangeable protons of the labelled ISTD must be considered. Homologous 
series, analog ues, or isomers of the analytes may also be used as internal standards, if 
isotopically labelled internal standards are unavailable.

2.2 Sensitivity 
Sensitivity is usually defined as a change in instrument response versus analyte 
concentration (i.e. slope of the calibration curve), and it is important in method development 
and monitoring of instrument performance. The sensitivity of the instrument can be assessed 
with a quality control sample or a reference sample of a target analyte. The response of the 
analyte should be sufficient to consistently control the status of the instrument. If the 
concentration level of the target analyte is known beforehand, the sensitivity of the 
instrument should be at least at the defined level. If the signal intensities do not fill the set 
criteria, cleaning, tuning, calibration, or other maintenance are needed. The matrix effect can 
be evaluated if the matrix spiked analytes are compared to the analytes in the solvent. The 
higher the sensitivity, the lower the limit of detection (LOD) and quantitation

be evaluated if the matrix spiked analytes are compared to the analytes in the solvent. The 
higher the sensitivity, the lower the limit of detection (LOD) and quantitation (LOQ). 
Limit of detection (LOD) and Limit of quantitation (LOQ) 
Limit of detection (L OD) is the lowest analyte concentration that can be detected and 
identified with a given degree of certainty from the background noise. The principles for 
defining limit of quantitation (L OQ) are simila r to those for L OD; however , the 
multiplication coefficient is larger. Note that the LOD of the whole method differs from the 
instrumental LOD, as it takes into account the whole sample preparation process. There are 
several alternative approaches to evalu ate and determine L OD and L OQ. These may be 
estimated from signal to noise ratios (S/N), and for all diagnostic ions signal to noise ratio 
should be for LOD S/N ≥ 3, and for LOQ S/N ≥ 10.

The method must be selective for the analyte to conform the identity of the analyte. Selective 
method discriminates between the analyte and other compounds in the sample matrix or 
interfering components in the sample mixture. 
The solvent/matrix blank is run to prove the absence of analysed chemicals in the reagents, 
solvents, or equipment used prior to the analysis of samples. The solvent blank contains the 
same solvents, including the possible derivatising agents. According to the OPCW reporting 
guidelines, a solvent blank run is performed with the same analysis method, and it must be 
run directly before sample, and no other analyses must be performed in between solvent 
blank and sample.15,16 
Contamination or carryover may cause false positive results, and must always be 
investigated. The matrix blank sample should be analysed after the highest calibration 
standard to study the possible carryover effects of the instrument. The number of extra blanks 
needed between the reference standards and samples should also be defined to avoid false 
positive results.

According to the OPCW reporting guidelines, at least two different analytical techniques are 
required for each identified chemical. The identification criteria inc lude various 
chromatographic and mass spectrometric parameters, such as retention time, retention index, 
relative retention time, mass accuracy, spectrum library match factors, diagnostic ions, and 
ion ratios. Comparison of the analysed chemical in the sample to reference chemical must 
fulfil OPCW reporting guidelines.15,16

3. Process of validation at LAVEMA 
This chapter describes the process of validation of the qualitative analytical method for the 
analysis of CWA and related compounds in environmental samples by HPLC and GC-based 
techniques performed at LAVEMA. The purpose is the evaluati on of the efficiency of the 
procedure to analyze environmental samples contaminated with CWAs and related 
compounds in a concentration of 1 mg/l or higher. 
The val idation covers not only the preparation of samples but also the chromatographic 
analysis. 
Selectivity and specificity of HPLC and GC-based techniques 
Different parameters are established to assure selectivity and specificity of HPLC and GC-
based techniques, including: 
 Confirmation of the chemical by two chromatograms of different concentration 
obtained from one or several standards, 
 The increase in area in both chromatograms must be proportional to the amount of 
standard, 
 Retention times of the chemical shall not differ more

obtained from one or several standards, 
 The increase in area in both chromatograms must be proportional to the amount of 
standard, 
 Retention times of the chemical shall not differ more than ± 0.5 minutes during the 
validation process. 
Identification by mas s spectrometry will match by 80% in the comparison between the 
standard and the chemical in the sample. 
According to the Spanish Accreditation Body, i f a chemical is reported under ISO 17025, 
the validation of the analytical method used to identify this c hemical in the environmental 
sample must be performed. 
Firstly, the purity of the chemical (commercial or synthesized in the laboratory) is calculated 
by GC-FID. Relevant information, such as the internal code, name, CWC schedule, CAS, 
structure, internal file where the chemical was reported , and the technique used for the 
identification, is summarized in a table. This information will be summarized in the 
validation report. 
Secondly, standards and samples are prepared. The standards are used to calculate the Limit 
of Detection (LOD). After that, three samples are spiked with the chemical at a concentration 
of 1 ppm or above . Sample preparation i

The regression curve is obtained from a series of standards of different concentrations. The 
concentration value of the sample is calculated by interpolation to the calibration curve. This

Statement of proficiency 
The analytical procedures established in the LAVEMA laboratory assure the detection and 
identification of CWC -related chemicals in environmental samples at a concentration of 
1 ppm or higher in the matrices covered by the scope of its accreditation according to

Validation report 
The validation report is prepared for every validated chemical in a specific environmental 
sample. This report will be evaluated by the Spanish Accreditation Body.

4. On-the-job validation at VERIFIN 
The scope of VERIFIN ISO 17025 accreditation is flexible, and it covers chemicals related 
to the Chemical Weapons Convention in environmental and material samples and 
biomedical samples (blood, urine). The most suitable procedures are sele cted for sample 
preparation and analysis for the type of sample matrix in question (Blue Book ROPs). The 
procedures have been tested in various interlaboratory comparison tests and OPCW 
proficiency tests. In addition, VERIFIN has the working instruction On-the-job-validation 
of the Sample Preparation and Analysis of Chemical Warfare Agents and Related 
Chemicals. The working instruction ensures reliable and unambiguous analytical results in 
cases where the method to be applied has not been tested in advance. If CWC -related 
chemicals are not found in the sample, the sample matrix is spiked with a known amount of 
chemicals. The sample preparation procedure and analysis are carried out for the s
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
advance. If CWC -related 
chemicals are not found in the sample, the sample matrix is spiked with a known amount of 
chemicals. The sample preparation procedure and analysis are carried out for the spiked 
sample using the same approach as for the real sample. This ve rifies that the selected 
chemicals can be found in the spiked sample matrix with similar selected analytical 
procedures at the used concentration level. The detection limits of the chemicals are 
estimated on the basis of spiking experiments. 
5. Conclusions 
In summary, the basic requirements for method validation have been discussed in this 
chapter. The level and criteria for the validation must be defined by the laboratory (or are set 
by the authorities or client). The selection of method performance parameters depends on 
the type of the validation, and whether it is qualitative or quantitative. Overall, 
interlaboratory proficiency tests organized by OPCW are a good way to monitor the method 
performance of qualitative analysis of CWAs and related compounds.

Section 1. General 
Part B. Analytical Strategy 
Chapter I. Screening 
 
Version 1.1 ROP 1-B-I 
Date 11 December 2017 Page 55 
1. Scope 
This chapter describes the screening step in the analysis of chemicals related to the Chemical 
Weapons Convention (CWC). In this step, various characteristics of the CWC -related 
chemicals are used to detect them among the irrelevant background chemicals. The next step 
is the identification, which is discussed in the following chapters. Generally, the methods 
aim to detect around 1 mg/kg or 1 mg/l concentration levels. In practice, many of the 
screening methods are able to detect traces of relevant chemicals at the µg/kg or µg/l level. 
This chapter discusses the screening of only CWC-related small molecule weight chemicals. 
The analysis of toxin molecules is discussed separately in Section 3, Part F: Other Analysis. 
2. Summary of the methods 
A wide range of different methods is available for the screening step in the analysis of CWC-
related chemicals. The gas chromatography (GC) -based techniques, GC using selective 
detectors and gas chromatography–electron ionisation mass spect
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ble for the screening step in the analysis of CWC-
related chemicals. The gas chromatography (GC) -based techniques, GC using selective 
detectors and gas chromatography–electron ionisation mass spectrometry (GC–EI/MS) are 
the most used and most sensitive screening techniques. It should, however, be re membered 
that other techniques, such as liquid chromatography –mass spectrometry ( LC–MS) and 
nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR), can be used very efficiently in screening. 
One major advantage these two methods have over GC -based techniques is the ability to 
screen aqueous samples with a minimal amount of sample preparation. 
The most important feature of a screening technique is to be able to detect a CWC -related 
chemical among other chemicals in the samples. Thi s ability is based on various chemical 
properties, but the screening methods are divided into two distinct groups: targeted screening 
methods and non -targeted screening methods. In the former group, only a defined set of 
known chemicals is being searched for, typically using mass spectrometry (either GC or LC-
based). In the latter group, a more universal property, such as an element (typically 
phosp
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
defined set of 
known chemicals is being searched for, typically using mass spectrometry (either GC or LC-
based). In the latter group, a more universal property, such as an element (typically 
phosphorus, sulphur or nitrogen) or a common part of the molecule is being targeted. 
Typically, the instruments and methods used for screening (especially spectrometric 
methods) are the same as those used for actual identification. The screening must be based 
on a pre-existing screening strategy, which contains lists of all compounds to be searched 
for. The screening s trategy must be carefully planned and evaluated in advance. It is 
important to understand what the advantages and limitations of each screening technique are 
and, especially, the screening step as a whole.

3. Screening strategies 
To enable a reliable and comprehensive analysis of CWC -related chemicals, it must be 
assured that all relevant chemicals can be detected and identified. One of the tool sets applied 
to this task is screening samples using various techniques. 
Each screening technique relies on one or more properties of the CWC -related chemicals, 
which separate them from irrelevant chemicals. Table 1 shows examples of selected CWC-
related chemicals and some typical screening methods for each chemical. 
It should be remembered that the screening step has to be a combination of various 
techniques. The nature of the sample impacts the selection of screening methods. Paragraph 
7 will shortly discuss the selection of screening methods and paragraph 8 gives two examples 
of screening strategies applied by a n OPCW designated laboratory for analysi s of CWC -
related chemicals.

3.1 Targeted and non-targeted screening 
There are different ways of approaching the screening task: one possibility is to use the most 
general method as possible (non-targeted screening ) and the other is to try to look for 
individual chemicals (targeted screening ). In reality, many of the screening methods are 
somewhere in between these two limits. 
The advantage of non-targeted screening is that the method searches for a common property 
of a chemical or a chemical group and, therefore, one doesn ’t have to know each of the 
chemicals to be screened. On the other hand, the screening result is very tentative and 
requires confirmation by other methods. 
Very typical non-targeted screening methods are mass screening methods such as selective 
GC detectors (paragraph 4.1). While still quite general, 31P NMR (paragraph 6) gives already 
more information on the actual structure of the target molecule. 
Mass spectrometric screening methods are mostly targeted methods. In the least targeted 
modes,
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
31P NMR (paragraph 6) gives already 
more information on the actual structure of the target molecule. 
Mass spectrometric screening methods are mostly targeted methods. In the least targeted 
modes, MS methods are looking for chemical groups based on characteristic ions 
(paragraph 5.1) such as m/z 99 for sarin -type chemicals, m/z 97 for dialkyl 
alkylphosphonates or m/z 109 and 63 for mustard-type agents (see Figure 1 for structures). 
When LC–MS is used in a non-targeted mode (using in-source CID), the characteristic group 
ions can be screened in a similar way to the GC–EI/MS screening. 
In the most targeted modes, specific chemicals are being searched for. This method , for 
example, can be used in GC–EI/MS to find chemicals that are not detectable using selective 
GC detectors (paragraph 5.1 .1). The most selective MS screening method is the multiple 
reaction monitoring (MRM) of CWC-related chemicals in LC–MS (paragraph 5.2.2.1).

type chemicals, b) dialkyl alkylphosphonates and c) mustard-type chemicals.

4. Elemental Screening 
The most comprehensive coverage in screening can be gained by screening for the 
heteroatoms in CWC-related chemicals. Almost all of the relevant chemicals contain at least 
one or several of the following elements: phosphorus, sulphur or nitrogen. Additionally 
many of the intact agents also contain halogen atoms (either chlorine or fluorine). 
Naturally, a huge amount of irrelevant chemicals will also contain one of the above elements, 
but the number of possible target chemicals is normally reduced to a much more manageable 
number. Figure 2 shows an example of the removal of the hydrocarbon background from a 
sample and the detection of mustard gas using a flame photometric detector (FPD) in sulphur 
mode.

4.1.1 Flame photometric detector (FPD) 
A flame photometric detector (FPD) uses an optical band-pass filteri for the selection of the 
detected element: phosphorus, FPD(P), or sulphur, FPD(S) . To convert the detector from 
one element to the other requires a change of filter. The detector is more sensitive to 
phosphorus than sulphur.ii 
Note! The photomultiplier tube is very sensitive to am bient light. Therefore, it has to be 
switched o ff before opening the detector. Also, the open end of the photomultiplier tube 
should always be covered (e.g. , by using aluminium foil) when it is not connected to the 
detector body. 
In the dual flame photomet ric detector systems (dual FPD), two photomultiplier tubes are 
fitted into one detector body. This way both phosphorus and sulphur can be monitored 
simultaneously without splitting the column flow. 
On some occasions, a very strong phosphorus peak can creat e a small ghost peak on the 
sulphur channel. This is due to an increased width of the phosphor
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
taneously without splitting the column flow. 
On some occasions, a very strong phosphorus peak can creat e a small ghost peak on the 
sulphur channel. This is due to an increased width of the phosphorus emission peak so that 
the signal is also increased in the sulphur wavelength. To avoid the wrong interpretation of 
these signals, one has to pay attention to the relative signal intensities. Comparison to a 
known sample, for example, a column performance test, helps to evaluate the correct signal 
levels. For sulphur, however, the detector is not linear and suffers from quenching by co-
eluting hydrocarbons. 
4.1.2 Pulsed FPD (PFPD) 
The pulsed flame photometric detector (PFPD) is able to detect phosphorus, sulphur, arsenic 
and nitrogen-containing compounds. iii The ability to detect arsenic or nitrogen -containing 
chemicals makes the PFPD very useful for screening CWC-related chemicals. 
PFPD exploits the time -dependence of the photon emission process during combustion of 
the compounds in the flame, which is not continuous, but turned on and off every 300 ms. 
The flame pulse profile over time is dependent on the elements in the chemicals, and thus 
the signal may be selecti
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
mpounds in the flame, which is not continuous, but turned on and off every 300 ms. 
The flame pulse profile over time is dependent on the elements in the chemicals, and thus 
the signal may be selectively associated to an element. The PFPD does not suffer the 
quenching of co-eluting hydrocarbon chemicals. Unfortunately, the emission spectra of the 
elements frequently overlap with others. 
Note! Avoid the use of chlorinated solvents with the PFPD detector due to the risk of 
photomultiplier degradation. 
The sensitivity of the PFPD is better as compared to the FPD detector for a single element 
in conditions optimised specifically for the detection of that element. 
The main optimisable parameters affecting the selectivity and sensitivity of the PFPD are 
the gate width and the gate delay. Careless maximisation of the sensitivity towards a single 
element may result in false positive detections, due to a decrease in selectivity. Conversely, 
the optimisation of selectivity is detrimental to sensitivity. It is important to realise that subtle 
variations in these parameters of the detector have a strong influence on signal emission, 
acquisition and processing.

text:

variations in these parameters of the detector have a strong influence on signal emission,

4.1.3 Nitrogen-Phosphorus Detector (NPD) 
The nitrogen-phosphorus detector (NPD) gives signals for both phosphorus and nitrogen 
simultaneously, which means that it is not possible to say whether a chemical contains only 
phosphorus, only nitrogen or both. 
An NPD is very selective and more sensitive towards phosphorus than towards nitrogen. The 
sensitivity of the detector depends strongly on the temperature of the NPD bead and the flow 
rate of the detector gases. In addition, some models are not compatible with chlorinated 
solvents and/or silylation reagents and, in this case, th
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
gly on the temperature of the NPD bead and the flow 
rate of the detector gases. In addition, some models are not compatible with chlorinated 
solvents and/or silylation reagents and, in this case, the analysis of silylate d samples 
(i.e., after derivatisation using BSTFA) results in the reduced performance of the detector. 
This is due the silicon-containing residue depositing on the collector surface of the detector. 
To avoid problems with non-silylated samples, it is recommended that the silylated samples 
are run after the other samples. 
4.1.4 Atomic Emission Detector (AED) 
The a tomic emission detector (AED) is particularly well -suited to screening complex 
samples for CWC-related chemicals containing heteroatoms such as phosphorous, sulphur, 
nitrogen, chlorine, fluorine and arsenic. 
This detector uses microwave -induced plasma in which molecules eluting from the 
chromatographic system are atomised in excited states. The relaxation of excited atoms 
results in the emission of photons at wavelengths characteristic to various elements , which 
are, in turn, detected by means of a spectrometer. 
The AED is a sensitive technique for the detection of carbon, hydrogen, sulph
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
of photons at wavelengths characteristic to various elements , which 
are, in turn, detected by means of a spectrometer. 
The AED is a sensitive technique for the detection of carbon, hydrogen, sulphur, phosphorus, 
arsenic and silicon (for silylated chemical s). Chlorine, fluorine, nitrogen and oxygen can 
also be detected but with poorer limits of detection. 
During the acquisition, specific reagent gases are required for optimal sensitivity for 
different elements. The elements form groups where the reagent gas mixture is the same and 
the used wavelengths are close to each other , as shown in Table 4. Elements within one 
group can be analysed in the same chromatographic run. If it is necessary to analyse elements 
from more than one group, several runs have to be made.

4.1.5 Electron Capture Detector (ECD) 
Some CWC -related compounds containing chlorine atoms, e.g. , vesicants, are detectable 
with an ECD, but the sensitivity for some compounds is rather low depending on the low 
electron affinity of the these compounds. 
The sensitivity of the ECD towards fluorine is quite poor. Therefore, NPD or FPD(P) would 
give better sensitivity for most CWC -related fluorine-containing chemicals as they usually 
also contain phosphorus. 
The ECD can be considered as moderately sensitive towards vesicants, but, in most cases, 
not selective enough. This is especially true for environmental and biological samples, which 
often contain irrelevant ECD-active chemicals, which will interfere with the detection of the 
CWC-related compounds. 
4.2 Other methods 
4.2.1 Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) Spectroscopy and ICP–MS 
Some CWC-related compounds containing special elements like arsenic can be detected by 
ICP–MS. The sensitivity is quite good for arsenic, which can be detect
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
led Plasma (ICP) Spectroscopy and ICP–MS 
Some CWC-related compounds containing special elements like arsenic can be detected by 
ICP–MS. The sensitivity is quite good for arsenic, which can be detected in the low ppb -
range even in diluted samples. 
The technique is quite simple to use. Water samples can be run directly or after dilution with 
diluted nitric acid. Organic samples or solids can be analy sed after digestion in nitric acid 
followed by oxidation with hydrogen peroxide. In this case, the samples are normally diluted 
with water to a nitric acid concentration in the range of 0.65% to 6.5%. 
The ICP–MS analysis can be done either as a single element analysis or as a multi -element 
analysis. In the latter case, it will often be possible to verify the presence of other heteroatoms 
such as phosphorous and sulphur.

5. Mass spectrometric screening 
Mass spectrometric screening has to rely on searching for ions typical of the target 
chemicals. These ions can be a molecular ion (typically in LC –MS), a fragment ion or 
combined as an MRM transition. Various levels of screening methods can be selected from 
relatively non-targeted to specifically targeted methods. 
5.1 GC–EI/MS-based screening 
As electron ionisation almost always produces fragment ions, the screening methods for GC–
EI/MS typically rely on more or less characteristic fragments. 
5.1.1 Screening phosphorus-, nitrogen- and sulphur-deficient chemicals 
Even though selective detectors for phosphorus, nitrogen and sulphur are often used for 
screening CWC-related samples, not all relevant chemicals are detected with these detectors. 
The reason for this is that there are some relevant chemicals that do not contain any of these 
three elements. The number of these chemicals is so small that they can be specifically 
screened with GC-EI/MS using their

5.1.2 AMDIS-based screening 
It is recommended that AMDIS screening is used for all samples analysed with GC–EI/MS. 
AMDIS is a software designed automatic analysis of GC–EI/MS data: deconvolution of GC–
EI/MS data followed by automated spectral cleaning (i.e. removal of background) and 
subsequent searching for target chemicals in a library. Originally, this tool was intended for 
the use by OPCW inspectors for on -site GC –MS analysis, but it has also proven very 
successful for off-site laboratory use. 
As AMDIS relies on library search, th e availability of comprehensive and reliable libraries 
is the critical requirement for successful use of AMDIS for any type of screening. The 
OPCW has been developing a thoroughly validated analytical database for both its inspectors 
and any other laboratory that needs to perform CWC-related analysis. The Official OPCW 
Analytical Database (OCAD) contains among other data EI spectra and GC retention data 
for Scheduled chemicals and their analytical derivat
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
at needs to perform CWC-related analysis. The Official OPCW 
Analytical Database (OCAD) contains among other data EI spectra and GC retention data 
for Scheduled chemicals and their analytical derivatives. The database is available to all 
Member States of the CWC upon request from the OPCW Laboratory. 
The major advantage of the software is the combination of automatic deconvolution and 
library search of each of the components in the GC run. The system can often find relevant 
low-concentration components that would be missed by a human analyst. 
The automatic library search is also the weakest point of the system, although, proper use of 
selective detectors can resolve many problems. First, if a spectrum of a chemical (or a closely 
related chemical) is not present in the library, it is not possible to detect the chemical. Second, 
the library search – as normal – may result in several close matches , which might lead to 
false positive identification without careful manual checking of the results (or use of 
retention indices discussed below). 
AMDIS is also able to perform automatic calculations of retention indices for all components 
of the run. For this calculation, it is
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
g of the results (or use of 
retention indices discussed below). 
AMDIS is also able to perform automatic calculations of retention indices for all components 
of the run. For this calculation, it is necessary to calibrate the retention indices using an 
alkane mixture [typic ally from typically octane (C 8) to tetracosane (C 24) or even to 
octacosane (C28)] which is included in the normal quality control mixture for GC and GC –
MS [see discussion in Section 3, Part B, Chapter II: Gas c hromatography–electron 
ionisation/mass Spectrometry (GC–EI/MS)]. The combination of mass spectral search and 
retention index search can solve most of the problems with the false positive detections, 
e.g. arising from closely related chemicals. 
The normal retention index calculation is always limited to values between the first and last 
component of the retention index standard series – typically starting from C8 up to C24 or C28. 
AMDIS offers an easy – but unofficial – way to extrapolate for very early eluting chemicals 
such as 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol (example shown in Figure 5 below) . This helps in 
differentiating it from other similar alcohols.

5.2 LC–MS-based screening 
In contrast to GC–MS, LC–MS cannot generally benefit from element selective detectors or 
data libraries as discussed above. Therefore, LC–MS-based screening has to rely on the mass 
spectral “properties” of the target chemicals. With modern instruments, a variety of 
experiments are available for screening of unknown samples. Some strategies for CWC-
relevant chemicals by LC–MS/MS will be given in this chapter. For further information on 
LC–MS/MS analysis and the ions used for screening, refer to Section 3, Part C, Chapter II: 
Liquid chromatography-atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass spectrometry (LC-API/MS). 
Atmospheric pressure ionisation (API) techniques , including electrospray ionisation (ESI) 
and atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation (APCI), are the most commonly used LC-MS 
ionisation techniques. As ESI and APCI are soft ionisation techniqu es, deprotonated or 
protonated molecul es or adduct ions with a usually low degree of fragmentation are 
generated de
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
y used LC-MS 
ionisation techniques. As ESI and APCI are soft ionisation techniqu es, deprotonated or 
protonated molecul es or adduct ions with a usually low degree of fragmentation are 
generated depending on the analysed chemical and its polarity. 
There exist several different types of mass spectrometers available for LC-MS. They can be 
divided roughly into two groups, “unit resolution” and “high resolution” instruments. To the 
first group belong single quadrupole instruments, triple quadrupole instruments (QqQ), ion 
traps and combinations thereof. These instruments (except for single quadrupoles) allow 
different scan techniques: 
 full scan MS 
 product ion scan 
 precursor ion scan 
 selected reaction monitoring (SRM) and multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) 
 neutral loss 
For the high or even ultra-high resolution mass spectrometers (HRMS), such as the hybrid 
quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer (Q-TOF) or the (hybrid) Orbitrap™ 
instruments, screening will make use of the high mass accuracy of these instruments. 
Some specific uses for HRMS: 
 measure in full scan and MS/MS mode simultaneously, 
 determine the m/z values with very high accuracy of typicall
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
use of the high mass accuracy of these instruments. 
Some specific uses for HRMS: 
 measure in full scan and MS/MS mode simultaneously, 
 determine the m/z values with very high accuracy of typically lower than 5 ppm, 
 determine molecular formulas of unknown chemicals based on high mass accuracy 
and isotopic pattern, 
 screening: use of m/z values with narrow mass windows, typically in the mDa-range 
 use “in-silico” molecular formula databases, 
 retrospective analysis. 
5.2.1 Chemicals 
To appropriately screen unknown samples by LC–MS/MS the nature and specific properties 
of the different chemicals must be taken into account. For a simplified discussion of different 
screening strategies, CWC-related chemicals can be divided into “knowns” and “unknowns”. 
At first glance, the “known” chemicals pose the least problem for screening and detection, 
because their structure and molecular weight are known . With the measurement of the

obtained. This very specific information can then be used to set up a selective screening 
method. For this type of chemical , an SRM/MRM-based method can be developed, with 
transitions using the molecular ion and one or two fragment ions. With HRMS full scan data 
can be obtained and searched for accurate m/z values of the target chemicals. 
The “unknown” chemicals pose an inherently more difficult problem: how to screen for 
chemicals which have unknown structures and molecular weights? This situation arises in 
all labs where samples are analysed for unknown chemicals. Many approaches are therefore 
published. Most of the proposed solutions to this so called ‘general unknown screening ’ 
(GUS) problem make use of at least known common substructure elements, or of 
characteristic isotopic distributions and other common phys icochemical properties of the 
“unknowns”. The same holds true for CWC -related chemical

characteristic isotopic distributions and other common phys icochemical properties of the 
“unknowns”. The same holds true for CWC -related chemicals: substructures and fragment 
ions typical for distinct substance classes can be used as targets for the screening process. 
These chemical class specific fragment ions ar e discussed in Section 3, Part C, Chapter II: 
Liquid chromatography–atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass spectrometry (LC–API/MS). 
5.2.2 Mass spectrometric techniques for CWC-related screening 
An LC –MS/MS based screening strategy for CWC -related chemicals has to take into 
account: 
 instrumental possibilities, i.e. what kind of mass spectrometers are available, 
 the broad chemical variety of relevant chemicals, 
 specific chemical properties of the CWC -related chemicals which separate them 
from irrelevant chemicals. 
“Unit resolution” instruments such as QqQ or ion traps offer different scan modes such as 
SRM/MRM, MS/MS, precursor ion, neutral loss and more. With HRMS instruments on the 
other hand screening is straightforward: one run in positive ion mode and one run in negative 
ion mode to gather all
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
RM/MRM, MS/MS, precursor ion, neutral loss and more. With HRMS instruments on the 
other hand screening is straightforward: one run in positive ion mode and one run in negative 
ion mode to gather all necessary data . These instruments permit measuring in the full scan 
mode and acquiring in-source CID or MS/MS data during the same LC run. Such data sets 
contain all information and allow retrospective analysis. 
5.2.2.1 Screening with “Unit resolution” LC–MS/MS 
Let’s first focus on “unit resolution” LC -MS/MS instrument, which can be found in many 
laboratories today. Taking into account the capabilities of these LC–MS/MS systems several 
approaches can be used. Some of these methods are summarised in Table 6 together with 
their advantages and disadvantages. 
Screening of known chemicals is based on the molecular weight, the retention time , the 
MS/MS spectra and other specific properties - it is referred to as target screening. To set up 
a target screening method, the respective reference substance must be available in order to 
optimise and test the method. 
The screening of an “unknown” must be based on properties common to the respective 
chemical family and it is here ref

optimise and test the method.

Target screening using SRM/MRM 
The method of choice for the selective detection of known chemicals in complex matrices is 
the SRM or MRM method. It is widely used for the detection and quantification of toxins, 
metabolites, drugs, dopes and environmental pollutants. 
The procedure to develop and optimise an MRM method entails the following steps and can 
be quite labour intensive (Q1 and Q3 refer to the quadrupoles of a trip le quadrupole mass 
spectrometer): 
1. Obtain a reference chemical. 
2. Measure the MS/MS spectrum of the reference chemical. 
3. Based on the MS/MS spectrum, choose specific fragment ions for Q3. Normally, the 
most intense fragment ion is chosen as “quantifier”. A second transition is used as 
“qualifier”. Fragments formed by the loss of water are not recommended for MRM 
transitions. 
4. Use split infusion to optimise the SRM/MRM parameters such as spray parameters, 
collision energy, collision gas pressure and quadrupole and ion trap potentials. Use 
an infusion pump, a T
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
itions. 
4. Use split infusion to optimise the SRM/MRM parameters such as spray parameters, 
collision energy, collision gas pressure and quadrupole and ion trap potentials. Use 
an infusion pump, a T-union and the LC pump. The pump delivers the LC solvent 
(flow and composition) that will be used during analysis. 
5. This optimisation has to be done for every chemical of interest. 
6. Check if the optimised method is still specific for the chemical of interest ( a matrix 
injection without the chemical should yield no signal). 
7. Determine the retention time. 
8. Optional: Determine the LOD of the method with a serial dilution. 
Some instruments allow automatic SRM/MRM optimization. 
If the number of MRM transitions, i.e. , the number of screened chemicals is high, a 
scheduled MRM method may be used. Be careful not to exclude chemicals when setting the 
retention time windows for the transitions. 
Non-target screening using LC–MS/MS with in-source CID 
In MS/MS experiments, the Q1 filter is set to the parent ion mass of the known target 
chemical. As the molecular mass of “unknowns” is not known, the SRM/MRM mode cannot 
be applied or has to be modified . For example, the nerve
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ilter is set to the parent ion mass of the known target 
chemical. As the molecular mass of “unknowns” is not known, the SRM/MRM mode cannot 
be applied or has to be modified . For example, the nerve agents and their degradation and 
by-products form a large number of chemicals with closely related substructures. This 
common property can be used for the screening of these chemicals. The API sources offer 
the possibility to perform in-source CID. Under in-source CID conditions the O-alkyl moiety 
is (partially) cleaved, reducing the chemical to its common substructure (Figure 6). Thus the 
intrinsically large number of nerve agent -related chemicals is reduced to a few typical m/z 
values. An example of in-source CID fragmentation for alkyl alkylphosphonates is shown 
in Figure 6.

The degree of in-source fragmentation should be controllable. The parameter which controls 
the fragmentation has to be set to a compromise value at which most of the chemicals 
produce sufficient in-source CID fragments but still showing the molecular ion [M+H] + or 
[M-H]-, respectively.

SRM/MRM for non-target screening 
The boundary between targeted and non-targeted screening is not sharp. Consequently, the 
target screening method SRM/MRM can be adapted for non-target screening. If a group of 
chemicals produces similar in-source CID frag
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
rgeted and non-targeted screening is not sharp. Consequently, the 
target screening method SRM/MRM can be adapted for non-target screening. If a group of 
chemicals produces similar in-source CID fragments, their m/z values can be used in an 
SRM/MRM method to detect all chemicals of this group. 
As an example, when fragmenting alkyl methylphosphonates (hydrolysed sarin -type nerve 
agents) under appropriate in-source CID conditions, fragment m/z 95 [MeP(O)(OH)O] - in 
the negative or m/z 97 [MeP(OH)(OH)OH]+ in the positive ion mode are generated. Under 
CID conditions, these chemicals further decay into fragment m/z 79 [PO3]- in the negative 
mode or m/z 79 [MeP(O)OH] + in the positive mode. Thus, a n MRM method using the 
transition m/z 9579 (negative mode) wil l detect all alkyl methylphosphonates that 
fragment into m/z 95 and 79, respectively, provided the ion source parameters are set to 
sufficiently generate these in-source CID fragments. A subsequent precursor ion scan of 
m/z 95 (-) or m/z 97 (+), respectively, can reveal the molecular weight of the intact chemicals 
and structural elements (the molecular weight of the O-alkyl group) can be determined.

5.2.2.2 Screening with HRMS instruments 
The specific properties of the HRMS systems, high mass resolution and high mass accuracy, 
allow a different screening approach. With these instruments it is possible to acquire full 
scan MS and MS/MS via in-source CID (as the molecular mass is not known) data 
simultaneously. Such combined data contain all mass spectrometric information about 
“knowns” and “unknowns” and screening can be carried out as follows: 
 Search for exact mass of the molecular ion (if known) 
 Search for exact mass of typical fragments 
 Use very narrow mass windows which enable the generation of a highly selective 
extracted ion chromatogram s (EIC) reducing the chemical interferences from the 
matrix background. 
For the analysis of the data t

text:
row mass windows which enable the generation of a highly selective 
extracted ion chromatogram s (EIC) reducing the chemical interferences from the 
matrix background. 
For the analysis of the data t he mass tolerance window is set to narrow values (typically 
<10 mDa) which enables highly selective extracted ion chromatograms. Consequently, even 
in a full scan spectrum, co -eluting chemicals are blocked (unless they have the same 
molecular formula), and thus chemical interferences are greatly reduced . In addition, the 
HRMS inst ruments produce exact masses (< 5 ppm), which can be used to calculate the 
elemental composition. Additionally, isotopic distribution s for typical common fragment 
ions, specific fragment ions and quasi-molecular ions can be obtained, leading to a reduced 
set of possible molecular formulas and giving information about the presence of 
heteroatoms. Exact fragment ion masses and retention times improve the selectivity of the 
screening process. 
Databases containing only molecular formula would already be sufficient for screening. 
To confirm the identity of chemicals, the reference chemical has to be measured. In this 
respect, there is no difference

6. NMR-based screening techniques 
Screening for the heteroatoms like phosphorus and fluorine in the CWC -related chemicals 
is feasible using NMR spectroscopy. 
Direct observation of phosphorus and fluorine with 31P{1H} NMR and 19F NMR, 
respectively, provides a selective overview of the compounds containing these heteroatoms. 
The resonance multiplicity in 19F NMR also provides information about the structure of the 
alkyl chain bonded to phosphorus in the Schedule 1.A.1 chemicals. The sensitivity for 
fluorine can be increased at least twofold by 19F{1H} compared to 19F but the information 
about the structure of the alkyl chain bonded to the phosphorus is lost. 
The screening for hydrogen in CWC related chemicals is feasible, provided the signals are 
not obscured by signals from matrix components. It is also possible to use the characteristic 
nJHP couplings found in organophosphorus compounds that are related to t he CWC, and 
screen the samples with 1D /2D 1H-31P correlation techniques. The m
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
It is also possible to use the characteristic 
nJHP couplings found in organophosphorus compounds that are related to t he CWC, and 
screen the samples with 1D /2D 1H-31P correlation techniques. The main advantage of e.g. 
the 1D 1H-31P HSQC experiment is its selectivity: signals from protons with a scalar 
coupling to 31P nuclei are observed exclusively while the signals from the sample 
background of obscuring signals from organophosphorus compounds in 1H NMR spectra are 
efficiently removed. Compared to the 31P{1H} NMR experiment, the sensitivity is 
considerably enhanced.

7. Selection of screening methods 
The actual selection of the screening methods depends on the available instrumentation. 
Most common methods for screening are element selective GC detectors and different mass 
spectrometric methods (both GC –MS- and LC –MS-based methods). Additionally, other 
methods such as NMR can be successfully applied. 
When the actual analysis is being carried out, it is important to get the screening information 
as early as possible to allow the location of the peaks of interest in more complex data, such 
as GC–EI/MS chromatograms. This requirement puts emphasis on the speed and simplicity 
of the screening analysis. It would, for example, be preferable to obtain the screening results 
with minimal sample preparation. A good example of this is the screening of water samples 
using both NMR and LC –MS techniques, which do not require the time consuming 
evaporation of water and derivatisation that is required for GC -based techniques. On the 
other hand, sample s in organ
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
using both NMR and LC –MS techniques, which do not require the time consuming 
evaporation of water and derivatisation that is required for GC -based techniques. On the 
other hand, sample s in organic solvents can very easily be screened using GC -based 
techniques, but may require more complicated sample preparation and cleaning procedures 
before LC-based analysis. 
Many laboratories use element detective screening techniques for screening, for example, in 
the OPCW Proficiency Tests, but do not actually report them. The emphasis in reporting is 
normally put on spectrometric techniques. Additionally, co -eluting chemicals may prevent 
the reporting of a GC-based technique. In mass spectrometry, by carefully selecting the ions, 
the co-eluting peaks can be removed from the extracted ion chromatograms (EICs).

8. Usage of screening in various laboratories 
The choice of the methods used for screening depends on the available instrumentation. In a 
typical OPCW designated la boratory, GC, GC –EI/MS, LC –MS and NMR are always 
available for screening. In the following, examples of screening strategies us ed in two 
OPCW designated laboratories are discussed. 
8.1 AMMS 
After proper sample preparation, samples are screened for the presence of CWC -related 
chemicals by GC coupled with element selective detectors, GC –EI/MS, LC –HRMS and 
NMR in Laboratory of Toxicant Analysis, Academy of Military Medical Sciences (AMMS). 
To further confirm the identity of the potential candidates detected in initial screening, other 
techniques such as GC–CI/MS, GC–HRMS, and LC–MS/MS may also be used. 
8.1.1 GC-based screening 
GC–FID/dFPD, GC –FID/NPD and GC –AED are employed to screen for CWC -related 
chemicals containing heteroatoms such as phosphorous, sulphur, nitrogen and arsenic. dFPD 
with both phosphorous and sulp
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
GC–FID/dFPD, GC –FID/NPD and GC –AED are employed to screen for CWC -related 
chemicals containing heteroatoms such as phosphorous, sulphur, nitrogen and arsenic. dFPD 
with both phosphorous and sulphur mode can give detection of phosphorus and sulphur 
simultaneously. NPD is able to monitor phosphorus and nitrogen-containing chemicals. The 
combination of dFPD and NPD helps to differentiate the signals that only contain nitrogen, 
but still cannot distinguish the signals containing only phosphorus and those containing both 
phosphorus and nitrog en. Meanwhile, carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and arsenic -containing 
chemicals are detected by GC–AED simultaneously in a single chromatographic run, due to 
the fact that the emission wavelengths of these four elements are close to each other. If 
necessary, nitrogen, chlorine or other elements can be monitored by running more runs. 
Since the columns fitted on the GC instruments (HP-5, 30 m x 0.25 mm x 0.25 μm) and the 
columns fitted on the GC–MS instruments (HP-5ms, 25 m x 0.20 mm x 0.33 μm) are of the 
same type of stationary phase but different dimension, the RI values of the selective detected 
chemicals are calculated, related and
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
GC–MS instruments (HP-5ms, 25 m x 0.20 mm x 0.33 μm) are of the 
same type of stationary phase but different dimension, the RI values of the selective detected 
chemicals are calculated, related and used to pinpoint the location of the chemicals in total 
ion chromatograms of GC–MS. To achieve this, the QC test mixture is measured in advance 
with FID or AED in carbon -channel to obtain the retention times of the relevant n -alkanes 
which is also called alkane pattern. The RI values of the specific signals during the sample 
analysis are then calculated with external standard method using the n-alkanes in the QC test 
run as retention index standards. In general, the alkane pattern is very stable and only has to 
be measured again after changing chromatographic condition or system maintenance such 
as column shortening. 
GC–EI/MS with scan mode are used to screen for all chemicals of interest. By using AMDIS 
combined with proper target library (OCAD, Validation Group Working Database (VGWD) 
or in -house libraries), data acquired can be anal ysed automatically and the chemicals of 
interest are extracted. The search control factors of AMDIS are always set leniently to get 
more
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e (VGWD) 
or in -house libraries), data acquired can be anal ysed automatically and the chemicals of 
interest are extracted. The search control factors of AMDIS are always set leniently to get 
more hits, hence some analogues not in the library may also be extracted. Special attention 
will be paid to the CWC-related chemicals that do not contain phosphorus, sulphur, nitrogen 
and arsenic and are not detectable with the selective detectors mentioned above, such as 
pinacolyl alcohol, chloropicrin and benzilic acid. If necessary, the characteristic ions for 
these chemicals are extracted for screening.

Except automatic library search performed by AMDIS, manual peak by peak check of GC -
EI/MS chromatograms is also carried out. After blank subtraction, every extra signal in the 
sample chromatogram are checked by searching in all relevant databases such as OCAD, 
VGWD, NIST library and in -house libraries. This is time -consuming but very helpful in 
minimizing “missing” target chemicals especially for those not included in OCAD and 
VGWD. 
8.1.2 LC-MS-based screening 
Water samples, or ganic liquids, and aqueous/organic extracts of soil or solid samples are 
analysed directly or after solvent change by LC–HRMS to screen for a wide range of CWC-
related chemicals, especially degradation products of CW agents. 
Analyses are performed on a LC –QTOF/MS instrument combined with ESI. A C18 LC 
column and a relatively neutral elution condition (acetonitrile: water system with ammonium 
formate buffer, without pH adjustment) are used for the primary screening carried out in 
both positive and negative ion
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
relatively neutral elution condition (acetonitrile: water system with ammonium 
formate buffer, without pH adjustment) are used for the primary screening carried out in 
both positive and negative ion mode. If necessary, columns of other type (e.g. HILIC) and 
mobile phase with different pH (acidic or basic) can be used to improve the chromatographic 
behavior or ionization of the target chemicals. 
HRMS data are acquired in full scan mode. Automatic screening for peak detection is 
processed using the special data processing software such as ChromaLynx XS running with 
the in -house theoretical library for CWC -related chemicals. Possible candidates in the 
sample are found depending on accurate mass measurement and then checked manually for 
further confirmation. Manual screening is also performed after blank subtraction. Elemental 
composition of the main ions in the extra peaks is calculated based on their accurate masses 
and isotopic pattern. Special attention will be paid to chemicals containing heteroatoms such 
as phosphorous, sulphur and nitrogen. 
In addition, in negative ion mode analyses, ten N, N -dialkylaminoethane-2-sulfonic acids 
with C1–C3 alkyl substituents are
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
micals containing heteroatoms such 
as phosphorous, sulphur and nitrogen. 
In addition, in negative ion mode analyses, ten N, N -dialkylaminoethane-2-sulfonic acids 
with C1–C3 alkyl substituents are monitored in particular since their BSTFA derivatives are 
unstable and difficult to be analysed by GC–MS. 
8.1.3 NMR-based screening 
Original or concentrated aqueous or organic liquid samples/extracts are screened for 
phosphorus-containing chemicals by NMR spectroscopy after adding corresp onding 
deuterated solvent. 1H NMR, 1D 1H-31P HSQC, 2D 1H-31P HMQC and 31P{H} NMR are 
performed to reveal organophosphorus chemicals and confirm their chemical shift. 
8.2 VERIFIN 
VERIFIN routinely uses GC–FPD(P)/FPD(S), GC–EI/MS, LC–MS (both ESI and APCI) 
and NMR for screening CWC-related samples. The purpose of the screening is to cover all 
CWC-related chemicals in the samples. All positive chemicals will be identified, if possible, 
and their relevance will be determined. 
Several screening -related sample p reparation steps are always done. Typically, separate 
sample aliquots are prepared to screen for Lewisites, arsenic trichloride and inorganic 
chlorides from Schedule 3. To allow rapid

text:
lated sample p reparation steps are always done. Typically, separate 
sample aliquots are prepared to screen for Lewisites, arsenic trichloride and inorganic 
chlorides from Schedule 3. To allow rapid screening of the received samples using LC–MS

Typically, GC –EI/MS and 1H NMR are used to determine the composition of sample

8.2.1 GC-based screening 
The main instrument used for GC-based screening is fitted with one column which is to a 
two-splitter. The effluent is split 1:1 between MSD and dual FPD (two FPDs in S and P 
modes). The MSD operates in EI mode. This way one instrument measures mass spectra as 
well as phosphorus and sulphur traces. 
The GC –EI/MS instrument is normally fitted with SE-54-type column (typically 30 m, 
0.25 mm i.d., 0.25 µm film thickness). In addition to the screening instrument, two other 
GC–MS instruments are configured: 
 GC–EI/MS instrument with different type of column (typically OV -1071 or 
Carbowax, depending on the sample composition) 
 GC

text:
the screening instrument, two other 
GC–MS instruments are configured: 
 GC–EI/MS instrument with different type of column (typically OV -1071 or 
Carbowax, depending on the sample composition) 
 GC–CI/MS instrument with the same type of column as the screening GC–dFPD/MS 
instrument 
The flow of the GC–CI/MS instrument is adjusted so that the retention times match those on 
the GC–dFPD/MS instrument. This way, the comparison of the data is much easier. The 
same quality control sample is run with both instruments and can be used to check the 
retention times. 
The GC–EI/MS data is routinely screened using two methods: 1) manual searching of ions 
– as discussed in paragraph 6.1 – and 2) automatic analysis using AMDIS software and the 
OCAD database. If necessary, the characteristic ions for various chemicals can also be used 
based on other screening information. 
The retention indices are automatically calculated for all detected chemicals by AMDIS. 
These are often used as a tool for identification of chemicals, but are normally not reported. 
These first two screening procedures are repeated for each sample fraction suitable for GC 
analysis. 
8.2.2 LC–MS-based screening in l

text:
for identification of chemicals, but are normally not reported. 
These first two screening procedures are repeated for each sample fraction suitable for GC 
analysis. 
8.2.2 LC–MS-based screening in low resolution 
All possible sample aliquots suitable for LC–MS analysis are screened in both positive and 
negative ion modes with both ESI and APCI using non -targeted in-source fragmentation 
method (see paragraph 5.2.2.1). Both acidic and basic elution conditions are used to modify 
the elution and ionisation of the acidic and basic tar get chemicals. iv The chromatography 
method is based on C18 separation ( 100 mm x 2.1 mm, 2.5 or 1.7 µm particle size) with a 
flow of 0.6 ml/min, which is suitable for both ESI and APCI sources. 
 
iv Basic conditions: Methanol: water system with ammonium acetate buffer. The pH is adjusted to 
8.6 using NH 4OH. Acidic conditions: Methanol-water system with formic acid as an additive. 
The pH is around 2.6.

Saxitoxin in screened separately using an MRM-based targeted screening method using LC–

8.2.3 LC–MS-based screening in high resolution 
In addition to the routinely performed LC–low resolution MS (LRMS) screening, screening 
using high resolution is often done using hybrid Orbitrap instrument. The LC runs are 
typically performed with UHPLC instrument using C18 column (50 mm x 2.1 mm, 1.7 µm 
particle size) with a flow of 0.5 ml/min. Both positive and negative ion modes can be used. 
The typical screening resolution of 120,000 gives 2 scans/s. 
The screening is based on accurate masses of target chemicals. The screening can be done 
manually using extracted ion chromatograms (typicall y 3 ppm mass windows) or 
automatically using suitable software (e.g. Thermo Scientific TraceFinder). 
The critical

manually using extracted ion chromatograms (typicall y 3 ppm mass windows) or 
automatically using suitable software (e.g. Thermo Scientific TraceFinder). 
The critical steps in this type of screening are 
 to include all potential target chemicals in the screening process and 
 to set the parameters for allowed elemental composition correctly. 
8.2.4 NMR-based screening 
All liquid state samples are screened as such using NMR spectroscopy; the only sample 
preparation that is needed is an addition of a small amount of a compatible deuterated solvent 
for lock reference; additionally for aqueous samples a small amount of TSP-d4 vis added for 
a chemical shift reference. The water and dichloromethane extracts of soil samples are also 
screened as such after the addition of the deuterated solvent (D 2O with TSP -d4 and 
dichloromethane-d2, respectively). The screening is perfo rmed with 1H NMR, 1D 1H-31P 
HSQC and 2D 1H-31P HMQC techniques. Additionally, 31P{1H} NMR is used for 
confirmation of the phosphorus chemical shifts of the found organophosphorus compounds. 
If the presence of fluorine -containing CWC-related chemicals (i.e. , phosphonofluorid
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
31P{1H} NMR is used for 
confirmation of the phosphorus chemical shifts of the found organophosphorus compounds. 
If the presence of fluorine -containing CWC-related chemicals (i.e. , phosphonofluoridates 
and phosphonic difluorides) is detected with these techniques, the presence of fluorine is 
further confirmed with 19F NMR. While the organophosphorus chemicals can be fairly easily 
screened with the above techniques, the screening of other CWC-related chemicals that have 
protons (i.e. , Lewisites, sulphur mustards and nitrogen mustards as well as related 
degradation products) is also feasible, provided that the sample matrix does not obscure the 
peaks. The assignment of the relevant peaks can be assisted using proton-proton correlation 
experiments (COSY and TOCSY).

9. Evaluation of methods 
9.1 Area of applicability 
The screening methods should be applied to each sample and subsample from sample prep. 
Each specific technique has its own limitations, but when a screening strategy has been 
carefully designed, it should detect most of the scheduled chemicals in any type of sample. 
The more individual screening techniques a laboratory has, the more flexibility there is. 
9.2 Advantages/disadvantages 
The clear advantage of the screening step is that the relevant chemicals are easily picked up, 
even from quite difficult samples. 
However, the limitations of a screening method should always be remembered. Thus, the 
gaps in the overall screening method can be identified and, finally, closed.

1. Scope 
Verification analysis is based on the identification of chemicals by comparison between the 
measured data and the spectra libraries or structure elucidation when similar chemical 
spectra are available. The best and most reliable verification method is comparing the 
analytical data to the analytical data of authentic reference chemicals. 
This chapter provides guidelines for purchasing and prepar ing reference chemi cals for 
verification analysis, quality criteria for reference chemicals, and chain of custody. 
2. Commercially avail
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
This chapter provides guidelines for purchasing and prepar ing reference chemi cals for 
verification analysis, quality criteria for reference chemicals, and chain of custody. 
2. Commercially available reference chemicals 
2.1 Purchase of chemicals 
Treaty-related chemicals are often difficult to purchase. Some chemical companies offer at 
least analytical-level standards for most common CWAs. Purchasing of these products can 
be rather complicated because of legislation. The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) 
also has regulations for the transfer of Scheduled chemicals from one State Party to another. 
The t ransfer of Schedule 1 chemicals must be announced 30 days before the transfer . 
Nonetheless, some of the degradation products of Schedule 1 chemicals are commercially 
available. Hazardous chemicals may also have prolonged distribution time due to the 
transport regulations. 
3. Own synthesis of reference chemicals 
The own synthesis of reference chemicals on a miniature scale is quite simple and the safety 
measures are not too difficult. Good equipment and knowledge provide a good starting point 
for the synthesis.

3.1 Starting materials 
The starting materials for synthesis of treaty -related chemicals and their degradation 
products are sold by many chemical suppliers. Different kinds of alcohols and phosphorus 
chemicals are available for synthetic purposes. In addition , various sulfur- and nitrogen-
containing compounds are available for the preparation of mustards and their degradation 
products. For biological sample reference chemicals , various types of polypeptides can be 
ordered from the companies specialised for custom synthesis. For short polypeptides, ready-
made kits are available for own synthesis. The starting materials can be purchased in advance 
and stored properly. Thus, when a reference chemical is needed, a quick start of synthesis 
can be possible. An end-user certificate is obligatory for the purchase of certain reference 
chemicals. The commercially available chemicals can also be used for preparation of starting 
materials that are not sold. 
3.2 Synthetic methods 
In re
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ligatory for the purchase of certain reference 
chemicals. The commercially available chemicals can also be used for preparation of starting 
materials that are not sold. 
3.2 Synthetic methods 
In recent years several laboratory scale methods for synthesis of CWAs have been published 
in open scientific papers. Some scientific books contain methods for synthesising 
degradation products of CWAs. The OPCW also plans to arrange courses for synthesis of 
reference chemicals in the future. Furthermore, the collaboration with OPCW -designated 
laboratories can be useful. 
The demand for reference chemicals of the metabolites of CWAs has recently increased due 
to biomedical testing, and various protein and DNA adducts of CWAs being needed for the 
verification of exposure to CWAs. Typically , plasma protein adducts may be obtained 
e.g. by sp iking reactive nerve agents into blank matrix plasma. Ho wever, availability of 
Schedule 1 agents is limited, so other synthetic methods would be needed for these adducts. 
On the other hand, β-lyase metabolites of sulphur mustard cannot be synthesised via spiking 
of sulfur mustard into biomatrix, and these have to be synthesized separately. The
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
eded for these adducts. 
On the other hand, β-lyase metabolites of sulphur mustard cannot be synthesised via spiking 
of sulfur mustard into biomatrix, and these have to be synthesized separately. The normal 
laboratory synthesis of CWA metabolites may be very time-consuming, e.g. the nonapeptide 
adducts of nerve agents are synthesised via several synthetic steps. 
Isotopically labelled compounds are important as internal standards , and they are needed 
especially in method development and quantitative analysis . The availability of labelled 
compounds is limited, and synthetic methods are needed. 
3.3 Equipment 
Micro-scale synthesis does not have special requirements for glassware. The amounts of the 
used chemicals and solvents are minimal, as well as the heat energy formed in the reaction. 
Usual vials (typically 1.5–2 ml) can be used for most of the synthesis. The reaction may be 
stirred using miniature magnetic stirring bars and liquid volumes measured by digital pipette. 
Synthesis products may be analysed by GC–MS, LC–MS, or NMR (the deuterated solvent 
can have a dual use as a reaction and analysis solvent ). For example, the concentration of 
the reagents can be set so
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
thesis products may be analysed by GC–MS, LC–MS, or NMR (the deuterated solvent 
can have a dual use as a reaction and analysis solvent ). For example, the concentration of 
the reagents can be set so that the dilution of the reaction mixture (1:100) leads to a suitable 
concentration for the GC–MS analysis.

3.4 Safety aspects 
Due to the high toxicity of CWAs, all the synthetic steps have to be pla nned properly, and 
the properties of the chemicals must be known. 
Normal laboratory safety measures, such as wearing protective lab coats, gloves, and goggles, 
should be employed while handling toxic samples, and decontamination solution should be 
available. All chemicals are to be handled in a fume hood or glove box with good ventilation 
and proper active charcoal filters. 
4. Identification of reference chemical 
4.1 Analytical methods 
At least two separate analytical methods are needed for identification and purity check of 
the synthesised chemical . It is prefer able to have the same analytical method for 
identification that was used for the analysis. For qualitative analysis, the exact purity of the 
chemical is often unrequired. 
5. Synthesis of reference chemicals as a part of quality system 
Good laboratory procedures are important in the synthesis of reference chemicals. The 
syn
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
urity of the 
chemical is often unrequired. 
5. Synthesis of reference chemicals as a part of quality system 
Good laboratory procedures are important in the synthesis of reference chemicals. The 
synthetic route, starting materials , and identification of the chemical must be described. 
Book-keeping of the prepared reference chemicals must be accurate. The origin of the 
chemical must be clearly identified. 
The Quality systems standard often defines, in detail, how the information of the synthesis 
of the reference chemical has to be written. The guidelines for the synthetic work can be 
described in the quality system working instructions.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the issues related to the possible false positive identifications during 
analysis of chemicals related to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). The reporting 
of a false positive for a c

text:
r describes the issues related to the possible false positive identifications during 
analysis of chemicals related to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). The reporting 
of a false positive for a chemical – i.e., a chemical that is in actuality not present in the 
sample – in CWC-related analysis might have serious political consequences. 
This discussion concentrates on gas chromatography–electron ionisation mass spectrometry 
(GC–EI/MS), which is used both during on -site analysis carried out by OPCW inspection 
teams and in, for example, designated laboratories for off-site analysis. See Section 3, Part 
B, Chapter II: Gas chromatography–electron ionisation/mass spectrometry (GC–EI/MS). 
Issues related to analytical data searched against both mass spectral and retention index 
databases are also discussed.

spectral search results. Data are presented for false positive matches between non-relevant 
chemicals and CWC-related chemicals.

The OPCW Central Analytical Database (OCAD)* is an excellent database for CWC-related 
chemicals, but a problem inherent such a limited spectral database is that chemicals which 
are not in the database that have similar spectra may be incorrectly identified as chemicals 
in the database leading to false positive identifications. Larger and more complete databases, 
such as the NIST database used in addition to the OCAD can remove these false positives. 
Different types of false positive hits are discussed and several possible ways of recognising 
and avoiding these false positives are introduced. One of the main methods for 
circumventing false positives is by using a combination of mass spectral and retention index 
searches for identification of the chemicals. In addition, some otherwise difficult cases may 
be addressed by examining small peaks in the mass spectrum that are important to the 
identification, but do not contribut
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
tification of the chemicals. In addition, some otherwise difficult cases may 
be addressed by examining small peaks in the mass spectrum that are important to the 
identification, but do not contribute to the match factor. 
Other analytical methods can be used to help rule out possible false positive matches. For 
example if a non-relevant chemical that produces good mass spectral and retention index 
matches with a scheduled chemical but does not contain phosphorus, then the use of an 
element specific detector or specific experiments can rule out the non-phosphorus containing 
chemicals. 
Finally, the m isidentification of one scheduled chemical for another different scheduled 
chemical is discussed. These types of false positive matches arise due to the very similar 
spectra of some groups of scheduled chemicals. 
The behaviour of some of the scheduled chemical s that produce false positive hits can be 
used in a productive manner. Matches with similar chemicals can be used in classification 
of scheduled chemicals, while keeping in mind that the match is not correct. 
3. Introduction 
While misidentification of a compound in an analysis is to be avoided in all cases, the 
conse

text:

of scheduled chemicals, while keeping in mind that the match is not correct. 
3. Introduction 
While misidentification of a compound in an analysis is to be avoided in all cases, the 
consequences of false positives in the area of chem ical weapons are particularly serious. 
False positives in civil or military defence-related analysis could give rise to false alarms 
and consequent extra costs. In the context of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), the 
occurrence of a false positive identification during an inspection or an investigation of 
alleged use could have adverse diplomatic consequences. 
Two broad areas are covered in this discussion: 
1. Identification of a chemical unrelated to chemical weapons as a CWC-related 
chemical (false positive identification) 
2. Identification of one CWC-related chemical as another (misidentification) 
The terms in parenthesis are often viewed as the same thing. In this discussion, the stronger 
term “false positive” will be used to focus on the greater risk associated with this type of 
identification. The identification of one Schedule 1.A.1 chemical as another is also a false 
positive identification, but typically the conse
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
o focus on the greater risk associated with this type of 
identification. The identification of one Schedule 1.A.1 chemical as another is also a false 
positive identification, but typically the consequences are less serious. 
Emphasis in thi s discussion will be placed on the analysis using gas chromatography – 
electron ionisation mass spectrometry (GC–EI/MS) instruments, since these are common to

and 1391 NMR spectra.

EI/MS requires understanding the nature of the components of the identification. The GC–
EI/MS analysis produces two independent measures of the component: the spectrum and the 
retention index. Most of the details of the spectra of CWC related chemicals are beyond the 
scope of this chapter , so the focus here is only on those details of the spectra that result in 
false positive identification and upon the underlying algorithms that are used for 
identification. 
The specific issue of false positive identification during on-site inspections is derived in part 
from the fact that these analyses rely on the OPCW Central Analytical Database (OCAD) as 
the sole resource for primary identification. This means that a spectrum of an unknown may 
have a good match with something in the OCAD and therefore would be identified as a CW-

have a good match with something in the OCAD and therefore would be identified as a CW-
related chemical, whereas it would actually have a far better match to a non -CWC-related 
chemical if such a spectrum was available. However, this is not readily evident since the 
data for a broader set of chemicals are unavailable due to confidentiality requirements in the 
inspection. 
Note! OCAD contains only CWC -related chemicals , with the exception of the chemicals 
included in the QC test for GC and GC –MS. The more general purpose databases, such as 
NIST or Wiley, are allowed on OPCW inspections due to confidentiality constraints.

The identification of chemicals by mass spectra requires that the experimental spectrum of 
the unknown to be identified can be compared to a library of spectra that have been measured 
for known chemicals. The criterion for identification is that the unknown spectrum matches 
one of the library spectra to a preset degree and does not match any other spectrum to a 
similar degree. This identification
