The only difference between the MF and RMF is that the denominator of the RMF does not 
have any information about the search spectrum. As a result, extra peaks that are in the search 
spectrum, but not in the library spectrum , do not increase the denominator and thus do not 
decrease the match factor. The reverse match factor is more likely to produce false positives, 
but it is also more likely to be able to reveal true positives in very complex matrices. 
Note ! Some mass spectrum search programs present only one value, which is normally the 
MF. 
A combined Net Match Factor (NMF) that combines both MF and RMF is defined by 
formula (3): 
 Net Match Factor (NFM) = (1-fR)*MF + fR*RMF (3) 
where fR is the fraction of the reverse match factor (RMF) that is included in the calculation. 
The value of fR used in the OPCW onsite software is 0.3. As indicated above, the spectrum 
is tentatively identified if the net ma tch factor is gr
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
h factor (RMF) that is included in the calculation. 
The value of fR used in the OPCW onsite software is 0.3. As indicated above, the spectrum 
is tentatively identified if the net ma tch factor is greater than some preset value – typically 
80 (out of 100). Note that the relative proportion of the MF and RMF in the NMF is 
somewhat arbitrary. The 3:1 ratio used above has been found to give good results – that is, 
relatively few additional false positives are added by the use of the RMF and some increase 
is seen in the ability to detect CWC-related compounds in practical situations. 
From the point of view of the analysis of chemical weapons related compounds, two distinct 
problems could o ccur – first, the spectrum is that of a compound that is related to the 
chemical weapons convention (CWC), but the data are not in the database; and second, the 
spectrum is of a compound that is not related to the CWC but the spectrum is similar to one 
of the spectra in the database. The first case, as will be discussed in detail subsequently, is 
quite unlikely to occur for the most important CWC -related chemicals, given the current 
state of the OCAD. The second case, which is the false

quite unlikely to occur for the most important CWC -related chemicals, given the current 
state of the OCAD. The second case, which is the false positive case, does occur in practice. 
While it is impossible to look at every case where a false positive might occur, determining 
to what extent the spectra in the OCAD might lead to false positives is useful. To assess this 
risk, the spectra in the OCAD can be compared to a large database representing a significant 
fraction of the possible chemicals.

OCAD against the NIST database. The search criteria were set up so that no scheduled 
compounds (of which there are many in the NIST database) are found. The result is a set of 
match factors for each compound in the OCAD against non-scheduled chemicals in the NIST 
database.

However, the possibility still exists that a compound may match a spectrum in the OCAD 
with MF > 80 and not be among the spectra present in the larger database. 
Note! In an off -site laborat ory (e.g. an OPCW designated laboratory ), no limitation is 
imposed for the usage of different databases. Use of as large a database as possible is 
advisable to prevent the false positive identification, by actually identifying the chemicals in 
question. 
6. Use of retention index to reduce false positive risk 
Even in the absence of a larger database (as is the case for on -site inspections) , other 
information may be used to resolve false positives. The discussion above has focused on one 
of the two parameters that are available in a GC –EI/MS experiment, the mass spectrum. In 
addition to the mass spectrum, the GC –EI/MS data gives a retention time – the time that a 
compound takes to elute from the column. This can be converted to a
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
EI/MS experiment, the mass spectrum. In 
addition to the mass spectrum, the GC –EI/MS data gives a retention time – the time that a 
compound takes to elute from the column. This can be converted to a retention index (RI) 
by comparing the retention time to the time for a set of standards – typically straight chain 
hydrocarbons. The times of elution for the hydrocarbons are assigned a n RI equal to 
100 times their carbon number (octane = 800, dodecane = 1200, etc.) and the e xperimental 
retention time is converted to a retention index by interpolation between adjacent standard 
times. 
Retention index is an independent parameter that is uncorrelated with the mass spectra. As 
such, it can be used to resolve the multiple identifications that are based solely on the mass 
spectral match factor. As will be discussed subsequently, the RI is especially useful in 
resolving the multiple matches that occur within the various schedules, but the initial focus 
is on reducing the risk of false positive identifications of unscheduled chemicals. 
For practical identification, both the difference in the spectral pattern of the library chemical 
and the unknown (the match factor) and the diff
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e positive identifications of unscheduled chemicals. 
For practical identification, both the difference in the spectral pattern of the library chemical 
and the unknown (the match factor) and the difference between the RI of a library hit and 
the experimental RI of the unknown are used. Typically, the RI difference [RI – RI(lib)] is 
either used as a cut -off filter – that is, if the retention index of the unknown is more than 
some predefined distance from the library value, the identification is rejected – or as variable 
filter, where the MF is reduced more and more as the difference between the experimental 
RI and the library RI increases, but without an absolute cut-off. The latter mode is used in 
the AMDIS software† for on-site analysis with the OCAD. 
In AMDIS, if the retention index of the unknown is within a user definable window (e.g., ±20 
retention index units) of the library match, no penalty is given. If the absolute difference is 
outside the window, an increasing penalty will be incurred, typically increasing by 10 match 
factor points (out of 100) per window – again, a user-definable parameter. Thus, if the 
experimental value of RI is 1825, the spectrum of a ch
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
alty will be incurred, typically increasing by 10 match 
factor points (out of 100) per window – again, a user-definable parameter. Thus, if the 
experimental value of RI is 1825, the spectrum of a chemical from the library has MF = 87 
and the RI of that chemical in the library was 1789 (i. e., a difference of 36), using the 
example values for the window and penalty level, the NMF would be 79 – the RI difference 
minus the window (36 – 20 = 16), to allow for the no penalty region, divided by the window

8. Summary of GC–EI/MS identification 
For the most part , the risks of false positive identification are very small , even with the 
limitations of using the OCAD , so long as both RI and MS data are used. The majority of 
the remaining risks can be eliminated – when possible – by using a larger set of spectral data 
to show that the best match is not the scheduled chemical but a non-scheduled chemical with 
a similar spectrum. This will still leave a very small number of cases where the spectral 
similarity and the retention similarity are sufficiently great that no clear cut way exists to 
eliminate the possibility for false positive identifications. The worst of these types of cases 
will occur when the compound yielding the false positive is not in any larger database and 
thus no way is available to show that the identification is incorrect. 
9. Spectroscopic methods for resolving false positive identifications

9. Spectroscopic methods for resolving false positive identifications 
The discussion above has focused on a single technique – GC–EI/MS. This technique is 
typically the most powerful currently available since , for most chemicals of concern for 
chemical weapons analysis , the sensitivity of GC –EI/MS is very high ( detection limits of 
<0.1 ppm are normal). The method can also be applied to the identification of most CWC -
related chemicals when used with derivatisation techniques [see Section 2, Part A, Chapter 
III: Derivatisation for gas chromatography]. However, as noted above, some cases still exist 
where the risk of false positive is present. Several analytical techniques can be of great 
assistance in eliminating these risks. 
To understand these methods, looking at the types of false positives that are encountered is 
useful. In both the Schedule 1.A.1 and 1.A.3 cases (where the bulk of the false positives are 
found), the false positives s hare one common feature – they do not contain phosphorus. In 
the very few cases where false positives might be seen
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
A.3 cases (where the bulk of the false positives are 
found), the false positives s hare one common feature – they do not contain phosphorus. In 
the very few cases where false positives might be seen in Schedule 1.A.2, these also do not 
contain phosphorus. For the other schedule 1 chemicals – Schedule 1.A.4 (the sul phur 
mustards), 1.A.5 (Lewisites) or 1.A.6 (the nitrogen mustards) – no false positives have been 
encountered. Therefore, the GC–EI/MS analysis is sufficient for these schedules. 
A number of other analytical methods can be used for the analysis of chemical weapons 
related compounds. Two of these methods have special value in relation to the issue with 
false positives: n uclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy ( NMR) and GC with flame 
photometric detector (GC–FPD). 
NMR suffers from limitations on the sensitivity of the methods and th us may be of limited 
use if a very low level signal is producing the false positive. The ability of NMR to detect 
phosphorus-containing chemicals at low ppm levels makes it a very useful technique in 
resolving false positive matches in GC –EI/MS. Typically, in an OPCW Proficiency test , 
NMR can detect the number and types of the
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ng chemicals at low ppm levels makes it a very useful technique in 
resolving false positive matches in GC –EI/MS. Typically, in an OPCW Proficiency test , 
NMR can detect the number and types of the phosphorus -containing chemicals at normal 
spiking levels (1 –10 µg/g). This helps in ruling out the impossible false positive matches. 
The main limitation of NMR is that its use is limited to off-site laboratories only and it may 
not be utilised on on-site inspections. 
GC–FPD is a method that, while not being sufficiently specific for general identification of 
scheduled chemicals, it is perfect for resolving false positives. Flame photometric detectors 
(FPD) will give signals that are unique for chemicals containing specific elements. The 
normal FPD detectors that are used for CWC-related work are sensitive to either sulphur or 
phosphorus. These detectors are routinely used for screening, as discussed in [see Section 1, 
Part B, Chapter I: Screening], but can be invaluable in eliminating false positives.

alternative method of resolving false positives – searching for phosphorus. 
Under acidic conditions, both the phosphonofluoridates and the phosponothiolates undergo

concentration of the material was too low to show up

the TMS esters are not found after acid degradation and derivatization, it means either the

was of a false positive.

indices covered by these chemicals is very large. Therefore, the u se of just the retention 
parameters to resolve the false positives may not be sufficient. Since the issue here is a 
fundamental one related to the stability of the ions themselves, no real way is available to 
avoid the problem. 
For the schedule 1.A.1 chemicals, two classes of problems are recognised. One is where the 
O-alkyl end of the molecule carries a significant portion of the charge, in which case the 
spectra may be very similar to the corresponding alcohol or alkene. In these cases, the use 
of re tention information will completely eliminate the false positive since the scheduled 
chemicals will have retention indices 200 to 300 greater than the corresponding non -
scheduled chemical. The second class is more difficult in that some chemicals are present 
that, on a random basis, have similar spectra to the schedule 1.A.1 chemicals. These are rare 
and predicting what the retenti

text:
l. The second class is more difficult in that some chemicals are present 
that, on a random basis, have similar spectra to the schedule 1.A.1 chemicals. These are rare 
and predicting what the retention index difference will be is not possible. 
In every case except one seen to date, the use of a larger database – such as the NIST database 
carried with the inspection equipment – would have resolved the problem of false positive.

1. Scope 
This section describes generally the preparation of environmental samples for the analysis 
of chemical warfare agents (CWAs) and their degradation products. 
2. General considerations 
Chemical analysis of samples normally involves sample preparation followed by 
instrumental analysis. The sample preparatio n is the key and limiting step for the whole 
analytical process. In most cases, sample preparation is directed towards a certain 
instrumental analytical method. These two activities are linked together and sometim
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
d limiting step for the whole 
analytical process. In most cases, sample preparation is directed towards a certain 
instrumental analytical method. These two activities are linked together and sometimes 
completely integrated. Furthermore, in t he case of the determination of analytes at low 
concentrations in a complicated matrix (target chemical analysis), additional clean-up might 
sometimes be necessary after the initial instrumental analyses have been carried out. 
Well-planned, effective, and reasonably simple sample preparations suitable for the method 
of analysis are needed for analysis of CWAs and their degradation products. Proper 
preparation of samples requires a thorough understanding of the behavior of the various 
types of chemicals in s ample matrices, both before and during the sample preparation, and 
an awareness of the limitations of the chosen instrumental method of analysis. The sample 
type, the chemicals that are analysed, the amount of the chemicals as well as the background 
chemicals in samples, and the method used for analysis affect the selection of the sample 
preparation method. 
Proper sample preparation is an important step in the chemical analysis
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
the background 
chemicals in samples, and the method used for analysis affect the selection of the sample 
preparation method. 
Proper sample preparation is an important step in the chemical analysis and is a prerequisite 
for the whole identification process. It prevents erroneous results due to cross-contamination 
or other interferences being reported. To prevent these possibilities, it is necessary to always 
perform the same sample preparation method on one or more matrix or glassware blank 
samples. 
Ideally, the recovery efficiency should be 100%, which, however, will seldom be obtained. 
For accurate quantitative analysis, a determination of the recovery will be necessary. This 
may be performed by spiking a blank background sample and carrying out the sample
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

preparation method on the spiked sample. However, verification analysis is focused on 
unambiguous identification rather than on producing accurate quantitative results. Moreover, 
for accurate quantitative results, stable analytes are presumed, which is certainly not the case 
with some chemical warfare agents in environmental samples. 
Due to a large variety of matrices (environmental samples: soil, decont amination solution, 
concrete, etc.; complex mixtures: diesel fuel, etc .) and target chemicals (CWC -scheduled 
chemicals, precursors, starting materials, analogues, analytical artefacts, degradation (break-
down) products, additives), rather universal procedures should be used. The Recommended 
Operating Procedures ( ROPs) are designed to be comprehensive enough to allow the 
analysis of all CWC-related chemicals. Accordingly, some of the procedures contain many 
sample preparation steps. It is also recommended that the ROPs should be used as a first 
choice in the analysis, with ot
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
f all CWC-related chemicals. Accordingly, some of the procedures contain many 
sample preparation steps. It is also recommended that the ROPs should be used as a first 
choice in the analysis, with other approaches not excluded. 
2.1 Safety 
Handle CWC-related chemicals with great care. Be sure that decontamination solution, 
protective masks, and autoinjectors of nerve agent antidotes are available when toxic 
samples or samples of unknown toxicity are handled. These samples must always be 
prepared in a fume cupboard and no-one must ever work alone. During sample preparation, 
individual protective gear such as laboratory coat, chemically resistant protective gloves, 
and safety goggles must be used. 
Clean the fume cupboard directly after sample preparation. Mater ials requiring 
decontamination must be treated with a proper decontamination solution and disposed of in 
designated waste containers. 
2.2 Purity 
The solvents should be as pure as possible. Their purity should preferably be checked in 
advance of the analysi s. Also, the glassware used during the extraction and for the storage 
of the extracts (vials, bottles) must be thoroughly clean. Moreover, separate glassware s
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
y be checked in 
advance of the analysi s. Also, the glassware used during the extraction and for the storage 
of the extracts (vials, bottles) must be thoroughly clean. Moreover, separate glassware should 
be used for samples, matrix, and glassware blank samples as well as reference standards. 
Appropriate labeling of the various extracts is another consideration. 
2.3 Storing of samples 
Store the samples in a freezer at -20 C prior to sample preparation. Aqueous samples and 
wet samples are stored in a refrigerator at +4 °C to prevent the bottles and vials from getting 
broken, however. 
The prepared sub -samples are also stored in a freezer at -20 C (aqu eous samples in 
refrigerator at +4 C) after the sample preparation. 
2.4 Warming of samples 
Open the sample packages carefully in a fume cupboard, pl ace sample bottles on the 
cupboard table, check that they are tightly closed, and let the samples warm up to room 
temperature slowly without external heating before opening the sample vessels.

1. Scope 
This section describes methods for the concentration of liquid samples containing chemical 
warfare agents (CWAs) and th eir degradation products. The analysis takes place by gas 
chromatography (GC) or liquid chromatography (LC) as an introduction technique for 
spectrometers. The concentration methods for analysis by nuclear magnetic resonance 
(NMR) spectroscopy are performed in the same ways in cases in which the concentration or 
evaporation of samples is needed. 
2. Summary of the method 
Extracts of different sample preparation procedures are often concentrated, e specially 
organic extracts. The purpose is to increase the concentration of the analytes in extracts in 
order to increase the sensitivity of the analysis. When the sample size is small and the solvent 
is volatile, the samples are concentrated by mild nitrogen flow. For larger sample volumes 
and quantities , laboratory equipment such as a TurboVap ® evaporator or a centrifuge 
evaporator should be used. These instruments are designed for the evaporation of liquid 
samples in glass vials and tubes.

5.1 Concentration of samples with mild nitrogen flow 
In concentration with nitrogen flow, a stream of nitrogen removes the solvent vapor from 
the surface of the sample. Mild flow is needed to keep the analytes in the sample and 
evaporate the solvent away. 
5.1.1 Concentration of organic solvents 
The sample or the extract is concentrated usually 5- or 10-fold with mild nitrogen flow: 1 ml 
to 200 µl or 100 µl. Attach a clean Teflon tube to the nitrogen cylinder. Protect the end of 
the tube from contamination, e.g. with a Pasteur pipette. Place the tip of th e Pasteur pipette 
just above the surface of the extract and adjust the nitrogen flow with pressure regulator to 
cause a gentle depression on the surface of the solution (Figure 1). Let the solution cool 
down during evaporation. The rate of the evaporation can be controlled by the degree of 
immersion of the Pasteur pipette in the vial. Concentration of 1 ml of dich, hexane or acetone 
extracts takes ca. 10 minutes. 
Note! Do
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
he rate of the evaporation can be controlled by the degree of 
immersion of the Pasteur pipette in the vial. Concentration of 1 ml of dich, hexane or acetone 
extracts takes ca. 10 minutes. 
Note! Do not concentrate the organic extract to dryness since certain volatile CWC-related 
chemicals such as sarin are lost from the sample and, on the other hand, certain less volatile 
CWC-related chemicals such as VX in residues of organic extracts are fir mly adsorbed to 
glass surfaces. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 1. Adjusting the mild nitrogen flow. 
5.1.2 Concentration of aqueous samples 
Concentration of water samples with mild nitrogen flow is time-consuming. For this reason, 
it is recommended to concentrate aqueous samples in the TurboVap® evaporator, in a 
centrifuge evaporator or in a rotary evaporator as described in the following sections. Small 
amounts of aqueous samples can be concentrated with mild nitrogen flow, but heating of the 
vial in a block heater or a sand bath at 40 –50 °C is recommended to avo id prolonged 
evaporation.

The TurboVap® evaporators direct the nitrogen flow into the sample tubes at a precise angle. 
The vortex created by the blowing gas travels down the tube to the solvent surface, where it 
increases the gas/solvent interface — providing faster evaporation than with conven tional 
methods. 
Two TurboVap ® concentration workstations can be used for automatic evaporation of 
samples. 
 The TurboVap II ® evaporator (Figure 2A) allows evaporation of up to six samples 
and uses optical sensors to provide fast and efficient evaporation. Either 50 ml or 200 
ml unit glassware with either 0.5 ml or 1.0 ml endpoint stems can be used. 
 The TurboVap LV® evaporator (Figure 2B) provides simultaneous evaporation of up 
to 50 samples. Many interchangeable tube racks are available, ranging in volumes 
from 1.5 ml to 30 ml , giving the flexibility for automated low-volume sample 
preparation. The microprocessor control provides monitoring of the
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:

from 1.5 ml to 30 ml , giving the flexibility for automated low-volume sample 
preparation. The microprocessor control provides monitoring of the timed operation 
and water bath temperature. 
When the TurboVap® evaporator is used, the shorter the concentration times, the better the 
recoveries. Nitrogen pressure should be kept as high as possible, but without splashing; 
thereby increasing the pressure as the volume decreases. 
Bath temperatures for dichloromethane and acetone should be 40–45 °C and nitrogen 
pressures 10–20 psi.

5.3 Concentration of samples in a centrifuge evaporator 
A centrifugal evaporator is a device used for the efficient and gentle evaporation of various 
solvents from many samples at the same time . The instrument consists of a vacuum pump 
connected to a centrifuge chamber in which the samples are placed. Many systems also have 
a cold trap or solvent condenser placed in line between the vacuum pump and the centrifuge 
chamber to collect the evaporated solvents. Some systems also have a cold trap on the pump 
exhaust. 
The pressure is lowered in the centrifuge using a vacuum pump , e.g. the samples are 
centrifuged before and during vacuum evaporation. The sample is forced down into the 
bottom of th e tube and for this reason the chamber is heated to ensure evaporation. The 
heating level and the depth of the vacuum are selected based on the particular samples 
(analytes and solvent) evaporated. The advantage of centrifugation is that the finished 
sample is in a pellet at the bottom of the evaporation tube and not distributed over the sides 
of th

sample is in a pellet at the bottom of the evaporation tube and not distributed over the sides 
of the evaporation tube. 
Note! When using the centrifugal evaporator, always place a centrifuge tube of the same 
size with the same filling level as a counterbalance on the opposite side of the centrifuge 
rotor.

 Set the temperature of the water bath to 50 °C or 60 °C 
 Load the sample and adjust rotation speed to ca. 100 rpm 
 Adjust the vacuum at 35 mbar and start pumping 
 When the vacuum is reached , set the sample step by step as low as possible in the 
water bath 
 Take care that the sample is not foaming out of the evaporation vessel when you 
adjust it in the water bath 
 Once the sample is dry, remove the tube from the unit and let it cool to room 
temperature before derivatisation 
 Derivatise the sample without delay 
To evaporate 5–10 ml of water to dryness in the recommended conditions (35 mbar, 50 °C, 
100 rpm) takes 20–30 minutes.

The following procedure is recommended for alcohol-based samples and extracts: 
 Turn on the evaporator

1. Scope 
This chapter describes derivatisation procedures recommended for the gas chromatographic 
analysis of polar precursors/degradation products of toxic chemicals listed in Schedules 1 
and 2 of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). Also described are derivatisation 
procedures for reactive, corrosive, or highly volatile analytes such as Lewisite 1, phosgene, 
and some precursors to Schedule 1 chemicals. Most of the procedures described h ave been 
applied predominantly for identifying chemicals at concentrations above 1 part per million 
in a variety of environmental and man -made matrices, typical of routine or challenge 
inspections and OPCW Proficiency Tests. Some alternative derivatisation procedures are 
included that are better suited to identifying relevan
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
and man -made matrices, typical of routine or challenge 
inspections and OPCW Proficiency Tests. Some alternative derivatisation procedures are 
included that are better suited to identifying relevant chemicals at concentrations down to 
low parts per billion, e.g. in investigations of alleged use and the analysis of biomedical 
samples (blood and urine). 
2. The requirement for derivatisation 
The major requirement for derivatisation of CWC-related analytes is for the analysis of polar 
precursors/degradation products of Schedule 1 chemical warfare ( CW) agents. These 
analytes chromatograph very poorly or degrade at the high temperatures required for gas 
chromatography. Examples are alkyl alkylphosphonic acids and alkylphosphonic acids, 
derived from the hydrolysis of organophosphorus nerve agents, and thiodiglycol and 
ethanolamines, which are precursors and hydrolysis products of sulfur and nitrogen mustards 
respectively.

Derivatisation is also used to reduce the reactivity and/or volatility of certain scheduled 
compounds prior to gas chromatography. Examples are the reactive Lewisites 1 and 2 
(Schedule 1), which chromatograph poorly, the highly volatile chemicals 
perfluoroisobutylene (Schedule 2) and phosgene (Schedule 3), and reactive and corrosive 
precursors such as arsenic trichloride (Schedule 2) and sulfur monochloride and sulfur 
dichloride (Schedule 3). 
For some applications, particu larly the analysis of biomedical or environmental samples 
associated with investigations of alleged use, analyte concentrations may be in the low parts 
per billion range. In these cases , derivatisation may also be used to enhance the selectivity 
or sensitivity of detection. Examples are the conversion of alkyl alkylphosphonic acids and 
thiodiglycol to perfluorinated derivatives, to enable analysis by the very sensitive technique 
of negative ion chemical ionisation (NICI) mass spe
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e the conversion of alkyl alkylphosphonic acids and 
thiodiglycol to perfluorinated derivatives, to enable analysis by the very sensitive technique 
of negative ion chemical ionisation (NICI) mass spectrometry. 
Increasingly, novel sample preparation techniques are being applied to the extraction and 
derivatisation of target analytes from complex matrices. These techniques include hollow 
fibre liquid phase membrane extraction (HFLPME), single drop micro -extraction (SDME), 
on-cartridge/solid supported and on -matrix derivatisation and ion -pairing assisted liquid 
extraction combined with derivatisation and the use of molecular imprinted polymers. The 
aim is selective extraction combined with subsequent or simultaneous derivatisation 
procedures under mild conditions. 
Novel reagents that confer superior identification potential for isomeric analytes, tolerance 
to traces of water, ease of use and enhanced sensitivity are still being developed and are 
described in the section below. 
3. Overview of the methods 
A detailed review of derivatisation methods of chemicals related to the CWC was published 
in 2003.1

3. Overview of the methods 
A detailed review of derivatisation methods of chemicals related to the CWC was published 
in 2003.1 
3.1 Silyl derivatives 
The most broadly applicable procedure for the derivatisation of polar CW agent 
precursors/degradation products i s conversion to trimethylsilyl (TMS) or tert-
butyldimethylsilyl (TBDMS) esters or ethers. Conversion to TMS derivatives is the 
approved procedure for OPCW on -site analysis during inspections. For off -site analysis, 
some OPCW designated laboratories prefer to use TBDMS derivatives. These have the 
advantage of greater robustness with regard to traces of water and stability on storage. 
Silylation can be used for alkyl alkylphosphonic acids (and their thio analogues), 
alkylphosphonic acids, degradation products derived from the side chain of V agents 
(N,N-dialkylaminoethane-2-thiols, N,N-dialkylaminoethan-2-ols), thiodiglycol and related 
mustard degradation products, ethanolamines derived from nitrogen mustards, and BZ and 
its degradation products benzilic acid and 3 -quinuclidinol. For 2 -(N,N-dialkyl-
amino)ethanesulfonic acids, derived from oxidative decontamination of V -agents, only 
TBDMS derivatives ap
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
nd BZ and 
its degradation products benzilic acid and 3 -quinuclidinol. For 2 -(N,N-dialkyl-
amino)ethanesulfonic acids, derived from oxidative decontamination of V -agents, only 
TBDMS derivatives appear to be stable. For thiodiglycol sulfoxide, TMS derivatisation is 
used to avoid Pummerer rearrangement or reduction. 
The silylating agents and derivativ es produced are sensitive to moisture. Consequently 
current recommended sample preparation procedures require concentration of aqueous

derivatisation. Residues are derivatis ed in an organic solvent usually with heating, 
particularly for the bulkier TBDMS derivatives, and analysed by gas chromatography using 
generic or selective detectors, or preferably by gas chromatography –mass spectrometry 
(GC–MS). 
Hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS) has been reported as a reagent for on-matrix derivatisation 
of a range of CWC -related alcohols recently.2 Use of this reagent results in a minimal 
chemical background, but like other trimethylsilyl derivatives is sensitive to moisture. 
A range of CWC -relevant amino alcohols were derivatised to their dimethy lphenylsilyl 
derivatives with dimethylphenyl chlorosilane following activation with N-methyl-
imidazole.3 Room temperature conditions were employed and reaction times are short (1 h). 
N-Methylimidazole was shown to be more efficient than pyridine for effecting the 
conve
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
vation with N-methyl-
imidazole.3 Room temperature conditions were employed and reaction times are short (1 h). 
N-Methylimidazole was shown to be more efficient than pyridine for effecting the 
conversion to the SiMe 2Ph derivatives. The mass spectra of these chemicals gave a very 
small but detectable molecular ion which is an advantage over standard silyl derivatives such 
as TMS and TBDMS derivatives. The report did not report any detection limits or mention 
the stability of the derivatives. This approach was later applied to the derivatisation of 
pinacolyl alcohol, producing a derivative of moderate volatility distinguishable from similar 
alcohol derivatives through its retention index and mass spectrum (although the spectra from 
similar alcohols were similar).4 Although standard silylating reagents do produce detectable 
derivatives with pinacolyl alcohol, they can be masked by excess reagent; a problem 
alleviated using the this approach. 
Solid supported derivatisation using tert-butyldimethylsilyl chloride on commercially 
available Chem Elut ® (Agilent) cartridges provided a simple and rapid extractive 
derivatisation procedure for aque ous samples containing alkyl al
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
g tert-butyldimethylsilyl chloride on commercially 
available Chem Elut ® (Agilent) cartridges provided a simple and rapid extractive 
derivatisation procedure for aque ous samples containing alkyl alkylphosphonic acids and 
alkyl methylphosphonic acids.5 
Magnetic beads coated with anion exchange resin were used to extract alkyl alkylphosphonic 
and alkylphosphonic acids from water samples which were subsequently derivat ised with 
N,O-bis(trimethylsilyl)trifluoroacetamide (MTBSTFA).6 
Ion-pairing extraction and in situ derivatisation using MTBSTFA in micro -drops was 
successfully applied to the extraction and derivatisation of alkyl methylphosphonic acids and 
other CWC -related acids. 7 Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) was the most 
effective ion pairing agent. 
3.2 Methyl esters 
Alkyl alkylphosphonic acids, alkylphosphonic acids, 2 -(N,N-dialkylamino)ethanesulfonic 
acids, and benzilic acid are readily converted to their methyl or dimethyl esters with 
diazomethane. This provides a second GC–MS procedure for identification, particularly for 
laboratories that do not use liquid chromatography –mass spectrometry (LC –MS). An 
advantage of methyl esters is that they are muc
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
vides a second GC–MS procedure for identification, particularly for 
laboratories that do not use liquid chromatography –mass spectrometry (LC –MS). An 
advantage of methyl esters is that they are much less sensitive to moisture than silyl esters. 
Also, their mass spectra are generally more easily interpreted and are more informative than 
those of silyl esters. Diazomethane does not react with non -acidic analytes such as 
thiodiglycol. The development of methylation reagents that are easier to produce, store and 
handle than diazomethane has been an active a rea of research recently. 
Trimethylsilyldiazomethane (TMSCHN2, TMSD) has been used for methyla tion of CWC-
related alkyl alkyl phosphonic acids and alkylphosphonic acids. 8 Chemical background is

greater than with diazomethane ; however, the reagent is commercially available and 
convenient to use. 
Trimethyloxonium tetrafluoroborate (TMOTFB), a reagent that is easy and safe to handle , 
has been reported for the methylation of alkyl alkylphosphonic acids and alkylphosphonic 
acids under mild conditions (room temperature).9 
3.3 Perfluorinated derivatives 
Perfluorinated derivatives are not generally used for the analysis of polar CW agent 
precursors/degradation products where concentrations are more than ca.1 part per million. 
They are not recommended for use in OPCW Proficiency Tests. Their main application has 
been for samples where analyte concentrations are in the low parts per billion range, e.g. in 
investigations of alleged use of chemical weapons, particularly for the analysis of biomedical 
samples such as urine or blood. Pentafluorobenzoyl and heptafluorobutyryl derivatives are 
used for the trace analysis of thiodiglycol.10–12 Pentafluor
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ns, particularly for the analysis of biomedical 
samples such as urine or blood. Pentafluorobenzoyl and heptafluorobutyryl derivatives are 
used for the trace analysis of thiodiglycol.10–12 Pentafluorobenzyl esters are used for the trace 
analysis of alkyl alkylphosphonic acids 13-17 and alkyl phosphonic a cids.16 Recently, 
3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)benzyl derivatives have been advocated for phosphonic acids, on the 
basis of much simpler sample preparation compared to that currently used for 
pentafluorobenzyl esters. 18 This reagent has also been applied to the analysis of alkyl 
methylphosphonic acids in urine samples. 19 Trifluoroacetyl and heptafluorobutyryl 
derivatives have been explored for the environmental analysis of ethanolamines 20 and 
thiodiglycol.20-21 
3.4 Thioesters 
Lewisite 1 (and to a lesser extent Lewisite 2) is an exception among Schedule 1 CW agents 
in that it is too reactive for routine analysis by GC. Trivalent arsenic forms strong bonds with 
sulfur, and this is exploited for derivatisation by converting analytes to thioesters. Alkyl or 
aryl thiols are used as derivatising agents for Lewisites 1 and 2, and their primary degradation 
products 2 -chlorovin
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
is exploited for derivatisation by converting analytes to thioesters. Alkyl or 
aryl thiols are used as derivatising agents for Lewisites 1 and 2, and their primary degradation 
products 2 -chlorovinylarsonous acid and bis(2 -chlorovinyl)arsinous acid, respectively. In 
contrast to the silylating and esterifying reagents described above, thiols ar e nucleophilic 
rather than electrophilic, and can be used in aqueous solution if required. A recent reference 
reviewed the area.22 A disadvantage of thioesters is that they do not distinguish agents from 
their degradation products, both converting to the same As(III) thioesters. Butanethiol (BT) 
is approved for on -site analysis of Lewisites and is the most commonly used reagent for 
derivatising intact and hydrolysed Lewisites. Dimercapto toluene (4-methylbenzene-1,2-
dithiol, DMT) is also approved for on -site use but caution must be exercised when this 
reagent is used, particularly in proficiency tests, as it converts Lewisite 2 to the Lewisite 1 
derivative.23 DMT has been used to sample phosgene with low limits of detection.24 
Butanethiol is also used for the derivatisation of arsenic trichloride, and other arsenicals 
relevan
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
he Lewisite 1 
derivative.23 DMT has been used to sample phosgene with low limits of detection.24 
Butanethiol is also used for the derivatisation of arsenic trichloride, and other arsenicals 
relevant to old and abandoned chemical weapons such as Adamsite, Clark 1 and Clark 2. 
Thiols can also be used for derivatising perfluoroisobutylene. 
3.5 Isocyanate derivatives 
The reagent p-tolyl isocyanate was investigated for derivatization of a range of polar CWA 
degradation products containing hydroxyl or thiol groups (the reagent does not react with 
carboxylic or phosphonic acid groups).25

Despite the aromatic substituent , molecular ions were not observed in all the derivatised 
products of N,N-dialkylaminoethanols and those that were visible were present at only 2-5% 
relative abundance. Quinuclidin-3-ol (CWC Schedule 2.B.09) resulted in a stable derivative 
with a strong molecular ion. A range of sulfur mustard degradation products resulted in 
mono-derivatives; however, bis-derivatives also formed as demonstrated by flow injection 
MS techniques. 
3.6 Electrophilic addition 
The CWC Schedule 3 chemicals sulfur monochloride and sulfur dichloride are reactive 
electrophiles. They can be analysed directly but hydrolyse and oxidise rapidly in air. To 
avoid reactions during sampling , conversion to stable derivatives with 3 -hexyne was 
accomplished under mild conditions (30 °C).26 The derivatives have convenient analytical 
properties (presence of chlorine and sulfur isotopes) and form only one product , unlike the 
case when 1-hexyne is used,
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
under mild conditions (30 °C).26 The derivatives have convenient analytical 
properties (presence of chlorine and sulfur isotopes) and form only one product , unlike the 
case when 1-hexyne is used, which results in two diastereoisomer pairs . The reaction was 
shown to be viable in the presence of sulfur mustard. 
3.7 Picolinyl esters 
The reagent, 3-pyridyldiazomethane was used to prepare picolinyl ester derivatives of alkyl 
methylphosphonic acids. 27 The derivatives fragmented conveniently allowing structural 
elucidation of the O-alkyl moiety of a range of twelve hexyl methylphosphonic acid isomers. 
These derivatives were more effectively separated than the corresponding trimethylsilyl 
derivatives. 
4. Safety aspects 
Most derivatisation reactions do not require specific precautions concerning safety. Samples 
to be analyse d normally contain only small concentrations of toxic chemicals, and the 
reagents are treated as for any other volatile reactive chemical. Normal laboratory safety 
measures should be used during sample handling, such as protective gloves, goggles and 
fume hoods. Trimethylsilyl cyanide, if used, produces HCN on reaction with phosphonic 
acids and thiod
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
y safety 
measures should be used during sample handling, such as protective gloves, goggles and 
fume hoods. Trimethylsilyl cyanide, if used, produces HCN on reaction with phosphonic 
acids and thiodiglycol etc. Thiol derivatising agents produce a stench and should always be 
confined to well-ventilated fume hoods. Likewise pentafluorobenzyl bromide is a powerful 
lachrymator and should only be used under well-ventilated conditions. 
An exception is diazomethane if used for the conversion of phosphonic or benzilic acids to 
methyl esters. Diazomethane has relatively high toxicity (possibly carcinogenic) and has 
potential for detonation. Trimethylsilyldiazomethane, though not widely used, has been 
proposed as a safer derivatising agent for conversion of acids to methyl esters.28

7.4 Pentafluorobenzyl esters 
Pentafluorobenzyl (PFB) e sters are used mainly for trace -level detection of alkyl 
alkylphosphonic acids in biomedical fluids (usually blood, plasma, or urine).13-17 
The residue obtained from SPE of urine (1 ml) (e.g. from an Oasis HLB polymeric cartridge) 
is dissolved in acetonitrile (500 µl) and derivatised with pentafluorobenzyl bromide (PFBBr) 
(10 µl) in the presence of potassium carbonate (20 mg) in a sealed 1 ml reaction vial at 90 
C for 45 min. Th e reaction mixture is carefully concentrated to dryness under a stream of 
nitrogen at 50 C and re-dissolved in dichloromethane (300 µl). The derivatised sample is 
added to a 1 ml / 100 mg Florisil SPE cartridge, pre-conditioned with dichloromethane (1 ml), 
the cartridge is washed with dichloromethane (1 ml) to remove excess PFBBr, and the 
derivatised analyte eluted with 10% methanol in dichloromethane (2 x 0.75 ml). The eluate 
is evaporated to dryness under nitrogen a
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

derivatised analyte eluted with 10% methanol in dichloromethane (2 x 0.75 ml). The eluate 
is evaporated to dryness under nitrogen and redissolved in dichloromethane (100 µl) for 
analysis by GC–MS (NICI). 
For optimum derivatisation of alkylphosphonic acids , diisopropylamine has been used as a 
base.16 
7.5 Bis-heptafluorobutyryl derivative of thiodiglycol 
The bis-heptafluorobutyryl (HFB) derivative is used for the trace analysis of thiodiglycol in 
biomedical samples, usually urine.12 The dried residue from SPE of urine (1 ml) (e.g. from 
an Oasis HLB polymeric cartridge) in a 1 ml reaction vial is dissolved in acetonitrile (20 µl), 
heptafluorobutyrylimidazole (HFBI, 30 µl) is introduced, and the sample heated at 50 C for 
30 min. After cooling, water (200 µl) is added to destroy excess derivati sing agent. The 
acetonitrile/water mixture is extracted with heptane (2 x 300 µl), the two extracts combined, 
and concentrated to approximately 50 µl under a stream of nitrogen.

necessary, the dried extract is filtered into another 4 ml vial prior to GC–MS analysis 
7.7.2.4 Air samples 
Air samples can be collected into a Tenax tube spiked with DMT solution to analyse 
phosgene by thermal desorption (see Section 2, Part B, Chapter IV: Air samples). 
8. Applicability 
Silyl derivatives, methyl esters and thioesters are recommended for use in OPCW 
Proficiency Tests, and generally for the analysis of samples where concentrations are likely 
to be above ca. 100 parts per billion. Mass spectra for some derivatives, TMS, TBDMS, and 
methyl esters, butyl thioesters of L
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
d generally for the analysis of samples where concentrations are likely 
to be above ca. 100 parts per billion. Mass spectra for some derivatives, TMS, TBDMS, and 
methyl esters, butyl thioesters of Lewisites 1 and 2, and the dimercapto toluene ester of 
Lewisite 1, are included in the OCAD. 
The First O PCW Confidence Building Exercise on Biomedical Sample Analysis, held in 
2009, demonstrated that silyl derivat ives and methyl esters are well -suited to the 
identification of CW degradation products or metabolites at spiking levels of 100 ng/ml 
(in clean syn thetic urine). However, the se derivatives gave poor signal -to-noise ratios at 
analyte spiking levels of 10 ng/ml, and selected ion or selected reaction chromatograms 
usually showed several additional peaks across displayed chromatographic windows. At 
these lower concentrations, perfluorinated derivatives were clearly superior in terms of 
selectivity and sensitivity of detection, although they may be more restricted in terms of the 
number of ions or transitions available for monitoring.34

9. Advantages / disadvantages 
The clear advantage of derivatisation is that it extends the range of analytes amenable to gas 
chromatographic analysis. Some derivatives may enhance the mass spectrometric properties 
in terms of structurally characteristic high -mass ions. For trace analysis, derivatisation 
allows a degree of tailoring of the properties to suit different methods of detection, for 
example perfluorinated derivatives for use with NICI–MS. 
Derivatisation can be a source of error. R esidual traces of water or large amounts of 
extraneous materials extracted from the matrix can suppress derivatisation, or produce a 
complex chemical background. Most derivatising agents are reactive electrophiles; many 
environmental contaminants are nucleophiles that will also react with the derivatising agent. 
Polar analytes are most often present in aqueous samples, or aqueous extracts of complex 
matrices such as soil. Derivatisation of polar analytes using c
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
will also react with the derivatising agent. 
Polar analytes are most often present in aqueous samples, or aqueous extracts of complex 
matrices such as soil. Derivatisation of polar analytes using current ROPs requires 
concentration of aqueous solutions to dryness, a procedure that is time consuming and which 
can be an additional source of error. Residual traces of water may react with the reagent and 
the derivative, and losses of analyte may occur on evaporation of aqueous solutions if the 
analyte has a degree of volatility; examples are thiodiglycol and pinacolyl alcohol. 
Some derivatisation procedures, especially those involving the lowest limits of detection 
such as those using perfluorinated derivatives, can result in trace levels of analyte present in 
negative control samples.34 Great care must be taken to avoid trace contamination of injector 
liners and columns. 
Derivatisation may introduce artefacts. An example recently suspected in an OPCW 
Proficiency Test was the partial O-dealkylation of a V agent during derivatisation of the 
sample with a silylating agent. Lewisite 2 is converted to the Lewi site 1 derivative if 
dimercaptotoluene is used as derivatising ag
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
partial O-dealkylation of a V agent during derivatisation of the 
sample with a silylating agent. Lewisite 2 is converted to the Lewi site 1 derivative if 
dimercaptotoluene is used as derivatising agent. In the case of methyl esters of alkyl 
alkylphosphonic acids or alkylphosphonic acids, the esters themselves are important analytes, 
some of them being precursors or by -products in nerve agent production. It is therefore 
important to distinguish methyl esters as derivatives from methyl esters as analytes. The 
OPCW Laboratory requires laboratories participating in proficiency tests to demonstrate that 
any analyte identified as a methyl or other alkyl ester after derivatisation was not present as 
that derivative in the original sample.

1. Introduction 
Sample clean-up methods are important tools for successful and reliable analysis and 
especially important with chromatographic separations such as gas chromatography (GC) 
and liquid chromatography (LC) and also for electrophoresis (CE). Solid matrices, such as 
soil, and liquid matrices, such as wastewater, can contain hundreds of chemicals. 
Chromatograms of these may become complex, making identification difficult. This is true 
especially when the analyte concentration is much lower than the concentration of the 
interferences. This means that sample clean-up is needed before reliable analysis. Another 
case is when the sample contains very high boiling material, which can cause different 
problems, e.g. injection port or the front edge of the column can be polluted, which can cause 
adsorption of the analytes before the chromatographic separation. 
Many methods to clean the samples also have to be used in analysis of chemical warfare 
agents (CWAs) and
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
polluted, which can cause 
adsorption of the analytes before the chromatographic separation. 
Many methods to clean the samples also have to be used in analysis of chemical warfare 
agents (CWAs) and their degradation products. This chapter presents the most commonly 
used methods: filtration, centrifugation, solvent exchange and solid phase extraction (SPE) 
methods used for cation exchange and for isolation of water-soluble chemicals. Solid phase 
microextraction (SPME) and liquid phase microextraction (LPME) methods, which are used 
for extraction of CWC-related chemicals, are presented in Section 2, P art B, Chapter III: 
Aqueous liquid samples , however . Some of these recommendations are not clear 
recommendations, but discuss essential issues to use the method properly. 
2. Safety aspects and storing 
Safety aspects of sample preparation and storing of samples are presented in Section 2, 
Part A, Chapter I: Introduction. 
3. Filtration 
Filtration is an easy method to clear samples and extracts before analysis and before the next 
sample preparation step , e.g. before concentration or evaporation to dryness. Soil extracts 
and solid material extracts are usually filtered thr
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
les and extracts before analysis and before the next 
sample preparation step , e.g. before concentration or evaporation to dryness. Soil extracts 
and solid material extracts are usually filtered through traditional filter paper in a filtration 
funnel. Whatman 4 (pore size 20–25 µm) has proved to be a good choice for first filtration. 
It offers fast filtering with a good retention of coarse particles and gelatinous precipitates 
and is useful as a rapid filter for cleaning up extracts. 
Sometimes finer filtering is needed. The sample or extract can be filtered with a filter paper 
of smaller pore size. Whatman 1 with pore size of 11 µm still offers medium retention and 
flow rate. However, membrane filters with a pore size of 0.45 or 0.5 µm can also be used, 
especially when only a portion (<1 ml) of the sample or extract has to be filtered. 
When membrane filters are used, it should be noted that different membranes have different 
resistance to chemicals. In addition, hydrophilic membranes must be used with hydrophilic 
samples and hydrophobic membranes with hydrophobic samples, respectively. To easily 
resolve the last -mentioned problem of having many different types of filt
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
membranes must be used with hydrophilic 
samples and hydrophobic membranes with hydrophobic samples, respectively. To easily 
resolve the last -mentioned problem of having many different types of filters to different 
applications, it is recommended to use regenerated cellulose membrane filters with which 
both aqueous and organic samples and extracts can be filtered (e.g. Millex LRC and 
Whatman RC).

4. Centrifugation 
Centrifugation is a fast and efficient method to separate a heterogeneous mixture of s olid 
and liquid, e.g. to separate the extraction solvent of the soil sample from the matrix before 
filtration. After successful centrifugation, the solid precipitate is settled at the bottom of the 
test tube and the solution above it, and the centrifugate is clear. If the centrifugate is not 
clear, you can always increase the time of centrifugation or the centrifugal force. 
It should be noted that water-organic solvent emulsions can also efficiently be separated into 
two phases by centrifugation. 
Note! Centrifuge always has to be in balance. This means that in the opposite holder there 
has to be another sample of the same weight. 
Usually, a centrifugal force of 2000 G is recommended. The amount of revolutions per 
minute RPM (speed) for a specific rotor can be calculated using the following equation:

5. Solvent exchange 
Solvent exchange is used to make the sample more suitable for chromatographic separation, 
spectrometric analysis and derivatis ation, and also to clean the sample from matrix 
components: 
 Polar solvent can be evaporated totally or partly to get peaks of a polar analyte 
sharper and to avoid peak splitting when nonpolar column is used for analysis in GC 
 Organic solvent is changed to be more suitable for liquid chromatography –mass 
spectrometric (LC–MS) analysis 
 Buffers and components of sample disturbing ionisation are evaporated for LC–MS 
analysis 
 Organic solutions are concentrated and extracted with aceton itrile to remove 
hydrocarbon background: see section 5.1 
 Water is evaporated to dryness before methylation 
 Water and alcohols are evaporated to dryness before silylation 
Note! Solid phase extraction (SPE) is also a solvent exchange method when the analytes of 
interest are trap ped in the solid phase and extracted with another so
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
aporated to dryness before silylation 
Note! Solid phase extraction (SPE) is also a solvent exchange method when the analytes of 
interest are trap ped in the solid phase and extracted with another solvent. The sample is 
usually concentrated in tandem. 
Methods for solvent exchange by concentration and evaporation are presented in Section 2, 
Part A, Chapter II: Concentration. 
5.1 Acetonitrile extraction of organic solutions to remove hydrocarbon background 
Hydrocarbon background is removed from organic liquid by partitioning the analytes from 
nonpolar hydrocarbon solvent to relatively polar aprotic solvent. The method is applicable 
to organic solvents immiscible in acetonitrile.

hydrocarbons and silicon oil. In case of solvents miscible with acetonitrile, the organic

The acetonitrile extraction method of organic solutions is simple and robust. It has been

The acetonitrile extraction method of organic solutions is simple and robust. It has been 
tested with samples provided in OPCW Proficiency T ests. Recovery of very nonpolar 
phosphonates (e.g. dioctyl or didecyl alkylphosphonates) may be lower than their more polar, 
smaller homologs (e.g. dipropyl alkylphosphonates). Other polar aprotic solvents 
(e.g. dimethylformamide), which are immiscible in hexane, can be also used.1 
6. Solid phase extraction methods 
6.1 Cleaning of hydrocarbon background with silica cartridges 
Hydrocarbon and other relatively nonpolar background chemicals are removed from an 
organic liquid sample and organic extracts using a silica SPE (Si) cartridge by partitioning 
the analytes from a nonpolar hydrocarbon solvent to a polar Si sorbent . The sorbent is 
washed with a nonpolar solvent and the analytes are extracted out of the sorbent with a polar 
solvent. 
Equipment, supplies and chemicals 
The equipment, supplies and chemicals needed in SPE cleaning of hydrocarbon background 
are presented in Table 2. 
Procedure 
Elute a portion of 200–500 µl of the o
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
Equipment, supplies and chemicals 
The equipment, supplies and chemicals needed in SPE cleaning of hydrocarbon background 
are presented in Table 2. 
Procedure 
Elute a portion of 200–500 µl of the organic liquid sample slowly (a drop in second) through 
a Si cartridge. Wash the cartridge with 2 ml of n-hexane and extract with methanol to an end 
volume of 500 µl. 
This sample is analysed for volatile CWC-related chemicals (soluble in organic solvents). 
Alternatively, a Si cartridge can be preconditioned with 1 ml of n-hexane, the organic liquid 
sample can be diluted before elution with an equal volume of n-hexane, and 2 ml of methanol 
can be used for extraction.

Evaluation of method 
The most nonpolar CWC-related chemicals such as mustard gas do not efficiently retain on 
Si cartridge, and the amount that has been retained is extracted out of the cartridge with the 
washing solvent (n-hexane). This means that these chemicals are not present in the methanol 
extract of a Si cartridge. 
The cartrid

that has been retained is extracted out of the cartridge with the 
washing solvent (n-hexane). This means that these chemicals are not present in the methanol 
extract of a Si cartridge. 
The cartridge can be extracted with a more nonpolar solvent such as acetonitrile or ethyl 
acetate instead of methanol. However, the more polar CWC-related chemicals such as VX 
are not extracted with these solvents, but methanol is needed to release it from the cartridge. 
For this reason, methanol is recommended as the extraction solvent. 
Do not throw away the sample eluted through the cartridge, the washing solvent(s), and the 
cartridge itself before you have analysed the extract and are satisfied with the results of this 
purification step.

organic samples and extracts.

Procedure 
Condition the strong cation-exchange SCX cartridge with 2–3 ml of methanol and 3–5 ml of 
clean water. Do not let the cartridge dry. Elute 1 –2 ml of aqueous sample or extract 
(preferably under gravity) through the cartridge. After the sample has completely eluted 
through the cartridge, wash the cartridge with 3 ml of clean water. Purge the cartridge with 
nitrogen stream for 1 minute to remove water from the sorbent. Finally, extract with 2 ml of 
10% ammonium hydroxide in methanol . Separate a portion of eluate, filter through a 
0.45 µm (for HPLC) or 0.20 µm (for UHPLC) disposable syringe filter , and analyse with 
LC–MS. 
Evaporate the rest of the eluate to dryness with mild nitrogen flow at room temperature or 
on a rotary evaporator as described in Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: Concentration. The 
evaporation residue is dissolved in 100–200 µl of high-purity acetonitrile. A small portion 
of this acetonitrile can be filtered as described above for LC–MS an

evaporation residue is dissolved in 100–200 µl of high-purity acetonitrile. A small portion 
of this acetonitrile can be filtered as described above for LC–MS analysis, and the rest of it 
is s ilylated as described in Section 2, Part A, Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas 
chromatography. 
These samples are analysed for polar amino alcohols. 
Note! The extraction efficiency depends on pH and, hence, the sample pH must be lower 
than 8 and the extraction solvent (10% NH4OH) pH must be above 10. 
Evaluation of method 
The method is highly sensitive and can extract traces of amino alcohols. Aqueous 
ammonium hydroxide solution may also be used for extraction; however, methanolic 
solution is recommended to get the maximum recoveries. Methanol helps in disrupting 
secondary hydrophobic interactions between carbon chain of amino alcohols and SCX 
material.5

custody (documentation showing

assurance of chemical analysis. Safety aspects of sample preparation and storing of samples 
are presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter I: Introduction. This chapter describes different 
means for assuring and controlling the quality of sample preparation. 
1. Plan the sample preparation carefully and make it efficient and simple. 
2. Follow the recommended operating procedures in all sample preparations. 
3. Check the purity of solvents (also the concentrated solvent) and reagents before sample 
preparation with the same methods used for analysis. 
4. Go through the whole sample preparation procedure without samples, using the same 
solvents, same reagents, and similar glassware to investigate the background 
generated during the procedure (method blank). 
5. If possible, prepare at least two parallel samples. 
6. Determine the approximate recovery of the sample preparation method by spiking the 
blank matrix with a known amount of the compounds of interest and repeating the 
sample preparation (this assumes that a clearly marked blank sample of the same

1. Scope 
Organic samples are samples in organic solvents. They can be collected directly from the 
inspected sites or can be organic solvent extracts of aqueous, soil, wipe, active charcoal, 
concrete, paint, rubber , other polymeric samples and air sampling tubes . A wide range of 
organic solvents or their mixtures can be used. This chapter describes methods for the 
preparation of organic samples for the analysis of chemical warfare agents (CWAs) and their 
degradation products, where chromatographic methods such as gas chromatography (GC), 
liquid chromatography (LC) as an analysis technique or an introduction technique to 
spectrometers are used as the separation technique. The sample preparation methods 
required for analysis by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy are also presented. 
2. Summary of the method 
A general flowchart of sample preparation of organic sample is given in Figure 1. An organic 
sample is divided into several sub-samples, which are treated i
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
also presented. 
2. Summary of the method 
A general flowchart of sample preparation of organic sample is given in Figure 1. An organic 
sample is divided into several sub-samples, which are treated in manners described in this 
chapter. Three separate sub-samples of untreated organic sample are analysed directly by 
GC and gas chromatography mass spectrometry (GC–MS) as well as with minimum sample 
preparation with liquid chromatography mass spectrometry ( LC–MS) and NMR . Three 
other separate sub-samples are derivatised: methylated, silylated and derivatised with thiols 
for identification of the Lewisites. Still, a separate sub-sample is cleaned up, if needed, with 
normal-phase silica Si solid phase extraction (SPE). A sub-sample can also be analysed after 
solvent exchange using LC–MS for analysis and one sub-sample is treated for NMR analysis. 
Finally, one sub -sample can be extracted after solvent exchange with acetonitrile using 
liquid-liquid extraction. After extraction, a part of this sample is analy sed with GC –MS, 
while another part is evaporated almost to dryness and derivatised for GC–MS analysis. 
3. Safety aspects and storing 
Safety aspects of sample preparati
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
part of this sample is analy sed with GC –MS, 
while another part is evaporated almost to dryness and derivatised for GC–MS analysis. 
3. Safety aspects and storing 
Safety aspects of sample preparation and storing of samples a re presented in Section 2, 
Part A, Chapter I: Introduction. 
4. Equipment, supplies and chemicals 
The equipment, supplies and chemicals needed in this ROP are presented in Table 1. 
5. Procedure 
5.1 Division of the sample 
If the amount of the original organic sample is 5 ml or bigger, it is always better to take a 
fresh portion of sample for each step to assure good recovery of chemicals of interest.

The sample is placed in a 10 ml headspace vial. The vial is sealed using a silicone -PTFA 
septum and an aluminium cap and is kept at 80 °C for 10–15 minutes. The gas phase is drawn 
and analysed with GC and GC–MS. 
5.3 Direct analysis 
One sub-sample of the organic sample (e.g. 200 µl) is analysed directly with GC, GC–MS, 
and if possible depending the solvent (e.g. acetonitrile and methanol) of the organic sample 
with LC–MS (Fraction 2, Figure 1). 
The original sample is analysed for volatile CWC-related chemicals, but since the procedure 
does not contain sample clean-up steps, large amount s of background chemicals in the 
sample may make the reliable identification of the target chemicals difficult. 
Similarly, a small portion can be analysed with NMR depending the solvent (e.g. chlorinated 
solvents, acetonitrile and methanol). 0.4–0.5 ml of the organic liquid

Similarly, a small portion can be analysed with NMR depending the solvent (e.g. chlorinated 
solvents, acetonitrile and methanol). 0.4–0.5 ml of the organic liquid is diluted with 0.1 ml 
of corresponding deuterated solvent and transfe rred into a n NMR tube (5 mm) . If it is 
suspected that the concentration of chemicals is high in the sample, the organic liquid is 
diluted more (e.g. 0.05 ml of the organic liquid is diluted with 0.45 ml of the corresponding 
deuterated solvent). 
5.4 Concentration 
If the direct analysis of the organic liquid sample (Fraction 2) shows very small amounts of 
possible analytes of interest, take a portion of 1–2 ml of the sample for concentration. 
Concentrate the sample with mild nitrogen flow (Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: 
Concentration) (Fraction 3, Figure 1) to 0.1 or 0.2 ml, respectively. 
Note! Do not concentrate the organic extract to dryness since certain volatile CWC-related 
chemicals such as sarin are lost from the sample and, on the other hand, certain less volatile 
CWC-related chemicals such as VX in residues of organic extracts are firmly adsorbed to 
glass surfaces. 
The concentrated organic liq

CWC-related chemicals such as VX in residues of organic extracts are firmly adsorbed to 
glass surfaces. 
The concentrated organic liquid sample is analysed for volatile CWC-related chemicals. 
5.5 Methylation 
A portion of the organic liquid sample is methylated as described in Section 2, Part A, 
Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas chromatography (Fraction 4, Figure 1). 
If the sample is cloudy after methylation, filter it with a disposable syringe filter before 
analyses with GC based methods. This sample is analysed for polar, non- or slightly volatile 
CWC-related chemicals such as alkylphosphonic and alkylthiophosphonic acids.

This sample is analysed for polar, non- or slightly volatile CWC-related chemicals such as

5.7 Derivatisation to analyse Lewisites 
Another sub -sample of the original sample is derivatised with butanethiol for GC–MS 
analysis of Lewisite 1 and 2, and Lewisite oxide (Fraction 6, Figure 1). The derivatisation 
procedure is presented in Section 2, Part A , Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas 
chromatography. 
5.8 Cleaning of hydrocarbon background with silica cartridges 
One sub-sample of organic sample can be cleaned up of hydrocarbon and other relatively 
nonpolar background chemicals by Silica (Si) solid phase extraction (SPE), partitioning the 
analytes from a nonpolar hydrocarbon solvent to a polar Si sorbent. The sorbe

text:
ocarbon and other relatively 
nonpolar background chemicals by Silica (Si) solid phase extraction (SPE), partitioning the 
analytes from a nonpolar hydrocarbon solvent to a polar Si sorbent. The sorbent is washed 
with a nonpolar solvent and the analytes are extracted out of the sorbent with a polar solvent 
(Fraction 7, Figure 1) . The procedure for Si cleaning is described in Section 2, Part A, 
Chapter IV: Sample clean-up methods. 
Si cleaned extracts can be concentrated, if necessary ( Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: 
Concentration). Si cleaned e xtracts can also be a nalysed after silylation or methylation 
(Sections 5.6 and 5.5 above). 
5.9 Solvent exchange for LC analysis 
For LC and LC –MS analysis, the solvent of the organic liquid sample may have to be 
changed to be more suitable for analysis. For this reason, one sub-sample is concentrated 
with mild nitrogen flow as described in Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: Concentration. The 
residue is dissolved with a solvent suitable to the solvent c hemistry of the LC analysis 
(pH and amount of aqueous solvent) (Fraction 8, Figure 1). 
5.10 Solvent-exchange and acetonitrile extraction to remove hydrocarbon background 
The solven

text:
to the solvent c hemistry of the LC analysis 
(pH and amount of aqueous solvent) (Fraction 8, Figure 1). 
5.10 Solvent-exchange and acetonitrile extraction to remove hydrocarbon background 
The solvent of the organic sample can be changed to n-hexane. One sub-sample of the 
original sample is concentrated 10-fold with mild nitrogen flow as described in Section 2, 
Part A, Chapter II: Concentration. The residue is reconstituted with n-hexane (Fraction 10, 
Figure 1). 
Note! Take care that the organic sample is not evaporated to dryness since that will result 
in the loss of volatile CWC-related chemicals. 
This sub-sample (in hexane) can then be liquid-liquid extracted with acetonitrile to remove 
hydrocarbon background. The analytes are partitioned from nonpolar hydrocarbon solvent 
to acetonitrile, which is a relatively polar aprotic solvent. The method is applicable to organic 
solvents immiscible in acetonitrile and presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter IV: Sample 
clean-up methods.

Quality control of sample preparation is presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter V: Quality

7. Evaluation of method 
Generally, organic samples can be analy sed using GC and GC –MS without sample 
preparation, but sometimes it is difficult to detect the CWC-related chemicals with direct 
GC–MS analysis in presence of masking/background components, especially in complex 
hydrocarbon background.

text:

GC–MS analysis in presence of masking/background components, especially in complex 
hydrocarbon background. 1 Clean-up methods such as SPE or liquid-liquid extraction are 
often used to remove the background chemicals from the sample matrix. Changing the 
solvent into n-hexane and extracting it with acetonitrile can eliminate the hydrocarbons from

1. Scope 
This section describes methods for the preparation of soil samples for the analysis of 
chemical warfare agents (CWA) and their degradation products , where chromatographic 
methods such as gas chromatography (GC), liquid chromatography (LC), ion 
chromatography (IC), or capillary electrophoresis (CE) are used as the separation technique. 
The sample preparation methods requ ired for analysis by nuclear magnetic resonance 
(NMR) spectroscopy are also presented. 
2. Summary of the method 
A general flowchart of sample preparation of soil samples is given in Figure 1. The soil 
sample is divided into sub -samples, which are treated i n manners described in this section. 
Sub-samples of soil samples are extracted with organic solvents, under neutral and alkaline 
conditions, using traditional liquid -liquid extraction. A separate sub -sample of the original 
soil sample or the remaining soil fraction after
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ted with organic solvents, under neutral and alkaline 
conditions, using traditional liquid -liquid extraction. A separate sub -sample of the original 
soil sample or the remaining soil fraction after neutral extraction is extracted with water. 
This water fraction or part of it is evaporated and derivatised. Another fraction of this water 
extract can also be analysed after filtration and pH change using LC. Similarly, a new sub -
sample of the original soil sample is extracted again with water or the remaining water 
fraction of the first water extract is cation-exchanged. After ion exchange, this sub-sample 
can be analysed after pH adjustment with LC, IC and CE, but for the GC analysis, a part of 
it is evaporated to dryness and derivatised. Finally, one sub-sample is extracted-derivatised 
for identification of Lewisites. 
3. Safety aspects and storing 
Safety aspects of sample preparation and storing of samples are presented in Section 2, 
Part A, Chapter I: Introduction. 
4. Equipment, supplies and chemicals 
The equipment, supplies and chemicals needed in this ROP are presented in Table 1.

5.2 Organic extraction 
Homogenise the soil sample with the help of a spoon or spatula, if necessary (the agents are 
assumed to be homogeneously distributed in the soil). Take ca. 1–10 g of soil and place it in 
a screw -capped glass bottle. Add the same volume in millilitres (ml) of the high-purity 
organic solvent as the amount of the sample in grams (g) (e.g. 5 ml to 5 g of soil) and close 
the bottle tightly. Usually, dichloromethane is used as extraction solvent.i Extract the soil by 
sonication, shaking, tumbling, or agitation for 10 min. Sonication may reduce recoveries by 
creating new active sites for analytes in the soil. Quickly centrifuge the extract, decant the 
supernatant and filter, if necessary, through a filter paper or a disposable 0.45 µm syringe 
filter. If you want to filter the whole extract with a disposable syringe filter, it is 
recommended to centrifuge for 5 min at 5000 G. Otherwise, centrifugation for 3 minutes at 
2000 G is usually enough. 
Note! Gener
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
t to filter the whole extract with a disposable syringe filter, it is 
recommended to centrifuge for 5 min at 5000 G. Otherwise, centrifugation for 3 minutes at 
2000 G is usually enough. 
Note! General instructions for filtration and centrifugation are descri bed in Section 2, 
Part A, Chapter IV: Sample clean-up methods. 
Repeat the extraction process once or twice. Combine the extracts and dry the combined 
extract with anhydrous sodium sulfate, if needed. Usually ca. 1 g of the drying agent is 
sufficient for 5 ml of the final extract. The dried extract is analy sed with GC and gas 
chromatography mass spectrometry (GC –MS) as such (Fraction 1, Figure 1) or, where 
necessary, after approximately 2 –10-fold concentration (Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: 
Concentration) (Fraction 1A). 
Note! Do not concentrate the organic extract to dryness since certain volatile CWC-related 
chemicals such as sarin are lost from the sample and, on the other hand, certain less volatile 
CWC-related chemicals such as VX in residues of organic extracts are firmly adsorbed to 
glass surfaces. 
Note! If the amount of the original soil sample is 15 g or bigger, it is always better to take a 
fresh sub-
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
emicals such as VX in residues of organic extracts are firmly adsorbed to 
glass surfaces. 
Note! If the amount of the original soil sample is 15 g or bigger, it is always better to take a 
fresh sub-sample to each extraction step to assure good recovery of chemicals of interest. 
This organic extract is analysed for nonpolar CWC-related chemicals. 
5.2.1 LC sample 
For LC and liquid chromatography mass spectrometric (LC –MS) analysis, the solvent has 
to be changed to be more suitable for LC analysis. For this purpose, the dichloromethane 
extract has to be concentrated with mild nitrogen flow as described in Section 2, Part A, 
Chapter II: Concentration. The residue is dissolved in a solvent suitable to the solvent 
chemistry of the LC analysis (pH and amount of aqueous solvent) (Fraction 1B). 
5.2.2 NMR sample 
Dichloromethane extracts can be analy sed with NMR. 0.4–0.5 ml of the extract is diluted 
with 0.1 ml of deuterated solvent (dichloromethane or chloroform) and transferred into an 
NMR tube (5 mm) (Fraction 1C). 
 
 
iOther organic solvents (ethyl acetate, chloroform, n-hexane….) can also be used.
