5.3 Aqueous extraction 
Take the same soil sample as above, or a new 1 –10 g portion of soil. Place it in a screw -
capped glass bottle. Add the same volume in millilitres (ml) of deionised, redistilled water 
as the amount of the sample in grams (g) (e.g. 5 ml to 5 g of soil) and close the bottle tightly. 
Extract similarly to the first extraction. Rapidly centrifuge the extract for 5 min at 2000 G, 
decant the supernatant and filter, if necessary, through a filter paper or a disposable 0.45 µm 
syringe filter. If you want to filter the whole extract with a disposable syringe filter, it is 
recommended to centrifuge for 5 min at 5000 G. Repeat the extraction process o

Measure the pH of the combined extracts. Divide the extract into four sub-samples. 
This extract is analy sed for polar water -soluble CWC -related chemicals (Fraction 2, 
Figure 1). 
Note! General instructions for filtration and centrifugation are described in Section 2, Part 
A, Chapter IV: Sample clean-up methods. 
Note! Sonication may reduce recoveries of the polar CWC -related chemicals by creating 
new active sites for analytes in the soil. 
5.3.1 Evaporation and derivatisation for GC and GC–MS analysis 
A portion of a water extract of the soil sample is evaporated to dryness (without cation -
exchange) and silylated. Evaporation and derivatisation procedures are presented in Section 
2, Part A, Chapter II: Concentration and Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas chromatography 
(Fraction 2A, Figure 1). 
The derivatised sample is analy sed for polar CWC -related chemicals such as thiodiglycol 
and amino alcohols. Polar alkylphosphonic and alkylthiophosphonic acids can

(Fraction 2A, Figure 1). 
The derivatised sample is analy sed for polar CWC -related chemicals such as thiodiglycol 
and amino alcohols. Polar alkylphosphonic and alkylthiophosphonic acids can also be 
recovered from this fraction, but since the procedure does not include a cation-exchange step, 
a large amount of inorganic cations in the sample may mean that the recoveries of smaller 
acids such as methyl or ethylphosphonic acid may be low, or the chemicals may not be

5.3.2 Cation-exchange, evaporation and derivatisation for GC and GC–MS analysis 
Another portion of a water extract of the soil sample is cation exchanged to remove inorganic 
cations, alkali and earth alkali metal ions such as Na +, Ca 2+, Mg 2+, etc. to help the 
derivatisation procedure for the GC analysis and to remove ion background for LC, CE, IC 
and sometimes also for NMR analysis (Fraction 2B, Figure 1). The pH of the eluate is 
determined in order to check the efficiency of the cation-exchange. 
The cation -exchanged sample or the most part of it (see Section 5.3.3) is evaporated to 
dryness and methylated for GC and GC –MS analysis. Cation-exchange, evaporation and 
derivatisation procedures and presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter IV: Sample clean-up 
methods, Chapter II: Concentration, and Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas chromatography 
(Fraction 2B2, Figure 1). 
Cation-exchanged samples are analysed for polar alkylphosphonic and alkylthiophosphonic 
acids.

Concentration, and Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas chromatography 
(Fraction 2B2, Figure 1). 
Cation-exchanged samples are analysed for polar alkylphosphonic and alkylthiophosphonic 
acids. 
Note! Amino alcohols remain in the cation-exchanger and cannot be recovered. 
5.3.3 LC sample 
Filter part of the water extra ct through a disposable 0.45 µm (for HPLC) or 0.20 µm (for 
UHPLC) syringe filter and adjust to a suitabl e pH for LC, CE and IC analysis 
(Fraction 2C, Figure 1). 
To avoid salt formation of organic bases and acids, a portion of a cati on-exchanged water 
extract should be analysed similarly (Fraction 2B3, Figure 1) directly or after concentration. 
5.3.4 NMR sample 
One portion of the water extract is diluted with deuterated water and transferred into an NMR 
tube (Fraction 2D, Figure 1 ); e.g. ca. 0.4–0.5 ml of the cation -exchanged water extract of 
soil sample is diluted with ca. 0.1 ml of deuterated water and transferred into an NMR tube 
(5 mm). 
Cation-exchange can also be useful to remove background chemicals, e.g. paramagnetic 
metal ions from aqueous samples. 
5.3.5 Solid phase microextraction and hollow fiber microextraction 
Water extracts of soil sampl

can also be useful to remove background chemicals, e.g. paramagnetic 
metal ions from aqueous samples. 
5.3.5 Solid phase microextraction and hollow fiber microextraction 
Water extracts of soil samples can be analy sed for water -soluble degradation products of 
CWC-related chemicals as an aqueous sample using solid phase microextraction (SPME) 
and hollow fiber liquid phase microextraction HF -LPME (Section 2, Part B, Chapter III: 
Aqueous liquid samples).

Take the same soil sample as above or a new 1 –10 g portion of soil. Place it in a screw -
capped glass bottle. Add the same volume in millilitres (ml) of methanol containing 1% of 
triethylamine (TEA) as the amount of the sample in grams (g) (e.g. 5 ml to 5 g of soil) and

5.5 Extraction/derivatisation to analyse Lewisites with GC–MS 
Another sub-sample of 1–10 g of the original sample is placed in a screw-capped glass bottle 
and prepared for analysis of the sample for Lewisite 1 and 2, and Lewisite oxide (Fraction 
4, Figure 1). The thiol derivatisation procedure is presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter III: 
Derivatisation for gas chromatography. 
6. Instrumental extraction 
Organic, water, and alkaline extraction can be performed in a pressurised solvent extraction 
(PSE) instrument designed for ext raction of solid and semisolid sample matrices. PSE 
reduces solvent consumption and sample preparation time. Solvent is pumped into an 
extraction vessel containing the sample and is heated and press

text:
raction of solid and semisolid sample matrices. PSE 
reduces solvent consumption and sample preparation time. Solvent is pumped into an 
extraction vessel containing the sample and is heated and pressuri sed. The pressuri sed 
solvent at high temperature accelerates the extraction process by increasing the solubility of 
the analyte in the solvent and also increasing the kinetic rate of desorption of the analyte 
from the sample matrix. High temperature makes possible the high solubility and high 
diffusion rate wh ile the high pressure keeps the solvent below its boiling point. At high 
pressures and high temperatures, the solvents penetrate the solid samples at a much higher 
rate. The extraction process is fast and efficient. In addition to PSE, the method is also called 
accelerated solvent extraction (ASE) and pressuri sed fluid extraction. The extraction 
parameters (extraction pressure, temperature, time and number of cycles) have to be 
optimised to obtain the best efficiency of the extraction process.1, 2

Quality control of sample preparation is presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter V: Quality

8. Evaluation of method 
Analysis of nonpolar chemicals from soil samples using GC and GC–MS is usually trouble-
free. In OPCW proficiency tests, most of the problems have been faced in sample preparation 
of water extracts for water-soluble chemicals before GC analysis, because the water must be 
displaced and the analytes derivatised.3 
Only a few results of analysis of real soil samples have been published, but identification of 
chemicals has been possible after several years from the collection of samples. The methods 
used have been quite similar with this ROP. 
D'Agostino analysed soil samples in the late 1980s from Iran/Iraq, suspected to have been 
contaminated with mustard. Mustard and 17 other mustard related impurities were identified 
after chloroform extraction. 4 Also Black et al . analy sed soil samples
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
Iran/Iraq, suspected to have been 
contaminated with mustard. Mustard and 17 other mustard related impurities were identified 
after chloroform extraction. 4 Also Black et al . analy sed soil samples collected from a 
Kurdish village after a chemical attack. GC–MS using headspace analysis, solvent extraction 
with organic solvent (dichloromethane or ethyl acetate) and thermal desorption methods 
successfully confirmed the presence of sulphur mustard and 21 related compounds.5 A year 
later they p ublished results of identification of sulphur mustard and/or thiodiglycol in six 
soil samples collected also from Kurdistan. In addition to these chemicals, isopropyl 
methylphosphonic acid and methylphosphonic acid, the hydrolysis products of the nerve 
agent sarin, were detected in six different soil samples. The neat agent was identified in 
dichloromethane extract and the hydrolysis products in water extracts, which were 
evaporated and silylated for GC–MS and GC-MS/MS analysis.6 
Several years later aqueous extracts of the same soil samples were successfully analy sed 
with LC–APCI–MS/MS for thiodiglycol and methylphosphonic acid.7 D'Agostino et al. have 
also used a LC–MS (LC–ESI–M
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
l years later aqueous extracts of the same soil samples were successfully analy sed 
with LC–APCI–MS/MS for thiodiglycol and methylphosphonic acid.7 D'Agostino et al. have 
also used a LC–MS (LC–ESI–MS/MS) method to identify thiodiglycol and nine longer chain 
diols in aqueous extracts of soil samples. These samples were taken from a former mustard 
storage site.8 
Recoveries of aqueous extraction may be low especially for the most polar degradation 
products and depend on the soil type. Kataoka et al. determined recoveries of four al kyl 
phosphonates on 21 different soil types. Compared to the recoveries measured directly by 
CE, the yields obtained after silylation and GC –MS analysis were low. The efficiencies of 
derivatisation depended on the amount of alkali earth metals extractable from soils as well 
as high total carbon content of the soil.9 
As with aqueous water samples, SPME methods have been tested to analy se both the neat 
agents and water-soluble CWC-related chemicals extracted from soil samples.10–17 
Ethyl acetate suits very well for extraction solvent of nonpolar and semipolar CWC-related 
chemicals when GC and GC –MS is used for analysis. Ethyl acetate is less
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
extracted from soil samples.10–17 
Ethyl acetate suits very well for extraction solvent of nonpolar and semipolar CWC-related 
chemicals when GC and GC –MS is used for analysis. Ethyl acetate is less volatile than 
dichloromethane. In addition, ethyl acetate does not react so easily as dichloromethane with 
chemicals in the sample background, especially with the chemicals containing nitrogen or 
sulfur.

1. Scope 
This section describes methods for the preparation of environmental aqueous liquid samples 
for the analysis of chemical warfare agents (CWAs) and their degradation products, where 
chromatographic methods such as gas chromatography (GC), liquid chromatography (LC), 
ion chromatography (IC) or capillary electrophoresis (CE) as an analysis technique or an 
introduction technique to spectrometers, are used as the separation technique. The sample 
preparation methods required for analysis by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) 
spectroscopy are also presented. 
2. Summary of the method 
A general flowchart of sample preparation of aqueous liquid sample is given in Figure 1. An 
aqueous liquid sample is d

2. Summary of the method 
A general flowchart of sample preparation of aqueous liquid sample is given in Figure 1. An 
aqueous liquid sample is divided into sub-samples, which are treated in manners described 
in this section. Sub-samples of aqueous samples are extracted with organic solvents, under 
neutral and alkaline conditions, using traditional liquid -liquid extraction or solid-supported 
liquid extraction Extrelut® (Merck) or Chem Elut® (Agilent) extraction cartridges. The 
neutral unpreserved aqueous sub-sample is alternatively extracted with a C 18 solid-phase 
extraction (SPE) cartridge. A separate sub -sample of the original aqueous sample or the 
remaining aqueous fraction after neutral extraction is evaporated and derivatised. Similarly, 
a new sub-sample of the original aqueous sample or the remaining aqueous fraction after 
neutral extraction is cation-exchanged. After ion-exchange, this sub-sample can be analysed 
after pH adjustment with LC, IC and CE, but for the GC analysis, a part of it is evaporated 
to dryness and derivati sed. A sub -sample can also be analysed after filtration or 
centrifugation and pH

text:
after pH adjustment with LC, IC and CE, but for the GC analysis, a part of it is evaporated 
to dryness and derivati sed. A sub -sample can also be analysed after filtration or 
centrifugation and pH change using LC. Finally, one sub -sample is derivat ised for 
identification of Lewisites and one sub-sample is treated for NMR analysis.

5.2 Liquid-liquid extractions 
If the aqueous sample is acidic, neutralise it with dilute ammonium hydroxide solution and 
if it is alkaline, neutralise with dilute hydrochloric acid. Liquid–liquid extract the neutralised 
sample with two portions of water-immiscible high purity organic solvent using a one -to-
two (1:2) volume ratio of solvent to sample. Usually, dichloromethane is used as extraction 
solventi and liquid–liquid extraction times are two to five minutes. Combine the extracts and 
dry the combined extract with anhydrous sodium sulfate by adding the sulfate to the extract. 
Usually ca. 1 g of the drying agent is a proper amount for 5 ml of the final extract. The dried 
extract is analysed with GC and GC–MS as such (Fraction 1A, Figure 1) or, where necessary, 
after approximately 2–10-fold concentration (Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: Concentration). 
Note! Do not concentrate the organic extract to dryness since certain volatile CWC-related 
chemicals such as sarin are lost from the
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ld concentration (Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: Concentration). 
Note! Do not concentrate the organic extract to dryness since certain volatile CWC-related 
chemicals such as sarin are lost from the sample and, on the other hand, certain less volatile 
CWC-related chemicals such as VX in residues of organic extracts are fir mly adsorbed to 
glass surfaces. 
This organic extract is analysed for nonpolar and semipolar CWC-related chemicals.

Fibers have to be conditioned before use. Turn on the split vent of the GC injection port and 
set a carrier gas flow of at least 50 ml/min. Insert the fiber into the injection port and 
condition it according to the recommendations of the manufacturer .2 The PDMS/DVB is 
conditioned at 250 °C for 30 min while the CAR/PDMS at 300 °C for 1–2 h, respectively. 
6.2 GC–MS analysis 
Immediately before every sample, an injection of the blank fiber is performed to ascertain 
the chemical background of the fiber. The SPME fiber is desorbed at the GC injection port 
either manually using the GC in the manual injection mode or automatically using a sampler 
capable to operate in SPME mode. The fiber is desorbe

either manually using the GC in the manual injection mode or automatically using a sampler 
capable to operate in SPME mode. The fiber is desorbed by exposing the fiber at the injection

10. Evaluation of method 
Analysis of nonpolar chemicals from aqueous samples using GC and GC –MS is us ually 
trouble-free. Most nonpolar CWAs hydrolyse in aqueous solution and efforts should be paid 
on analysis of degradation products in water samples, however. In this respect, surprisingly 
few results of analysis of real aqueous samples have been published. D'Agostino et al. used 
LC–MS for the analysis of aqueous samples collected at a former mustard destruction site. 
Both thiodiglycol and the corresponding hydrolysis product of O-mustard were identified in 
these samples.12 A few years later they analysed (also with LC–MS) a snow sample that was 
accidentally contaminated with an organophosphorus chemical warfare agent during the 
destruction of a chemical munition. Sarin, its hydrolysis products an
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ed (also with LC–MS) a snow sample that was 
accidentally contaminated with an organophosphorus chemical warfare agent during the 
destruction of a chemical munition. Sarin, its hydrolysis products and a number of related 
compounds were identified.13 
Aqueous liquid sample has been the othe r of the most popular sample types in OPCW 
proficiency tests. Most of the problems in these tests have been faced in sample preparation 
of water-soluble chemicals before GC analysis, because the water must be displaced and the 
analytes derivatised.14 Isolation of highly polar analytes from an aqueous matrix prior to 
derivatisation is problematic. Liquid –liquid extraction is inefficient, SPE m ay be 
unworkable for some matric es, and concentration of aqueous solutions to dryness is time -
consuming and a source of error. For these reasons, approaches such as ion-pair SPE15,16 and 
derivatisation directly in the aqueous medium11 or on a solid support have been tested. New 
miniaturised extraction techniques such as surfactantless microextraction and HF -LPME 
have been used to isolate the derivatives formed in aqueous media.17,18 Similarly, HF-LPME 
has been explored in on -support derivati
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
on techniques such as surfactantless microextraction and HF -LPME 
have been used to isolate the derivatives formed in aqueous media.17,18 Similarly, HF-LPME 
has been explored in on -support derivatisation where a mixture of solvent and derivati sing 
agent was held in the hollow f iber for in -situ derivati sation-extraction of water-soluble 
CWC-related chemicals from aqueous samples.5, 8 
HF-LPME method is simple and requires small amount of organic solvents. Main advantages 
of the method over SPME are its cost effectiveness and no carryover of analytes. SDME in 
turn requires careful handling as drop may dislodge during stirring. HF-LPME is robust and 
can extract analytes from aqueous samples containing suspended particles. Method has been 
tested with proficiency test samples. 7,8 On the other hand, SPME has been the most tested 
method of these modern extraction techniques and a review of its use in analysis of CWC 
related chemicals was published in 2007.19 
Alkyl alkylphosphonic acids can be extracted with HF from aqueous sample for LC–MS 
analysis down to the concentration of 1–10 ng/ml.20 Addition of 10% NaCl in water sample 
(the donor phase) further enhances the sens

analysis down to the concentration of 1–10 ng/ml.20 Addition of 10% NaCl in water sample

importance when nitrogenous and non polar impurities are present in the sample.

1. Scope 
This section describes a method for the collection of air samples in Tenax ® tubes and their 
analysis by thermal desorption –gas chromatography –mass spectrometry (TD –GC–MS). 
Specific sample preparation is not required and the samples are analysed on -line. Thus, the 
analysis of sample tubes requires specific analytical equipment; sa mpling and analysis 
procedures are described here together. Other methods using SPME fibers, canisters or 
Tedlar bags can also be used for sampling chemical warfare agent s (CWAs) in air, but are 
not described in this chapter. 
Sampling on Tenax® tubes is very efficient for the collection of most volatile CWA (sarin, 
soman, tabun, mustard gas,1 and chloropicrin). However, because of the low specific surface 
area (25 m2g-1), Tenax® is not suitable for the trapping of very highly volatile chemicals. It 
cannot also be used for thermolabile and chemicals of very low volatility such as V agents 
and polar degradation products. 
Because sample preparation is not required before
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
volatile chemicals. It 
cannot also be used for thermolabile and chemicals of very low volatility such as V agents 
and polar degradation products. 
Because sample preparation is not required before analysis, s olvent or derivatising agent is 
not added into the sample. Thus, no risk of interference or reactivity with relevant chemicals 
can occur during sample analysis. In addition, results are o btained more quickly (within 
30 minutes). 
The higher the sampled volu me is, the bigger the mass of collected chemicals in the tube. 
This means that the concentration of chemicals in the tube is significant and sensitivity is 
good. Therefore, TD–GC–MS can be used for the detection and identification of CWA in 
air both at high and low concentration levels (down to 10 µgm-3). 
It should be also noted that collected Tenax® samples could be extracted with organic solvent 
instead of thermal desorption. However, chlorinated solvents such as dichloromethane must 
not be used due to the degradation of Tenax® material. 
2. Summary of the method 
Air samples are collected into sampling tubes packed with at least 200 mg of Tenax® GR or 
Tenax® TA with a handheld pump working at a constant air
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ation of Tenax® material. 
2. Summary of the method 
Air samples are collected into sampling tubes packed with at least 200 mg of Tenax® GR or 
Tenax® TA with a handheld pump working at a constant air flow (50 - 200 ml/min). It is 
strongly r ecommended to collect onto two sample tubes at the same time in order to 
overcome possible problems during sampling or analysis. Recommended sampling volume 
is 0.2–2.0 liters depending on the concentration. If the concentration level is not known, the 
sampling volume must be adjusted to 2 liters. 
After sampling, tubes are capped with ¼-inch brass Swagelok®-type caps and stored at low 
temperature (< 4 °C) before analysis.

To verify the correct performance of the analytical system, a quality control run ( QC test, 
see below) is carried out before each sample batch, followed by a blank run to verify the 
absence of CWC-related chemicals. 
Collected chemicals are thermally desorbed from the sample tube and eluted to the analytical 
column using a two-stage thermal desorption system interfaced to a GC–MS. 
A 25–30-m-long non- or semipolar fused silica capillary column (0.25 mm i.d. and 0.25 m 
film thickness) is used. Adjust the GC–MS EI scan range to 29–400 amu. The chemicals are 
identified comparing the measured EI spectra to those in relevant libraries or to spectra of 
authentic reference chemicals or interpretating the spectra. 
3. Safety aspects 
The thermal desorber requires specific safety precautions. During the thermal desorption, 
only a part of sample is tr ansferred into the GC –MS. The rest of the sample – possibly 
containing a large amount of toxic chemicals – is flushed through the spl
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ons. During the thermal desorption, 
only a part of sample is tr ansferred into the GC –MS. The rest of the sample – possibly 
containing a large amount of toxic chemicals – is flushed through the split valve to the 
laboratory. Therefore, the thermal desorber must be installed under a filtering hood, or 
alternatively, the split valve exit flow must be connected to a charcoal filter. 
In addition, the hot parts of the instrument, e.g. valve and transfer line (>200 °C) must be 
taken into account during maintenance operations. 
GC–EI/MS safety recommendations are described in S ection 3, Part B, Chapter II: Gas 
chromatography–electron ionisation/mass spectrometry (GC–EI/MS). 
4. Instrumentation, reagents and chemicals 
4.1 Thermal desorber 
A two-step thermal desorption system must be necessarily used in order to maintain capillary 
column efficiency. 
The following requirements are recommended for optimal results: 
 coupling with the gas chromatograph must be performed with a heated deactivated fused-
silica transfer line; 
 tube desorption temperature must be adjustable from 50 °C to 350 °C; 
 cold trap temperature must be down to 0 °C during primary desorption and must reach
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
deactivated fused-
silica transfer line; 
 tube desorption temperature must be adjustable from 50 °C to 350 °C; 
 cold trap temperature must be down to 0 °C during primary desorption and must reach 
at least 200 °C in a few seconds during secondary desorption; 
 valve must be temperature controlled and manufactured from an inert material. 
4.2 Tenax® tubes 
Two forms of Tenax® are commercially available: Tenax® TA and Tenax® GR. Tenax® TA 
is a porous polymer resin based on 2,6 -diphenylene-oxide. Tenax® GR is a composite 
material containing 70 % of Tenax ® TA polymer and 30% of graphiti zed carbon. The 
resulting material gives higher breakthrough volume for most compounds and superior 
trapping of volatile compounds. It presents also a low affinity for water, avoiding hydrolysis 
and minimising disturbances of the gas chromatographic analysi s, for example, damage of 
the stationary phase. The properties of Tenax® are presented in Table 1.

4.4 Sampling pumps 
It is recommended that the pumps meet the following requirements: 
 small and light in weight (less than 1 kg); 
 equipped with a nickel-cadmium battery allowing long operating life; 
 allow constant flow rates of 0.0–0.5 l/min through the sampling tube; 
 the flow rate must not deviate more than 5% from the initial set value throughout 
the sampling period; 
 as an option, the pump can have a timer allowing run time and delayed start time 
programs; 
 if possible, sampling pump must also have a regular calibration schedule.

5. Sampling 
5.1 Tube conditioning 
After analysis, Tenax ® tubes must be carefully conditioned, regenerated, to eliminate all 
traces of chemicals still adsorbed on the sorbent that could cause false positive results during 
the analysis. 
The conditioning procedure consists of heating the tubes to a higher value than the normal 
desorption temperature under purified helium or nitrogen flow.

Optimal conditioning is achieved by heating Tenax® tubes at 310 °C for at least 2 hours with 
a 100 ml/min gas flow. 
Tube conditioning can be performed with a thermal desorber or with a specific tube 
regeneration device (Figure 1), which allows regeneration of up to 20 tubes simultaneously. 
 
Figure 1. MARKES tube conditioner TC20. 
After conditioning, clean tubes are sealed with ¼ -inch brass Swagelok ®-type screw caps 
fitted with combined PTFE ferrules or in air -tight containers (depending on the tube 
manufacturer). Tubes can be stored in this way at ambient temperature for 6 months. Beyond 
6 months, it is advisable to proceed with reconditioning of the tubes. 
5.2 Tube testing 
For good results and repeatability, it is recommended to control the quality of Tenax ® 
packing in the sampling tubes. As the sorbent is not visible in a stainless steel tube, a control 
can be performed by measuring the air flow rate through the tube with a flowmeter. This 
control must be performe
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
he sampling tubes. As the sorbent is not visible in a stainless steel tube, a control 
can be performed by measuring the air flow rate through the tube with a flowmeter. This 
control must be performed in the laboratory. 
Connect the air pump to one side of the tube and the flow meter to the other side. Adjust the 
pump flow rate to the required value. 
Repeat the operation to all Tenax® tubes without readjusting the pump flow rate. Write down 
the obtained value of each tube. 
Calculate the average flow rate Fav of all the measured tubes. Discard all tubes having flow 
rate values ±5% of the average value. 
Flow rate of accepted tube = Fav ±5% ml/min

5.3 Air sampling on Tenax® tubes 
5.3.1 Flow adjustment 
Flow adjustment must be performed before sampling in order to determine with accuracy 
the collected volume for quantitative analysis. This step can be achieved in the laboratory. 
At least two Tenax ® tube samples must be collected at the same sampling location, 
preferably in parallel or alternativ ely, one after the other. For parallel sampling, use a dual 
channel tube holder connected to the pump with a short piece of tygon tubing. Connect the 
tubes chosen randomly among the batch of tubes to both channels of the holder. Connect a 
flowmeter to one channel and precisely adjust the airflow rate through the tube by tightening 
of the screw at the dual channel tube holder with a screwdriver. 
Repeat the operation for the other channel. 
5.3.2 Sampling procedure 
Remove the caps from the sampling tube and co nnect it to the sampling pump with tygon 
tubing. Note the sampling tube direction on the tube, because the desorption
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
hannel. 
5.3.2 Sampling procedure 
Remove the caps from the sampling tube and co nnect it to the sampling pump with tygon 
tubing. Note the sampling tube direction on the tube, because the desorption must always be 
performed in the reverse direction to that from which the sample entered. Most stainless steel 
tubes have a groove that must be directed to the opposite of the pump during sampling. 
Because of the high sensitivity of modern mass spectrometers, collected volumes are not 
critical. Recommended volumes are 0.2 liter for high concentration (more than 1 mg/m 3), 
1 liter for medium concentration (between 0.1 mg/m 3 and 1 mg/m 3) and 2 liters for low 
concentration (less than 0.1 mg/m3). In the absence of information on the concentration level, 
the sampling volume must be adjusted to 2 liters. 
Optimal trapping is obtained with 50 –200 ml/ min air flow depending on the amount of 
Tenax® in the tube. High amount of humidity in the sampling tube may cause problems for 
the desorption and analysis. If samples must be collected during rainfall, protect the tube so 
that the rain will not be in direct contact.

that the rain will not be in direct contact. 
After sampling tubes are sealed with ¼ -inch brass Swagelok ®-type caps and transferred to 
the laboratory preferably in a cooler. They must be stored in the laboratory at low 
temperatures (<4 °C) before analysis. 
5.4 Field (transport) blanks 
Field blanks are conditioned Tenax ® tubes, which are transported with the tubes to be used 
for sample collection. Once at the monitoring location, all the processes carried out on the 
sampling tubes (uncapping, recapping, storage, etc.), except sample collection itself, should 
also be carried out on the field blanks. They provide important controls for all tube handling, 
storage, and transport procedures. 
5.5 Storage 
Sampled tubes must preferably be stored at low temperature (< 4 °C) before analysis. 
However, care should be taken to ensure that the atmosphere inside the refrigerator or freezer

Recommended MS conditions are given in Table 6. The given conditions correspond to the

6.4 Background interferences caused byTenax® 
As with all porous polymers, degradation of Tenax ® is constantly observed during analysis

3-heptanone, and heptanal5 can be detected at lower concentration levels. 
Nitrogen oxides, which are more predominant in an urban location, can also produce 
aromatic chemicals.

The reliable identification of CWC-related chemicals requires that the data produced by the

The performance of a TD –GC–EI/MS instrument is checked by carrying out a column 
performance test sample run, in which the mass spectrometric behaviour of test compounds 
and the condition of the column, transfer line, and cold trap are confirmed to be acceptable. 
The test is performed using a test solution containing the following compounds at 10 ng/µl 
each in a solvent, which is not well retained by the sorbent in use: 
 trimethylphosphate 
 2,6-dimethylphenol 
 5-chloro-2-methylaniline 
 tri-n-butylphosphate 
 dibenzothiophene 
 methyl stearate 
 n-alkanes (C8–C24, even members)

part of the solvent in the tube particularly if the solvent is poorly retained.

(see Table 7).

8. Determination of phosgene 
8.1 Summary of the method 
Phosgene is a toxic industrial chemical, which is listed in the Schedule 3 of the Chemical 
Weapons Convention and it cannot be collected directly in Tenax® because it is too volatile. 
Trapping of phosgene on more adsorptive materials such as molecular sieves, which have 
higher specific surface area but adsorb substantial amounts of water, is not possible because 
phosgene quickly hydrolyses in the tube when ambient air is collected.6 
Nevertheless, phosgene vapors can be collected in a Tenax® tube which is in advance spiked
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:

phosgene quickly hydrolyses in the tube when ambient air is collected.6 
Nevertheless, phosgene vapors can be collected in a Tenax® tube which is in advance spiked 
with a mixture of 3,4-dimercaptotoluene (DMT; CAS 207-828-3) and triethylamine (TEA; 
CAS 121-44-8). Phosgene is derivatised with this reactive mixture during sampling to stabile 
5-methyl-1,3-benzodithiole-2-one which is easy to analyse with TD- GC-MS/EI (Figure 3). 
The same analytical conditions presented above are used except that outle t split flow must 
be increased significantly. 
The detection limit is 150 µgm-3 for1 liter of air collected.

1. Scope 
This section describes methods for the preparation of concrete, paint, rubber, and other 
polymeric, as well as wipe samples, when chemical warfare agents (CWAs) and their 
degradation products are analy sed with chromatographic methods such as gas 
chromatography (GC), liquid chromatography (LC), ion chromato graphy (IC), or capillary 
electrophoresis (CE) as the separation technique or an introduc tion technique to 
spectrometers. The sample preparation methods required for analysis by nuclear magnetic 
resonance (NMR) spectroscopy are also presented. Chapter V.A. describes the preparation 
of concrete samples, Chapter V.B. preparation of paint, rubber, and other polymeric samples, 
and Chapter V.C. preparation of wipe samples. 
Other solid material samples such as wood, metal, cloth, garment, wool, vegetation (leaves, 
grass), etc. can be pre pared in a similar way as the described sample types. However, no 
detailed ROP has been written, because analysis of such types of samples, excluding metal, 
has not been tested in any international comparison (round-robin) and proficiency tests and 
are, thus, not validated.

2. Preparation of solid material samples 
Division of solid samples can be problematic and may cause loss of analytes of interest 
because of heterogeneity of the analytes in the sample material. Physical conditions 
(e.g. hardness) and too small an amount of available sample can make division of the sample 
impossible. 
The solid material sample is commonly extracted successively with an organic and an 
aqueous solvent. 
2.1 Organic extraction 
Place the sample into a small glass vial or use the original sample container as an extraction 
vessel. Check that the selected solvent does not dissolve the sampling matrix to avoid matrix 
interferences. Pour the selected organic solvent (acetone, ethyl acetate, dichloromethane )i 
over the sample matrix. Increasing the surface by cutting or crushing the sample into smaller 
pieces will enhance the efficiency. The amount of solvent used will depend on the sample. 
In general, care must be taken to soak, cover, or rinse the material with
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
r crushing the sample into smaller 
pieces will enhance the efficiency. The amount of solvent used will depend on the sample. 
In general, care must be taken to soak, cover, or rinse the material with the solvent. As a rule, 
1 g of a material needs to be extracted with a few ml of a solvent. 
Extraction by agitating, shaking, rinsing, or sonicating for 3–10 minutes is usually sufficient 
to obtain good extraction efficiencies. Centrifugation or f iltration of the extract through a 
membrane filter is recommended . If concentration of the extract is required, apply mild 
nitrogen flow, but not to concentrate to dryness ( Section 2, Part A, Chapter II : 
Concentration). 
This organic extract is analysed for non- and semipolar CWC-related chemicals. 
The extract should also be analysed with GC after silylation (Section 2, Part A, Chapter III: 
Derivatisation for gas chromatography ), because it might be possible that the extract 
contains polar CWC-related chemicals soluble in the used solvent. 
If the organic extract is analysed with LC and/or LC–MS, the solvent (e.g acetone, 
dichloromethane or ethyl acetate) can be exchanged or diluted with a solvent more suitable 
for LC analysis
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
olvent. 
If the organic extract is analysed with LC and/or LC–MS, the solvent (e.g acetone, 
dichloromethane or ethyl acetate) can be exchanged or diluted with a solvent more suitable 
for LC analysis (e.g. acetonitrile). After concentration with mild nitrogen flow as described 
in Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: Concentration, the residue is dissolved in a solvent suitable 
to the mobile phase chemistry of the LC analysis (pH and the amount of aqueous solvent). 
The organic extract can be analysed with NMR directly if deuterated solvent was used for 
the extraction . In other cases, 0.4–0.5 ml of the extract is diluted with 0. 1 ml of the 
corresponding deuterated solvent and transferred into an NMR tube. 
2.2 Aqueous extraction 
Repeat the procedure on the sample using water or aqueous soluble solvent (e.g.acetonitrile 
or methanol). 
The aqueous extract is analy sed for semipolar and polar CWC-related chemicals such as 
alkylphosphonic and alkyl thiophosphonic acids, thiodiglycol, and amino alcohols. 
 
i Deuterated analogues can be used for NMR analysis.

For GC analysis of polar CWC-related chemicals, derivatisation is needed. Evaporation and 
derivatisation procedures are presented in Section 2, Part A Chapter II: Concentration, and 
Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas chromatography. 
Water, acetonitrile and methanol extracts can be analy sed with LC and LC –MS as such 
without derivatisation. If a pre -column is not used, t he extract is usually filtered through a 
disposable syringe filter before injection. 
Polar extracts can be analy sed with NMR directly if deuterated solvent was used for the 
extraction. In other cases, 0.4–0.5 ml of the extract is diluted with 0. 1 ml of deuterated 
solvent and transferred into an NMR tube (5 mm). 
2.3 Extraction/derivatisation to analyse Lewisites with GC–MS 
Both organic and aqueous extracts can be prepared for analysis of Lewisites 1 and 2, as well 
as Lewisite oxide. The derivatisation procedure is presented in Section 2, Part A Chapter III: 
Derivatisation for gas chromatography.

3. Quality control 
If available, perform the entire extraction procedure with matrix blank material. Quality 
control is presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter V: Quality assurance and quality control 
in sample preparation. 
4. Evaluation of method 
Evaluation and references of the specific methods for concrete, polymeric samples and wipe 
samples are summarised in their individual chapters V.A., V.B., and V.C. Considering other 
types of solid material samples, Black et al. published their experiences of analysis of real 
wool samples, which were collected from a Kurdish village three months after a chemical 
attack in 1988. Clothing and metal fragment samples were collected four years later. 1,2 The 
wool samples were extracted with dichlo romethane and the clothing and metal samples in 
addition with water. The water extracts were silylated after evaporation to dryness . Nerve 
agent sarin as well as its pol ar hydrolysis products were identified from the extracts of the 
metal fr
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
n 
addition with water. The water extracts were silylated after evaporation to dryness . Nerve 
agent sarin as well as its pol ar hydrolysis products were identified from the extracts of the 
metal fragments, although the samples were collected four years after the attack. 
Ethyl acetate suits very well for extractio n solvent of non - and semi polar CWC -related 
chemicals when GC and G C–MS is used for analysis. Ethyl acetate is less volatile than 
dichloromethane. In addition, ethyl acetate does not react so easily as dichloromethane with 
chemicals in the sample background, especially with the chemicals containing nitrogen or 
sulfur. 
A disadvantage of ethyl acetate is that it does not suit for NMR analysis and for this reason 
another extraction by dichloromethane, chloroform or their deuterated solvent analogs has 
to be performed. 
Difficulties met in OPCW proficiency tests in the last few years when dichloromethane has 
been used as an extraction solvent are described below.

1. Summary of the method 
If necessary, the sample is homogenised by crushing, and thereafter first extracted with 
organic solvent (e.g. acetone or dichloromethane ), subsequently water, and 1 M HCl. 
Extractions can be done successively on the same sample or on different samples. The 
extracts are prepared for analysis accordi
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
t (e.g. acetone or dichloromethane ), subsequently water, and 1 M HCl. 
Extractions can be done successively on the same sample or on different samples. The 
extracts are prepared for analysis according to the type of extract. A general flowchart 
describing the sample preparation of concrete samples is given in Figure 1. 
Note! Concrete is an alkaline matrix and rapid degradation of most chemical warfare agents 
deposited on the untreated surface would be expected. Accordingly, the sample preparation 
procedure includes an efficient extraction step with acidic water for polar degradation 
products. 
2. Safety aspects and storing 
Safety aspects of sample preparation as well as storage of samples are presented in Section 2, 
Part A, Chapter I: Introduction. 
3. Equipment, supplies and chemicals 
The equipment, supplies and chemicals needed in this ROP are listed in Table 1.

4. Procedures 
4.1 Organic extraction 
Transfer ca. 2–5 g of concrete into a glass vial/bottle or use the original sample container as 
an extraction vessel. If sample pieces are large, homogenising by crushing will be necessary 
before extraction; small pieces may be extracted without crushing. Add ca. 2–5 ml of acetone 
or dichloromethane . For problems using dichloromethane as an extraction solvent see 
Section 2, Part B, Chapter V: Solid samples. 
Note! Use m
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e extracted without crushing. Add ca. 2–5 ml of acetone 
or dichloromethane . For problems using dichloromethane as an extraction solvent see 
Section 2, Part B, Chapter V: Solid samples. 
Note! Use more solvent if the whole sample is not covered by it. 
Close the bottle tightly and sonicate for 30 min. Monitor the temperature of the water bath 
and add ice, if necessary, to maintain ambient temperature. 
Quickly transfer the solvent into another screw-capped vial or centrifuge tube, close the tube, 
centrifuge for 3 min at 2000 G , and filter the supernatant through a 0.45 µm filter. Repeat 
the procedure with another portion of solvent and combine the extracts (Fraction 1, Figure 1).

4.4 Liquid Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry (LC–MS) sample preparation 
Aqueous extracts can be analysed with LC and LC–MS as such without derivatisation. If a 
pre-column is not used, the extract is usually filtered through a disposable syringe before 
injection (Fraction 2C and 3B, Figure 1). 
Note! Depending on the chromatographic method used for analysis, it can be useful to adjust 
the pH of the sample for optimal chromatographic performance before injection. For pH 
adjustment, volatile buffers as ammonium hydroxide and formic acid should be used to avoid 
signal suppression when LC–MS is used for analysis. 
If organic extracts are subjected to analysis by LC or/and LC-/MS analysis , the solvent 
(e.g. acetone or dichloromethane) can be exchanged to or diluted with a solvent more

for analysis of the sample for Lewisites 1 and 2, as well as Lewisite oxide (Fraction 2E and 
3D, Figure 1). The derivatisation procedure required for Lewisites is presented in Section 2, 
Part A, Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas chromatography.

6. Evaluation of method 
This ROP of concrete samples was established after the third i nterlaboratory comparison 
(round-robin) test held in 1992,1,2,3 but thereafter, the method has not been further evaluated 
or tested in any proficiency test s a rranged by OPCW . D’Agostino et al . published their 
results of analysis of acetonitrile extracts of concrete samples of the this round-robin test.4,5 
Later concrete samples have been extracted with acetonitrile or deuterated chloroform when 
degradation of mustard gas and sarin on concrete or cement have been investigated.6,7,8,9 
Based on the results of the round-robin test, in which this ROP in based on, as well as based 
on the mentioned later publications, it is impossible to say which solvent produce s the best 
extraction efficiencies. Concrete samples should simply be extracted with an organic solvent 
in which the material is not soluble (e.g. acet

extraction efficiencies. Concrete samples should simply be extracted with an organic solvent 
in which the material is not soluble (e.g. acetonitrile and acetone). To increase the recovery 
of polar CWC-related chemicals water should be chosen for the second extraction. Because 
concrete is an alkaline matrix and rapid degradation of most chemical warfare agents 
deposited on the untreated surface would be expected, the sample preparation procedure also

4. Procedures 
4.1 Organic extraction 
If required, crush or cut the sample into smaller pieces and transfer the sample into a small 
glass vial or use the original sample container as an extraction vessel. Before extraction, use 
a small piece of sample to check that the intended organic s olvent does not dissolve the 
sample. Pour the selected solvent (acetone, ethyl acetate, dichloromethane, or deuterated 
analogues if NMR is used for analysis) over the sample matrix . For problems using 
dichloromethane as an extraction solvent see Section 2, Part B, Chapter V: Solid materials. 
As a general rule, use solvent volume twice the volume of the sampling matrix (e.g. 10 ml) 
or enough to cover the sample. Sonicate the sample for 10 minutes and quickly transfer the 
solvent to a new container. If necessary, discard particles and debris by centrifuging briefly. 
(Fraction 1, Figure 1). 
If concentration of the extract is required, apply a gentle stream of
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
er the 
solvent to a new container. If necessary, discard particles and debris by centrifuging briefly. 
(Fraction 1, Figure 1). 
If concentration of the extract is required, apply a gentle stream of nitrogen , but caution 
should be taken to prevent the sample from going to dryness (Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: 
Concentration), (Fraction 1A, Figure 1). 
This organic extract is analysed for nonpolar CWC-related chemicals. 
The extract should also be analysed by GC after silylation, because it might be possible that 
the extract contains also polar CWC-related chemicals that have a tendency to be extracted 
by the selected solvent (Section 2, Part A, Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas 
chromatography). 
4.2 Water extraction 
After the first extraction, extract the same sample, or another if available, in a similar way 
but using pure (deionised) water. (Fraction 2, Figure 1). 
Note! Extraction of a new piece of sample with water could lead to erroneous conclusions 
regarding the presence of degradation products (e.g. degradation products can be 
unintentionally formed by adding water to the sample). 
The water extract is analysed for polar CWC-related chemicals such as alkylphosp
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ence of degradation products (e.g. degradation products can be 
unintentionally formed by adding water to the sample). 
The water extract is analysed for polar CWC-related chemicals such as alkylphosphonic and 
alkylthiophosphonic acids, thiodiglycol, and aminoalcohols. 
For GC analysis of polar CWC-related chemicals, derivatisation is usually needed. Water 
extracts must be evaporated to dryness before silylation. Evaporation and derivati sation 
procedures a re presented in Section 2, Part A , Chapter II : Concentration, Chapter III: 
Derivatisation for gas chromatography and Chapter IV: Sample clean-up methods (Fraction 
2A, Figure 1). 
4.3 Liquid Chromatography/Mass Spectrometry (LC–MS) sample preparation 
Water extract can be analy sed with LC and LC –MS as such with out derivati sation. If a 
precolumn is not used, the extract is usually filtered through a disposable syringe before 
injection (Fraction 2C, Figure 1).

4.4 Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) sample preparation 
Both extracts can be analysed directly with NMR if the extraction was done with deuterated 
solvents. In other cases, 0.4–0.5 ml of the extract is diluted with 0.1 ml of the corresponding 
deuterated solvent and transferred into an NMR tube (5 mm) (Fractions 1C and 2B, Figure 1).

required for Lewisites is presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter III: Derivatisation for gas

If available, perform the entire extraction procedure with matrix blank paint, rubber, or other 
polymeric material. Quality control of sample preparation is presented in Section 2, Part A, 
Chapter V: Quality assurance and quality control in sample preparation.

6. Evaluation of method 
This ROP of paint, rubber, and other polymeric samples was e stablished after the third 
interlaboratory comparison (round-robin) test.1,2,3 Wils et al. (1992) have shortly described 
their results of analysis of paint and rubber samples using dichloromethane or thermal 
desorption for analysis of mustard gas.4 The ROP method has later been successfully tested 
in the trial proficiency test for rubber and paint samples, in the first proficiency test for 
polymer samples, and in the third proficiency test for paint samples. OPCW arranged these 
tests. Two groups have pub lished their results of analysis of paint and rubber samples of 
these tests.5,6,7 n-Hexane or acetone were used for organic extraction and water, if used, for 
aqueous extraction, respectively. These organic solvents were used because paint or 
polymeric materials are less soluble in acetone than in chlorinated solvents or ethyl acetate. 
In addition, to increase the recovery of the polar CWC-related chemicals organic extraction 
should be followed by water extraction as Greasy et al. have also shown.8 
It should be noted that many CWC-related chemicals diffuse deep into polymeric m

should be followed by water extraction as Greasy et al. have also shown.8 
It should be noted that many CWC-related chemicals diffuse deep into polymeric materials 
relatively quickly, meaning that a low recovery would be estimated by non-infusive solvents 
recommended in this method. In the recent 29th OPCW proficiency test, it was shown that

charcoal matrix and analy sed with chromatographic methods such as gas chromatography 
(GC), liquid chromatography (LC), ion chromato graphy (IC), or capillary electrophoresis

5. Procedures 
5.1 Extraction 
Place the active charcoal material in a glass vial. Add the extracting solvent (twice the 
volume of the charcoal), cap the vial, and sonicate the mixture for three minutes. Suitable 
solvents are acetone, carbon disulfide, dichloromethane , chloroform, ethyl acetate , 
acetonitrile. If NMR is used for analysis, deuterated solvents (e.g. acetone -d6, 
dichloromethane-d2 or chloroform-d1) can be used. 
Where necessary, remove the supernatant by brief centrifugation and quick filtration. If 
concentration of the extract is required, do it under a gentle stream of nitrogen , but not to 
dryness (Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: Concentration). 
This organic extract is analysed for nonpolar and semipolar CWC-related chemicals. 
5.2 Thermal desorption 
If the origin and nature of the active charcoal sample material, as well as the sampling 
procedure, are known, the sample or a few grains of it may also be analy sed by thermal 
desorption. 
5.3 LC–
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
If the origin and nature of the active charcoal sample material, as well as the sampling 
procedure, are known, the sample or a few grains of it may also be analy sed by thermal 
desorption. 
5.3 LC–MS sample preparation 
For LC and liquid chromatography mass spectrometric (LC–MS) analysis, the solvent of the 
extract can be changed to be more suitable for analysis (e.g. acetonitrile). For this reason , 
dichloromethane and ethyl acetate extract especially has to be concentrated with mild 
nitrogen flow as described in Section 2, Part A, Chapter II : Concentration. The residue is 
dissolved with a solvent suitable to the solvent chemistry of the LC analysis (pH and amount 
of aqueous solvent). 
5.4 NMR sample preparation 
The extract can be analysed with NMR as if deuterated solvent was used. In other cases, ca. 
0.4–0.5 ml of the extract is diluted with ca. 0.1 ml of deuterated solvent and transferred into 
a NMR tube (5 mm). If needed, the extract can be concentrated with mild nitrogen flow as 
described in Section 2, Part A, Chapter II: Concentration. 
6. Quality control

assurance and

Quality control of sample preparation is presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter V: Quality 
assurance and quality control in sample preparation. 
7. Evaluation of method 
This recommendation is based on the results obtained in the second international 
interlaboratory comparison (round -robin) test held in 1990. 1,2,3 This means that the ROP 
method for active charcoal samples has not been validated in interlaboratory or proficiency 
tests. In addition, only a few, quite old, successful uses of charcoal in battlefield conditions

have been reported.5,6,7 Furthermore, active charcoal is not recommended for the collection 
of organophosphorus chemicals (nerve agents) because it may induce their decomposition.4 
In general, the recoveries of CWC-related chemicals tend to be lower from active charcoal 
than from other air sampling materials. Therefore, active charcoal as a strong adsorbent 
requires more effective extraction methods than, e.g., Tenax® tubes. 
The use of active charcoal as a sampling mater ial of CWC -related chemicals is overall 
problematic. The materials used in filters, protective clothing, respiratory canisters, etc. are 
usually impregnated with chemicals according to the needs of the use. These chemicals have 
often catalytic and chelating properties, which mean that the chemicals desorbed from such 
charcoal materials might be different from those originall y adsorbed. This problem arise s 
especially if the charcoal is analysed by thermal desorption. In this respect, it is ess
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
esorbed from such 
charcoal materials might be different from those originall y adsorbed. This problem arise s 
especially if the charcoal is analysed by thermal desorption. In this respect, it is essential for 
successful sample pre-treatment that the origin and contents of active charcoal m aterial 
should be known. Unfortunately, this will seldom be possible, for both military and 
commercial reasons. 
Ethyl acetate suits very well for extraction solvent of non-polar and semi-polar CWC-related 
chemicals when GC and GC –MS is used for analysis. Ethyl acetate is less volatile than 
dichloromethane. In addition, ethyl acetate does not react so easily as dichloromethane with 
chemicals in the sample background, especially with the chemicals containing nitrogen or 
sulfur. 
A disadvantage of ethyl acetate is that it does not suit for NMR analysis a nd for this reason 
another extraction by dichloromethane, chloroform or their deuterated solvent analogs has 
to be performed. 
Difficulties met in OPCW proficiency tests in the last few years when dichloromethane has 
been used as an extraction solvent are described below. 
In the 35th OPCW proficiency test dichloromethane which was use

s met in OPCW proficiency tests in the last few years when dichloromethane has 
been used as an extraction solvent are described below. 
In the 35th OPCW proficiency test dichloromethane which was used as an extraction solvent 
of aqueous sample reacted with the background chemical N,N,N' ,N'-tetramethyl-1,2-
ethanediamine (CAS 110 -18-9) forming a sample preparation artefact 2 -N,N- 
dimethylaminoethylchloride (CAS 107-99-3).8 
In the 40 th OPCW proficiency test it was shown that tertiary amines, such as BZ and 3 -
quinuclidinol, can easily react with dichloromethane if it is used as extraction solvent. 9 BZ 
was in a metal plate sample and 3 -quinuclidinol in an aqueous sample. Most laboratories 
extracted the metal (aluminium) plate with dichloromethane. In the same test DGA (France) 
used both dichlorom ethane and ethyl acetate as extraction solvents and did not observe 
formation of additional chemicals with ethyl acetate. 
In the 41st OPCW proficiency the laboratory which evaluated the test results, DSO National 
Laboratories (Singapore), demonstrated that dichloromethane which was used as an 
extraction solvent of alkaline (pH 12) aqueous sample reacted with the background c

Laboratories (Singapore), demonstrated that dichloromethane which was used as an

Author Robin Black†

1. Scope 
This chapter introduces the techniques that are used for the identification of scheduled 
chemicals in verification activities associated with the Chemical Weapons Convention 
(CWC). Analysis in support of verification may be performed on-site at an inspected facility, 
or off-site in Designated Laboratories in cases where on-site analysis is equivocal or in cases 
of alleged use of chemical weapons (CW) in which more extensive analysis is required.
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ected facility, 
or off-site in Designated Laboratories in cases where on-site analysis is equivocal or in cases 
of alleged use of chemical weapons (CW) in which more extensive analysis is required. 
Analytical methods can be broadly divided into those that combine a separation technique 
with identification, and those that analyse an aliquot or extract of the sample without 
separating the components. Section 3 on analytical methods is divided into five parts: 
 GC-based techniques 
 LC-based techniques 
 Other separation techniques 
 Spectroscopy-based techniques 
 Other analysis (saxitoxin, ricin, sediment analysis, analysis of CNS acting chemicals) 
2. GC-based techniques 
Most CW agents have a degree of volatility , and historically the separation technique of 
choice has been gas chromatography (Section 3, Part B, Chapter I: Gas chromatography 
(GC)). Agents are usually chromatographed directly without derivati sation. Exceptions are 
Lewisites I and II and phosgene because of their reactivity and, in the case of phosgene, very 
high volatility. Gas chromatography combined with element selective detection ( GC–FPD, 
GC–NPD, GC–AED) is useful for screening, but the major
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
of their reactivity and, in the case of phosgene, very 
high volatility. Gas chromatography combined with element selective detection ( GC–FPD, 
GC–NPD, GC–AED) is useful for screening, but the major technique for iden tification of 
volatile scheduled chemicals is gas chromatography combined with mass spectrometry using 
electron ionisation (Section 3, Part B, Chapter II : Gas chromatography –electron 
ionisation/mass spectrometry (GC–EI/MS). In support of verification, the Organisation for 
 
†represented the organization in 2011.

text:

Section 3. Analytical methods

Chapter I Introduction

Date 11 December 2017 Page 260 
the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), in cooperation with Member States, has 
compiled an extensive database of electron ionisation (EI) spectra (OCAD). GC–EI/MS may 
be used as the sole technique for on-site analysis. For analysis at the parts per million level, 
simple bench top quadrupole and ion trap instruments are commonly employed, although 
mass spectra acquired on ion traps may show some differences, e.g. from self -protonation. 
Time of flight (TOF) instruments, employing high acq uisition rates, are seeing increasing 
application in GC–MS analysis . Additional GC–MS analysis using chemical ionisation 
(Section 3, Part B, Chapter III: G as chromatography –chemical ioni sation/mass 
spectrometry (GC–CI/MS)) is used to confirm the molecular mass of an analyte for off-site 
analysis and in OPCW Proficiency Tests. 
Some scheduled precursors, and most environmental degradation products of CW agents, 
are more polar than the agents , and much less volatile. These require conversion,
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
and in OPCW Proficiency Tests. 
Some scheduled precursors, and most environmental degradation products of CW agents, 
are more polar than the agents , and much less volatile. These require conversion, e.g. , to 
trimethylsilyl (TMS), tert-butyldimethylsilyl (TBDMS) or methyl ester derivatives, in order 
to facilitate analysis by GC–MS. In the case of aqueous solutions, this usually requires 
isolation of the analyte or complete removal of the water, processes th at are both time 
consuming and prone to error. 
GC–tandem mass spectrometry is not used extensively for identification at the parts per 
million levels typical of OPCW Proficiency Tests . It is a key technique in trace analysis, 
particularly for biomedical samples, where analyte levels may be in the low parts per billion 
range. Applications will be described in the Section 3, Part B, Chapter IV: Gas 
chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (QQQ)(GC–MS/MS) (not in the 2017 edition). 
High resolution MS allows the determination of the molecular formula of unknowns, e.g. in 
OPCW Proficiency Tests, and may be used to increase selectivity in trace analysis. As MS 
instrumentation is evolving, the use of high resolution magne
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
n of the molecular formula of unknowns, e.g. in 
OPCW Proficiency Tests, and may be used to increase selectivity in trace analysis. As MS 
instrumentation is evolving, the use of high resolution magnetic sector instruments is 
declining, whilst the use of other types of instruments capable of high resolution is increasing. 
The Section 3, Part B, Chapter V: Gas chromatography-high resolution mass spectrometry 
(GC–HRMS): sector instruments, selective reaction monitoring mode and Section 3, Part B, 
Chapter VI: Gas chromatography–high resolution mass spectrometry (GC–TOF) describe 
the use of sector instruments and GC–TOF/MS for high resolution applications. 
3. LC-based techniques 
An alternative approach to the analysis of more polar chemicals is liquid chromatography–
mass spectrometry ( LC–MS) (Section 3, Part C, Chapter I: Liquid chromatography (LC) 
separation for mass spectrometry (not in the 2017 edition). This has the advantage that it 
can be applied directly to aqueous solutions. Modern LC–MS is performed almost 
universally using one of two atmospheric pressure ionisation (API) techniques, electrospray 
ionisation (ESI) and atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation (APCI)
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ons. Modern LC–MS is performed almost 
universally using one of two atmospheric pressure ionisation (API) techniques, electrospray 
ionisation (ESI) and atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation (APCI) (Section 3, Part C, 
Chapter II: Liquid chromatography –atmospheric pressure ionisation/ mass spectrometry, 
(LC–API/MS)). Single stage LC–MS provides molecular mass information, similar to GC–
CI/MS, and provides a very rapid screening procedure in OPCW Proficiency Tests. 
Additional structural information can be obtained by LC–tandem mass spectrometry. The 
increasing use of LC–TOF/MS is described in the Section 3, Part C, Chapter III : Liquid 
chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). Usage of new high resolution 
instruments are described in Section 3, Part C, Chapter IV : Liquid chromatography –high 
resolution mass spectrometry and tandem mass spectrometry (LC –HRMS and LC –
MS/HRMS). LC–MS and LC–MS/MS are now widely used by Designated Laboratories.
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

These techniques are essential for the analysis of biomedical samples , and f or the 
identification of saxitoxin and ricin. 
4. Other separation techniques 
Capillary electrophoresis and ion chromatography are used by only a small number of 
Designated Laboratories. Both are used primarily for the screening and identification of alkyl 
alkylphosphonates and alkylphosphonic acids. The Section 3, Part D, Chapter I: Capillary 
electrophoresis (CE) describes the use of CE in combination with UV detection. The Section 
3, Part D, Chapter II: Ion chromatography (IC) describes the use of IC with conductivity 
detection or ESI/MS. 
5. Spectroscopy-based techniques 
The principle technique used without separating the components of the sample is nuclear 
magnetic resonance spectrometry (NMR). Advances in instrumentatio n and techniques, 
including 2D and correlation techniques, have increased the sensitivity of NMR and the 
ability to discriminate between individual chemicals in mixtures. NMR is widel
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
instrumentatio n and techniques, 
including 2D and correlation techniques, have increased the sensitivity of NMR and the 
ability to discriminate between individual chemicals in mixtures. NMR is widely used in 
OPCW Proficiency Tests, and is particularly useful in identifyi ng isomers. Traditional 1D 
NMR, more advanced 1D/2D NMR experiments as well as general guidelines for NMR 
parameter analysis and reference spectrum simulation are described in the Section 3, Part E, 
Chapters I -VIII: Basic 1H NMR techniques , Basic 31P NMR t echniques, Basic 19F NMR 
techniques, Nonselective 1D 1H–31P correlation techniques, 2D 1H–31P correlation 
techniques, 2D 1H-1H correlation techniques, Spectral parametrization for reference data 
and 2D 1H-13C correlation techniques. 
6. Other analysis (saxitoxin and ricin , sediment analysis, analysis of CNS acting 
chemicals) 
The Scientific Advisory Board of the O PCW (through its Temporary Working Group on 
Sampling and Analysis) and the Technical Secretariat of the OPCW have began to address 
the identification of the two toxins included in Schedule 1 of the CWC, saxitoxin and ricin. 
These cannot be analysed by GC–MS; rather, LC–MS/MS is the major
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
tariat of the OPCW have began to address 
the identification of the two toxins included in Schedule 1 of the CWC, saxitoxin and ricin. 
These cannot be analysed by GC–MS; rather, LC–MS/MS is the major method of 
identification. However, in order to meet the requirement for at least two identification 
techniques, additional methods are required. 
Analysis of saxitoxin is described in the Section 3, Part F, Chapters I-II: Analysis of 
saxitoxin: LC–MS/MS and Analysis of saxitoxin: LC–FLD and immunoassays. 
Analysis strategy of ricin is described in the Section 3, Part F, Chapter III: Analysis of ricin: 
Analysis strategy. Analysis of ricin is de scribed in the Section 3, Part F, Chapters I V-VII: 
Analysis of ricin: ELISA, Analysis of ricin: immunocapture, Analysis of ricin: MALDI–MS, 
Analysis of ricin: LC–MS/MS. 
Sediment analysis to study environmental effects of sea-dumped munitions are described in 
Section 3, Part F, Chapter VIII : Analysis of sediment samples for sea -dumped chemical 
weapons. 
CNS active compounds include anaesthetics, sedatives and analgesics tha t have been 
developed for medical purposes. Such compounds are designed to be delivered intravenously
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

only under strict medical supervision with concurrent monitoring of the health of the patient. 
As such chemicals might be aerosolised and misused, verification methods could be usefully 
developed and tested, and such methods are described in the Section 3, Part F, Chapter IX: 
Analysis of Central Nervous System acting chemicals.

1. Scope 
This chapter covers the gas chromatographic (GC) analysis of chemical warfare agents, their 
precursors, and degradation products or derivatives, i.e. chemicals related to the C hemical 
Weapons Convention, CWC . Generally , the procedure is for identifying and screening 
chemicals above the 0.1 mg/kg concentration level. However, the procedure can also be 
utilised for identifying and screening relevant chemicals down to low μg/kg concentration 
levels with some selective detectors. This procedure alone gives in most cases only tentative 
identification and final ide
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
dentifying and screening relevant chemicals down to low μg/kg concentration 
levels with some selective detectors. This procedure alone gives in most cases only tentative 
identification and final identification should be done by spectrometric methods. 
2. Summary of the method 
Chemicals extracted from samples i nto organic solvent are separated on properly selected 
columns and detected with appropriate detectors. Before and at the end of each sample batch, 
a quality control run to verify the correct performance of the instrument, and a blank run to 
verify the absence of CWC -related chemicals is carried out . Identifications are made with 
absolute retention times against the absolute retention times of authentic reference chemical 
or with retention indices (RI) measured against n-alkane series C 8–C24 and comparing the 
measured RI values to those in the library. 
3. Safety aspects 
GC analysis does not require any specific precautions concerning safety. Samples to be 
analysed normally contain only small concentrations of toxic chemicals and the used 
detectors destroy the sample molecules. Normal laboratory safety measures like protective 
gloves and goggles during sample
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
normally contain only small concentrations of toxic chemicals and the used 
detectors destroy the sample molecules. Normal laboratory safety measures like protective 
gloves and goggles during sample handling in manual injections should be used. 
Hot parts of instruments, e.g. hot septum nut (>250 °C), must be taken into account during 
operation and maintenance of instruments.

4. Instrumentation 
4.1 Gas Chromatograph 
Any modern, preferably a two-channel GC instrument, can be used. 
4.2 Injectors 
Injection technique plays an important role in chromatographic separation. On -column and 
splitless injections are the most useful techniques for trace analysis. On -column injection 
has some advantages over other techniques, es pecially in the analysis of thermally labile 
compounds such as chloropicrin and compounds with adsorptive properties such as VX 
homologues and dialkyl methylphosphonates. However, for environmental samples such as 
soil and plant extracts and biological samples , on-column injection may lead to rapid 
contamination of the analytical column. For the on-column technique, a separate injector is 
needed while splitless and split injections can be carried out with the same injector. The split 
injection technique provides good separation efficiency for volatile compounds when the 
concentrations of these are high enough,
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
plit injections can be carried out with the same injector. The split 
injection technique provides good separation efficiency for volatile compounds when the 
concentrations of these are high enough, but discrimination against high boiling components 
is evident. 
4.3 GC columns 
The non-polar phases tend to have better characteristics in terms of resistance to oxygen, 
separation efficiency of the column and higher maximum temperatures. Laboratories should 
have at least two or three columns of different polarity available for situations when the 
target chemical elutes together with a bac kground chemical on standard SE -54-type (5%-
phenyl-95%-dimethylpolysiloxane) phase material . Non -polar OV -1 ( 100% 
dimethylpolysiloxane) and medium-polar OV -1701 ( 14%-cyanopropylphenyl-86%-
dimethylpolysiloxane) phase materials are suitable for solving such co-elution problems . 
A polar CW-20M (polyethyleneglycol) column can only be used in limited applications for 
the analysis of the most polar compounds. Some of the CWC-related compounds do not elute 
through CW-20M column due to the ir strong retention and to the quite low maximum 
temperature allowed for the phase material. 
The in
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
polar compounds. Some of the CWC-related compounds do not elute 
through CW-20M column due to the ir strong retention and to the quite low maximum 
temperature allowed for the phase material. 
The inner diameter of a column has a direct influence on retention, efficiency, and capacity 
of the column. The on -column injection technique requires an internal diameter (i.d.) of at 
least 0.25 mm. This is also a good choice for MS analysis, as it facilitates a proper adjustment 
of the carrier gas flow. Narrower bore columns are typically used in various kinds of fast GC 
applications. Columns of i.d. 0.2 5–0.32 mm can be considered most suitable for the GC 
analysis of CWC-related compounds. 
Thin stationary phase film columns (below 0.15 µm) should be avoided because they tend 
to give poor peak shapes for strongly adsorptive compounds such as thiodiglycol, dialkyl 
methylphosphonates, and aminoalcohols, especially at low concentration levels. Thick film 
columns (above 2 µm) are ideal for the separation of very volatile compounds such as 
hydrogen cyanide , phosgene, and cyanogen chloride . However, they are unsuitable for 
higher molecular weig ht compounds such as BZ or VX . Stand
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
or the separation of very volatile compounds such as 
hydrogen cyanide , phosgene, and cyanogen chloride . However, they are unsuitable for 
higher molecular weig ht compounds such as BZ or VX . Standard (0.25 –0.33 µm) film 
thickness offers the best compromise between resolution and sample capacity.
