The selection of the length of the column depends on the required resolution and analysis 
time. Short columns (10 –15 m) are useful for fast GC and for screening purposes. 
Intermediate column lengths of 25 –30 m, providing sufficient separation power and 
reasonable analysis time, are recommended. 
4.4 Detectors 
Critical properties of detectors are sensitivity, selectivity, line arity of response, 
reproducibility and reliability of operation. Spectrometric detectors, MS and FTIR, are 
described in more detail in other sections. 
Precise recommendations for the choice of a detector cannot be given, because it depends 
much on the requirements of the analytical task like the use of RI values for identification 
and the need for sample screening. Despite the great separation power of capillary columns, 
the analysis of trace compounds in some complex matrices may be difficult if only universal 
detectors are used. Many selective detectors are available for monitorin
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ation power of capillary columns, 
the analysis of trace compounds in some complex matrices may be difficult if only universal 
detectors are used. Many selective detectors are available for monitoring CWC-related 
compounds containing heteroatoms. Chromatograms are simplified with these detectors and 
the sensitivity of analysis is increased. The following detectors are useful for CWC-related 
compounds: 
Flame ionisation detector (FID) is the most popular universal detector, having both a wide 
linear range and great reliability. The detection limits of CWC-related compounds are from 
0.1 ng to 1 ng depending on its structure. Sensitivity can be poor for some chemicals such 
as hydrogen cyanide. In addition, phosgene and chloropicrin because of their thermal 
decomposition cannot be detected as such with the FID. 
Phosphorus-selective detectors are of greatest importance for verification analysis. The 
nitrogen-phosphorus detector (NPD) is very sensitive and selective towards compounds 
containing phosphorus and/or nitrogen, reaching detection limits of 10–50 pg for phosphorus 
and 50–100 pg for nitrogen. Flame photometric detector (FPD) is the most widely used 
detector for sulf
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ds 
containing phosphorus and/or nitrogen, reaching detection limits of 10–50 pg for phosphorus 
and 50–100 pg for nitrogen. Flame photometric detector (FPD) is the most widely used 
detector for sulfur-containing compounds. Besides sulfur, it is selective for phosphorus, 
which makes it a suitable for both nerve agents and sulfur-containing mustards. Detection 
limits are ca. 100–500 pg in phosphorus mode and ca. 500–1000 pg in sulfur mode. Two-
channel FPD detectors operating simultaneously in S - and P -mode are commercially 
available. 
Some CWC-related compounds containing chlorine atoms, e.g. vesicants, are detectable 
with the electron capture detector (ECD) . However, t he sensitivity of ECD for some 
compounds is rather low depending on the electron affinity of the compounds. The ECD can 
be considered as moderately sensitive but not selective enough, especially for environmental 
and biological samples, many of which contain irrelevant ECD-active compounds, 
interfering the detection of the CWC-related compounds. 
FID, NPD and FPD are the most relia ble, easy to set up and most commonly used non-
spectrometric detectors for the detection of CWC-related chemicals. By using
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
etection of the CWC-related compounds. 
FID, NPD and FPD are the most relia ble, easy to set up and most commonly used non-
spectrometric detectors for the detection of CWC-related chemicals. By using two detectors 
in parallel, it is possible to increase the information obtained from a single GC run. For 
screening it is recommended that the same stationary phase is used with selective detectors 
and spectrometers.

One of most attractive detectors for screening purposes is the atomic emission detector 
(AED), which is particularly well-suited in CWC analysis, where extensive screening for a 
large variety of chemicals containing various heteroatoms (P, S, N, As, F, Cl) is often 
required, and where other GC detectors may be insufficient. 
Large variations in detection limits are observed between elements when using AED. Better 
sensitivity is reached for carbon, phosphor us, sulfur, arsenic and silicon. Sensitivity for 
nitrogen and chlorine is moderate and poor for oxygen and fluorine. Sensitivity for Sarin is 
ca. 1 ng detected with carbon line at 193 nm, 2 ng with phosphorus line at 186 nm and only 
50 ng with fluorine line at 690 nm. Sensitivity for mustard gas is ca. 2 ng detected with sulfur 
line at 181 nm and chlorine line at 479 nm. 
With AED, it is also possible to calculate an approximate total or partial empirical formula 
for unknown compounds. 
Large variety of ga
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
cted with sulfur 
line at 181 nm and chlorine line at 479 nm. 
With AED, it is also possible to calculate an approximate total or partial empirical formula 
for unknown compounds. 
Large variety of gases (nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, mixed nitrogen/methane 90/10 v/v) can 
be used as reagent gas es to improve sensitivity and v ery high purity helium is required as 
carrier and plasma gas. Maintenance operations such as discharge tube replacement have to 
be made periodically in order to maintain a good AED performance. 
In addition to GC–MS, GC–AED offers the most powerful combination of techniques for 
obtaining data for unambiguous qualitative characterisation of CWC-related chemicals.

Run conditions may be modified depending on the type of samples or used injector, column 
and detector. For example concentrated samples (>100 ng/μl) should be injected in split 
injection mode with split ratio 1:20 or higher to avoid column overloading and to achieve 
better separation of low boiling chemicals. For splitless injections , concentrated samples 
must be diluted. 
Note! OCAD RI-values are not valid with split-injection. 
For standard GC analysis, it is recommended to use a 25–30 m long SE-54-type fused silica 
capillary column (0.25 mm i.d. and film thickness 0.25 µm), preferably so called low bleed 
MS column. If the column is sp lit between two detectors the use of three-way press -fit 
connector, a Y-splitter, is recommended.

6. Quality control 
The reliable identification of CWC -related compounds requires that the data produced by 
the instrument is correct. Therefore, it is essential to run quality control tests on regular basis 
to confirm correct and stable instrument performance during the samp le analysis and to 
check any possible contamination. 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
6.1.1 Column test 
The goal of this test is to control the performance of the column (See Table 2). This test can 
also be used for estimation the sensitivity of the instrument. The QC test must be run at the 
beginning and at the end of each sample batch and , in the case of a long sample batch , at 
least after every fifteenth sample. 
The peak shape of trimethylphosphate can be used to estimate the column activity. The acidic 
and basic properties of the column can be estimated by comparing the peak heights and /or 
peak areas of phenol and aniline peaks. Poor peak shape or reducing peak height of 5-Chl
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ctivity. The acidic 
and basic properties of the column can be estimated by comparing the peak heights and /or 
peak areas of phenol and aniline peaks. Poor peak shape or reducing peak height of 5-Chloro-
2-methylaniline indicates an acidic nature of the column that is not good for basic 
compounds. Poor peak shape or reducing peak height of 2,4-dimethylphenol indicates a 
basic nature of the column and the column is not good for acidic compounds. 
The column is satisfactory if the following criteria of the QC-test chemicals are met: 
 Absolute retention times of detected compounds are within ±15 s retention index 
window compared to the QC-test performed after the column installation. 
 The trimethylphosphate peak asymmetry measured at half height of peak is below 4. 
 The peak height ratio of 2,6-dimethylphenol / 5 -chloro-2-methylaniline is between 
0.5 and 2 
 Signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio for each test chemical is >10:1 in the chromatogram. 
Figure 1 shows typical chromatograms of a QC test sample indicating good instrument 
performance obtained from the FID, NPD and FPD(S).

6.2 Blank tests 
A system blank (blind test) is used to check any possible contamination coming from the 
sample preparation or from the instrument. This test is run at least in the beginning and at 
the end of each sample series and sometimes before every sample. 
If blank test shows contamination, a solvent blank run with the same solvent used in sample 
preparation must be carried out to eliminate the possibility of c ontamination of the 
equipment (e.g. contamination from the syringe or the memory effect of the equipment). 
Note! This is extremely important for silylated samples. The memory effect is possible, for 
example, in the analysis of alkyl phosphonic acids. If th e derivatisation of these chemicals 
has not been complete, the non -derivatised acids are adsorbed on the injector liner. A 
silylation reagent may in such case react in situ with the adsorbed acids in the liner yielding 
false positive results. 
If CWC-related chemicals are found in any blank chromatogram, the blank tests are repeated 
after elimination of t
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
react in situ with the adsorbed acids in the liner yielding 
false positive results. 
If CWC-related chemicals are found in any blank chromatogram, the blank tests are repeated 
after elimination of the possible contamination source. All contamination coming from 
glassware, solvents, standard solution s (or authentic reference solution s), syringe, injector 
system, or columns must be eliminated before new sample analysis is started.

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1 Sequence of analysis 
In the beginning of an analysis batch , a QC test and a system blank test are run. When all 
tests have been accepted, samples can be analysed. Generally, 1.0 µl of the sample is injected 
on each run. 
7.2 Screening 
The use of selective detectors for screening of samples is presented in Section 1, Part B, 
Chapter I: Screening and the use of extracted ion chromatograms of selective ions for 
screening with GC –EI/MS are presented in Section 3, Part B, Chapter I I: Gas 
chromatography-electron ionisation/mass spectrometry (GC-EI/MS). 
7.3 Identification 
The peak of an identified chemical and the peak of a corresponding reference chemical must 
have a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 5:1. For non-spectrometric GC techniques, if there are 
peaks in the chromatogram within the retention time window of ±0.1 min of the peak of the 
identified chemical, standard addition of the reference chemical should be used to confir
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ques, if there are 
peaks in the chromatogram within the retention time window of ±0.1 min of the peak of the 
identified chemical, standard addition of the reference chemical should be used to confirm 
the identity of the identified peak in the chromatogram. Add ca. 50% of the estimated 
original amount of the chemical of interest into the sample to see a clear increase of the peak 
of interest. 
7.3.1 Absolute retention times 
Absolute retention times are the most useful identification parameters if reference chemicals 
are available. A pure standard of the identified chemical is run as a reference as soon as 
possible after the sample run. The identification is accepted if the absolute retention time of 
the GC peak of interest in the sample falls within a window ±0.1 min of the retention time 
of reference chemical. 
7.3.2 Retention indices 
The use of RI-values for identificati on is particularly advantageous when reference 
chemicals are not available. The ease of use of RIs is increased significantly if a computer 
program for calculation of RI values is available. It is recommended to calculate RI values 
with external standard method using the n-alkanes in the QC test run

program for calculation of RI values is available. It is recommended to calculate RI values

8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
GC method can be applied to all chemical warfare agents, their degradation products , 
precursors or derivatives, except saxitoxin and ricin . Extremely volatile (e.g. DF), non-
volatile (e.g. phosphonic acids), and reactive (e.g. lewisite 1) CWC-related chemicals can be 
analysed after derivatisation. The method is suitable for analysing and identifyi
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
olatile (e.g. DF), non-
volatile (e.g. phosphonic acids), and reactive (e.g. lewisite 1) CWC-related chemicals can be 
analysed after derivatisation. The method is suitable for analysing and identifying any 
chemical at the 0.1 mg/kg concentration level with FID and at the 0.01 mg/kg concentration 
level with selective detectors. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
Advantages of the method are good separation of chemicals, sensitivity, and possibilities for 
selective detection. Modern instruments are easy to use and AMDIS software provides 
automated RI analysis. GC screening with selective detectors before GC–MS identification 
is important in producing useful information from complex mixtures. 
The disadvantage of using GC alone is that identification is based on retention data giving 
only tentative identification and for final identification a spectrometric method is required 
as a second technique.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of gas chromatography–electron ionisation mass spectrometry 
(GC–EI/MS) in screening and identifying chemical warfare agents, their precursors , 
degradation products or derivatives , i.e., chemicals related to the C hemical
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ectron ionisation mass spectrometry 
(GC–EI/MS) in screening and identifying chemical warfare agents, their precursors , 
degradation products or derivatives , i.e., chemicals related to the C hemical Weapons 
Convention (CWC). Generally , this procedure is used to identify chemicals above the 
1 mg/kg or mg/l concentration level. However, the procedure can also be used to identify 
relevant chemicals down to low μg/kg or µg/l concentration levels. 
2. Summary of the method 
GC–EI/MS measurements are carried out with modern GC–EI/MS instruments operating in 
full scanning mode. Samples are analy sed with a GC–MS instrument equipped with a 
25−30 m capillary column with SE -54-type stationary phase material. Before each sample 
batch, a quality control run (QC test, see below ) is carried out to verify the correct 
performance of the instrument , and a blank run to verify the absence of CWC -related 
chemicals. Screening of relevant chemicals is carried out with the Automated Mass Spectral 
Deconvolution and Identification System (AMDIS) with an appropriate target library or by 
selecting characteristic ions of chemical families or individual chemicals (extracted ion 
chromatograms,
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ral 
Deconvolution and Identification System (AMDIS) with an appropriate target library or by 
selecting characteristic ions of chemical families or individual chemicals (extracted ion 
chromatograms, EICs) from the total ion chromatograms (TICs). Relevant chemicals are 
identified by comparing the measured EI spectra to those in CWC-relevant libraries or to 
spectra of authentic reference chemicals or interpretation of spectra. 
If needed, linear retention indexes are measured against n-alkane series C8–C24 [included in 
the QC test; see the Section 3, Part B, Chapter I: Gas chromatography (GC)].

3. Safety aspects 
GC–EI/MS analysis does not require any specific precautions concerning safety. Samples to 
be analysed typically contain only small concentrations of toxic chemicals , and electron 
ionisation will destroy the sample molecules. Normal laboratory safety measures such as 
wearing protective gloves and goggles while handling samples in manual injections should 
be used. 
It should be noted that in samples related to investigations of alleged use the concentration 
of toxic chemicals can be high. In these cases, laboratories should take appropriate measures 
to screen the samples using e.g. portable detectors and to guarantee safe handling of the 
samples. 
Hot parts of the instrument, e.g. the hot septum nut (> 250 °C), must be taken into account 
while operating and maintaining the instrument. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 GC–EI/MS instrument 
Any modern GC –EI/MS instrument capable of a scanning speed of at least 1

while operating and maintaining the instrument. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 GC–EI/MS instrument 
Any modern GC –EI/MS instrument capable of a scanning speed of at least 1 scan/s and 
covering a mass range of at least m/z 40–500 can be used. 
4.2 GC columns 
A 25 to 30-m-long SE-54-typei fused silica capillary column (0.20 –0.25 mm i.d. and film 
thickness 0.25 µm), preferably the low-bleed MS column, is used. 
GC–EI/MS analysis can also be done using fast -GC, but fast-GC method is not covered by 
this chapter. 
4.3 Reagents and chemicals 
The reagents and chemicals needed for GC–EI/MS analysis are given in Table 1. 
 
 
i SE-54-type column means a stationary phase consisting of 95% -methyl-5%-phenylpolysiloxane. 
Polyarylene-type columns that are virtually equivalent to the SE -54-type columns can also be 
used.

5.3 Recommended tuning and mass calibration of the MS 
Use the tuning method recommended for the instrument. An automatic tuning and calibration 
procedure should be used, if available. Tuning and calibration should be performed once a 
week or more often if indicated by the QC test. Printouts of tuning and calibration reports 
should be archived for further reference. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
Reliable identification of CWC -related compounds requires that the data produced by the 
instrument is correct. Therefore, quality control tests must be run on a regular basis to 
confirm the instrument is performing correctly and stably while analysing the samples. 
The performance of a GC–EI/MS instrument is controlled by carrying out a QC test run, in 
which the mass spectrometric behavior of the test compounds and the adsorption behavior 
of the column are confirmed to be acceptable. The QC test must be ru
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
trolled by carrying out a QC test run, in 
which the mass spectrometric behavior of the test compounds and the adsorption behavior 
of the column are confirmed to be acceptable. The QC test must be run at the beginning and 
the end of each sample batch and in the case of a long sample batch e.g. after every fifteenth 
sample. 
The instrument is accept able for use if the MS and GC data produced from each test 
compound meet the following requirements: 
1. The signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio for each test chemical >10:1 (with a modern GC –MS 
system the S/N is much higher than this) in the total ion chromatogram ( TIC). The 
evaluation is done visually or automatically if available (the sensitivity of the GC–EI/MS 
equipment can be estimated with the QC test sample containing each test chemical at the 
10 ng/µl concentration level). 
2. The m/z values of the major ions of each test chemical are correct and no extra ions above 
5% are present (the mass range to be printed must extend 10 m/z beyond the molecular 
mass, so that the whole relevant mass spectrum is registered). 
3. The intensity ratios of the isotopic ions are within the following limits (the values are 
expressed as percent
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
beyond the molecular 
mass, so that the whole relevant mass spectrum is registered). 
3. The intensity ratios of the isotopic ions are within the following limits (the values are 
expressed as percentages of the less abundant isotopic ions relative to the more abundant 
ones  the acceptable error limits): 
 m/z 143/141 (37Cl/35Cl) for 5-chloro-2-methylaniline is 32.6±3.0% 
 m/z 186/184 (34S/32S) for dibenzothiophene is 5.3±1.0%. 
4. The peak height of trimethylphosphate is at least 20% of that of dibenzothiophene. The 
evaluation is done visually using the TIC.

6.2 Blank tests 
A system blank run (blind test) using the same solvents/reagents used in sample preparation 
is highly recommended to check any possible contamination coming from the sample 
preparation or the instrument. 
Note! The system blank should contain the same silylation reagent as the sample to prove 
the absence of instrument contamination . This is extremely important for sily
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
preparation or the instrument. 
Note! The system blank should contain the same silylation reagent as the sample to prove 
the absence of instrument contamination . This is extremely important for silylated samples 
as injecting silylation reagent-containing samples can produce in-situ silylation of 
remaining CWC-related chemicals in the injector. 
If CWC-related chemicals are found in any system blank chromatogram, the blind tests are 
repeated after the possible contamination source has been identified and eliminated . All 
contamination from glassware, solvents, standard solutions (or authentic reference solutions), 
syringes, the injector system, or columns must be eliminated before sample analysis is started.

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
In the beginning of an analysis batch , a QC test and a blank test are run. When all tests are 
acceptable, the samples can be analy sed. Blank tests in between sample series are 
recommended. Generally, 1.0 µl of the sample is injected. If retention indices are used, they 
can be calculated with an external method using the n-alkanes in the QC test run as retention 
index standards. AMDIS softwareii is recommended for calculating the retention index (refer 
to the GC ROP for detailed instructions). According to the current OPCW rules, a blank run 
is required before each sample analysis! 
7.2 Screening 
If GCs coupled to selective detectors are used to screen the samples, extracted ion 
chromatograms (EICs) from GC–EI/MS analyses can be used to locate chemicals without 
CWC-specific elements such as phosphorus, nitrogen, sulphur, arsenic, fluorine, chlorine 
and others. A list

7.3 Identification 
The final identification must always be approved by an experienced analyst. 
Identification can be based on comparison with an authentic reference chem ical or by 
comparing the recorded spectrum with the reference spectrum in the OPCW Central 
Analytical Database (OCAD) (when identifying isomers having similar EI /MS spectra, the 
retention index (RI) may be used to distinguish which isomer is in question) . Commercial 
databases may also be used for identification (e.g., NIST, Wiley). If a reference chemical or 
reference spectra are not available, the identification can be done with spectral interpretation. 
The recorded spectrum (reference and unknown) must be at least ten mass units above the 
molecular weight of the proposed molecule. No ions having mass-to-charge ratio above the 
molecular weight (excluding the isoto
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ctrum (reference and unknown) must be at least ten mass units above the 
molecular weight of the proposed molecule. No ions having mass-to-charge ratio above the 
molecular weight (excluding the isotope ions) must be present. Ions having intensities above 
10% in relative scale and not belonging to the reference spectrum must not be present. The 
signal-to-noise ratio of a recorded TIC peak must be greater than five (visual inspection). If 
identification is based on spectral interpretation, a spectrum of a closely related chemical 
together with a spectral interpretation and a fragmentation pathway must be provided. More 
details can be found in the OPCW reporting criteria for GC–EI/MS.iii 
Note! If extra peaks are present in the spectrum, use extracted ion chromatograms by 
selecting the impurity ion together with two ions, which belong to the spectrum of an 
authentic reference chemical. If the ion profiles are different, try to extract as pure spectrum 
as possible of the chemical of interest . If the target chemical co-elutes with a background

7.4 Fragmentation scheme of main CWA 
The results of identification using commercial and user´s databases should be verif ied with 
spectral interpretation, whic h is based on fragmentation rules. To make spectral 
interpretation easier, the fragmentation scheme of typical chemical warfare agents are 
presented below. 
7.4.1 Alkyl/cycloalkyl alkylphosphonofluoridates 
Alkyl/cycloalkyl alkylphosphonofluoridates give a common fragment ion [RPF(OH)2+] with 
the exception of methyl esters (which will give a methoxy -containing fragment 
[RPF(OH)(OCH3)+] instead). For methyl methylphosphonofluoridates, the characteristic ion 
of m/z 99 will be either the base peak or a highly abundant peak (> 90%) . This structure 
results from the loss of an alkenyl/cycloalkenyl radical from the molecular ion and it is 
typical of the sarin h
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
/z 99 will be either the base peak or a highly abundant peak (> 90%) . This structure 
results from the loss of an alkenyl/cycloalkenyl radical from the molecular ion and it is 
typical of the sarin homologues. 
Other characteristic ions are the low mass ions at m/z 81 ([CH3FOP]+), m/z 65 ([H2O2P]+), 
m/z 63 ([O2P]+) and m/z 47 ([OP]+). The O-alkyl group will also have a large effect on the 
mass spectra of the alkylphosphonofluoridates. Branched chain compounds are usually 
causing the high mass fragments at m/z 111, 125, 139, etc. (due to the loss of alkyl radicals) 
or at m/z 112, 126, 140, etc. (due to the loss of alkenes). Generally, spectra of the compounds 
with unbranched O -alkyl groups are less informative because the phosphorus-containing 
high mass fragments have a low abundance (< 5%). 
Methyl methylphosphonofluoridate gives the base peak at m/z 82 due to the loss of 
formaldehyde from the molecular ion (m/z 112). This compound is the only one of the known 
alkyl/cycloalkyl methylphosphonofluoridates, which produces a molecular ion (about 5%).

7.4.2 Alkyl/cycloalkyl N,N-dialkylphosphoroamidocyanidates 
There are big differences betwee n fragmentation of N,N -dimethylphosphoroamido-
cyanidates and the other N,N-dialkyl-containing chemicals, especially between “symmetric” 
and “unsymmetric” N,N-dialkyl analogues . The best known example of the family of 
N,N-dimethylphosphoroamidocyanidates is the O-ethyl ester: tabun. 
Dominant ions of tabun are m/z 42, 43 (base peak) and 44, originating from the 
dimethylamino group. The intensive peak at m/z 70 is produced with rearrangement of this 
group (see Figure 4). The loss of ethyl group leads to the moderate abundance ion at m/z 133, 
but in the mass spectra of N,N-dimethyl analogues with longer alkyl chains, the loss of the 
alkenyl radical from the molecular ion produces strong peak at m/z 135, which corresponds 
to the structure [C 3H8N2O2P]+. This ion is very typical for the alkyl/cycloalkyl 
N,N-dimethylphosphoroamidocy
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
kenyl radical from the molecular ion produces strong peak at m/z 135, which corresponds 
to the structure [C 3H8N2O2P]+. This ion is very typical for the alkyl/cycloalkyl 
N,N-dimethylphosphoroamidocyanidates. For C4 to C10 alkyls, it is the base peak. 
Molecular ion is present only in the mass spectra of the smaller N,N-dimethyl analogues, 
while for the O-methyl and O-ethyl esters the molecular ion is 30–40 %. For C5 esters and 
larger, the molecular ion is not present. 
The elimination of ethene or propene and HCN leads to the most intensive peaks in the mass 
spectra of N,N-dialkyl analogues of tabun. Base peaks are at m/z 147 (for N,N-diethyl) or at 
m/z 161 ( for N,N-dipropyl and N,N-diisopropyl), other intense ions are a t m/z 119 ( for 
N,N-diethyl or N,N-diisopropyl) or at m/z 133 (for N,N-dipropyl).

7.4.3 Alkyl/cycloalkyl S-2-(dialkylamino)ethyl alkylphosphonothiolates 
The family of V agents is the largest group of chemical warfare agents as there are 
theoreticaly more than eighty thousand possible structures of this type of compounds 
(compounds related to Schedule 1.A.03 of the Chemical Weapons Convention). 
The EI mass spectra of the O -alkyl/cycloalkyl S -2-(dialkylamino)ethyl 
alkylphosphonothiolates are dominated by the S -2-dialkylaminoethyl moieties. For VX,

8. Method evaluation 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The GC–EI/MS method can be applied to all chemical warfare agents, their degradation 
products, precursors or derivatives, except saxitoxin and ricin. Extremely volatile (e.g. alkyl 
phosphonyldifluorides), non-volatile (e.g. alkylphosphonic acids) and reactive (e.g. arsenic 
trichloride) CWC -related chemicals can be analysed after being converted in derivatives 
with an appropriate volatility . The method is suitable for analysing and identifying any 
chemical at the 1 mg/kg or 1 mg/l level in full scan mode and at the 0.01 mg/kg or 0.01 mg/l 
level in selective ion monitoring (SIM mode, target analysis only). 
8.2 Adva
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
alysing and identifying any 
chemical at the 1 mg/kg or 1 mg/l level in full scan mode and at the 0.01 mg/kg or 0.01 mg/l 
level in selective ion monitoring (SIM mode, target analysis only). 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The advantages of the GC–EI/MS method are reliability and sensitivity. Modern instruments 
are easy to use , and AMDIS software provides automated data analysis and identification. 
Thousands of chemicals using commercial libraries or OCAD can be identified within a very 
short period. 
The disadvantage in identification using GC–EI/MS is the similarity of the mass spectra of 
isomers. This problem may be solved by simultaneously using the retention index data of 
possible isomers found from the OCAD.

1. Scope 
This chapter deals with the application of gas chromatography –chemical ioni sation/mass 
spectrometry (GC–CI/MS) to determine molecular weight and identify relevant chemicals, 
hereafter chemical warfare agents, their precursors and degradation products regardin
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
chemical ioni sation/mass 
spectrometry (GC–CI/MS) to determine molecular weight and identify relevant chemicals, 
hereafter chemical warfare agents, their precursors and degradation products regarding the 
schedules of the Convention for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. Chemical ionisation 
is essential for confirming the structures of relevant chemicals after performing experiments 
with gas chromatography–electron ionisation/mass spectrometry ( GC–EI/MS). Generally, 
this technique is applied to identify chemicals above the 1 mg/kg concentration level. 
However, the technique can also be used to identify relevant chemicals below 1 mg/kg 
concentration levels.

2. Summary of the method 
GC–CI/MS experiments are carried out with modern GC–MS instruments used in chemical 
ionisation. The principle of the technology is based on a quadrupole or ion trap mass analyser 
operating in full scanning mode. Samples are introduced in the GC typically equipped with 
a 25 - to 30-m capillary column, generally coated with the same chemical phase used in 
previous experiments run in GC–EI/MS. 
A quality control run (QC test sample) is performed to check the GC–MS performance and 
to ensure the reliability of the analysis in each sample batch. 
Every relevant chemical, previously detected in GC–EI/MS, is examined in GC–CI/MS. 
Relevant chemicals are identified by comparing them with authentic reference chemicals 
when available or by interpreting the spectra. 
Determining the molecular weight is of key importance to elucidate the structure. Methane, 
ammonia and isobutane are widely used as reagent g
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
hemicals 
when available or by interpreting the spectra. 
Determining the molecular weight is of key importance to elucidate the structure. Methane, 
ammonia and isobutane are widely used as reagent gases to confirm the molecular weight of 
CWC-related chemicals in GC–CI/MS experiments. 
Methane (proton affinity (PA) ca. 135 kcal/mol) is the most common reagent gas for CWC 
scheduled compounds .1–3 Even if the [M+H]+ quasi-molecular ion is not systematically 
observed, positive chemical ioni sation (PCI) with methane allows information about the 
structure of relevant chemicals to be obtained that complements the information obtained in 
electron ionisation. 
For instance, because of the relatively huge difference in the proton affinity (PA) between 
methane and dialkyl alkylphosphonates ( ca. 65 kcal/mol), many fragmentations can be 
observed in their CI mass spectra. These fragmentations can differ from those observed in 
the EI mass spectra. Indeed, odd -electron species (i.e., M +.) can dissociate following 
different pathways than those occurring from the even-electron ions (i.e., [M+H]+). 
Extensive fragmentation, the non-systematic presence of the [M+H]+ ion and the two addu
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
) can dissociate following 
different pathways than those occurring from the even-electron ions (i.e., [M+H]+). 
Extensive fragmentation, the non-systematic presence of the [M+H]+ ion and the two adduct 
ions [M+C 2H5]+ and [M+C 3H5]+ are characteristic of positive chemical ioni sation using 
methane as a reagent gas. 
Because of methane’s low proton affinity, this reagent gas can protonate other organic 
compounds (backgrounds) together with relevant chemicals present at low concentrations in 
complex mixtures. It can be difficult to extract a good-quality mass spectrum for the target 
chemicals. 
Isobutane (PA ca. 192 kcal/mol) is a reagent gas softer than methane. Isobutane is more 
selective and causes less fragmentation. 
The simple fragmentation pattern, large abundance of the [M+H]+ ion and the presence often 
observed of [M+C 3H3]+, [M+C3H5]+and [M+C4H9]+ are characteristic of positive chemical 
ionisation using isobutane4 as a reagent gas. 
Ammonia (PA ca. 204 kcal/mol) is a more specific reagent gas due to its high proton affinity. 
Ammonia is recommended for confirming the molecular weight of organophosphorus 
compounds (OPC)5–8 and for chemicals containing sulfur and ni
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ore specific reagent gas due to its high proton affinity. 
Ammonia is recommended for confirming the molecular weight of organophosphorus 
compounds (OPC)5–8 and for chemicals containing sulfur and nitrogen atoms with a proton 
affinity higher than 204 kcal/mol. 
If the difference of (PA OPC – PANH3) is ±10 kcal/mol, the [M+NH 4]+ ion is stable enough 
to be detected.

Negative chemical ioni sation9,10 is particularly recommended for analysing halogenated 
compounds. However,  deprotonation of organophosphorus compounds is possible and can 
yield RH-C–P(=O) (OR)2 as well as high acid reagents (e.g., HCl  Cl-). 
Elimination can lead to the formation of RCH2–P(=O) (OR’) O- instead of deprotonation that 
could yield [M-H]-. The difference in behavior allows complementary dissociative processes 
to be obtained, and thus, specific ions can be obtained.11 
Chemical ionisation (CI) with liquid reagents 
Liquid CI reagents12,13 offer several important benefits over pressurised gases. These benefits 
include safety, convenience, cost and ease of use. 
Liquid CI uses the room temperature vapor pressure of the liquid as the reagent gas. This is 
possible only with an internal source ion trap and not an external source instrument be it an 
ion trap or a quadrupole. Liquid CI is highly selective becaus
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
of the liquid as the reagent gas. This is 
possible only with an internal source ion trap and not an external source instrument be it an 
ion trap or a quadrupole. Liquid CI is highly selective because of the wide variety of common 
reagents available in a typical laboratory. The different types of liquids used give specific 
adduct ions particular to the reagent and the compound class of the analyte. 
There is a list of the typical CI reagents (methanol, acetonitrile, acetone, including deuterated 
forms). Acetonitrile has become the most common reagent because it reacts extremely well 
with hydrocarbon14 and any compound containing nitrogen, phosphorus and/or sulphur. 
Acetonitrile’s (ACN) molecular weight is 41, and the CI reagent is the M+1, which is mass 
42. The adduct ion is M+13, which is an attachment of CH. 
3. Safety aspects 
Analysing chemical warfare agents requires specific safety precautions be adopted. For the 
bulk of the molecules arriving in the ion source of the mass spectrometer, only a fraction is 
ionised and thus destroyed. The majority of the samples go through the instrument ation 
directly to the primary pump. Although quantities injected into the GC –MS
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
s spectrometer, only a fraction is 
ionised and thus destroyed. The majority of the samples go through the instrument ation 
directly to the primary pump. Although quantities injected into the GC –MS are at low 
concentration levels, after several experiments, precautions have to be taken when the oil of 
the primary pump has to be changed. That is why the operations mentioned above should be 
carried out with masks and butyl gloves under a suction and filtering hood. In addition, some 
parts of the GC–MS are hot (e.g., the GC’s injector and the GC–MS’s transfer line). This is 
why precautions should be taken to avoid damage or injury during maintenance. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 GC columns 
Generally, the 25- to 30-m capillary column used in GC–CI/MS is coated with the same 
chemical phase used in previous experiments by GC–EI/MS. 
Note! According to the Proficiency Test criteria, the same phase column must be used in 
GC–EI/MS and GC–CI/MS, if the target chemical is identified against a library instead of 
an authentic reference chemical.

6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
Identifying CWC-related compounds reliably requires that the data is correct. Therefore, 
running quality control tests periodically to confirm that the instrument works correctly and 
the performance of the instrument remains stable during the sample analysis is essential. 
The performance of a GC–CI/MS instrument is assessed by carrying out a QC test run, in 
which the mass spectrometric behavior of the test compounds and the adsorption behavior 
of the column are confirmed to be acceptable. 
The instrument is accepted for use if the MS and GC data produced from each test compound 
is in accordance with the following requirements: 
1. Signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio for each test chemical 10:1 in the total ion chromatogram 
(TIC). The evaluation is done visually or automatically if available. 
2. The m/z values of the major ions of each test chemica
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
(S/N) ratio for each test chemical 10:1 in the total ion chromatogram 
(TIC). The evaluation is done visually or automatically if available. 
2. The m/z values of the major ions of each test chemical are correct and no extra ions 
above 5% are present (the mass range to be printed must be extended until 60 m/z 
beyond the molecular weight so that the overall relevant mass spectrum is registered). 
3. The relative ion abundances deviation regarding the abundances of the main ions 
could be around ±50%, compared with the values of the reference spectra.

6.2 Blank tests 
A solvent blank run must be conducted between two analy sed samples to avoid cross 
contamination of the GC –MS, and thus to ensure the reliability of the measurements. If 
CWC-related compounds are found in the blank chromatogram, the solvent blank test is 
repeated until the contamination source is completely eliminated. 
After a silylated sample is analysed, some memory effects could remain due to the presence 
of non-volatile chemicals in the injector. In this case, a solvent used in sample preparation 
containing a silylation agent is injected to remove contamination. 
7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
In the beginning of an analysis batch, a QC test sample and a blank test are run. When both 
tests have been accepted, the samples can be analy sed. Generally, 1.0 µl of the sample is 
injected in the splitless mode. 
During sample analysis, the QC test sample is run every 15 to 20 injectio
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
tests have been accepted, the samples can be analy sed. Generally, 1.0 µl of the sample is 
injected in the splitless mode. 
During sample analysis, the QC test sample is run every 15 to 20 injections to validate the 
GC–MS performance. 
At the end of the batch samples, the QC test sample is run to validate the GC –MS 
performance. 
7.2 Screening 
Screening is typically performed in GC and GC–EI/MS systems. GC–CI/MS analysis is 
generally performed to confirm the molecular weight of the relevant chemicals previously 
identified with GC–EI/MS. However, screening in GC–CI/MS is recommended to help in 
identifying CWC-related chemicals. Some scheduled chemicals are no t detected with 
phosphorus, sulfur and nitrogen selective detectors. These chemicals and their specific ions 
for GC–CI/MS screening are listed in Table 4. Appendix 1 contains the specific ions of the 
most important groups of CWC-related chemicals. The ion intensity depends on the reagent 
gas, the repeller voltage and the ion source temperature, and therefore, the intensity scale is 
not included in Table 4.

7.3 Identification 
The final identification must always be approved by an experienced analyst. The recorded 
spectra (reference chemicals if available and relevant ch emicals) must be presented from 
80 to at least 60 mass units above the mono -isotopic molecular weight to include all 
expected adducts, including those when isobutane is the reagent gas. The isotopic ions ratio 
must be consistent with the proposed structure. 
All background ions present in the mass spectrum of the relevant chemical with an intensity 
>10% must be labeled as background ions. In this case, the extracted ion chromatogram 
(EIC) should be shown by selecting an impurity ion with one or two charact eristic ions of 
the relevant chemical. In most cases, the profile ions are not perfectly overlapped , and a 
good-quality spectrum can be extracted. 
There are two possibilities for confirming the structure of CWC -related chemicals in GC –
CI/MS in a Proficiency Tes
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ons are not perfectly overlapped , and a 
good-quality spectrum can be extracted. 
There are two possibilities for confirming the structure of CWC -related chemicals in GC –
CI/MS in a Proficiency Test. 
 The best way to confirm the structure and the identification is to compare the GC–
CI/MS mass spectrum of a relevant chemical against the GC–CI/MS mass spectrum 
of a reference chemical. The retention time of the relevant chemical and the reference 
chemical must remain within ±0.1 min. 
 GC–CI/MS data without comparison to similarly obtained data from a reference 
chemical, is accepted only as a supporting technique to GC–EI/MS data. Where no 
GC–EI/MS data has been submitted or the GC–EI/MS data is insufficient, GC–
CI/MS data without comparison to similarly obtained data from a reference chemical 
will be rejected.

8. Method evaluation 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The GC–CI/MS method can be applied to all volatile chemical warfare agents , 15 their 
degradation products16 and their precursors, except saxitoxin and r

text:
Method evaluation 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The GC–CI/MS method can be applied to all volatile chemical warfare agents , 15 their 
degradation products16 and their precursors, except saxitoxin and ricin. Non -volatile polar 
CWC-related chemicals with alcohol 17 and/or acid groups (e.g. , thiodiglycol,18 
triethanolamine, alkylphosphonic acids 18) can be derivati sed with silylating reagents 
(e.g., BSTFA, MTBSTFA ); chemicals with acid groups (e.g. , alkylphosphonic acids, 
benzilic acid) can be derivatised with methylating reagents (e.g., diazomethane). 
CWC-related chemicals with arsenic atoms are typically derivati sed with thiol reagents 
(e.g., propanethiol, buthanethiol, DMT19). 
This technique can be used in full scan mode for chemicals with a concentration around the 
mg/kg level. The technique can be used in Selected Ion Monitoring (SIM) mode to search 
target chemicals with a concentration around the 0.1 mg/kg20 level, although the SIM mode 
is not accepted in Proficiency Test reports. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
Advantages 
The GC–CI/MS is a reliable and sensitive identification technique if the mass spectrometer 
is regularly calibrated and if the sensitivity of t

8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
Advantages 
The GC–CI/MS is a reliable and sensitive identification technique if the mass spectrometer 
is regularly calibrated and if the sensitivity of the GC –MS is checked with the use of test 
compounds (e.g., QC test sample). Many reagent gases can be used to confirm the molecular 
weight of CWC-related chemicals. Positive and negative chemical ioni sation often reveals 
several characteristic ions in addition to those obtained under electron ioni sation (EI). 
Positive and negative chemical ioni sation contributes to the structure elucidation of CWC -
related chemicals. 
Disadvantages 
The ion intensities in the CI spectra are different depending on the ion source temperature, 
the repeller voltage and the pressure of the reagent gas. That is why CI databases do not exist. 
To switch from operating in the EI to the CI mode in a quadrupole system, the ioni sation 
source has to be changed. This requires venting of the MS system. Approximately two hours 
are required to get the vacuum and an additional 6 hours or more for the reagent gas to

Chapter V. 
Gas chromatography–high resolution mass 
spectrometry (GC–HRMS): sector instruments, 
selective ion monitoring mode 
 
Author Vesa Häkkinen 
 Finnish Institute for Verification of the Chemical Weapons Convention (VERIFIN) 
 PO. Box 55, FI-00014 University of Helsinki, Finland. 
 E-mail: vesa.hakkinen@helsinki.fi 
 
Reviewer Martin Söderström 
 Finnish Institute for Verification of the Chemical Weapons Convention (VERIFIN) 
 PO. Box 55, FI-00014 University of Helsinki, Finland. 
 E-mail: martin.soderstrom@helsinki.fi 
 
1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of gas chromatography–high resolution mass spectrometry 
(GC–HRMS) using magnetic sector instruments in selective ion monitoring mode (SIM) in 
the identification of chemical warfare agents, their precurs ors, degradation products , or 
derivatives, i.e., chemicals related to the C hemical Weapons Convention (CWC). Th
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
onitoring mode (SIM) in 
the identification of chemical warfare agents, their precurs ors, degradation products , or 
derivatives, i.e., chemicals related to the C hemical Weapons Convention (CWC). This 
method is used for volatile chemicals in an organic solvent when interfering background 
chemicals prevent the analysis and identification of relevant chemicals using low resolution 
GC–EI/MS. 
2. Summary of the method 
GC–HRMS measurements using electron ioni sation can be carried out with modern GC –
HRMS magnetic sector instruments operating in selected ion monitoring (SIM) mode for 
target analysis. Samples are analysed with a GC–MS instrument equipped with a 25 –30 m 
capillary column with SE-54-type stationary phase material. For GC–HRMS SIM, reference 
material (e.g., perfuorokerosine, PFK) is introduced into the ion source, and the instrument 
is tuned to high resolution (R>8000). Before each sample batch, a quality control run (QC 
test, see below) is carried out to verify the correct performance of the instrument , using a 
SIM method created for the QC test sample. After a passed QC test, a specific SIM method 
for the sample of interest is created, and the sample is ana
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
correct performance of the instrument , using a 
SIM method created for the QC test sample. After a passed QC test, a specific SIM method 
for the sample of interest is created, and the sample is analysed. QC tests should be run daily 
before any sample(s) of interest are analysed. 
The target analysis of chemicals of interest using GC–HRMS SIM is carried out by selecting 
the exact masses of characteristic ions for the individual chemicals (at least three ions must 
be selected for each target chemical ). A chemical is identified when each selected ion 
produces a peak with the correct ion abundance (±20%) in comparison with the reference EI 
spectrum.

3. Safety aspects 
GC–HRMS analysis does not require any specific precautions concerning safety. Samples 
to be analysed normally contain only small concentrations of toxic chemicals , and the 
electron ionisation will destroy the sample mole cules. Normal laboratory safety measures , 
such as the use of protective gloves and goggles during sample handling in manual injections, 
should be followed. 
Hot parts of instruments, e.g., hot septum nuts (>250 °C), must be taken into account during 
the operation and maintenance of instrument. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 GC–HRMS instrument 
Any modern GC–HRMS magnetic sector instrument that is capable of at least a resolution 
of 8000 and covers a mass range of at least 40–500 m/z can be used. 
4.2 GC columns 
A 25 –30 m-long SE-54-typei fused silica capillary column (0.20 –0.25 mm i.d. and film 
thickness 0.25 µm), preferably a so-called low bl
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ass range of at least 40–500 m/z can be used. 
4.2 GC columns 
A 25 –30 m-long SE-54-typei fused silica capillary column (0.20 –0.25 mm i.d. and film 
thickness 0.25 µm), preferably a so-called low bleed MS column, is used. 
Note! As the GC –HRMS SIM data is normally almost clear of background chemicals, the 
actual amount of background introduced to the system or any possible column bleed will not 
be seen. It is essential to the QC test to verify the condition of the GC column during and 
after the GC–HRMS work. 
 
i A SE-54-type column means a stationary phase consisting of 95% -methyl-5%-phenylpolysiloxane. Also , 
polyarylene-type columns, which are virtually equivalent to the SE-54-type columns, can be used.

5.3 Tuning and mass calibration of the HRMS SIM 
Follow the instructions given by the instrument manufacturer. Modern instruments have 
automatic tuning and calibration procedures that must be carried out for each individual SIM 
measurement. Perfuorokerosine (PFK) or some other reference chemical recommended 
by the in strument instructions is used for tuning and calibration , and the reference 
material must be present in the ion source during HRMS SIM measurements. Check 
that the correct reference file , which contains the reference ions of the reference chemical 
used, has been selected before you begin tuning. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The reliable identification of CWC -related compounds requires that the data produced by 
the instrument is correct. Therefore, it is essential to continu ally run quality control tests to 
confirm correct and stable instrument performance during the sample ana
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
s that the data produced by 
the instrument is correct. Therefore, it is essential to continu ally run quality control tests to 
confirm correct and stable instrument performance during the sample analysis. 
The performance of a GC–HRMS instrument is controlled by carrying out a QC test run, in 
which the mass spectrometric behaviour of test compounds and the adsorption behaviour of 
the column are confirmed to be acceptable. The QC test must be run at the beginning and at 
the end of each sample batch, and in the case of a long sample batch, it must be run at least 
after every fifteenth sample. The selected ions for each test chemical are given in Table 1.

For the QC test, three different SIM sets should be created: 
1. m/z 110.013, 140.025 for trimethylphosphate 
m/z 107.050, 122.073 for 2,6-dimethylphenol and 
m/z 106.066, 141.035, 143.032 for 5-chloro-2-methylaniline 
2. m/z 155.047, 211.110 for tri-n-butylphosphate, 
m/z 152.066, 184.035, 186.031 for dibenzothiophene and 
m/z 158.058, 173.081 for malathion 
3. m/z 255.232, 298.287 for methyl stearate 
The retention time window for each set can be checked by running the same QC test with 
the full scan GC–EI/MS method under same run conditions and observing the corresponding 
retention times. 
The instrument is accepted for use if the MS and GC data produced from each test compound 
meet the following requirements: 
1. The s ignal-to-noise (S/N) ratio for each test chemical >10:1 for all selected ion 
chromatograms. The evaluation is done visually. 
2. The intensity ratios of the iso
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
the following requirements: 
1. The s ignal-to-noise (S/N) ratio for each test chemical >10:1 for all selected ion 
chromatograms. The evaluation is done visually. 
2. The intensity ratios of the isotopic ions are within the following limits: (the values 
are expressed as percentages of the less abun dant isotopic ions relative to the more 
abundant ones  the acceptable error limits) 
 m/z 143.032/141.035 (37Cl/35Cl) for 5-chloro-2-methylaniline is 32.4±3.0% 
 m/z 186.031/184.035 (34S/32S) for dibenzothiophene is 4.4±1.0% 
6.2 Blank tests 
A system blank (blind test) is highly recommended for each target chemical to check for any 
possible contamination coming from the sample preparation or the instrument. If the blind 
test shows contamination, a solvent blank run with the same solvent used in the sample 
preparation must be carried out to eliminate the possibility of contamina tion of the 
equipment (e.g., contamination from the syringe or the memory effect of the equipment). 
Note! This is extremely important when silylated target chemicals are analysed. 
If target chemicals are found in any blank chromatogram, the blank tests are repeated after 
the elimination of the possi
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
te! This is extremely important when silylated target chemicals are analysed. 
If target chemicals are found in any blank chromatogram, the blank tests are repeated after 
the elimination of the possible contamination source. All contamination coming from 
glassware, solvents, standard solutions (or authentic reference solutions), syringes, injector 
systems, or columns must be eliminated before sample analysis is begun. 
7 Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
In the beginning of an analysis batch , a QC test (always) and blank tests are run. When all 
tests have been performed successfully, samples can be analysed. Generally , 1.0 µl of the 
sample is injected.

7.2 Identification 
The final identification must always be approved by an experienced analyst. 
A chemical is i dentified when each selected ion produces a peak with the same retent ion 
time. Additionally, each ion must have a correct ion abundance (±20%) in comparison with 
the reference EI spectrum. 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The GC–HRMS SIM method can be applied to all chemical warfare agents, their degradation 
products, precursors, or derivatives, except saxitoxin and ricin. Extremely volatile (e.g., DF), 
non-volatile (e.g., alkylphosphonic acids), and reactive (e.g., Lewisite I ) CWC-related 
chemicals can be analysed after their derivatisation to volatile der ivatives. The method is 
suitable for analysing and identifying any chemical at the 1 mg/kg level. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The advantages of the method are reliability and selectivity in
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
le der ivatives. The method is 
suitable for analysing and identifying any chemical at the 1 mg/kg level. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The advantages of the method are reliability and selectivity in analysing extremely complex 
sample mixtures. Modern HRMS sector instruments are easy to use with automatic tuning 
and calibration. 
The disadvantage of identification using GC–HRMS SIM is that in practice, only a limited 
number of target chemicals can be analysed from a single run. Also, the selection of at least 
three characteristic ions for certain relevant chemicals may be problematic.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of gas chromatography–high resolution mass spectrometry 
(GC–TOF) in screening and identifying chemical warfare agents, their precursors , 
degradation products or derivatives , i.e., chemicals related to the C hemical Weapons 
Convention, CWC. The descriptions in chapter s II and III of GC–EI/MS and CG –CI/MS, 
respectively, are for the most part valid for GC–TOF. This chapter will focus on issues that 
differ from low-resolution methods. 
2. Summary of the method 
GC–TOF instr
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
II of GC–EI/MS and CG –CI/MS, 
respectively, are for the most part valid for GC–TOF. This chapter will focus on issues that 
differ from low-resolution methods. 
2. Summary of the method 
GC–TOF instruments differ from other GC –MS instruments by being non -scanning 
instruments. Instead, ions are measured in the time frame at a frequency of 15–30 kHz with 
either a TDC (Time-to-Digital Converter) or a Continuous Averager (ADC, also known as 
DSA or ITR). The detector is normally not an electron multiplier, but a micro-channel plate 
(MCP). The measurements are summed over time giving the apparent scan rate. This gives 
the possibility of having either very fast “scan rates” or high resolution. Here we will focus 
on the high-resolution GC–TOF. 
The high-resolution GC–TOF has most of the characteristics of the modern GC–EI/MS and 
GC–CI/MS described in Section 3, Part B, C hapters II and III , respectively . One major 
difference is that the dynamic range of the GC–TOF is lower than the dynamic range of the 
typical quadrupole-based GC–MS. The dynamic range could, depending on the instrument, 
be enhanced by alternating scans with two different sensitivity settings (Dynamic Range
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e dynamic range of the 
typical quadrupole-based GC–MS. The dynamic range could, depending on the instrument, 
be enhanced by alternating scans with two different sensitivity settings (Dynamic Range 
Enhancement) resulting in a halving of the apparent scan rate.

3. Safety aspects 
GC–TOF analysis does not requir e any specific precautions concerning safety. Samples to 
be analy sed normally contain only small concentrations of toxic chemicals , and the 
ionisation will destroy the sample molecules. Normal laboratory safety measures such as 
wearing protective gloves and goggles while handling samples in manual injections should 
be used. 
Hot parts of the instrument, e.g., the hot septum nut (>250 °C) , must be taken into account 
while operating and maintaining the instrument. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 GC–TOF instrument 
Any modern GC –TOF instrument with a resolution of 5000 –10,000 and covering a mass 
range of at least m/z 40–500 can be used. 
4.2 GC columns 
A 25- to 30-m-long SE-54-typei fused silica capillary column (0.20 –0.25 mm i.d. and film 
thickness 0.25 µm), preferably the low-bleed MS column, is used. 
4.3 Reagents and chemicals

ed silica capillary column (0.20 –0.25 mm i.d. and film

4.3 Reagents and chemicals 
The reagents and chemicals needed for GC –TOF analysis are the same as those given in 
Table 1 of Section 3, Part B, C hapters II: Gas chromatography–electron ionisation/mass 
spectrometry (GC –EI/MS) and III : Gas chromatography –chemical i onisation/mass 
spectrometry (GC–CI/MS) for GC–EI/MS and GC–CI/MS, respectively. 
5. Experimental 
5.1 Recommended GC conditions 
The recommended GC conditions are given in Table 1. 
The run conditions may be modified depending on the sample type. Due to the lower 
dynamic ra nge of the GC –TOF, the split injection mode is used more frequently. For 
example, samples with concentrations < 10 ng/µl are typically done with a 1:5 split ratio. 
More concentrated samples (>100 ng/μl) should be injected in the split injection mode with 
a split ratio of 1:50 or higher to avoid column overloading and to achieve better separation 
of low-boiling chemicals. For splitless injections, most samples must be diluted.

5.3 Recommended tuning and mass calibration of the MS 
Use the tuning method recommended for the instrument. An automatic tuning and calibration 
procedure should be used, if available. Tuning should be carried out once a week or more 
often if indicated by the QC test. Mass calibration should be carried out before each batch 
of samples to achieve accurate mass. Printouts of tuni ng and calibration reports should be 
archived for future reference. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
Reliably identifying CWC-related compounds requires that the data produced by the 
instrument is correct. Therefore, quality control tests must be run continuously to confirm 
the instrument will perform correctly and stably while analysing samples. 
The instrument performance test for GC–TOF analysis is the same as given in 6.1 of Section 
3, Part B, Chapters II and III for GC–EI/MS and GC–CI/MS, respectively. 
6.2 Blank tests 
A system
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
samples. 
The instrument performance test for GC–TOF analysis is the same as given in 6.1 of Section 
3, Part B, Chapters II and III for GC–EI/MS and GC–CI/MS, respectively. 
6.2 Blank tests 
A system blank (blind test) should be performed to check for any possible contamination in 
the sample preparation or the instrument. If the blind test shows contamination, a solvent 
blank run with the same solvent used in sample preparation must be performed to eliminate 
the possibility of contamina tion of the equipment (e.g., contamination from the syringe or 
the memory effect of the equipment). 
Note! Extremely important for silylated samples. 
If CWC-related chemicals are found in any blank chromatogram, the blank tests are repeated 
after the possible contamination source has been eliminated . All contamination from 
glassware, solvents, standard solution s (or authentic reference solution s), syringes, an 
injector system or columns must be eliminated before sample analysis is started. 
7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
In the beginning of an analysis batch, a QC test (always) and a blank test are run. When all 
tests have been accepted, the samples can be analy sed.
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
In the beginning of an analysis batch, a QC test (always) and a blank test are run. When all 
tests have been accepted, the samples can be analy sed. Generally, 1.0 µl of the sample is 
injected. If retention indices are used, they can be calculated with an external method using 
the n-alkanes in the QC test run as retention index standards . Automated Mass Spectral 
Deconvolution and Identification System (AMDIS) softwareii should be used to calculate 
the retention index (refer to the GC ROP for detailed instructions). According to the current 
OPCW rules, a blank run is required before each sample analysis! 
 
ii Available at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) website 
(chemdata.nist.gov)

III for GC–EI/MS and GC–CI/MS, respectively. One major difference is that selective ion 
monitoring (SIM) cannot be conducted at the instrumental level. Instead of SIM, extracted 
ion chromatograms (EICs) are very useful due to the high resolution, which allows the mass

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of liquid chromatography –atmospheric pressure ionisation 
mass spectrometry (LC–API/MS) in the screening and identification of degradation products 
of chemical warfare agents in aqueous samples or in aqueous extracts of solid samples. LC–
API/MS is also applicable to some intact chemical warfare agents. The procedures described 
are generally suitable for identifying chemicals at concentrations above 1 mg/kg or 1 mg/l 
and may be applicable at lower concentrations. The most widely used atmospheric pressure 
ionisation methods are (heated) electrospray ionisation ( LC–ESI/MS) and atmospheric 
pressure chemical ionisation (LC–APCI/MS). A detailed review of the application of these 
techniques to CWC-related analytes has been published.1 
2. Summary of the method 
LC–ESI/MS and LC–APCI/MS for analysis at parts-per-million levels are performed using 
quadrupole or ion trap instruments operating in full scanning mode, or using time -of-flight 
instruments. Screening and identification of CWAs with LC –HRMS is
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
er-million levels are performed using 
quadrupole or ion trap instruments operating in full scanning mode, or using time -of-flight 
instruments. Screening and identification of CWAs with LC –HRMS is described in 
Section 3, Part C, Chapter IV: Liquid chromatography–high resolution mass spectrometry 
and tandem mass spectrometry (LC –HRMS and LC –MS/HRMS). Samples are most 
commonly analysed using a reversed phase (C18 or C8) LC column.2–4 Column dimensions 
are left to laboratory preference, but 50–150 × 2.1–4.5 mm columns packed with 1.7–5 µm

ESI,5–6 but this is exper imentally more demanding. Both ESI and APCI are broadly 
applicable to CWC -related chemicals, e.g. degradation products of nerve agents and 
vesicants. ESI is used for thermally labile and highly polar ionic analytes such as saxitoxin 
and high molecular mass materials such as ricin. 
A recent modification has been hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) for 
improved separation of highly polar chemicals (e.g. saxitoxin). HILIC is performed using 
mobile phases with high organic content (usually acetonitrile) and is highly compatible with 
ESI. Analytes elute from the column in the order opposite to that in reverse phase LC; 
analytes poorly retained in reverse phase LC are strongly retained in HILIC.7–9

analytes poorly retained in reverse phase LC are strongly retained in HILIC.7–9 
Before analysis of samples, a quality control run (QC test, see below) is carried out to verify 
correct instrument performance. Screening of relevant chemicals is performed by selecting 
ions characteristic of chemical classes or individual chemicals (extracted ion chromatograms, 
EICs) from the total ion chromatograms (TICs). Identification of relevant chemicals is made 
by comparison of the measured spectra to those in relevant libraries, if available, or to spectra 
of authentic reference chemicals, or by interpretation of spectra. 
3. Safety aspects 
LC–API/MS analyses do not require any specific safety precautions. Samples to be analysed 
usually contain low concentrations of intact chemical warfare agents or their less toxic 
degradation products. However, some components of the mobile phases used are hazardous. 
Normal laboratory safety measures such as protective gloves and eyewear should be used. 
Some parts of the LC–MS instrument are hot (>250 °C). Typically, these are located in the 
ion source. During normal operations touching the hot parts should
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ective gloves and eyewear should be used. 
Some parts of the LC–MS instrument are hot (>250 °C). Typically, these are located in the 
ion source. During normal operations touching the hot parts should be avoided and before 
maintenance operations they must be let to cool down before handling them. 
The ion sources typically use high voltages (e.g. 2 –3 kV) for the ionisation process. Care 
must be taken to follow the manufacturers’ instructions for safe operation of the instrument. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 LC–API/MS instrument 
Any modern LC–API/MS instrument can be used . It should have a scan -speed capacity of 
at least 1 scan/s and cover a mass range of at least m/z 50–400. 
4.2 LC columns 
A 50–150 mm long C18 or C8 column (2.1–4.5 mm i.d.) packed with 1.7–5 µm particles is 
commonly used. 
4.3 Reagents and chemicals 
The reagents and chemicals needed for LC–API/MS analysis at Dstl and VERIFIN are given 
in Table 1. Other QC test chemicals may alternatively be used.

QC samples are essential to assess instrument sensitivity, chromatographic separation, 
column condition, and mass calibration for reliable identification of CWC-related chemicals. 
QC samples may comprise v arious CWC relevant chemicals for which test criteria should 
be established to measure instrument performance. Examples of QC test criteria used by Dstl 
(6.1.1) and VERIFIN (6.1.2) are shown below. QC samples should be analysed at the 
beginning and end of each sample batch to ensure adequate instrument performance 
throughout the analytical run.

6.2 Sensitivity test 
The sensitivity of the LC–API/MS instrument is estimated with the QC test sample 
containing each test chemical. If the QC criteria are not passed, instrument maintenance must 
be performed according to manufacturer’s instructions until the QC passes the performance 
criteria. 
6.3 Blank test 
A solvent (water) blank must be run to show possible contamination or carry-over effects of 
CWC related chemicals, which may be present in the QC test mix, samples, or analysed as 
reference standards. Blank water samples must be run directly before samples are analysed 
to demonstrate that there are no peaks observed relating to CWC relevant chemicals. If such 
peaks are evident, the blank run, or runs, should be repeated or the instrument cleaned until 
no peaks are detected. All carry-over or contamination from glassware, solvents, QC test 
mix, or authentic reference s tandards, syringe, auto -s
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
, should be repeated or the instrument cleaned until 
no peaks are detected. All carry-over or contamination from glassware, solvents, QC test 
mix, or authentic reference s tandards, syringe, auto -sampler, columns, or equipment must 
be eliminated before sample analysis is started. Matrix blanks are prepared by processing a 
blank (often water) sample using the same sample preparation procedures as for authentic 
samples. Matrix blanks are analysed to ensure that there is no contamination in the sample 
preparation procedure. 
Note! VERIFIN QC test mixture does not contain scheduled chemicals, and the selected QC 
test chemicals are only mimicking the scheduled chemicals. Dstl QC test mixture contains 
scheduled chemicals, so care must be taken in order to avoid possible carry-over effects. 
7. Analysis of samples 
7.1 Sequence of analysis 
A QC test and water blank are always run at the beginning of an analysis batch. When both 
tests have been accepted samples can be analysed. Typically 5–10 µl of the sample is injected. 
Water blank should be run before injection of a ne w sample in the sequence. Blanks need 
not be run between multiple injections of the same sample. 
7.2 Scre
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
cally 5–10 µl of the sample is injected. 
Water blank should be run before injection of a ne w sample in the sequence. Blanks need 
not be run between multiple injections of the same sample. 
7.2 Screening 
Extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) are used to locate chemicals or classes of chemicals 
which may be masked by interfering chemicals in the total ion chromatogram (TIC). Specific 
ions for screening with API+/MS and API-/MS are given in Tables 7 and 8, respectively. 
Note! The diagnostic ions for methyl alkylphosphonates and O -methyl 
alkylphosphonothioates differ from the diagnostic ions of other alkyl alkylphosphonates and 
alkyl alkylphosphonothioates 
Note! The list s of specific ions for screening with API +/MS and API -/MS are not 
comprehensive.

7.3 Identification 
The final identification must always be approved by an experienced analyst. 
The identity of target chemical is preferably confirmed by comparison with a spectrum from 
an authentic reference chemical . Identification can also be based on interpretation of a 
spectrum or comparison with a library spectrum if available. Commercial (or OPCW) 
databases of LC–API/MS spectra of CWC -related chemicals are not currently available, 
although many such spectra have been published in scientific journals , and an OPCW 
database is currently in development. 
A quasi -molecular ion or adduct io n of the target chemical must be visible in the mass 
spectrum and recorded spectra

spectrum and recorded spectra (unknown and reference) must be presented from ≤60 to at 
least 60 mass units (M+70 recommended) above the molecular weight of the proposed 
structure.10 The S/N ratio of a peak in the TIC or EIC must be ≥ 5:1 and retention time of the 
target chemical in the sample must be within ± 0.2 min of the reference chemical . If 
identification is based on spectral interpretation, a spectrum of a closely related chemical 
together with a spectral interpretation must be provided.

chemical. If extra peaks are present in spectrum, use extracted ion chromatograms by 
selecting the impurity ion together with two ions present in the spectrum of the authentic 
reference chemical. If the ion profiles are different, try to extract as pure a spectrum as 
possible of the chemical of interest. If the target chemical co -elutes exactly with a 
background chemical, a column possessing different selectivity or a diff

8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
LC–API/MS methods can be applied to many degradation products of chemical warfare 
agents and to some intact agents that are more or less stable in aqueous solution. Sensitivity 
varies depending on the type of chemical and may be better with either ESI or APCI methods. 
Negative ion mode methods are selective for acidic chemicals. The screening of CWAs 
should be performed both with acidic and basic LC eluents, with positive and negative ion 
modes and utilizing both ESI and APCI techniques. 
8.2 Advantages / disadvantages 
Advantages of the method are speed of analysis of aqueous samples or extracts, removing 
the need for evaporation and derivatisation , which are required for GC–MS methods. API 
usually provides confirmation of the molecular mass and, if fragment ions are detected with 
API/MS, these generally result from simple neutral losses. 
ESI spectr
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
are required for GC–MS methods. API 
usually provides confirmation of the molecular mass and, if fragment ions are detected with 
API/MS, these generally result from simple neutral losses. 
ESI spectra may be more complex than APCI spectra owing to the greater tendency to form 
adduct ions with solvent and metal ions such as Na +. Where there is a substantial chemi cal 
background, ion suppression can occur, which is also more prevalent with ESI. 
Disadvantages for identification are the low content of structural information in API spectra, 
the limited 'fingerprint' compared to GC –EI/MS, plus the lack of a spectral database. For 
confirmation of identification MS/MS is recommended, and is essential for differentiating 
isomers other than by known retention time .11–12 For trace analysis LC–MS/MS is 
recommended rather than single-stage LC–MS, because the reduction in noise usually gives 
substantially enhanced S/N ratios. The identification of CWAs with LC–MS/MS is described 
in the next chapter ( Section 3, Part C, Chapter II I: Liquid chromatography–tandem mass 
spectrometry (LC–MS/MS).
