1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry ( LC–
MS/MS) for the identification of non-volatile chemical warfare agents and their polar or 
semi-polar degradation products ; i.e., chemicals related to the C hemical Weapons 
Convention, CWC. The scope of analysable compounds by LC –MS/MS is similar to the 
scope of analysable compounds by LC–MS [see Section 3, Part C, Chapter II: Liquid 
chromatogr
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
the C hemical Weapons 
Convention, CWC. The scope of analysable compounds by LC –MS/MS is similar to the 
scope of analysable compounds by LC–MS [see Section 3, Part C, Chapter II: Liquid 
chromatography–atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass spectrometry (LC–API/MS).] In 
general, the procedure is applied to identify chemicals present at above 1 mg/kg 
concentration level. However, the procedure can also be used to identify relevant chemicals 
down to low μg/kg concentration levels. 
Note! Not all LC–MS/MS instrument s are described in this version ( e.g., Q–TOF and 
Orbitrap instruments are covered in Section 3, Part C, Chapter IV: Liquid chromatography–
high resolution tandem mass spectrometry. 
Note! Some features typical of most instruments from different manufacturers are referred 
to throughout the text. These are the features that the authors are aware of at the time of the 
writing of this Chapter. It is possible that similar features are also available on other 
manufacturers’ systems. 
2. Summary of the method 
LC–MS/MS measurements are carried out with modern LC–MS/MS instruments like triple 
quadrupole (QqQ) or quadrupole–time-of-flight (Q–TOF; in this Chapter also QqTO
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
systems. 
2. Summary of the method 
LC–MS/MS measurements are carried out with modern LC–MS/MS instruments like triple 
quadrupole (QqQ) or quadrupole–time-of-flight (Q–TOF; in this Chapter also QqTOF for 
clarity) or ion trap (linear or 3D) mass analysers operating in MS/MS mode. Samples are 
analysed with a LC–MS/MS instrument equipped with a similar LC column as would be 
used for a LC–MS experiment. Before each sample batch, a quality control run (QC test, see 
in Chapter 3-C-II) is carried out to verify the correct performance of the instrument (LC 
column and ionisation performance) . A quality control run, especially for a MS/MS 
experiment, is necessary to verify proper calibration of the equipment with respect to 
frequency for isolation and excitation (see paragraph 6).

LC–MS/MS techniques have two applications. The first case is where LC–MS has already 
been carried out and the chemical of interest is identified. In this case, LC –MS/MS is used 
for confirmation by the generation of characteristic product ions to strengthen the 
identification. Indeed, LC –MS with a soft ionisation source (APCI or ESI) often gives 
relatively few diagnostic ions and in most cases only the protonated or de protonated ion 
and/or the sodium adduct are present. 
Note! In-source CID could be used to fragment the quasi -molecular ions. This method, 
however, would fragment all co-eluting chemicals and would result in a mixture of fragment 
ions. In-source CID can be used for screening purposes (see Section 1, Part B, Chapter I: 
Screening). 
In the second case, LC–MS/MS could be used for s creening and identification of relevant 
chemicals by selecting characteristic product ions of chemical families or individual 
chemica
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
: 
Screening). 
In the second case, LC–MS/MS could be used for s creening and identification of relevant 
chemicals by selecting characteristic product ions of chemical families or individual 
chemicals (extracted ion chromatograms, EICs) from the total ion chromatograms (TICs) 
obtained by automated MS/MS experiments done on the more intense ions (this option is 
currently available on modern instruments, especially ion traps). In the case of a QqQ or a 
QqTOF, multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) and/or precursor ion scan experiments could 
be performed. These types of experiments (see paragraph 4.1.2) allow to selection of only 
characteristic product ions beyond the collision cell and identification of the precursor ion. 
Identification of relevant chemicals is made by comparison of the measured LC–MS/MS 
spectra to authentic reference chemical spectra or by spectrum interpretation. 
3. Safety aspects 
LC–MS/MS analyses do not require any specific safety precautions. Samples for analysis 
normally contain degradation products and are automatically injected. I n some case s, a 
sample could contain small concentrations of toxic chemicals, if the hydrolysis does not go 
to completi
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ysis 
normally contain degradation products and are automatically injected. I n some case s, a 
sample could contain small concentrations of toxic chemicals, if the hydrolysis does not go 
to completion. Normal laboratory safety measures , such as wearing protective gloves and 
goggles during sample handling in manual injections, should be used. 
Hot parts (>250 °C) of the instrument (e.g., some metallic interfaces in the external ionisation 
source) must be taken into account during operation and maintenance of instrument. 
The ion sources typically use high voltages (e.g. 2 –3 kV) for the ionisation process. Care 
must be taken to follow the manufacturers’ instructions for safe operation of the instrument. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 LC–MS/MS instrument 
Any modern LC–MS/MS instrument, capable of a scan speed of at least 1 scan/s and 
covering a mass range of at least m/z 50–600, can be used. This type of instrument allows a 
good quality of spectra and enables new applications. In practice, the mass range covered by 
the first quadrupole for QqQ or by the ion trap begins from m/z 50 due to the presence of 
water, nitrogen and carbon dioxide in the sample. 
Triple quadrupole and 3D

the first quadrupole for QqQ or by the ion trap begins from m/z 50 due to the presence of 
water, nitrogen and carbon dioxide in the sample. 
Triple quadrupole and 3D or 2D ion trap systems are unit resolution instruments over the 
entire mass range, and correspond to a resolving power of 1000 ( for QqQ) or 5000 (for ion

(ITMS) for the most efficient instruments. 
Two types of MS/MS instruments are available. First are the sequential MS/MS instruments, 
where the MS/MS experiment is performed in the same place but at different times (e.g., ion 
traps). Second are the spatial MS/MS instruments , where the MS/MS experiment is 
performed at different site with in the instrument (e.g., triple quadrupole and Q –TOF 
instruments). 
4.1.1 Characteristics of the instruments 
4.1.1.1 Triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (QqQ) 
The most common tandem -in-space mass spectrometers are triple quadrupole instruments 
that consist of two quadrupole mass analyzers separated by an RF -only (radio frequency) 
quadrupole collision cell. 
The main characteristics of a triple quadrupole instrument are the following: 
Transmission (impact on sensitivity and stability of signals) 
The rat

nly (radio frequency) 
quadrupole collision cell. 
The main characteristics of a triple quadrupole instrument are the following: 
Transmission (impact on sensitivity and stability of signals) 
The ratio of the number of ions having identical properties entering and exiting the 
quadrupole is generally 1:20. Triple quadrupole instruments are generally more sensitive for 
detecting target analytes, even in complex mixtures, and are therefore better ins quantitation 
than in screening tools. 
Scan speed (impact on sampling rate and quantitation results) 
Today, quadrupole mass spectrometer systems routinely scan at 10 ,000 u/s. Therefore, a 
comprehensive scan, even one of short duration ( e.g., an LC peak with the width of 1 s) 
would nevertheless capture each ion ten times or more in each second. Nevertheless, triple 
quadrupoles are relatively simple, easy -to-use, highly utilitarian instruments that offer a 
variety of interfaces at a relatively low cost, which explains their popularity. 
4.1.1.2 Ion trap mass spectrometer (ITMS) 
The main characteristics of ion traps are the following: 
Analytical cycle time (impact on resolution, sampling rate, quantitation results) 
In an ion t

4.1.1.2 Ion trap mass spectrometer (ITMS) 
The main characteristics of ion traps are the following: 
Analytical cycle time (impact on resolution, sampling rate, quantitation results) 
In an ion trap, the analytical cycle time consists of the following major events: 
- ICC ( Ion Charge Control, Bruker) or AGC (Automatic Gain Control, Thermo 
Scientific) pre-scan in order to ensure that the trap is always filled with the optimum 
number of charges for mass accuracy and sensitivity; 
- Ion injection (usually the rate-determining step); 
- Isolation and activation of the precursor ion within the trap; 
- Scan of the ions out of the trap (mass analysis). 
The ion injection time (filling the trap) accounts for the largest proportion of the cycle time, 
particularly for low-level components. The use of an ICC/AGC pre-scan allows a maximum

concentrations. 
Low mass cut -off (has an impact on the structural information obtained by MS/MS 
and on sensitivity) 
The low mass cut -off (LMCO) corresponds to the smallest m/z value of ions with a stable 
trajectory in the ion trap. Usually, only the product ions with a n m/z > 1/4 (3D ion trap) or 
m/z > 1/5 (linear trap used with resonant excitation) of the precursor ion have a stable 
trajectory and are trapped and detected. 
Note! Linear ion trap instruments from Thermo Scientific can be used for an experiment 
called “Pulsed Q Collision Induced Dissociation (PQD)”. This type of experiment can allow 
measurement of ions with m/z > 1/6.5.1 
Different MS/MS experiments can be run depending of the type of MS/MS instrument.

Product Ion Scan (also called Fragment Ion Scan o

text:
Different MS/MS experiments can be run depending of the type of MS/MS instrument. 
4.1.2 Tandem mass spectrometry scan modes for spatial instruments2 
Product Ion Scan (also called Fragment Ion Scan or Daughter Ion Scan) 
Firstly, ions of a chosen m/z are selected on the first quadrupole (Q1). Secondly, these ions 
collide inside the collision cell and fragment. Thirdly, product ions resulting from the 
fragmentation of the selected precursor ions are analyzed by the third quadrupole (Q3). 
For example, for analysis of diethyl methylphosphonate (DEMP): 
Selection on Q1 of precursor ions m/z 153 ([M+H]+), and then fragmentation of m/z 
153 in the collision cell . The product ions m/z 125 (loss of CH2=CH2) and m/z 97 
(losses of two CH2=CH2) are generated and detected in Q3. 
Precursor Ion Scan (also called Parent Scan) 
All ions generated from the sample are initially scanned using the first quadrupole (Q1 or 
Q). Then, these ions collide inside the collision cell and fragment. Finally, Q3 (in QqQ) or 
TOF (QqTOF) is focused on a selected m/z. All of the precursor ions that produce ions with 
the selected m/z through reaction or fragmentation are therefore detected. 
For example, fo
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
Q3 (in QqQ) or 
TOF (QqTOF) is focused on a selected m/z. All of the precursor ions that produce ions with 
the selected m/z through reaction or fragmentation are therefore detected. 
For example, for analysis of alkyl methylphosphonates: 
Selection on Q3 of product ion s m/z 95 (in negative mode). Scanning on Q1 of all 
precursor ions; this generates product ions m/z 95. This scan mode enables detection 
of the presence of alkyl methylphosphonates in an unknown sample. 
Neutral Loss Scan 
In this mode, both the first quadrupole (Q1 or Q) and the third quadrupole Q3 (QqQ) or TOF 
(QqTOF) are scanned together, but with a constant mass offset between the two. Thus, for a 
mass difference a, when ions of mass m go through first quadrupole, detection occurs if these 
ions have produced fragment ions of mass (m – a) when they leave the collision cell. This is 
a neutral loss scan, with the neutral having the mass a. 
For example, for analysis of ethyl methylphosphonic acid (EMPA): 
Precursor ion [M-H]- m/z 123 produces product ion m/z 95 by losing a CH2=CH2 alkene 
(a for this example is equal to 28 u).

Selected Reaction Monitoring (or Multiple Reaction Monitoring) 
For SRM, both the first quadrupole (Q1) and third quadrupole (Q3) are focused on selected 
masses. The ions selected by the first quadrupole (Q1) are only detected if th ey produce a 
given fragment, by a selected reaction (SRM) or by multiple reactions (MRM). The absence 
of scanning allows one to focus on the precursor and fragment ions over longer times, 
increasing the sensitivity as for Selected Ion Monitoring (MS mode), but this sensitivity is 
now associated with a high increase in selectivity. This method is often used to detect a 
selected compound in an elution timeframe during chromatography. The high selectivity 
corresponds to a low probability of detecting an interf ering compound. This reduces the 
background noise and eliminates most interference due primarily to the matrix, thereby 
improving the specificity. 
An analysis obtained by SRM or MRM on a triple
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
rf ering compound. This reduces the 
background noise and eliminates most interference due primarily to the matrix, thereby 
improving the specificity. 
An analysis obtained by SRM or MRM on a triple quadrupole is more sensitive than a 
MS/MS analysis acquired on an ion trap. This scan mode is particularly dedicated to 
quantitative analyses or confirmation analyses when the compound was already identified 
by another technique or technology. It should be mentioned that , at present, the SRM or 
MRM mode is not acce pted for Official OPCW Proficiency Tests dedicated to 
environmental samples.

4.1.3 Tandem mass spectrometry scan modes for temporal instruments 
Product Ion Scan (also called Fragment Ion Scan or MS2) 
Firstly, ions of a chosen m/z are selected by ejecting all other ions from the ion trap. Secondly, 
these chosen ions are excited (supplementary RF voltage applied) and collision induced 
dissociations (CID) with the He buffer gas inside the ion trap are produced , leading to 
product ions. Thirdly, product ions are analyzed in the ion trap by rescanning all of the mass 
range. 
Multistage tandem mass spectrometry experiments (MSn) 
Because all of the steps of the MS/MS experiment are performed at the same location, these 
steps can be run again with product ions obtained by MS/MS. After the MS/MS step, product 
ions of a chosen m/z are selected by ejecting all other product ions from the ion trap. The 
product ions at the chosen m/z are excited and fragmented to product ions (MS3 experiment). 
This process can be

4.3 Reagents 
The reagents and chemicals needed for LC–MS/MS analyses are discussed in the following

5.3 Recommended MS/MS conditions 
For each compound, several parameters must be optimized to obtain the best response in 
MS/MS. If possible, this optimization occurs by infusion with an ESI interface. This means 
that the compound is available to study. 
A solution of the compound of interest has to be prepared in a solvent mixture relatively 
close to the solvent composition at the elution time of that compound; i.e., generally, a 
mixture deionized water/acetonitrile 50/50 (v/v) with 0.2% formic acid (or acetic acid) or a 
mixture deionized water/methanol with 0.02 M ammonium formate can be used . These 
solvent proportions correspond to the elution solvent composition of many compounds and 
provide the best surface tension to obtain a stable spray. The formic acid facilitates ionisation 
in positive mode.

5.3.1 Triple quadrupole 
5.3.1.1 Optimization of MS/MS parameters 
The reference chemical must be diluted to obtain a concentration equivalent to 1 µg/ml (or 
generally between 0.5 and 20 µg/ml). 
1. The first step consists of determination of the precursor ion, based on the obtained 
MS spectra obtained both in positive and negative ion (if applicable) modes (see 
Section 3, Part C, C hapter II : Liquid chro matography–atmospheric pressure 
ionisation/mass spectrometry (LC–API/MS)). Occasionally, the protonated molecule 
[M+H]+ or the deprotonated molecule [M-H]- are not detected or are present at very 
low abundance, so that only a fragment ion ( as is the case for thiodiglycol) or an 
adduct ion, often with sodium, [M+Na]+, is observed. The ionisation mode that gives 
the best response in terms of intensity is used. The selection of the [M+Na]+ as 
precursor ion is not recommended because the sodium ion retains the charge and the 
fragments of the chemical are not detected as neutrals. 
2. The solution
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
y is used. The selection of the [M+Na]+ as 
precursor ion is not recommended because the sodium ion retains the charge and the 
fragments of the chemical are not detected as neutrals. 
2. The solution is then directly infused into the mass spectrometer by the ESI interface 
to obtain a MS/MS spectrum of the compound under standard conditions 
3. The MS/MS experiment cou ld also be used to determine the transitions of interest 
from precursor ion → product ion for MRM experiments 
4. To obtain an optimal MS/MS fragmentation, the collision energy of a given transition 
for a given capillary value must be optimized. This parameter optimization is done 
manually (by testing different values and register spectra) or automatically by the 
software (for example, use of the “MS/MS Breakdown” option), which provides the 
searched value. 
5. Capillary and collision energy values can be more prec isely optimized again by 
injecting the compound directly in to the MS source using the diverter valve while 
the mobile phase is at its elution composition and as it passes at a determined LC 
flow through the system.

First, automated MS/MS experiments can be utilised with generic collision induced 
dissociation (CID) conditions on the main precursor ions. This means that during the LC 
peak elution, MS and MS/MS experiments on the more intensive ion are alternatively 
performed. It is possible to exclude a list of ions ( for example, known interferents) or to 
include a list of preferential ions for MS/MS scan (for example, m/z of certain alkyl 
methylphosphonates). Several precursor ions during the same LC peak can be isolated and 
excited for fragmentation depending of their intensity, if option allows exclusion of the 
MS/MS spectrum registration of an already fragmented ion. The excitation voltage (tickle, 
if a resonant excitation) should be chosen in the middle of the excitation values usually used. 
If possible, a ramp of excitation values can be added in order to ensure the fragmentation of 
main precursor ions; for example, an excitation vo

main precursor ions; for example, an excitation voltage of 0 .6 Vpp with a ramp (30–200%) 
means that an averaged MS/MS spectrum is obtained per scan, corresponding to the 
combined spectra from 0.2 to 1.2 Vpp excitation voltage.

The solution is then directly infused into the mass spectrometer by the ESI interface to detect

1. To obtain an optimal fragmentation in MS/MS, the excitation voltage value must be 
optimized with a s tandard isolation window (2 u is a good compromise for unit 
resolution instrument) . This parameter optimization is done manually by t esting 
different values and register spectra. The optimized value corresponds to the value 
for which the precursor ion is presented in the MS/MS spectrum at 20 –33% of the 
main product ion. A ramp of excitation voltage can be used, depending on whether 
an important difference in fragmentation is noted for close values. 
2. After optimization of the excitation voltage step, the best isolat
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ramp of excitation voltage can be used, depending on whether 
an important difference in fragmentation is noted for close values. 
2. After optimization of the excitation voltage step, the best isolation window is then 
defined. In the case of isotopic pattern or co-eluted compounds in the real sample , 
testing an isolation window at 1 u can be helpful for selecting only the monoisotopic 
peak of your chemical of in terest. This optimization is a compromise between 
sensitivity (which increases with a large excitation window) and specificity (no 
selection of ions that do not correspond to the precursor ion fragments). 
3. Verify your optimized conditions by analysing the r eference chemical by LC –
MS/MS. 
4. Perform the LC–MS/MS analysis of your system blank and then for your real sample 
with the optimized fragmentation conditions. 
5.4 Recommended tuning and mass calibration of the MS 
Use the recommended tuning method of the inst rument. Automatic tuning and calibration 
procedures should be used, if available. Tuning and calibration in MS and MS/MS modes 
should be carried out once a month, or more often if indicated by the QC test. Printouts of 
tuning and calibration repor
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
es should be used, if available. Tuning and calibration in MS and MS/MS modes 
should be carried out once a month, or more often if indicated by the QC test. Printouts of 
tuning and calibration reports should be archived for further reference. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test in LC–MS 
The reliable identification of CWC -related compounds requires an operating system. 
Therefore, running quality control tests continuously is essential to confirm that the 
instrument is working correctly and the performance of the instrument remains stable during 
the sample analysis. 
The performance of a LC–MS instrument is controlled by carrying out a QC test run (see 
Section 3, Part C, Chapter II: Liquid chromatography–atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass 
spectrometry (LC–API/MS), where two examples of QC test mixture are described), in which 
the mass spectrometric behaviour of test compounds and the adsorption behaviour of the 
column are confirmed as acceptable.

Since performance depends on the nature of the analyzed molecules, compounds chosen as

The use of this kind of QC test mixture imposes the absolute need to verify the absence of a 
QC compound in the system by performing a blank sample run prior to the real sample run. 
6.2 Sensitivity test in LC–MS/MS or LC–MRM

6.3 Blank test 
A s olvent blank run must be carried out to avoid cross contamination of the equipment 
(e.g., contamination from the injection needle or a memory effect of the column) and thus to 
ensure the reliability of the samples analysis by eliminating all risks of false positives . 
Running a solvent blank is therefore recommended before each sample analysis by injecting 
10 µL of the same solvent (or solvent mixture) used in sample preparation. If CWC-related 
chemicals are found in the blank chromatogram, the solvent blank test should be repeated 
until the total elimination of the contamination source is confir med. All contamination 
coming from glassware, solvents, standard solution (or authentic reference solution), syringe, 
injector system, or columns must be eliminated before sample analysis is started. 
A system blank also needs to be run if a sample preparation (concentration, matrix extraction, 
etc.) is performed be
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
injector system, or columns must be eliminated before sample analysis is started. 
A system blank also needs to be run if a sample preparation (concentration, matrix extraction, 
etc.) is performed before the LC –MS/MS analysis. In this case, the solvent blank is the 
system blank. 
7 Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
At the beginning of an analysis batch, a QC test (always) and a blank test are run. When both 
tests have been accepted, samples can be analysed. Generally, 10 µl of the sample is injected.

8. Evaluation of methods 
8.1 Area of applicability 
An LC–MS/MS method can be applied to non-volatile, polar or semi -polar degradation 
products of chemical warfare agents, and some chemical warfare agents (VX, tabun ). The 
method is suitable for analyzing and identifying any chemical at a level of 10 mg/kg in the 
full scan mode and at a level of 0.1 mg/kg in the selective ion monitoring mode (SIM mode, 
target analysis only, MRM mode). 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The a dvantage of the method is the direct analysis of degradation products of chemical 
warfare agents. Thus, the sample preparation is simple and rapid due to the absence of a 
derivatization step. Furt
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
a dvantage of the method is the direct analysis of degradation products of chemical 
warfare agents. Thus, the sample preparation is simple and rapid due to the absence of a 
derivatization step. Furthermore, the LC –MS/MS method is complementary to GC –MS or 
NMR techniques. 
The disadvantage in identification using LC–MS/MS is the absence of commercial or OCAD 
databases. In -house LC –MS/MS databases should be used, but the spectra are strongly 
dependent on the configuration of the instrument used. Few characteristic ions are produced 
in LC–MS/MS compared to GC–EI/MS.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of liquid chromatography–high resolution mass spectrometry 
(LC–HRMS) in the screening and identification of degradation products of chemical warfare 
agents in aqueous samples or in aqueous extracts of solid samples. LC –HRMS is also 
applicable to some intact chemical warfare agents. The procedures described are generally 
suitable for identifying chemicals at concentrations above 1 mg/kg or 1 mg/ l and may be 
applicable at lower concentrations. 
The purpose of this chapter is to discuss the issues related to the high-resolution aspects of 
LC–MS measurements. General issues related to LC –API/MS and LC –API/MS/MS 
measurements are discussed in Section 3, Part C, Chapters II and III: Liquid 
chromatography–atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass spectrometry (LC –API/MS) and 
Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). 
2. Summary of the method 
There are several types of LC–HRMS instruments currently available: time-of-flight (TOF), 
Orbitrap, Fourie
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
) and 
Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). 
2. Summary of the method 
There are several types of LC–HRMS instruments currently available: time-of-flight (TOF), 
Orbitrap, Fourier -transform ion cyclotron (FTICR) , and magnetic sector instruments. 
Measurement with these instruments can be carried out by operating in full scanning mode 
for screening and in some instruments also in selected ion monitoring (SIM) mode for target 
analysis.
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

In order to classify as a high-resolution instrument, it must operate at resolution higher than 
10,000. High -end instruments will normally operate at much higher resolution settings. 
Mass calibration is very important to guarantee high-quality results. The frequency of the 
mass calibration depends on the instrument and can vary from daily to weekly calibration. 
In many HRMS instruments, a chemical is introduced into the instrument during the run to 
produce so-called “lock mass”, which can be used to calibrate the mass scale for each scan. 
Both ESI and APCI are broadly applicable to CWC -related chemicals, e.g. degradation 
products of nerve agents and vesicants, although some analytes will be more easily detected 
and identified using one of these ionization methods. ESI is used for thermally labile and 
highly polar ionic analytes such as saxitoxin and high molecular mass mat
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ytes will be more easily detected 
and identified using one of these ionization methods. ESI is used for thermally labile and 
highly polar ionic analytes such as saxitoxin and high molecular mass materials such as ricin. 
Samples are most commonly analysed using a reversed phase (C18 or C8), HPLC or UHPLC 
column. Column dimensions are left to personal preference, but for HPLC analysis 100 –
150 x 2.1 mm columns packed with 3 –5 μm particles are broadly applicable . For UHPLC 
analysis, columns can be 50–100 mm long with < 2 µm particles. 
For more details on LC analysis and ionisation, please refer to Section 3, Part C, Chapters II 
and III: Liquid chromatography–atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass spectrometry (LC –
API/MS) and Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). 
Before each sample batch, a quality control run (QC test, see below) should be carried out 
to verify the correct performance of the instrument, using a method created for the QC test 
sample. The correct mass calibration of the instrument should be check ed using the QC 
sample data. After a passed QC test, a method for the sample of interest is cre ated, and the 
sample is analysed. In some in
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
orrect mass calibration of the instrument should be check ed using the QC 
sample data. After a passed QC test, a method for the sample of interest is cre ated, and the 
sample is analysed. In some instruments the analysis would be best carried out using a full 
scan method and in some instruments using a SIM method. 
The target analysis of chemicals of interest is carried out by selecting the exact masses of 
characteristic ions for the individual chemicals (at least three ions must be selected for each 
target chemical). In SIM methods, the ions must be defined before the run, which limits the 
collected data but enhances the sensitivity. On the other hand, full scan methods collect large 
amount of data, which can be analysed, e.g. by extracting high resolution ion chromatograms 
using narrow mass windows. The full scan methods are less sensitive than SIM methods. 
Identification of a chemical using HRMS requires that molecular ion or adduct ion is found 
with correct mass accuracy (mass error ≤ 5 ppm) and that the retention time of the 
chromatographic peak is within acceptable range from the reference, e.g. ±0.2 min. 
The higher information content of the high -resolution data
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
(mass error ≤ 5 ppm) and that the retention time of the 
chromatographic peak is within acceptable range from the reference, e.g. ±0.2 min. 
The higher information content of the high -resolution data makes the use of full scan LC–
HRMS very useful for screening and identification of unknown chemicals. Therefore, many 
laboratories measure LC–HRMS data (and store it for possible later use) in addition to more 
targeted LC–MS/HRMS. A full scan method can be quite generic and does not need to be 
modified. Naturally, generic ion source conditions would not be optimal for all chemicals. 
Structure elucidation of unknown chemicals that are not present in databases is a significant 
challenge in OPCW Proficiency Tests. The accurate masses of the molecular, fragment ions, 
or isotopic ratio can be measured using LC –MS/HRMS. The corresponding elemental 
compositions can then be calculated and used to elucidate possible molecular structure. 
Examples for structure elucidation using HRMS are in Paragraph 7.2 below.

3. Safety aspects 
LC–HRMS analyses require no specific safety precautions. Samples for analysis normally 
contain degradation products and are automatically injected. In some cases, a sample could 
contain small concentrations of toxic chemicals, if the hydrolysis does not go to completion. 
Normal labor atory protective gear , such as gloves and goggles , should be used when 
handling chemicals or samples. 
Some parts of the instrument are hot (>250 °C). Typically, these are located in the ion source. 
During normal operations touching the hot parts should be avoided and before maintenance 
operations they must be let to cool down before handling them. 
The ion sources typically use high voltages (e.g. 2 –3 kV) for the ionisation process. Care 
must be taken to follow the manufacturers’ instructions for safe operation of the instrument. 
Grounding of the ESI source is necessary to
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
gh voltages (e.g. 2 –3 kV) for the ionisation process. Care 
must be taken to follow the manufacturers’ instructions for safe operation of the instrument. 
Grounding of the ESI source is necessary to avoid electric shocks and must always be carried 
out according to the manufacturers’ instructions. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 LC–HRMS instruments 
Any modern LC–HRMS instrument – including TOF, Orbitrap, FTICR and magnetic sector 
instruments – that is capable of at least a resolution of 10,000 and covers a mass range of at 
least m/z 50–1000 can be used. The mass range naturally depends on the application, but this 
range covers most CWC-related applications. In practice, the mass range upper limit for the 
scan should be adjusted to suitable value, typically between m/z 400 and 600 depending on 
the application. 
The mass accuracy of ± 5 ppmi or better – limit for high resolution measurementsii,iii – should 
also be obtainable with most modern instruments. It should be noted that in many 
instruments, the mass accuracy will be come worse at low m/z values. For low molecular 
weight chemicals, e.g. methylphosphonic acid ([M+H]+ = m/z 97.00491), it may be difficult 
to meet the requirem
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
instruments, the mass accuracy will be come worse at low m/z values. For low molecular 
weight chemicals, e.g. methylphosphonic acid ([M+H]+ = m/z 97.00491), it may be difficult 
to meet the requirement for ± 5 ppm accuracy. However, the ± 5 ppm accuracy requirement 
is set in OPCW criteria and it must be met in reporting of HRMS data. Typically, instruments 
operating at higher resolution, e.g. R > 40,000, can measure the masses more accurately as 
the mass peaks are narrower.iv 
 
 
i Mass accuracy is defined as (measured m/z value – theoretical value)/theoretical value * 
1,000,000 and presented as parts per million (ppm). 
ii Work Instruction for the Reporting of the Results of the OPCW Profi ciency Tests 
(QDOC/LAB/WI/PT04) (Note! This document is updated for each OPCW Proficiency Test) 
iii Work Instruction for the Reporting of the Results of the OPCW Biomedical Proficiency Tests 
(QDOC/LAB/WI/BioPT04) (Note! This document is updated for each OPCW Biomedical 
Proficiency Test) 
iv Example: High-frequency Orbitrap instrument at resolution 120,000 is expected to produce mass 
accuracy < 3 ppm with external calibration and < 1 ppm with internal calibration.

4.2 LC–MS/HRMS instruments 
LC–MS/HRMS experiment can be conducted on high -resolution mass spectrometers with 
some kind of collision cell and is capable of performing at least two mass analysis stages . 
Instrumentation performance requirements for LC –MS/HRMS are the same as for LC –
HRMS and are met by most modern instruments. 
In most tandem HRMS instruments, the first mass analysis is performed using a low 
resolution analyser, e.g. quadrupole (Q–TOF and some Orbitrap instruments) or ion trap 
(some TOF and some Orbitrap instruments). In these cases, the ion selection is an inherently 
low-resolution process and precursor ions cannot be selected by their exact masses. 
The advantage of using quadrupole as the first MS stage is that it can rapidly and 
continuously filter the precursor ions. In many instruments, the mass range of the quadrupole 
can be adjusted. In addition , if
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e of using quadrupole as the first MS stage is that it can rapidly and 
continuously filter the precursor ions. In many instruments, the mass range of the quadrupole 
can be adjusted. In addition , if a quadrupole -Orbitrap is used in LC -HRMS mode, the 
quadrupole can be used to limit the range of precursor ions entering the Orbitrap, which will 
increase the sensitivity of the measurement. 
Instruments using ion traps for the first MS stage are capable of producing LC–
MS/MS/HRMS (and higher) data. In ion trap -Orbitrap systems, the ion trap stages will be 
much faster than the Orbitrap stage and therefore will not considerably change the total scan 
time. In the high-end instruments, such as Orbitrap Fusion (with both quadrupole and linear 
ion trap), the ion trap and Orbitrap can operate in a parallel manner and, therefore, operate 
at optimal scan rates. It should be noted that ion trap will produce softer fragmentation – 
only fragmenting the precursor ion – compared to quadrupole collision cells. 
Magnetic sector instruments can be built as tandem mass spectrometers, but they are mostly 
LC–HRMS instruments. In sector instruments, the configuration will determine the availab
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e collision cells. 
Magnetic sector instruments can be built as tandem mass spectrometers, but they are mostly 
LC–HRMS instruments. In sector instruments, the configuration will determine the available 
measurement modes, e.g. in EBEQ v instrument, the selection of precursor ions would be 
performed using high mass accuracy a nd the product ions would be measured using low 
resolution. 
FTICR can always use high mass accuracy for all mass analysis stages. These instruments 
are also capable of producing the highest mass resolution, which can be up to 1,000,000 
depending on the field strength of the magnet. 
5. Experimental 
The following paragraphs highlight the issues related to HRMS measurements. For more 
details on conditions for LC and MS analysis in general, please refer to Section 3, Part C, 
Chapters II and III: Liquid chromato graphy–atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass 
spectrometry (LC–API/MS) and Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC –
MS/MS). 
 
 
 
v EBEQ means configuration where there the instrument consists of electric, magnetic and electric 
sectors followed by a quadrupole.

5.1 Scan speed 
In high resolution instruments , the scan speed can be dependent on the resolution settings: 
e.g. in Orbitrap instruments, the scan speed is halved when the resolution is doubled. The 
parameters of the chromatographic separation, which affect the width of the 
chromatographic peak must be matched with the selected resolution setting to produce 
enough data points for the chromatogram. 
5.2 Mass calibration 
For maintaining mass accuracy in high resolution measurements, the instrument needs to be 
tuned and calibrated according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Automatic tuning and 
calibration procedures are us ed if available. Full tuning and calibration is carried out 
following instrument servicing. Mass calibration should be performed before commencing 
analysis of sample batches. 
In many high resolution instruments, a calibration chemical is injected in the
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ut 
following instrument servicing. Mass calibration should be performed before commencing 
analysis of sample batches. 
In many high resolution instruments, a calibration chemical is injected in the in strument 
continuously to serve as internal mass reference. This so -called lock mass in then used by 
the instrument software to correct for small shifts in mass axis. The chemical and the way it 
is introduced depend on the instrument and the application. In most instruments, in addition 
to the chemicals suggested by the manufacturer, users can use their own chemicals provided 
that their mass peaks do not overlap with the peaks in the analyte spectra. Nonetheless, great 
care should be taken to choose the lock mass chemical and its concentration as it can cause 
ion suppression in ESI source due to electrospray charge competition, thus reducing the 
sensitivity of the analyses. The reference chemical may be introduced using an external

5.4 Scan modes for LC–HRMS2 and LC–HRMSn measurements 
There are several ways to achieve LC–HRMS2 and LC–HRMSn measurements in the current 
instruments. 
Most instrument types would have a quadrupole or ion trap as the first MS stage for selecting 
the precursor ion for collision experiment. The ion trap instruments are capable of producing 
MS2 or MS n fragmentations of the precursor ion. FTICR instruments would typically 
perform MS 2 or MS n consecutively in the ICR cell. In general, the methods HRMS 
instruments would
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:

MS2 or MS n fragmentations of the precursor ion. FTICR instruments would typically 
perform MS 2 or MS n consecutively in the ICR cell. In general, the methods HRMS 
instruments would be similar to those on the low resolution instruments described in Section 
3, Part C, Chapter III: Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS)]. 
It should be noted that in methods using quadrupole or ion traps for precursor ion selection, 
these stages are performed in low resolution. Only FTICR and TOF/TOF instruments can 
produce real LC–HRMS/HRMS data. 
In other types of instruments, this data could be produced by measuring both LC–HRMS 
and LC–MS/HRMS consecutively in one scan cycle, where both precursor and product ion 
can be measured at high resolution. The OPCW would consider this a LC –HRMS/HRMS 
data, even though the actual parent selected for collision experiment is selected at low 
resolution. True LC–HRMS/HRMS data can be achieved only in an FTICR instrument.

MS/HMRS scan where all precursor ions in a mass range (e.g. m/z 400–1000) are selected 
in wide windows (typically

5.5 Calculation of accurate masses and molecular formulae 
When calculating theoretical m/z values at high resolution for target chemicals, care should 
be taken to obtain the correct result. The following parameters/procedures should be used: 
 use monoisotopic masses, not the average massed including all isotopesvii 
 calculate the mass using at least four decimals 
 add the correct ionisation in the molecular structure, i.e. positive or negative charge 
as well as any radical as shown in Figure 1. 
The calculation of molecular formulae from measure ments depends on the software in use, 
but the e.g. the following parameters may be possible to set: 
 Charge. You will have to set the charge of the target molecule correctly as this will 
impact the results as shown in Figure 1. 
 Is nitrogen rule being used? If it is, prediction of even-electron ions should be used 
for ions (bo
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e charge of the target molecule correctly as this will 
impact the results as shown in Figure 1. 
 Is nitrogen rule being used? If it is, prediction of even-electron ions should be used 
for ions (both cations and anions) and odd-electron ions should be used for radical 
ions. In LC –MS, ionization will typically produce protonated or deprotonated 
molecules. However, in some exceptional cases, also radical ions can be seen in LC–
MS or LC–MS/MS spectra. 
 Mass tolerance. Depending on the inst rument, resolution and mass accuracy 
different tolerance (e.g. 3 or 5 ppm) can be used for producing the list of candidate 
formulae. 
 Ranges for possible elements. This is critical parameter. If too few elements are 
included in the calculation, the correct formula may be missing from the result listing. 
Especially, isotopically labelled molecules require special attention. If an overly wide 
range of elements is incl uded, the result list will be too long , and it will be difficult 
to identify the correct formula. All available additional information should be used, 
e.g. isotope patterns, to limit the range of elements. 
 Unsaturation of the result formula (DBE). viii The DBE shoul
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
entify the correct formula. All available additional information should be used, 
e.g. isotope patterns, to limit the range of elements. 
 Unsaturation of the result formula (DBE). viii The DBE should always be positive 
number.ix It should be integer for radical ions and decimal number “x.5” for ions. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
vii For example, in ChemBioDraw software you should use “Exact mass” 
viii Unsaturation of a molecule is des cribed by Double Bond Equivalent (DBE), which can be 
calculated using formula DBE = X - Y/2 + Z/2 +1, where X is the sum of carbon and silicon, Y is 
the sum of hydrogen and halogens and Z is sum of nitrogen, phosphorus and arsenic in the 
molecule. 
ix There is one significant exception to this: adduct ions may produce a negative DBE, e.g. Na + 
adduct DBE = -0.5 and NH4+ adduct DBE = -1.5.

typically all be overlapping to a single isotope peak. At high resolution, these isotope ions

characteristic for different elements and can be used to confirm the presence of a certain 
element in the analyte . This can often be used to select the correct formula among several 
candidates. The values for fully separated isotopic peaks are shown in

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1 Screening 
Extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) may be used to locate chemicals or classes of chemicals 
which may be masked by interfering chemicals in the total ion chromatogram (TIC). Specific 
ions can be referred to chemicals in tables in Section 3, Part C, Chapter II: Liquid 
chromatography–atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass spectrometry (LC–API/MS), but for 
HRMS these have to be calculated with exact mass. 
Water samples, organic liquids, and aqueous/organic extracts of soil or solid samples are 
analysed directly or after solvent change by LC–HRMS to screen for a wide range of CWC-
related chemicals, especially degradation products of CW agents. 
The a nalyses are typically performed with ESI , but APCI can also be used from some 
compounds. The most typical column type for CWC-chemicals is C18. For some very polar 
chemicals (e.g. saxi toxin or a
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
a nalyses are typically performed with ESI , but APCI can also be used from some 
compounds. The most typical column type for CWC-chemicals is C18. For some very polar 
chemicals (e.g. saxi toxin or alkyphosphonic acids) a HILIC column could be a feasible 
option. For more detailed description see Section 3, Part C, Chapter II: Liquid 
chromatography–atmospheric pressure ionisation/mass spectrometry (LC–API/MS). 
For screening, the HRMS data are acquired in full scan mode . The search for relevant 
chemicals can be performed either automatically or manually. Automatic screening first 
performs peak detection and then searches the found exact masses against a database 
containing target chemicals. The database typically contains the molecular formulae, which 
the software uses to calculate exact mass values and possibly also isotopic patterns. The 
findings must always be verified by the user. Most manufacturers have data processing 
software for this kind of screening. 
Manual screening is based on the use of extract ion chromatograms (EICs). For HRMS data, 
the mass window used for the EIC can be very narrow. See paragraph 7.2.2 for the effects 
of different mass windows. Before t
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
g is based on the use of extract ion chromatograms (EICs). For HRMS data, 
the mass window used for the EIC can be very narrow. See paragraph 7.2.2 for the effects 
of different mass windows. Before the actual extraction of ion chromatograms, 
chromatogram of a blank sample can be subtracted from the sample chromatogram. In this 
case, care should be taken to avoid distortion of the data. Many data processing software can 
automatically assign molecular formulas to peak in a mass spectrum, which helps in 
evaluation of the data. Special attention will be paid to chemicals containing heteroatoms 
such as phosphorous, sulphur and nitrogen. 
A clear problem in HRMS screening is that if the database (automatic screening) or the list 
of target chemicals (manual screening) are incomplete, some chemicals may be missed. The 
list of possible target chemicals can be very long as a typical task for analysis of CWC -

7.2 Identification 
Identification can be based on interpretation of a spectrum or comparison with a library 
spectrum, if available. Confirmation of identity is preferably by comparison with a spectrum 
from an authentic reference chemical. Commercial or OPCW databases of LC –HRMS 
spectra of CWC -related chemicals are currently unavailable, although many such spectra 
have been published in scientific journals. 
The final identification must always be approved by an experienced analyst. 
Unknown chemicals in OPCW Proficiency tests are chemicals that are not in OPCW or 
public databases. They might be CWC-related chemicals or irrelevant chemicals spiked into 
the samples as background c
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
nknown chemicals in OPCW Proficiency tests are chemicals that are not in OPCW or 
public databases. They might be CWC-related chemicals or irrelevant chemicals spiked into 
the samples as background chemicals. Sometimes, these unknown background chemicals 
also need to be identified to make sure they are not CWC-related chemicals. However, 
structure elucidation of unknown chemicals that are not pre sent in databases is a big 
challenge in OPCW Proficiency Tests. The accurate masses of the molecular and fragment 
ions were measured using LC –MS/HRMS. The corresponding elemental compositions are 
calculated and used to elucidate possible molecular structure. 
The following paragraphs 7.2.1 through 7.2.4 provide examples of identification of 
chemicals by LC–HRMS or LC–MS/HRMS. 
7.2.1 Example 1: Identification of N, N-dialkylaminoethane-2-sulfonic acids and a 
similar compound in 21st PT 
The sample was directly analysed using LC–TOF. Two chemicals were found with the same 
nominal mass for the deprotonated molecule s. However, the exact masses differed by 
0.0326 u as shown in Figure 3. These two chemicals were clearly not isomer ic. Their 
elemental compositions were calculated fro
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
for the deprotonated molecule s. However, the exact masses differed by 
0.0326 u as shown in Figure 3. These two chemicals were clearly not isomer ic. Their 
elemental compositions were calculated from the exact mass and, from these, the degrees of 
unsaturation (DU). Based on the evaluation of the data the latter peak at 4.50 min was 
N,N-diisopropylaminoethane-2-sulfonic acid. The chemical eluting at 2.88 min had one 
additional double bond or ring based on the unsaturation. A possible cyclic structure has 
been presented for this chemical in Fig ure 3. This chemical would be further than one 
reaction step away from triethanolamine (Schedule 3.B.17) according to the current OPCW 
Proficiency Test rules.

This example presents the identification of bis(isopropyl-d7) methylphosphonate in 32nd PT. 
Aqueous sample 326 was extracted by DCM, the extraction was then analy sed by GC with 
different selective detectors and GC –MS. One chemical containing P, but no S or N was

The sample was then analysed by LC–Q-TOF to determine the elemental composition of the

Metal fragment (aluminum sheet at the size of 4 cm × 4 cm with sample code 739) was 
wiped by four cotton swabs previously moistened by DCM, and then these wiped cotton 
swabs were extracted with 10 mL DCM. An LC–MS sample was made from this extract and 
analysed using by LC–Q-TOF. 
This sample had been spiked with BZ by sample preparation lab, which was identified in the 
sample (peak at 5.27 min in ESI+ run in Fig ure 7). In the analysis, however, an additional 
chemical is seen at 5.41 min in ESI+. Calculated m olecular formula for this chemical was 
C22H25NO3Cl. No matching chemical could be seen in GC –MS analysis. In ESI run, an 
adduct with formic acid could also be seen. 
The spectra for BZ and the unknown chemical are shown in Figure 8. In the spectrum of the 
unknown

text:
emical could be seen in GC –MS analysis. In ESI run, an 
adduct with formic acid could also be seen. 
The spectra for BZ and the unknown chemical are shown in Figure 8. In the spectrum of the 
unknown chemical, a peak is seen at m/z 176.0851. This peak clearly contains a chlorine 
atom and, based on accurate mass, has the molecular formula C 6H7ClNO3. This peak was 
assigned to a quaternary chloromethyleneammonium 3-quinuclidinol fragment and matched 
the reference spectrum well. The unknown chemical was therefore identified as quaternary 
chloromethyleneammonium 3-quinuclidinyl benzilate. 
Based on the analysis results, it was determined that BZ probably forms quaternary 
chloromethyleneammonium compounds when DCM is used as the solvent. This reaction 
could happen to any tertiary aliphatic amine.

8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
LC–HRMS methods can be applied to many degradation products of chemical warfare 
agents and to some intact agents that are relatively stable in aqueous solution. The HRMS 
analysis can be performed for the same sample samples as for LC–MS. 
The sensitivity of the analysis varies depending on the type of chemical and may be better 
with either ESI or APCI methods. In most cases, non-targeted screening can be performed 
at the concentration level of the OPCW proficiency tests for environmental samples (i.e. 
down to 1 ppm level). Targeted screening can be performed at the concentration level 
suitable for OPCW proficiency test for biomedical samples as well as OPCW trace analysis 
sample (i.e. down 1–10 ppb level). 
Negative ion methods are selective for acidic chemicals. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The advantages and disadvantages
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
cal samples as well as OPCW trace analysis 
sample (i.e. down 1–10 ppb level). 
Negative ion methods are selective for acidic chemicals. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The advantages and disadvantages of LC–HRMS analysis are generally the same as for LC–
MS and LC–MS/MS. 
To maintain the high mass accuracy, the HRMS instruments require more frequent 
calibration than low-resolution instruments. 
One extra advantage is that the selectivity of HRMS methods is higher than that of the low-
resolution methods . Through the use of narrower EIC mass window s, clean er 
chromatograms of target chemical can be obtained as ions of background interference are 
more efficiently filtered from the data.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of capillary electrophoresis (CE) with indirect ultraviolet 
(UV) detection for the separation and subsequent analysis of alkylphosphonic acids and 
related monoesters. Species are separated in CE by the ir electrophoretic mobilities. This 
method has many advantages , including low sample consumption and narrow peak widths 
for excellent analyte separation. Detection (indirect UV) is achieved by using a buffer system 
containing a background electrolyte (phenylphosphonic acid) and continuously monitoring 
a
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
peak widths 
for excellent analyte separation. Detection (indirect UV) is achieved by using a buffer system 
containing a background electrolyte (phenylphosphonic acid) and continuously monitoring 
a specific UV-absorbing background. The loss of signal indicates when non-chromophore-
containing analytes have been detected. Generally, the procedure is used fo r qualitative 
identification of chemicals above 1 mg/l (ppm). However, the procedure can also be utilised 
for identifying relevant chemicals down to sub-ppm concentration levels. 
2. Summary of the method 
Alkylphosphonic acid degradation products of chemical warfare agents can be detected in 
aqueous samples and extracts . If necessary, aqueous samples are prepared by using a 
combination of On -Guard sample clean -up cartridges to remove chloride and /or sulfate 
interferences. Capillary electrophoresis with a reversed electro-osmotic flow (EOF) buffer 
system and indirect UV detection is used to separate and detect the alkylphosphonic acids. 
Before each sample batch, a quality control run (QC test, refer to Section 6.1) is carried out 
to verify the correct performance of the instrument, and a blank run is used to verify
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
hosphonic acids. 
Before each sample batch, a quality control run (QC test, refer to Section 6.1) is carried out 
to verify the correct performance of the instrument, and a blank run is used to verify the 
absence of alkylphosphonic acids and related monoesters. Screening for alkylphosphonic 
acids is carried out by comparing relative migration times of peaks in the electropherograms 
of unknowns versus the migration times of peaks in a sample made from authentic reference 
chemicals. 
3. Safety aspects 
CE analysis does not require any specific precautions concerning safety . Samples to be 
analysed normally contain only small concentrations of toxic chemicals. Normal laboratory 
safety measures such as donning appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) such as 
gloves, lab coats and safety glasses during sample handling should be used.

6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The reliable identification of Chemical Weapons Convention ( CWC)-related compounds 
requires that the data produced by the instrument is correct . Therefore, it is essential to 
continuously run quality control tests to confirm correct and stable instrument performance 
during the sample analysis. 
An instrument performance check is a suggested verification proced ure; instrument 
performance for use with CWC-related compounds is determined by anal ysing a check 
standard containing ca. 10.0 µg/ml isopropyl methylphosphonic acid (IMPA), each day the 
instrument is used to anal yse a sample. The instrument is accept able for use if the data 
produced from the test compound meets the following requirement : peak area of IMPA ( a 
10.0 µg/ml solution) shall be no less than 8.0 area counts on the diode array detector set at 
254 nm with indirect UV detection.

6.3 Blank tests 
The running of blanks is highly recommended to check for any possible contamination 
coming from the sample preparation (method blank) or the instrument (system blank). If the 
system blank shows contamination, a solvent blank run with the same solvent used in sample 
preparation must be run on the instrument to eliminate the possibility of contamination due 
to the equipment (e.g. contamination from the syringe or the memory effect of the 
equipment). A method blank will test for any contamination that would result from the 
sample preparation. 
If CWC -related chemicals are found in any blank electropherogram, the blank tests are 
repeated after eliminating the possible contamination source. All contamina tion coming 
from glassware, solvents, standard solutions (or authentic reference solutions), syringes, the 
autosampler system or columns must be eliminated before sample analysis is started. 
7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of anal

text:
standard solutions (or authentic reference solutions), syringes, the 
autosampler system or columns must be eliminated before sample analysis is started. 
7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
Multiple samples are anal ysed using the Agilent -CE autosampler with a sequence table 
containing the respective information for each sample . All sample s must have unique 
identifiers. In the beginning of an analysis batch, a QC test and a blank test are always run. 
When all tests have been acce pted, samples can be analysed. Identification of a compound 
determined by this method is based on a comparison of the sample migration time to the 
standard solution migrati on time. The relative migration time (RMT) of the sampl e 
component must be within ±0.20 RMT units of the RMT of the standard component within 
each batch (current OPCW criteria limit RTs to ±0.1 min of the reference standard ). The 
approximate migration times for each component are: MPA, 3.25 min; EMPA, 3.33 min ; 
IMPA, 3.41 min; iBMPA, 3.47 min; CMPA 3.56 min; and PMPA, 3.63 min. In order to track 
migration time changes, a QC standard should be run at least every 10 samples. It is 
recommended that batches
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
IMPA, 3.41 min; iBMPA, 3.47 min; CMPA 3.56 min; and PMPA, 3.63 min. In order to track 
migration time changes, a QC standard should be run at least every 10 samples. It is 
recommended that batches (sequences) should be kept under 25 total injections, incl uding 
all standards, samples and controls. A freshly ampoulised vial of electrolyte solution needs 
to be placed into the appropriate vial slot in the autosam pler before each batch is run. This 
will help to ensure that the electrolyte will not be depleted a nd migration time changes will 
be kept to a minimum. 
Note! According to the current OPCW rules, a blank run (method blank) is required before 
each sample analysis. 
7.2 Identification 
The final identification must always be approved by an experienced analyst. 
Identification is based on RMT and comparison with an authentic reference chemical. The 
recorded RMT in the electropherograms (reference and unknown) must be within ±0.1 
minutes of each other. The signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio of a recorded peak mus t be greate r 
than five . The S/N can be calculated by visual inspection or through the use of an S/N 
calculator in the software. 
Note! If extra peaks are present

8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
This CE method can be applied to identification of phosphonic acid degradation products of 
chemical warfare agents in aqueous samples and extracts . The method is suitable for 
analysing and identifying alkylphosphonic acids at ≥500 ng/ml (ppb) concentration levels. 
8.2 Advantages/disadvantages 
Advantages of the identification method using CE are reliability and sensitivity . Modern 
instruments are easy to use , and the identification does not rely on any derivatisation 
techniques. 
A d isadvantage is that the technique requires primarily aqueous samples, and the buffer 
system used in this method is specific for anal ysing and identifying alkylphosphonic acids 
and monoesters only. Other buffer systems and methods would need to be developed to 
expand the method for other CWC-related compounds.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of ion-exchange chromatography in the separation and 
analysis of alkylphosphonic acids using conductivity and/or mass spectrometry detection. 
Ion-exchange chromatography involves the separation of target analytes based on 
coulombic interactions of the charged species with an ionic stationary phase. This procedure 
uses anion ex change chromatography coupled with conductivity detection to identify 
analytes above a 1 mg/l (ppm) concentration level. The use of a mass spectrometer allows 
for the detection of analytes
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
anion ex change chromatography coupled with conductivity detection to identify 
analytes above a 1 mg/l (ppm) concentration level. The use of a mass spectrometer allows 
for the detection of analytes at much lower (sub-ppm) concentration levels. 
2. Summary of the method 
Ion chromatography (IC) is carried out using a modern IC instrument equipped with a 
conductivity detector (CD) and an optional mass spectrometry (MS) detector. Aqueous 
samples are anal ysed with an IC –CD instrument equipped with an analytical and guard 
column containing an anion -exchange medium. Before each sample batch an instrument 
performance test and quality control (QC) standard is run to verify the correct performance 
of the instrument. Additionally, a blank run is performed to verify the absence o f 
alkylphosphonic acids. Identification of analytes : methylphosphonic acid (MPA), ethyl 
methylphosphonic acid (EMPA), isopropyl methylphosphonic acid (IMPA), isobutyl 
methylphosphonic acid (iBMPA), cyclohexyl methylphosphonic acid (CMPA) and 
pinacolyl methylphosphonic acid (PMPA) is made by comparison of the retention times in 
chromatograms of the unknowns to that of authentic reference chemicals. Wit
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
yl methylphosphonic acid (CMPA) and 
pinacolyl methylphosphonic acid (PMPA) is made by comparison of the retention times in 
chromatograms of the unknowns to that of authentic reference chemicals. With MS 
detection, spectra of unknowns and authentic reference chemicals can also be compared.

5.3 Recommended tuning of the IC and MS instruments 
Use the recommended tuning method s of the instrument s. An a utomatic tuning and 
calibration procedure should be used, if available. Tuning and calibration should be carried 
out once a week , or more often if indicated by the QC test. Printouts of tuning and 
calibration reports should be archived for further reference. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The reliable identification of Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC )-related compounds 
requires that the data produced by the instrument is correct. Therefore, it is essential to 
continuously run QC tests to confirm correct and stable instrument performance during the 
sample analysis. 
An instrument performance check is a suggested verification procedure; instrument 
performance f or use with CWC -related compounds is determined by anal ysing a check 
standard containing ca. 5.0 µg/ml phenyphosphonic acid (PPA), each day the instrument is
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
procedure; instrument 
performance f or use with CWC -related compounds is determined by anal ysing a check 
standard containing ca. 5.0 µg/ml phenyphosphonic acid (PPA), each day the instrument is 
used to analyse a sample. 
The instrument is accepted for use if the MS and IC data produced from each test compound 
meet the following requirements: 
1. Signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio for each test chemical is >5:1 in the chromatograms. The 
evaluation is done visually or automatically if available. 
2. The m/z values of the major ions of each test chemical are correct, and no extra ions 
above 5% are present (the mass range to be printed must extend 10 m/z units beyond 
the molecular mass, so that the whole relevant mass spectrum is registered). 
Figure 1 shows a typical conductivity chromatogram of a QC test sample indicating good 
instrument performance.

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
Multiple samples are anal ysed using the Dionex autosampler (AS) with a sequence table 
containing the respective information for each sample. All samples must have unique 
identifiers. At the beginning of an analysis batch, a QC standard test and a solvent blank 
test are run. When all tests have been accepted, samples can be analysed. Identification of 
a compound determined by this method is based on a comparison of the sample retention 
time (RT) to the standard-solution RT. The RT of the analyte must be within ±0.2 minutes 
of the RT of the reference standard. The approximate RTs for each component using IC−CD 
are: EMPA, 8.93 min; IMPA, 9.22 min; iBMPA, 11.01 min; CMPA, 13.08 min; PMPA 
13.37 min; and MPA, 18.58 min. In order to track migration time changes, a QC standard 
should be run at least every 10 samples. It is recommended that batches (sequences) should 
be kept under 25 total injections, including
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
min. In order to track migration time changes, a QC standard 
should be run at least every 10 samples. It is recommended that batches (sequences) should 
be kept under 25 total injections, including all standards, samples, and controls. 
Note! According to the current OPCW rules, a blank run (method blank) is required before 
each sample analysis. 
7.2 Identification 
The final identification must always be approved by an experienced analyst. 
Identification is based on comparison with an authentic reference chemical. The recorded 
RT in the chromatograms (reference and unknown) must be within ±0.2 minutes of each 
other. The signal-to-noise ratio of a recorded peak must be greater than 5. The S/N can be 
calculated by visual inspection or through the use of a S/N calculator in the software. If 
mass spectrometric detection is used, then the recorded spectr a (reference and unknown) 
must be at least 10 m/z units above the molecular weight of the precursor and be similar in 
spectral quality. 
Note! If extra peaks are present in the chromatogram within the ±0.2 min window due to a 
complex matrix, a chromatogram with standard addition of the reference standard must also 
be provid
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
quality. 
Note! If extra peaks are present in the chromatogram within the ±0.2 min window due to a 
complex matrix, a chromatogram with standard addition of the reference standard must also 
be provided to confirm the identity of the peak in the chromatogram of the unknown sample. 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
This IC method can be applied to the identification of phosphonic acid degradation products 
of chemical warfare age nts in aqueous samples and extracts. The method is suitable for 
analysing and identifying alkylphosphonic acids at ≥1 µg/ml (ppm) concentration levels via 
conductivity detection and at ≥250 ng/ml (ppb) via mass spectrometric detection. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The a dvantages of both the I C–CD and the IC –MS methods are their reliability and 
sensitivity. Modern instruments are easy to use, and the identification does not rely on any 
derivatisation techniques. The use of an IC –MS/MS method with MRMs allows for the 
selectivity of individual ions corresponding to specific phosphonic acids. However, the use

of a full -scan MS method may be necessary as a screen to first qualitatively detect the 
presence of phosphonic acids in the samples. The IC–MS or IC–MS/MS methods can then 
be used as a positive identification and/or a quantitative analysis technique. Disadvantages 
in identification using anion-exchange chromatography are that the technique requires 
primarily aqueous samples, and other common anions, such as fluoride, chloride, bromide, 
nitrite, nitrate, sulphate, phosphate, carbonate, chlorate, chlorite and perchlorate , may 
potentially cause interference when using conductivity detection. It may be necessary to 
perform sample cleanup to remove some of these interferences or to use an MS detectio n 
technique. A mass spectrometer is significantly more expensive than an IC system with a 
conductivity detector.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of high-resolution nuclear magnetic r esonance (NMR) 
spectrometry utili sing one -dimensional 1H NMR experiments for the screening and 
identification of chemical warfare agents, their precursors and degradation /reaction 
products of chemicals related to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). Generally, the 
procedure is for identifying chemicals above the 1 µg/ml concentration level. NMR 
measurements are carried out with modern NMR instruments typically equipped with 
5-mm NMR probe heads.

2. Summary of the method 
NMR techniques are commonly used fo r structural elucidation. With the 1H NMR 
spectrum interpretation, a set of information is obtained in the form of NMR parameters 
(chemical shifts and coupling constants) that converge to a chemical structure. 1H NMR 
spectroscopy can also be used as a screening method and give information about chemical 
families. Identification of a compound is achieved by comparison with reference spectra 
included in a computer database or spectrum library, through comparison with a spectrum 
of the authentic compound , or w ith standard addition of the authentic compound . 
Identification of a chemical by 1H NMR may also be achieved by spectrum interpretation. 
The n umber of resonances, chemical shifts, coupling constants, and peak areas must be 
consistent. 
3. Safety aspects 
The samples can potentially contain a high dosage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Clo
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
stants, and peak areas must be 
consistent. 
3. Safety aspects 
The samples can potentially contain a high dosage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If the concentration of the agent 
is high, a special screw-cap tube can be used or the tube can be sealed by flame. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 General recommendations 
The requirements for spectrometers suitable for the analysis of treaty -related compounds 
by 1H NMR are as follows: 
1. capability to observe 1H nucleus, 
2. capability to decouple selected second (13C, 19F, or 31P) nucleus, 
3. capability to apply signal suppression on selected solvent peak(s), 
4. capability for shaping rf pulses and pulsed field gradients, 
5. capability for control ling of the sample temperature to an accuracy of within 
±0.5 °C, 
6. a proton resonance frequency preferably of 400 MHz or more, and 
7. a data system adequate for acquisition, processing, and storage of all necessary data. 
4.2 Probe head characteristics 
The 5-mm room-temperature probe heads generally used in NMR spectroscopy are
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
. a data system adequate for acquisition, processing, and storage of all necessary data. 
4.2 Probe head characteristics 
The 5-mm room-temperature probe heads generally used in NMR spectroscopy are 
suitable for the analysis of treaty -related compounds. The coil geometry and number of 
channels can vary depending on the type and manufacturer of the probe head. 
1H NMR experiments need a probe head with a 1H channel; optimal sensitivity is achieved 
with so -called inverse probe heads, where the innermost RF coil is used for proton 
detection. Using cryogenic and microcoil probe heads may also increase sensitivity (see 
section 7.5).

5. Experimental 
5.1 Recommended conditions 
Temperature: The temperature of the NMR sample must be controlled at between 20 and 
30 °C. The boiling point of the sample solvent should be noted. 
NMR sample: The volume of sample to analyse for a 5-mm NMR tube is 450 to 600 µl. To 
avoid cross-pollution, a new tube (e.g. disposable) should be used for each sample. 
NMR solvent: To lock the frequency of the spectrometer, addition of a miscible deuterated 
solvent to the liquid sample is required (50 to 150 µ l). If possible, using a deuterated 
solvent similar to the protonated solvent is recommended. To determine the solvent of a 
liquid sample, a first unlocked 1H NMR experiment can be performed. If pre -treatment is 
required to analyse a sample, the used solvent can be fully deuterated.

NMR acquisition parameters : A pulse angle of 30°, an acquisition time of 3.9 s, a 
relaxation delay of 0.1 s, and a spectral width of 12 ppm, ranging from -2 to 10 ppm , are 
recommended. For a more quantitative data, a pulse angle of 90° and relaxation delay of 
10 s are recommended. These experimental parameters may be optimi sed for particular 
samples using the guidelines provided in Table 1.

5.3 Optional modifications 
Solvent suppression techniques like presaturation, WET 1, PURGE 2 or ROBUST 3 are

been useful to remove overlapping 13C-satellites.

Testing of the spectrometer performance to meet specifications requires a variety of test 
samples, usually provided by the instrument manufacturer. A set of test samples may be as 
follows: 
1. 1H resolution test sample: 5% of orthodichlorobenzene in acetone-d6, 
2. 1H lineshape and spinning sideband test sample: 0.3–3% chloroform in acetone-d6, 
3. 1H sensitivity test sample: 0.1% ethylbenzene in chloroform-d1, 
Spectrometer performance tests consist of checking lineshape, sensitivity, and resolution of 
a probe head for 1H nucleus. Other tests include checking the radio frequency field 
strengths of the observation and decoupling channels. A six - to twelve -month interval 
should be observed between extensive test ing; otherwise, tests are performed whenever 
any degradation of performance is detected. Tests are performed according to procedures 
found in the spectrometer manuals or other literature (e.g. see ref. 4). 
Note! The chemical shift is sensitive to
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
degradation of performance is detected. Tests are performed according to procedures 
found in the spectrometer manuals or other literature (e.g. see ref. 4). 
Note! The chemical shift is sensitive to changes o f the sample temperature; therefore, the 
temperature of the sample during the NMR experiment should be known and controlled. 
Calibration of the temperature control unit can be performed with either the ethylene 
glycol or methanol sample when operating near the room temperature.5, 6 
6.2 Solvents 
Deuterated solvents should have a high enrichment of deuterium, >99.5 %. Chloroform-d1, 
deuterium oxide, acetone -d6, dichloromethane-d2, acetonitrile -d3, benzene -d6, and 
methanol-d4 are the most common solvents for NMR spectrometry. Dichloromethane-d2 
and deuterium oxide are considered to be the main solvents in CWC-related analysis, but 
some others may be preferred for better dis solution or to avoid overlap of resonances. The 
purity of the solvents should be checked by long-term NMR. 
6.3 Internal chemical shift references 
Tetramethylsilane [TMS, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] should be used in organic solvents as the 
chemical shift reference fo r proton NMR spectra. Sodium 4,4-dime
