Tetramethylsilane [TMS, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] should be used in organic solvents as the 
chemical shift reference fo r proton NMR spectra. Sodium 4,4-dimethyl-4-silapentane-
1-sulfonate-d6 [DSS-d6, δ(H) = 0.0 0 ppm; also known as sodium 3-(trimethylsilyl)propane 
sulfonic acid -d6, TSPSA-d6], or sodium 3-(trimethylsilyl)-3,3,2,2-tetradeuteropropionate 
[TSP-d4, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] are recommended as reference standards in water.

ppm vs. TSP-d4 δ(H) = 0.00 ppm. 
If unintentional reaction of DSS-d6 and TSP-d4 with the sample compounds is suspected in 
water, p-dioxane [δ(H) = 3.7 45 ppm vs. int. DSS-d6 δ(H) = 0.0 0 ppm] could be used 
instead. In chloroform , the shifts of p-dioxane are : δ(H) = 3.70 ppm, vs. int . TMS

in selected sample matrices has also been reported ,7, 8 which can be used as prima ry

6.4 External chemical shift references 
If appropriate reference samples or NMR tube inserts are used, internal chemical shift 
references can also serve as external references. 
7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
The NMR sample tube is first placed into the magnet. The sample temperature stabilization 
to the preset value can take up to 5 minutes depending on the temperature difference of the 
sample and the preset measurement temperature . Meanwhile, the field to the 2H resonance 
of the solvent should be locked (if no deuterated solvent is present, skip this step) and the 
appropriate experimental parameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homogeneity adjusted. The 90 
deg. proton pulse length can be calibrated if necessary ( in case of a new matrix) with the 
single scan stroboscopic nutation method.9 Once the receiver gain is adjusted, data 
acquisition may comm ence.
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
proton pulse length can be calibrated if necessary ( in case of a new matrix) with the 
single scan stroboscopic nutation method.9 Once the receiver gain is adjusted, data 
acquisition may comm ence. After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -
transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is performed if needed to obtain the real spectrum in pure absorption lineshape . 
The same conditions should always be used for spectrum processing . Appropriate shift 
referencing should be used to calibrate the spectrum . These operations can be automat ed 
by using a sample changer and an auto -tunable gradient probe head with appropriate 
software. 
Compared with the sample matrix, the experimental parameters have a minor effect on the 
spectral parameters. Experimental parameters such as spectral width, flip angle, repetition 
time, number of points in the FID and in the real spectrum, number of scans, and 
processing parameters need to be comparable with those used for the acquisition of the 
database spectrum or spectrum of the authentic reference compound. 
Note! It is not always possible nor feasible to use the same experimenta
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
o be comparable with those used for the acquisition of the 
database spectrum or spectrum of the authentic reference compound. 
Note! It is not always possible nor feasible to use the same experimental parameters, such 
as the number of s cans for the test sample as for the reference standard , due to , e.g., 
different concentration of the compound. 
7.2 Screening 
1H NMR experiments can be used for the screening of hydrogen -containing organic 
compounds, in which case 1H NMR may provide a high level of proof for the presence of a 
particular compound. However, the usefulness of the 1H NMR experiment may be limited 
if the sample contains a strong proton signal background due to the solvent or sample 
matrix. 
7.3 Identification 
First, the spectrum i s examined for resonance patterns, their positions, number of 
resonances, and their intensities or area s (Figure 1). This gives an idea of the functional 
groups of the compounds of interest. An immediate identification of a compound on the 
basis of familia r features may also result. Information obtained from each NMR

spectral library, or with the spectrum of an authentic compound (Figures 2–3). All 
available information, including that obtained by other techniques, is used to construct a 
complete picture. 
To obtain a positive identification, the NMR spectral parameters for a compound must 
agree within certain limits with those of the database or the authentic compound. If the 
sample of the compound to be identified has been prepared so as to correspond in solvent, 
concentration, pH, and chemical shift references to t he compound in the database 
(or authentic compound), the values of δ(H) must agree with the corresponding va lues in 
the database (or authentic compound) within limits of ±0.05 ppm. The values of coupling 
constants J(HH) must agree within limits of ±0.2 Hz. In addition, the resonance patterns 
and their intensities must match. An identification made by spiking a s amp

±0.05 ppm. The values of coupling 
constants J(HH) must agree within limits of ±0.2 Hz. In addition, the resonance patterns 
and their intensities must match. An identification made by spiking a s ample with the 
suspected chemical requires exact overlapping of the resonances. The amount of 
compound spiked should increase the signals of the compound by at least a factor of 2 and 
a maximum factor of 4. Identification of a chemical by 1H NMR may also b e achieved by 
spectrum interpretation. 
Note! It is not always possible to obtain the same conditions for the reference standard as 
for the test sample (e.g. matrix effect), thus differences in the NMR spectral parameters 
may be considerable. The identifica tion criteria may then be expanded within reasonable 
limits (e.g. doubled). In this case, identification by adding the authentic compound in the 
sample is recommended.

conditions, the signal intensity is directly proportional to the amount of nuclei pres ent. The 
combination of quantitative 1H NMR with metrological weighing can lead to measurement

for the given application . Quantification is performed most frequently using an internal

its relaxation time, the NMR tube diameter, the sample matrix, and the homogeneity of the

7.6 Remarks on analysis 
Non-deuterated solvents can be used if a small amount of the corresponding deuterated 
solvent is added to the sample to provide the lock conditions, if the experiment is 
performed unlocked, or if a lock nucleus other than deuterium is used. For strongly salty 
samples, cryogenic probe heads are disadvantageous, but it could be beneficial using 
smaller diameter tubes (e.g. 3-mm tube and spinner on a 5-mm probe head) or micro coil 
probe heads. The 90° pulse width should be recalibrated. Paramagnetic salts in aqueous 
samples can enhance relaxation so that the resonances became too broad to be observable. 
In this case, a pre-treatment must be performed (e.g. cation exchange, application of 
chelating agents). 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to all compounds containing hydrogen atoms other than 
exchangeable and dissolving to a sufficient degree in a solvent. The analysed liquid sample 
must b
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ea of applicability 
The method is applicable to all compounds containing hydrogen atoms other than 
exchangeable and dissolving to a sufficient degree in a solvent. The analysed liquid sample 
must be homogeneous and without paramagnetic properties. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The main advantage of 1H NMR spectroscopy is that the spectrum of a compound is in 
most cases specific and the measurement does not degrade the sample. The disadvantages 
are the non-selectivity causing overlap of signals and the modest sensitivity (several orders 
of magnitude compared to GC–MS if absolute amounts of compounds are considered). 
When unknown compounds ( without reference data ) are present, 1H NMR spectrometry 
may be the best so urce of structural information, with other techniques providing 
complementary information. Although they are not described here, other one -dimensional 
(e.g. techniques utili sing polari sation transfer) or two -dimensional homonuclear and 
heteronuclear correlation techniques can be used as well.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) 
spectrometry utili sing one -dimensional 31P NMR experiments for the screening and 
identification of chemical warfare agents, their precursors , and degradation /reaction 
products of chemicals related to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). Generally, the 
procedure is for identifying chemicals above the 1 to 5 µg/ml concentration level. NMR 
measurements are carried out with modern NMR instruments typically equipped with 5-mm 
NMR probe heads.

2. Summary of the method 
NMR techniques are commonly used for structural elucidation. With 31P NMR spectrum 
interpretation, a set of information is obtained in the form of NMR parameters ( chemical 
shifts and coupling constants) that converge to a chemical structure. 31P NMR spectroscopy 
is used as a screening method and to give information about chemical families. Identification 
of a compound is achieved by comparison with reference spectra included in a compu ter 
database or spectrum library, through comparison with a spectrum of the authentic 
compound, or with standard addition of the authentic compound . Number of resonances, 
chemical shifts, and coupling constants must be consistent. 
3. Safety aspects 
The samples can potentially contain a high dosage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If the
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If the concentration of the agent is 
high, a special screw-cap tube can be used or the tube can be sealed by flame. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 General recommendations 
The requirements for spectrometers suitable for the analysis of treaty-related compounds by 
31P NMR are as follows: 
1. capability to observe 31P nucleus, 
2. capability to decouple 1H nucleus, 
3. capability for controlling of the sample temperature to an accuracy of within ±0.5 °C, 
4. a phosphorus resonance frequency preferably of 161 MHz or more, and 
5. a data system adequate for acquisition, processing, and storage of all necessary data. 
4.2 Probe head characteristics 
The 5-mm room-temperature probe heads generally used in NMR spectroscopy are suitable 
for the analysis of treaty-related compounds. The coil geometry and number of channels can 
vary depending on the type and manufacturer of the probe head. 
31P NMR experiments need a probe head with a 31P channel; optimal sensitivity is achieved 
with so -called direct
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
mber of channels can 
vary depending on the type and manufacturer of the probe head. 
31P NMR experiments need a probe head with a 31P channel; optimal sensitivity is achieved 
with so -called direct probe heads, where the innermost RF coil is used for phosphorus 
detection. Using cryogenic and microcoil probe heads may also increase sensitivity (see 
section 7.5). 
The measurement of 31P{1H} NMR experiments needs a probe head with two channels 
tuneable to the 31P and 1H nuclei.

5. Experimental 
5.1 Recommended conditions 
Temperature: The temperature of the NMR sample must be controlled at between 20 and 
30 °C. The boiling point of the sample solvent should be noted. 
NMR sample: The volume of sample to analyse for a 5-mm NMR tube is 450 to 600 µl. To 
avoid cross-pollution, a new tube (e.g. disposable) should be used for each sample. 
NMR solvent: To lock the frequency of the spectrometer, addition of a miscible deuterated 
solvent to the liquid sample is required (50 to 150 µl). If possible, using a deuterated solvent 
similar to the protonated solvent is recommended. To determine the solvent of a liquid 
sample, a first unlocked 1H NMR experiment can be performed. If a pre-treatment is required 
to analyse a sample, the used solvent can be fully deuterated. 
NMR acquisition parameters : Optimised sensitivity for an interscan delay T c and 
longitudinal relaxation time T 1 is obtained by the application of an excitation angle αerns
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
an be fully deuterated. 
NMR acquisition parameters : Optimised sensitivity for an interscan delay T c and 
longitudinal relaxation time T 1 is obtained by the application of an excitation angle αernst 
(Ernst angle) given by the following relation: cos( αernst) = exp(-Tc/T1).1 Current 
recommended parameters corresponding to a longitudinal relaxation time T1 close to 4 s are 
as follows: a pulse angle of 45°, an acquisition time of 1 s, a relaxation delay of 0.3 s, and a 
spectral width of 200 ppm, ranging from 170 to -30 ppm. 
Note! If problems related to the duty cycle occur , inverse gated 1H decoupling , shorter 
acquisition time and longer relaxation time should be used. 
Alternatively, a spectral width of 350 ppm, ranging from 260 to -90 ppm can be used to 
cover possible Schedule 3 inorganic phosphorus compounds. In this case the reciprocal of 
the duration of the pulse (in 1/sec), which indicate the usable excitation bandwidth of the 
pulse, should exceed the spectral width of 350 ppm (in hertz). If the excitation bandwidth is 
not sufficient for the whole 350 ppm spectral width, two separate acquisitions a spectral 
width of 200 ppm, ranging from e.g. 260 to 60 ppm and 11
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
350 ppm (in hertz). If the excitation bandwidth is 
not sufficient for the whole 350 ppm spectral width, two separate acquisitions a spectral 
width of 200 ppm, ranging from e.g. 260 to 60 ppm and 110 to -90 ppm can be measured. 
These experimental parameters may be optimised for particular samples using the guidelines 
provided in Table 1.

5.3 Optional modifications 
The proton-decoupled 31P NMR experiment,(i.e. 31P{1H} NMR) is more common due to a 
better signal -to-noise ratio, simplified appearance of the multiplets and i ts useful ness to 
screen chemical families of organophosphorus compounds. The proton decoupling is 
achieved by standard composite pulse decoupling (CPD) like WALTZ or MLEV. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The most important quality control operations are the testing of the spectrometer 
performance and following the identification criteria. The operating procedures included in 
the Quality Manual for the laboratory should complement the Recommen ded Operating 
Procedures (ROP).

6.2 Solvents 
Deuterated solvents should have a high enrichment of deuterium, >9 9.5%. Chloroform-d1, 
deuterium oxide, acetone-d6, dichloromethane-d2, acetonitrile-d3, benzene-d6, and methanol-
d4 are the most common solvents for NMR spectrometry. Dichloromethane-d2 and deuterium 
oxide are considered to be the main solvents in CWC-related analysis, but some others may 
be preferred for better dissolution or to avoid overlap of resonances. The purity of the 
solvents should be checked by long-term NMR. 
6.3 Internal chemical shift references 
Triphenyl phosphate [TPP, δ(P) = -17.80 ppm] dissolves well in organic solvents and could 
serve as an internal chemical shift reference for phosphorus. 
Note! TPP gives resonances in the aromatic region of the 1H NMR spectrum.

6.4 External chemical shift references 
The most common external chemical shift reference in 31P NMR is 85% phosphoric acid. In 
aqueous samples, δ(P) = 0.00 ppm is measured in an ideal spherical container inside the 
solution.5 In practice, however, it is more convenient to use a cylindrical capillary tube to 
hold the standard, and a correction should then be applied to take into account the differences 
in diamagnetic susceptibility. To corr ect for diamagnetic susceptibility differences in 
aqueous samples, the signal of 85 % H3PO4 in a cylindrical capillary in superconducting 
solenoid spectrometers should be set at -0.73 ppm. If a narrower line is desired, a 0.2 M 
solution of crystalline phosp horic acid in 14 % aqueous perchloric acid 
(tetrahydroxyphosphonium perchlorate, P(OH) 4ClO4) 6 in a cylindrical capillary could be 
chosen, and the signal should then be set at δ(P) = 0.09 ppm in superconducting solenoid 
spectrometers. For other solvents , corrections to the phosphorus chemical shifts

chosen, and the signal should then be set at δ(P) = 0.09 ppm in superconducting solenoid

and tetrahydroxyphosphonium perchlorate would be different.

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1 Sequence of analysis 
The NMR sample tube is first placed into the magnet. The sample temperature stabilization 
to the preset value can take up to 5 minutes depending on the temperature difference of the 
sample and the preset measurement temperature . Meanwhile, the field to the 2H resonance 
of the solvent should be locked (if no deuterated solvent is present, skip this step) and the 
appropriate experimental parameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homogeneity adjusted. The 90 
deg. proton pulse length can be calibrated if necessary ( in case of a new matrix) with the 
single scan stroboscopic nutation method.11 Once the receiver gain is adjusted, data 
acquisition may commence. After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -

The same conditions should always be used for spectrum processing . Appropriate shift

Compared with the sample matrix, the experimental parameters have a minor effect on the

7.2 Screening 
31P NMR experiments can be used for screening of organophosphorus compounds, in which 
case 31P NMR may provide a high level of proof for the presence of a particular compound. 
The chemical shift range of phosphorus is broad in comparison with proton (from -80 to 250 
ppm with CWC -related compounds), and t he phosphorus chemical shift is generally 
characteristic of the phosphorus chemical family (i.e. number of valence, functional groups 
around phosphorus). 
7.3 Identification 
First, the spectrum is examined for resonances, their chemical shifts, number of resonances, 
and their intensities or area s (Figure 1A). This provides an idea of the chemical families 
(e.g. phosphonofluoridate, phosphonothiolate, phosphoramidocyanidate) of the compounds 
of interest. Information obtained from each NMR experiment is consolidated. Comparisons 
are made with spe

(e.g. phosphonofluoridate, phosphonothiolate, phosphoramidocyanidate) of the compounds 
of interest. Information obtained from each NMR experiment is consolidated. Comparisons 
are made with spectra in a computer database or spectral library, or with the spectrum of an 
authentic compound. However, derivation of the complete chemical structure solely with 31P 
NMR experiments may not be possible ; therefore, all available information, including that 
obtained by other techniques, is used to construct a complete picture. 
To obtain a positive identification, the NMR spectral parameters for a compound must agree 
within certain limits with those of the database or the authentic compound. If the sample of 
the compound to be identified has been prepared so as to correspond in solvent, 
concentration, pH, and chemical shift references to t he compound in the database 
(or authentic compound), the values of δ(P) must agree with the corresponding values in the 
database (or authentic compound) within limits of ± 0.2 ppm. The values of coupling 
constants must agree within certain limits, e.g. J(PH) must agree within limits of ±0.2 Hz, 
(except for 1J(PH)±2 Hz) and 1J(PF) must agree

7.4 Quantification 
NMR spectrometry is well -suited for quantification because, under certain experimental 
conditions, the signal intensity is directly proportional to the amount of nuclei present. The 
combination of quantitative 1H NMR with metrological weighing can lead to measurement 
uncertainties below 0.1 % when highly pure substances are used.12 The guidelines provided 
by EUROLAB13 can be applied to determine the precision and accuracy of quantification 
for the given application . Quantification is performed most frequently using an internal 
standard, although other approaches may also be applied (for example, using the ERETIC 
method, which utilises a reference signal synthesi sed by an electronic device to determine 
absolute concentrations.14 An alternative example is the PULCON method that correlates 
the absolute intensities of two spectra measured in different solution conditions . 15 A pulse 
angle of 90° and a repetition time (sum of the acquisition time and the relaxation delay) that 
equals five times the longest T1 are recommended, using a pulse program that does not build 
up NOE. Signal-to-noise of the quantified

7.6 Remarks on analysis 
Non-deuterated solvents can be used if a small amount of the corresponding deuterated 
solvent is added to the sample to provide the lock conditions. Due to long total measurement 
times, acquisition of 31P NMR spectra unlocked is no t recommended. For strongly salty 
samples, cryogenic probe heads are disadvantageous, but it could be beneficial using smaller 
diameter tubes (e.g. 3-mm tube and spinner on a 5-mm probe head) or microcoil probe heads. 
The 90° pulse width should be recalibr ated. Paramagnetic salts in aqueous sam

diameter tubes (e.g. 3-mm tube and spinner on a 5-mm probe head) or microcoil probe heads. 
The 90° pulse width should be recalibr ated. Paramagnetic salts in aqueous samples can 
enhance relaxation so that the resonances became too broad to be observable. In this case, a 
pretreatment must be performed (e.g. cation exchange, application of chelating agents). 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to all organophosphorus compounds dissolving in sufficient 
amount (concentration above the limit of detection) in a solvent. The analysed liquid sample 
must be homogeneous and without paramagnetic properties. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The main advantage of 31P NMR spectroscopy is its selectivity, since it reveals the presence 
of organophosphorus compounds in the sample, and the measurement does not degrade the 
sample. The disadvantages are the low information content of the spectrum in comparison

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) 
spectrometry utili sing one -dimensional 19F NMR experiments for the screening and 
identification of chemical warfare agents, their precursors , and degradation /reaction 
products of chemicals related to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). Generally, the 
procedure is for identifying chemicals above the 1 µg/ml concentration level. NMR 
measurements are carried out with modern NMR instruments equipped with 5-mm NMR 
probe heads.

2. Summary of the method 
NMR techniques are commonly used for structural elucidation. With 19F NMR spectrum 
interpretation, a set of information is obtained in the form of NMR parameters ( chemical 
shifts and coupling constants) that converge to a chemical structure. 19F NMR spectroscopy 
is used as a screening method and to give information about chemical families. Identification 
of a compound is achieved by comparison with reference spectra included in a computer 
database or spectrum library, through comparison with a spectrum of the authentic 
compound, or with standard addition of the authentic compound. The number of resonances, 
chemical shifts, and coupling constants must be consistent. 
3. Safety aspects 
The samples can potentially contain a high dosage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
sage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If the concentration of the agent is 
high, a special screw-cap tube can be used or the tube can be sealed by flame. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 General recommendations 
The requirements for spectrometers suitable for the analysis of treaty-related compounds by 
19F NMR are as follows: 
1. capability to observe 19F nucleus, 
2. capability to decouple 1H nucleus, 
3. capability for controlling of the sample temperature to an accuracy of within ±0.5°C, 
4. a fluorine resonance frequency preferably of 376 MHz or more, and 
5. a data system adequate for acquisition, processing, and storage of all necessary data. 
4.2 Probe head characteristics 
The 5-mm room-temperature probe heads generally used in NMR spectroscopy are suitable 
for the analysis of treaty-related compounds. The coil geometry and number of channels can 
vary depending on the type and manufacturer of the probe head. 
19F NMR experiments need a probe head with a 19F channel; optimal sensitivity is achieved 
with so-called direct

19F NMR experiments need a probe head with a 19F channel; optimal sensitivity is achieved

5. Experimental 
5.1 Recommended conditions 
Temperature: The temperature of the NMR sample must be controlled at between 20 and 
30 °C. The boiling point of the sample solvent should be noted. 
NMR sample: The volume of sample to analyse for a 5-mm NMR tube is 450 to 600 µl. To 
avoid cross-pollution, a new tube (e.g. disposable) should be used for each sample. 
NMR solvent: To lock the frequency of the spectrometer, addition of miscible deuterated 
solvent in the liquid sample is required (50 to 150 µ l). If possible, using the deuterated 
solvent similar to the protonated solvent is recommended. To determine the solvent of a 
liquid sample, a first unlocked 1H experiment can be performed. If a pre-treatment is required 
to analyse a sample, the used solvent can be fully deuterated. 
NMR acquisition parameters : Optimised sensitivity for an interscan delay T c and 
longitudinal relaxation time T 1 is obtained by the application of an excitation angle αernst
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
n be fully deuterated. 
NMR acquisition parameters : Optimised sensitivity for an interscan delay T c and 
longitudinal relaxation time T 1 is obtained by the application of an excitation angle αernst 
(Ernst angle) given by the following relation: cos( αernst) = exp(-Tc/T1).1 Current 
recommended parameters corresponding to a longitudinal relaxation time T1 close to 3 s are 
as follows: a pulse angle of 45°, an acquisition time of 0.5 s, a relaxation delay of 0.5 s and 
a spectral width of 230 ppm, ranging from 50 to -180 ppm. These experimental parameters 
may be optimised for particular samples using the guidelines provided in Table 1.

5.3 Optional modifications 
The proton-decoupled 19F NMR experiment (i.e. 19F{1H} NMR) can be used to simplify the 
appearance of the multiplets and to increase the sensitivity of the experiment . The proton 
decoupling is achieved by standard composite pulse decoupling (CPD) like WA LTZ or 
MLEV. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The most important quality control operations are the testing of the spectrometer 
performance and following the identification criteria. The operating procedures included in 
the Quality Manual for the laboratory should complement the Recommen ded Operating 
Procedures (ROP).

Testing of the spectrometer performance to meet specifications requires a variety of test 
samples, usually provided by the instrument manufacturer. A set of test samples may be as 
follows: 
1. 19F sensitivity test sample: 0.05% trifluorotoluene in chloroform-d1, 
2. A suitable sample for the calibration of the proton pulse width and the power on the 
decoupling channel. 
Spectrometer performance tests consist of checking lineshape and sensitivity for a probe 
head for the 19F nucleus. Other tests include checking the radio frequency field strengths of 
the observation and decoupling channels. A six- to twelve-month interval should be observed 
between extensive testing; otherwise, tests are performed whenever any degradation of 
performance is detected. Tests are performe d according to procedures found in the 
spectrometer manuals or other literature (e.g. see ref. 2). 
Note! The chemical shift is sensitive to changes of the sample temperature; therefore,
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
re performe d according to procedures found in the 
spectrometer manuals or other literature (e.g. see ref. 2). 
Note! The chemical shift is sensitive to changes of the sample temperature; therefore, the 
temperature of the sample during the NMR experiment should be known and controlled. 
Calibration of the temperature control unit can be performed with either the ethylene glycol 
or methanol sample when operating near the room temperature. 3, 4 
6.2 Solvents 
Deuterated solvents should have a high enrichment of deuterium, >99.5 %. Chloroform-d1, 
deuterium oxide, acetone-d6, dichloromethane-d2, acetonitrile-d3, benzene-d6, and methanol-
d4 are the most common solvents for NMR spectrometry. Dichloromethane-d2 and deuterium 
oxide are considered to be the main solvents in CWC-related analysis, but some others may 
be preferred for better dissolution o r to avoid overlap of resonances. The purity of the 
solvents should be checked by long-term NMR. 
6.3 Internal chemical shift references 
Trichlorofluoromethane (CCl3F) should be used in organic solvents as the chemical shift 
reference for fluorine spectra. The fine structure of the 19F signal of CCl3F results from the 
four isotopom
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
Trichlorofluoromethane (CCl3F) should be used in organic solvents as the chemical shift 
reference for fluorine spectra. The fine structure of the 19F signal of CCl3F results from the 
four isotopomers of the chlorine giving four lines with relative intensities (from down-field 
up) 8:8:3:1. The second line from down-field is used as the scale reference [δ(F) = 0.00 ppm]. 
Alternatively, fluorobenzene [C6H5F, δ(F) = -113.5 ppm] or hexafluorobenzene [C6F6, δ(F) 
= -163 ppm] 5 may be used . To calibrate the chemical shift scale in water , trifluoroacetic 
acid can be used [CF3COOH, δ(F) = -74.225 ppm vs. external CCl3F]. 6 
6.4 External chemical shift references 
If appropriate reference samples or NMR tube inserts are used, internal chemical shift 
references can also serve as external references. 
6.5 Unified scale chemical shift referencing 
The current IUPAC recommendation7, 8 is to use a unified scale for reporting chemical shifts 
of any nuclide X other than 1H in any sample relative to a primary internal reference. The 
primary internal reference is the proton resonance of tetramethylsilane (TMS) in a dilute

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1 Sequence of analysis 
The NMR sample tube is first placed into the magnet. The sample temperature stabilization 
to the preset value can take up to 5 minutes depending on the temperature difference of the 
sample and the preset measurement temperature . Meanwhile, the field to the 2H resonance 
of the solvent should be locked (if no deuterated solvent is p resent, skip this step) and the 
appropriate experimental parameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homogeneity adjusted. The 90 
deg. proton pulse lengt
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
appropriate experimental parameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homogeneity adjusted. The 90 
deg. proton pulse length can be calibrated if necess ary (in case of a new matrix) with the 
single scan stroboscopic nutation method.11 Once the receiver gain is adjusted, data 
acquisition may commence. After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -
transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is performed if needed to obtain the real spectrum in pure absorption lineshape . 
The same condition s should always be used for spectrum processing . Appropriate shift 
referencing should be used to calibrate the spectrum. These operations can be automated by 
using a sample changer and an auto-tunable gradient probe head with appropriate software. 
Compared with the sample matrix, the experimental parameters have a minor effect on the 
spectral parameters. Experimental parameters such as spectral width, flip angle, repetition 
time, number of points in the FID and in the real spectrum, number of scans, and processing

spectrum or spectrum of the authentic reference compound. 
Note! It is not always possible nor feasible to use the same experimental parameters, such 
as the number of scans for the test sample as for the reference standard, due to, e.g., different 
concentration of the compound. 
7.2 Screening 
19F NMR experiments can be used for screening of fluorine-containing organic compounds, 
in which case 19F NMR may provide a high level of proof for the presence of a particular 
compound. The fluorine chemical shift range is broad in comparison with protons (from -
180 to 50 ppm for CWC -related compounds), and the fluorine chemical shift is generally 
characteristic of the fluorin e chemical family (i.e. functional groups connected to the 
fluorine). 
7.3 Identification 
First, the spectrum is examined for resonance patterns, their positions, number of resonances, 
and their intens
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
emical family (i.e. functional groups connected to the 
fluorine). 
7.3 Identification 
First, the spectrum is examined for resonance patterns, their positions, number of resonances, 
and their intensities or area s (Figure 1). This gives an idea of the chemical families (e.g. 
phosphonofluoridate) of the compounds of interest . Information obtained from each NMR 
experiment is consolidated. Comparisons are made with spectra in a computer database or 
spectral library, or with the spectrum of an authentic compound. However, derivation of the 
complete chemical structure solely with 19F NMR experiments may not be possible ; 
therefore, all available information, including that obtained by other techniques, is used to 
construct a complete picture. 
To obtain a positive identification, the NMR spectral parameters for a compound must agree 
within certain limits with those of the database or the authentic compound. If the sample of 
the compound to be identified has been prepared so as to correspond in solvent, 
concentration, pH, and chemical shift references to the compound in the database (or 
authentic compound), the values of δ( F) must agree with the corresponding values in the
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
correspond in solvent, 
concentration, pH, and chemical shift references to the compound in the database (or 
authentic compound), the values of δ( F) must agree with the corresponding values in the 
database (or authentic compound) within limits of ±0. 2 ppm. The values of coupling 
constants 2-3J(FH) must agree within limits of ±0.2 Hz and 1J(FP) must agree within 2 Hz. 
Also, the resonance patterns and their intensities must match. An identification made by 
spiking a sample with the suspected chemical requires exact overlapping of the resonances. 
The amount of compound spiked should increase the signals of the compound by at least a 
factor of 2 and a maximum factor of 4. 
Note! It is not always possible to obtain the same conditions for the reference standard as 
for the test sample (e.g. matrix effect), thus differences in the NMR spectral parameters may 
be considerable. The identification criteria may then be expanded within re asonable limits 
(e.g. doubled). In this case, identification by adding the authentic compound in the sample 
is recommended.

7.4 Quantification 
NMR spectrometry is well -suited for quantification because, under certain experimental 
conditions, the signal intensity is directly proportional to the amount of nuclei present. The 
combination of quantitative 1H NMR with metrological weighing can lead to measurement 
uncertainties below 0.1 % when highly pure substances are used.12 The guidelines provided 
by EUROLAB13 can be applied to determine the precision and accuracy of quantification 
for the given application. Quantification is pe
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
when highly pure substances are used.12 The guidelines provided 
by EUROLAB13 can be applied to determine the precision and accuracy of quantification 
for the given application. Quantification is performed most frequently using an internal 
standard, although other approaches may also be applied (for example, using the ERETIC 
method, which utilises a reference signal synthesised by an electronic device to determine 
absolute concentrations. 14 An alternative example is the PULCON method that correlates 
the absolute intensities of two spectra measured in different solution conditions . 15 A pulse 
angle of 90° and a repetition time (sum of the acquisition time and the relaxation delay) that 
equals five times the longest T1 are recommended, using a pulse program that does not build 
up NOE. Signal-to-noise of the quantified compound of 10:1 is sufficient for estimation of 
the concentration for standard addition purposes. The signal -to-noise of the quantified 
compound and the internal reference must be comparable and much higher for low 
uncertainties, e.g. above 150:1 for the relative measurement uncertainty to be 1%.13 
7.5 Trace analysis 
The detection limit for a compound
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
rnal reference must be comparable and much higher for low 
uncertainties, e.g. above 150:1 for the relative measurement uncertainty to be 1%.13 
7.5 Trace analysis 
The detection limit for a compound depends on the magnetic field strength of the 
spectrometer, the probe, the number of scans, the flip angle, the observed nucleus and its 
relaxation time, the NMR tube diameter, the sample matrix, and the homogeneity of the 
magnetic field. With modern NMR spectrometers having a magnetic field of ca. 12 Tesla 
and a room-temperature probe head, a limit of detection of 1 µg/ml can be obtained. With

7.6 Remarks on analysis 
Non-deuterated solvents can be used if a small amount of the corresponding deuterated 
solvent is added to the sample to provide the lock conditions, if the experiment is performed 
unlocked, or if a lock nucleus other than deuterium is used. For strongly sa lty samples, 
cryoprobes are disadvantageous, but it co
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ple to provide the lock conditions, if the experiment is performed 
unlocked, or if a lock nucleus other than deuterium is used. For strongly sa lty samples, 
cryoprobes are disadvantageous, but it could be beneficial using smaller diameter tubes (e.g. 
3-mm tube and spinner on a 5-mm probe head) or microprobes. The 90° pulse width should 
be recalibrated. Paramagnetic salts in aqueous samples can enh ance relaxation so that the 
resonances became too broad to be observable. In this case, a pretreatment must be 
performed (e.g. cation exchange, application of chelating agents). 
Note! Most treaty-related chemicals with fluorine hydrolyse rapidly in aqueous conditions, 
hence losing the fluorine atom. Observation of 19F NMR signal from these compounds is, 
thus, not feasible. 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to all compounds containing fluorine atoms dissolving to a 
sufficient degree in a solvent (concentration upper to the limit of detection). The analysed 
liquid sample must be homogeneous and without paramagnetic properties.

8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The main advantage of 19F NMR spectroscopy is its selectivity, since it reveals the presence 
of organofluorine compounds in the sample, and the measurement does not degrade the 
sample. The disadvantages are the low information content of the spectrum in comparison 
with the information obtained in a 1H NMR spectrum and the modest sensitivity (several 
orders of magnitude compared to GC–MS if absolute amounts of compounds are considered). 
Although they are not described here, other one -dimensional (e.g. techniques utili sing 
polarisation transfer) or two -dimensional heteronuclear correlation techniques can be used 
as well. Generally, to determine a complete picture of an organo fluorine compound, 
complementary NMR techniques should be used.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) 
spectrometry utilising 1D 1H–31P correlation techniques like nonselective 1D 1H–31P HSQC 
experiments1 and nonselective 1D 1H–31P HMQC/HMBC experiments for the screening of 
samples for the presence of organophosphorus chemicals related to the Chemical Weapons 
Convention (CWC). Generally, the procedure is suitable for screening organophosphorus 
chemicals above a 1 µg/ml concentration level. NMR measurements are carried out with 
modern NMR instruments typically equipped with 5-mm NMR probe heads.

2. Summary of the method 
NMR techniques are commonly used for structural elucidation. With the nonselective 
1D 1H–31P correlation spectrum interpretation, a set of information is obtained in the form 
of NMR parameters (chemical shifts and coupling constants) that converge to a chemical 
structure. The main information obtained by the nonselective 1D 1H–31P correlation 
experiment is the structure of the alkyl group (e.g. methyl, ethyl, propyl or isopropyl) directly 
bonded to the phosphorus atom and the number of different organophosphorus compounds 
present in a sample . Usually, a subset of all proton signals of a given organop hosphorus 
compound is observed , and the experiment is mostly used for screening and rarely for 
identification of organophosphorus compounds (Figure 1b). If used for identification, 
identification of a compound is achieved by comparison with reference spectra included in 
a computer database or spectrum librar
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
f organophosphorus compounds (Figure 1b). If used for identification, 
identification of a compound is achieved by comparison with reference spectra included in 
a computer database or spectrum library, through comparison with a spectrum of the 
authentic compound, or with standard addition of the authentic compound. The number of 
resonances, chemical shifts, and coupling constants must be consistent. 
3. Safety aspects 
The samples can potentially contain a high dosage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If the concentration of the agent is 
high, a special screw-cap tube can be used or the tube can be sealed by flame. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 General recommendations 
The requirements for spectrometers suitable for the analysis of treaty-related compounds by 
the nonselective 1D 1H–31P HSQC are as follows: 
1. capability to observe 1H nucleus, 
2. capability to decouple 31P nucleus, 
3. capability to apply signal suppression on selected solvent peak(s), 
4. capability for shaping rf pulses and pulsed field gradients, 
5. capa
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ve 1H nucleus, 
2. capability to decouple 31P nucleus, 
3. capability to apply signal suppression on selected solvent peak(s), 
4. capability for shaping rf pulses and pulsed field gradients, 
5. capability for controlling of the sample temperature to an accuracy of within ±0.5 °C, 
6. a proton resonance frequency preferably of 400 MHz or more, and 
7. a data system adequate for acquisition, processing, and storage of all necessary data. 
4.2 Probe head characteristics 
The 5-mm room-temperature probe heads generally used in NMR spectroscopy are suitable 
for the analysis of treaty-related compounds. The coil geometry and number of channels can 
vary depending on the type and manufacturer of the probe head. 
The 1D 1H–31P HSQC experiment needs a probe head with two channels tuneable to 1H and 
31P. Optimal sensitivity is achieved with so-called inverse probe heads, where the innermost

5. Experimental 
5.1 Recommended conditions 
Temperature: The temperature of the NMR sample must be controlled at between 20 and 
30 °C. The boiling point of the sample solvent should be noted. 
NMR sample: The volume of sample to analyse for a 5-mm NMR tube is 450 to 600 µl. To 
avoid cross-pollution, a new tube (e.g. disposable) should be used for each sample. 
NMR solvent: To lock the frequency of the spectrometer, addition of a miscible deuterated 
solvent to the liquid sample is required (50 to 150 µl). If possible, using a deuterated solvent 
similar to the protonated solvent is recommended. To determine the solvent of a liquid 
sample, a first unlocked 1H NMR experiment can be performed. If a pre-treatment is required 
to analyse a sample, the used solvent can be fully deuterated. 
NMR acqu

sample, a first unlocked 1H NMR experiment can be performed. If a pre-treatment is required 
to analyse a sample, the used solvent can be fully deuterated. 
NMR acquisition parameters: 1H and 31P pulse widths corresponding to angles of 90° and 
180°, a coupling constant of 20 Hz, an acquisition time of 1 s, a relaxation delay of 2.5 s, an 
1H spectral width of 12 ppm, ranging from -2 to 10 ppm and setting the 31P transmitter to 30 
ppm are recommended. These experimental parameters may be optimi sed for particular 
samples using the guidelines provided in Table 1.

Table 1 and Table 2 provide guidelines for the selecti on of experimental parameters for

31P decoupling during a cquisition can be used with 1D 1H–31P HSQC to simplify t he 
appearance of the multiplets and to increase the sensitivity of the experiment . To increase 
the 31P sampling range, the hard 31P 180° pulses may be replaced by adiabatic pulses.

6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The most important quality control operations are the testing of the spectrometer 
performance and following the identification criteria. The operating procedures included in 
the Quality Manual for the laboratory should complement the Recommen ded Operating 
Procedures (ROP). 
Testing of the spectrometer performa nce to meet specifications requires a variety of test 
samples, usually provided by the instrument manufacturer. A set of test samples may be as 
follows: 
1. 1H resolution test sample: 5% of orthodichlorobenzene in acetone-d6. 
2. 1H lineshape and spinning sideband test sample: 0.3–3% chloroform in acetone-d6. 
3. 1H sensitivity test sample: 0.1% ethylbenzene in chloroform-d1. 
4. 31P sensitivity test sample: 0.0485 M triphenyl phosphate in acetone-d6. 
Spectrometer performance tests consist of checking lineshape, sensitivity, and resolution of 
a probe head for 1H nucleus and t
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
1P sensitivity test sample: 0.0485 M triphenyl phosphate in acetone-d6. 
Spectrometer performance tests consist of checking lineshape, sensitivity, and resolution of 
a probe head for 1H nucleus and the sensitivity of the 31P nucleus . Other tests include 
checking the radio frequency field strengths of the observation and decoupling channels. A 
six- to twelve-month interval should be observed between extensive testing; otherwise, tests 
are performed whenever any degradation of performance is detected. Tests are performed 
according to procedures found in the spectrometer manuals or other literature (e.g. see ref. 
2). 
Note! The chemical shi ft is sensitive to changes of the sample temperature, and therefore 
the temperature of the sample during the NMR experiment should be known and controlled. 
Calibration of the temperature control unit can be performed with either the ethylene glycol 
or methanol sample when operating near the room temperature.3, 4 
6.2 Solvents 
Deuterated solvents should have a high enrichment of deuterium, >99.5 %. Chloroform-d1, 
deuterium oxide, acetone-d6, dichloromethane-d2, acetonitrile-d3, benzene-d6, and methanol-
d4 are the most common solvents fo
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ents should have a high enrichment of deuterium, >99.5 %. Chloroform-d1, 
deuterium oxide, acetone-d6, dichloromethane-d2, acetonitrile-d3, benzene-d6, and methanol-
d4 are the most common solvents for NMR spectrometry. Dichloromethane-d2 and deuterium 
oxide are considered to be the main solvents in CWC-related analysis, but some others may 
be preferred for better dissolution or to avoid overlap of resonances. The purity of the 
solvents should be checked by long-term NMR. 
6.3 Internal chemical shift references 
The same chemical shift references as for the basic 1H NMR experiments should be used: 
Tetramethylsilane [TMS, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] should be used in organic solvents as the 
chemical shift reference for proton NMR spectra. Sodium 4,4-dimethyl-4-silapentane-
1-sulfonate-d6 [DSS-d6, δ(H) = 0.0 0 ppm; also known as sodium 3-(trimethylsilyl)propane 
sulfonic acid -d6, TSPSA-d6], or sodium 3-(trimethylsilyl)-3,3,2,2-tetradeuteropropionate 
[TSP-d4, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] are recommended as reference standards in water.

6.4 External chemical shift references 
If appropriate reference samples or NMR tube inserts are used, internal chemical shift 
references can also serve as external references. 1H NMR spectra are acquired from the 
external chemical shift reference, followed by a transfer of the relevant parameters to the 1D 
1H–31P correlation experiment. 
7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
The NMR sample tube is first placed into the magnet. The sample temperature stabilization 
to the preset value can take up to 5 minutes depending on the temperature difference of the 
sample and the preset measurement temperature. Meanwhile, the field to the 2H resonance 
of the solvent should be locked (if no deuterated solvent is present, skip this step) and the 
appropriate experimental parameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homogeneity adjusted. The 90 
deg. proton pulse length can be calibrated if necess
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
rameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homogeneity adjusted. The 90 
deg. proton pulse length can be calibrated if necessary ( in case of a new matrix) with the 
single scan stroboscopic nutation method.7 Once the receiver gain is adjusted, data 
acquisition may commence. After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -
transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is performed if needed to obtain the real spectrum in pure absorption lineshape . 
The same conditions should always be used for spectrum processing . Appropriate shift 
referencing should be used to calibrate the spectrum. These operations can be automated by 
using a sample changer and an auto-tunable gradient probe head with appropriate software. 
Compared with the sample matrix, the experimental parameters have a minor effect on the 
spectral parameters. Experimental parameters su ch as spectral width, flip angle, repetition 
time, number of points in the FID and in the real spectrum, number of scans, and processing 
parameters need to be comparable with those used for the acquisition
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ectral width, flip angle, repetition 
time, number of points in the FID and in the real spectrum, number of scans, and processing 
parameters need to be comparable with those used for the acquisition of the database 
spectrum or spectrum of the authentic reference compound. 
Note! It is not always possible nor feasible to use the same experimental parameters, such 
as the number of scans for the test sample as for the reference standard, due to, e.g., different 
concentration of the compound.

7.2 Screening 
Screening solutions for the presence of organophosphorus chemicals relevant to the CWC is 
the main application of the nonselective 1D 1H–31P correlation experiment. In this case, the 
1D 1H–31P correlation experiment may provide a high level of proof for the presence of a 
particular organophosphorus chemical. 
7.3 Identification 
First, the spectrum is examined for resonance patterns, their positions, number of resonances, 
and their intensities or areas. This gives an idea of the functional groups of the compounds 
of interest. Information obtained from each NMR experiment is consolidated. Comparisons 
are made with spectra in a computer database or spectral library, or with the spectrum of an 
authentic compound. All available information, including that obtained by other techniques, 
is used to construct a complete picture. 
To obtain a positive identification, the NMR spectral parameters for a compound must agree 
within

text:
information, including that obtained by other techniques, 
is used to construct a complete picture. 
To obtain a positive identification, the NMR spectral parameters for a compound must agree 
within certain limits with those of the database or the authentic compound. If the sample of 
the compound to be identified has been prepared so as to correspond in solvent, 
concentration, pH, and chemical shift references to the compound in the database (or 
authentic compound), the values of δ(H) should agree with th e corresponding values in the 
database (or authentic compound) within limits of ±0.05 ppm. The values of coupling 
constants J(HH) and J(PH) should agree within limits of ±0.2 Hz, (except for 1J(PH) ±2 Hz). 
In addition, the resonance patterns and their intensities must match. An identification made 
by spiking a sample with the suspected chemical requires exact overlapping of the 
resonances and is recommended for the identification of compounds by the nonselective 1D 
1H–31P correlation experiment. The amount of compound spiked should increase the signals 
of the compound by at least a factor of 2 and a maximum factor of 4. 
Note! It is not always possible to obtain the sa

text:
orrelation experiment. The amount of compound spiked should increase the signals 
of the compound by at least a factor of 2 and a maximum factor of 4. 
Note! It is not always possible to obtain the same conditions for the reference standard as 
for the test sample (e.g. matrix effect), thus differences in the NMR spectral parameters may 
be considerable. The identification criteria may then be expanded within reasonable limits 
(e.g. doubled). In this case, identification by adding the authentic compound in the sample 
is recommended.

7.4 Quantification 
The peak areas in the 1 D 1H–31P correlation spectra are dependent on a multitude of 
parameters. In the 1D 1H–31P correlation experiment, signal intensity is strongly dependent 
on the J(PH) of the protons and the used polari sation transfer delay, so the relative number 
of protons contributing to a signal cannot be deduced like in a 1H NMR spectrum. However, 
when taking these variations into account, the nonselective 1D 1H–31P HSQC experiment 
can be used for the quantification of organophosphorus analytes u
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
be deduced like in a 1H NMR spectrum. However, 
when taking these variations into account, the nonselective 1D 1H–31P HSQC experiment 
can be used for the quantification of organophosphorus analytes using an external 
calibration.8, 9

cryoprobes are disadvantageous, but it could be beneficial usi ng smaller diameter tubes 
(e.g. 3-mm tube and spinner on a 5-mm probe head) or microprobes. The 90° pulse width s 
should be recalibrated. Paramagnetic salts in aqueous

8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to all compounds containing hydrogen atoms other than 
exchangeable with a scalar coupling to a phosphorus atom and dissolving in sufficient 
amount in a solvent. The analy sed liquid sample must be homogeneous and without 
paramagnetic properties. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The main advantage of the 1D 1H–31P correlation experiment is its selectivity: signals 
exclusively from protons with a scalar coupling to 31P nuclei are recorded. Signals from the 
sample background obscuring signa ls from organophosphorus compounds in 1H NMR 
spectra are efficiently removed (Figure 1 and 2). Compared to the 31P{1H} experiment, the 
sensitivity is considerably enhanced. The disadvantage is the modest sensitivity compared 
to mass spectrometric techniques (several orders of magnitude compared to GC –MS if 
absolute amounts of compounds are considered). Another disadvantage i
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
advantage is the modest sensitivity compared 
to mass spectrometric techniques (several orders of magnitude compared to GC –MS if 
absolute amounts of compounds are considered). Another disadvantage is that not all proton 
signals of a compound are present in 1D 1H–31P correlation spectra – only protons with a 
scalar coupling with phosphorous are detectable. To obtain a complete picture of a 
compound (with all spin-systems assigned), other NMR techniques can be recorded.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) 
spectrometry utilising 2D 1H–31P correlation techniques like 2D 1H–31P HSQC 1 and 2D 1H–
31P HMQC 2 in multiple bond 1H–31P correlation for the screening and ide ntification of 
organophosphorus chemicals related to the C hemical Weapons Convention (CWC) . 
Generally, the procedure is suitable for identification of organophosphorus chemicals above 
the 1 µg/ml concentration level. NMR measurements are carried out with modern NMR 
instruments typically equipped with 5-mm NMR probe heads.

2. Summary of the method 
NMR techniques are commonly used for structural elucidation. With the 2D 1H–31P 
correlation spectrum interpretation, a set of information is obtained in the form of NMR 
parameters (chemical shifts and coupling constants) that converge to a chemical structure. 
The information obtained with these two experiments is virtually identical; only the 
appearance of the correlation peaks may vary due to different J(HH) evolution characteristics 
during the pulse sequences. The main information obtained by the 2D 1H–31P correlation 
experiments is the information about organophosphorus chemical family, the structure of the 
alkyl group (e.g. methyl, ethyl, propyl or isopropyl) directly bonded to the phosphorus atom, 
and the number of different organophosphorus compounds present in a sample . Usually, a 
subset of all proton signals with a scalar coupling to phosphorus of organop hosphorus 
compounds is observed . Identification of a com
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ent organophosphorus compounds present in a sample . Usually, a 
subset of all proton signals with a scalar coupling to phosphorus of organop hosphorus 
compounds is observed . Identification of a compound is achieved by comparison with a 
reference spectrum of the authentic compound. The number of resonances, chemical shifts, 
and coupling constants must be consistent. 
3. Safety aspects 
The samples can potentially contain a high dosage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If the concentration of the agent is 
high, a special screw-cap tube can be used or the tube can be sealed by flame. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 General recommendations 
The requirements for spectrometers suitable for the analysis of treaty-related compounds by 
the 2D 1H–31P correlation experiments are as follows: 
1. capability to observe 1H nucleus, 
2. capability to decouple 31P nucleus, 
3. capability to apply signal suppression on selected solvent peak(s), 
4. capability for shaping rf pulses and pulsed field gradients, 
5. capability for controlling of t
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ty to decouple 31P nucleus, 
3. capability to apply signal suppression on selected solvent peak(s), 
4. capability for shaping rf pulses and pulsed field gradients, 
5. capability for controlling of the sample temperature to an accuracy of within ±0.5 °C, 
6. a proton resonance frequency preferably of 400 MHz or more, and 
7. a data system adequate for acquisition, processing, and storage of all necessary data. 
4.2 Probe head characteristics 
The 5-mm room-temperature probe heads generally used in NMR spectroscopy are suitable 
for the analysis of treaty-related compounds. The coil geometry and number of channels can 
vary depending on the type and manufacturer of the probe head. 
The 2D 1H–31P correlation experiments need a probe head with two channels tuneable to 1H 
and 31P. Optimal sensitivity is achieved with so -called inverse probe heads, where the

cryogenic and microcoil probe heads may also increase sensitivity (see section 7.5). 
5. Experimental 
5.1 Recommended conditions 
Temperature: The temperature of the NMR sample must be controlled at between 20 and 
30 °C. The boiling point of the sample solvent should be noted. 
NMR sample: The volume of sample to analyse for a 5-mm NMR tube is 450 to 600 µl. To 
avoid cross-pollution, a new tube (e.g. disposable) should be used for each sample. 
NMR solvent: To lock the frequency of the spectrometer, addition of miscible deuterated 
solvent in the liquid sample is required (50 to 150 µl). If possible, using a deuterated solvent 
similar to the protonated solvent is recommended. To determine the solvent of a liquid 
sample, first an unlocked 1H NMR experi ment should be performed. If a pre treatment is 
required to analy se a sample, solvent exchange to the compatible
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
mended. To determine the solvent of a liquid 
sample, first an unlocked 1H NMR experi ment should be performed. If a pre treatment is 
required to analy se a sample, solvent exchange to the compatible deuterated solvent is 
recommended. 
NMR acquisition parameters: A 1H spectral width of 11 ppm ranging from -1 to 10 ppm and 
a 31P spectra l width of 200 ppm, ranging from -30 to 170 ppm , are recommended. The 
experimental parameters may be optimi sed for particular samples using the guidelines 
provided in Table 1 and Table 2.

Table 1 and Table 2 provide guidelines for the s election of acquisition and processing 
parameters for 2D 1H–31P correlation experiments.

5.3 Optional modifications 
The 2D 1H–31P HSQC experiment can be conducted in a phase-sensitive mode, which will 
provide narrower peaks in the spectrum. A 31P decoupling during acquisition can be used to 
simplify the appearance of the multiplets and to increase the sensitivity of the experiment. 
To increase the 31P excitation range, the hard 31P 180° pulses may be replaced by adiabatic 
pulses. 
The 2D 1H–31P HMQC experiment is not phase -sensitive and must be processed in 
magnitude mode. A better resolution can be achieved using squared sine weighting with 
128 and 147  shifted sine bell on proton and phosphorus dimensions, respectively. The 
experiment is accomplished using the Ernst angle excitat ion, which will provide the 
optimised sensitivity. The HMQC is less sensitive to the 31P 90° pulse value deviation 
compared to the HSQC sequence. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The most important quality control operations are the

compared to the HSQC sequence. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The most important quality control operations are the testing of the spectrometer 
performance and following the identification criteria. The operating procedures included in 
the Quality Manual for the laboratory should complement the Recommen ded Operating 
Procedures (ROP). 
Testing of the spectrometer performance to meet specifications requires a variety of test 
samples, usually provided by the instrument manufacturer. A set of test samples may be as 
follows: 
1. 1H resolution test sample: 5% of orthodichlorobenzene in acetone-d6. 
2. 1H lineshape and spinning sideband test sample: 0.3–3% chloroform in acetone-d6. 
3. 1H sensitivity test sample: 0.1% ethylbenzene in chloroform-d1. 
4. 31P sensitivity test sample: 0.0485 M triphenylphosphate in acetone-d6. 
 
Spectrometer performance tests consist of checking lineshape, sensitivity, and resolution of 
a probe head for 1H nucleus and the sensitivity for the 31P nucleus . Other tests include 
checking the radio frequency field strengths of the observation and decoup ling channels. A
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
resolution of 
a probe head for 1H nucleus and the sensitivity for the 31P nucleus . Other tests include 
checking the radio frequency field strengths of the observation and decoup ling channels. A 
six- to twelve-month interval should be observed between extensive testing; otherwise, tests 
are performed whenever any degradation of performance is detected. Tests are performed 
according to procedures found in the spectrometer manuals or other literature (e.g. see ref. 3). 
Note! The chemical shift is sensitive to chan ges of the sample temperature; therefore, the 
temperature of the sample during the NMR experiment should be known and controlled. 
Calibration of the temperature control unit can be performed with either the ethylene glycol 
or methanol sample when operating near the room temperature. 4, 5

6.2 Solvents 
Deuterated solvents should have a high enrichment of deuterium, >99.5 %. Chloroform-d1, 
deuterium oxide, acetone-d6, dichloromethane-d2, acetonitrile-d3, benzene-d6, and methanol-
d4 are the most common solvents for NMR spectrometry. Dichloromethane-d2 and deuterium 
oxide are considered to be the main solvents in CWC-related analysis, but some others may 
be preferred for better dissolution or to avoid overlap of resonances. The purity of the 
solvents should be checked by long-term NMR. 
6.3 Internal chemical shift references 
The same chemical shift reference s as for basic 1H NMR experiments and basic 31P NMR 
experiments should be used for the corresponding dimension: 
Tetramethylsilane [TMS, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] should be used in organic solvents as the 
chemical shift reference for proton NMR spectra. Sodium 4,4-dimethyl-4-silapentane-1-
sulfonate-d6 [DSS-d6, δ(H) = 0.0 0 ppm; also known as sodium 3-(trimethylsilyl)propane 
sulfonic acid

text:
nts as the 
chemical shift reference for proton NMR spectra. Sodium 4,4-dimethyl-4-silapentane-1-
sulfonate-d6 [DSS-d6, δ(H) = 0.0 0 ppm; also known as sodium 3-(trimethylsilyl)propane 
sulfonic acid -d6, TSPSA-d6], or sodium 3-(trimethylsilyl)-3,3,2,2-tetradeuteropropionate 
[TSP-d4, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] are recommended as reference standards in water. 
Note! DSS-d6 and TSP-d4 have a small chemical shift difference; for comparison of aqueous 
samples with different reference standards use convention DSS -d6 δ(H) = 0.015 ppm vs. 
TSP-d4 δ(H) = 0.00 ppm. 
If unintentional reaction of DSS-d6 and TSP-d4 with the sample compounds is suspected in 
water, p-dioxane [δ(H) = 3.745 ppm vs. int. DSS-d6 δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] could be used instead. 
In chloroform, the shifts of p-dioxane are: δ(H) = 3.70 ppm, vs. int. TMS δ(H) = 0.00 ppm. 
The precise chemical shift of several trace solvents with respect to TMS in selected sample 
matrices has also been reported,6, 7 which can be used as primary internal reference. 
Triphenyl phosphate [TPP, δ(P) = -17.80 ppm] dissolves well in organic solvents and could 
serve as an internal chemical shift reference for phosphorus. 
Note! TPP gives resonances in the a

Triphenyl phosphate [TPP, δ(P) = -17.80 ppm] dissolves well in organic solvents and could 
serve as an internal chemical shift reference for phosphorus. 
Note! TPP gives resonances in the aromatic region of the 1H NMR spectrum. 
As the se chemical shift references do not display a signal in a 2D 1H–31P correlation 
spectrum, a direct proton/phosphorus chemical shift calibration is not possible. Instead, 1H 
NMR and 31P NMR spectra should be acquired first, followed by a transfer of the relevant 
parameters to the 2D 1H–31P correlation experiments. 
6.4 External chemical shift references 
If appropriate reference samples or NMR tube inserts are used, internal 1H chemical shift 
references can also serve as external references. 
The most common external chemical shift reference in 31P NMR is 85% phosphoric acid. In 
aqueous samples, δ(P) = 0.00 ppm is measured in an ideal spherical container inside the 
solution.8 In practice, however, it is more convenient to use a cylindrical capillary tube to 
hold the standard, and a correction should then be applied to take into account the differences 
in diamagnet ic susceptibility. To correct for diamagnetic susceptibility differen

6.5 Unified scale chemical shift referencing 
The current IUPAC recommendation 10, 11 is to use a unified scale for reporting chemical 
shifts of any nuclide X other than 1H in any sample relative to a primary internal reference. 
The primary internal reference is the proton resonance of tetramethylsilane (TMS) in a dilute 
solution in CDCl 3 (volume fraction ϕ < 1 %), but other solvents can be used as the proton 
chemical shift of TMS is, by definition, in any solvent exactly zero. The precise chemical 
shift of several trace level solvents with respect to TMS in selected sample matrices has also 
been reported,6, 7 which can be used as primary internal reference. 
To relate data on the unified scale to chemical shifts expressed relative to a secondary 
reference of the same nuclide X, a quantity Ξ (Greek capital Xi) was defined as the ratio of 
the secondary (isotope-specific) frequency, ν obsX, to that for 1H of TMS in CDCl 3, νobsTMS, 
in the same magnetic field. Therefore, it is convenient to express Ξ as a percentage:

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
The NMR sample tube is first placed into the magnet. The sample temperature stabilization 
to the preset value can take up to 5 minutes depending on the temperature difference of the 
sample and the preset measurement temperature . Meanwhile, the field to the 2H resonance 
of the solvent should be locked (if no deuterated solvent is present, skip this step) and the 
appropriate experimental parameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homog eneity adjusted. The 
90 deg. proton pulse length can be calibrated if necessary (in case of a new matrix) with the 
single scan stroboscopic nutation method.12 Once the receiver gain is adjusted, data 
acquisition may commence. After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -
transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is performed if need
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:

transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is performed if needed to obtain the real spectrum in pure absorption lineshape . 
The same conditions should always be used for spectrum processing . Appropriate shift 
referencing should be used to calibrate the spectrum. These operations can be automated by 
using a sample changer and an auto-tunable gradient probe head with appropriate software. 
Record 1H NMR and 31P{1H} NMR spectra for projections, if necessary. Reference the 
spectra. 
Compared with the sample matrix, the experimental parameters have a minor effect on the 
spectral parameters. Experimental parameters such as spectral width, flip angle, repetition 
time, number of points in the FID and in the real spectrum, number of scans, and processing 
parameters need to be comparable with those used for the acquisition of the spectrum of the 
authentic reference compound. 
Note! It is not always possible nor feasible to use the same experimental parameters, such 
as the number of scans for the test sample as for the reference standard, due to,

as the number of scans for the test sample as for the reference standard, due to, e.g., different 
concentration of the compound. 
7.2 Screening 
The 2D 1H–31P correlation experiment can be used for screening solutions for the presence 
of organophosphorus chemicals relevant to the CWC. In this case, the 2D 1H–31P correlation 
experiment may provide a high level of proof for the presence of a particular 
organophosphorus chemical. 
7.3 Identification 
First, the spectrum is examined for resonance patterns, their positions, number of resonances, 
and their intensities or areas (Figure 1). This gives an idea of the organophosphorus chemical 
family, and the structure of the alkyl group of the compounds of interest. An immediate 
identification of a compound on the basis of familiar features may also result. Information 
obtained from each NMR experi ment is consolidated. Comparisons are made with spectra 
in a computer database or with the spectrum of an authentic compound. All available 
information, including that obtained by other techniques, is used to construct a

respectively. The values of coupling constants J(HH) and J(PH) must agree within limits of 
±0.2 Hz (except for 1J(PH) ±2 Hz). In addition, the resonance patterns and their intensities 
must match. An identification made by spiking a sample with the suspected chemical 
requires exact overlapping of the resonances. The amount of compound spiked should 
increase the peak integral of the compound by at least a factor of 2 and a maximum factor

7.4 Quantification 
The peak volumes in the 2D 1H–31P correlation spectra are dependent on a multitude of 
parameters. Therefore, these experiments are not recommended for routine quantification of 
sample compounds. However, the observed cross-peak volume can be regarded as linear

standard addition for identification of particular compound.

8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to all compounds containing hydrogen atoms other than 
exchangeable with a scalar coupling to a phosphorus atom and dissolving to a sufficient 
degree in a solvent. The analy sed liquid sample must be homogeneous and without 
paramagnetic properties. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The main advantage of the 2D 1H–31P correlation experiment is its selectivity: signals 
exclusively from protons with a scalar coupling to 31P nuclei are recorded. Signals from the 
sample background obscuring signals from organophosphorus compounds in 1H NMR 
spectra are efficiently removed (Figure 1). The experiment has better sensitivity compared 
to the 31P{1H} experiment with additional structural information about the structure of the 
alkyl group and partial characterisation of the ester side chain . The disadvantage is the 
modest sensitivity compared to mass spectrometric techniques (several ord
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
mation about the structure of the 
alkyl group and partial characterisation of the ester side chain . The disadvantage is the 
modest sensitivity compared to mass spectrometric techniques (several orders of magnitude 
compared to GC –MS if absolute amounts of compounds are considered). Another 
disadvantage is that all proton signals of a compound are not present in 2D 1H–31P correlation 
spectra – only proton signals with a scalar coupling with phosphorous are detectable. So to 
obtain a complete picture of a compound (with all spin -system assigned) , other NMR 
techniques can be recorded.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) 
spectrometry utilizing two dimensional (2D) 1H–1H homonuclear correlation experiments 
like COrrelation SpectroscopY (COSY)1 and TOt
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
cribes the use of high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) 
spectrometry utilizing two dimensional (2D) 1H–1H homonuclear correlation experiments 
like COrrelation SpectroscopY (COSY)1 and TOtal Correlation SpectroscopY (TOCSY)2 to 
give 2D NMR spectra where connectivi ty between protons is shown via J(HH) couplings. 
While COSY spectra show protons with direct J(HH) couplings, TOCSY spectra show 
extended networks of J(HH) couplings. 
2D 1H–1H correlation experiments can be performed for the screening and identification of 
chemical warfare agents, their precursors and degradation/reaction products of chemicals 
related to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). 2D 1H–1H correlation techniques are 
generally used to reveal the spin systems of a compound for which some signals o verlap 
with matrix or other chemicals in 1H NMR spectra. In screening, 2D correlation peaks 
provide sub-spectrum characteristics for part of a molecule , which in some case s form a 
specific pattern that attests to the presence of a compound related to the CWC. 
Depending on the nature of probe head, value of the magnetic field , and experiment time, 
2D 1H–1H correlation techniques are suitable f
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
hat attests to the presence of a compound related to the CWC. 
Depending on the nature of probe head, value of the magnetic field , and experiment time, 
2D 1H–1H correlation techniques are suitable for the identification of chemicals above the 
concentration of 1 µg/ ml. NMR measurements are carried out with modern NMR 
instruments typically equipped with 5-mm NMR probe heads.
