2. Summary of the method 
NMR techniques are commonly used for structural elucidation of organic chemical 
compounds. With the 2D 1H–1H correlation spectrum interpretation, a set of information is 
obtained in the form of proton -proton connectivit y through J(HH) scalar couplings that 
converge to a chemical structure. The information obtained with COSY and TOCSY is 
complementary to some degr ee; while COSY is typically optimized to reveal 2-3J(HH) 
correlations, TOCSY experiment (also called HOHAHA experiment for HOmonuclear 
HArtmann-HAhn) permits the assignment of a whole/full spin system. 
The main information obtained by the 2D 1H–1H correlation experiments is which protons 
belong to the same substructure of a compound, which aids the correct assignment of the 
proton resonances observed in 1H NMR spectrum, and possibly detect s resonances under 
obscuring background through off -diagonal cross pe aks. Identification of a compound is 
generally ac
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
nt of the 
proton resonances observed in 1H NMR spectrum, and possibly detect s resonances under 
obscuring background through off -diagonal cross pe aks. Identification of a compound is 
generally achieved by combination with 1H NMR and by comparison with a reference 
spectrum of the authentic compound. The number of resonances, chemical shifts, and c ross 
peak patterns must be consistent. 
3. Safety aspects 
The samples can potentially contain a high dosage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If the concentration of the agent is 
high, a special screw-cap tube can be used, or the tube can be sealed by flame. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 General recommendations 
The requirements for spectrometers suitable for the analysis of treaty-related compounds by 
the 2D 1H–1H correlation experiments are as follows: 
1. capability to observe 1H nucleus, 
2. capability to apply signal suppression on selected solvent peak(s), 
3. capability for shaping rf pulses and pulsed field gradients, 
4. capability for controlling the sample temperature
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
nucleus, 
2. capability to apply signal suppression on selected solvent peak(s), 
3. capability for shaping rf pulses and pulsed field gradients, 
4. capability for controlling the sample temperature to an accuracy of within ±0.5 °C, 
5. a proton resonance frequency preferably of 400 MHz or more, and 
6. a data system adequate for acquisition, processing, and storage of all necessary data. 
4.2 Probe head characteristics 
The 2D 1H–1H correlation experiments need a probe head with one channel tunable to 1H. 
Optimal sensitivity is achieved with so-called inverse probe heads, where the innermost RF 
coil is used for proton detection. Using cryogenic and microcoil probe head s may also 
increase sensitivity. The coil geometry can vary depending on the type and manufacturer of 
the probe head.

5. Experimental 
5.1 Recommended conditions 
Temperature: The temperature of the NMR sample must be controlled at between 20 and 30 
°C. The boiling point of the sample solvent should be noted. 
NMR sample: The volume of sample to analyse for a 5 -mm NMR tube is 450 to 600 µl. To 
avoid cross-pollution, a new tube (e.g. disposable) should be used for each sample. 
NMR solvent: To lock the frequency of the spectrom eter, addition of miscible deuterated 
solvent in the liquid sample is required (50 to 400 µl). To determine the solvent of a liquid 
sample, an unlocked 1H NMR experiment should first be performed. If the compound to 
identify is not volatile, nor subject to degradation (e.g. oxidation), a solvent exchange with 
the compatible deuterated solvent can be achieved. For screening method, the solvent 
exchange is not recommended. 
NMR acquisition parameters: For screening method, a 1H spectral width of 11 ppm ranging 
from -1 to 10 ppm is recommende

text:
n be achieved. For screening method, the solvent 
exchange is not recommended. 
NMR acquisition parameters: For screening method, a 1H spectral width of 11 ppm ranging 
from -1 to 10 ppm is recommended. The experimental parameters may be optimized for 
particular samples using the guidelines provided in Table 1 for TOCSY and Table 2 for 
COSY.

Table 1 and Table 2 provides guidelines for the selection of acquisition and processing

5.3 Optional modifications 
The TOCSY experiment is conducted in a phase -sensitive mode, which will provide 
narrower peaks in the spectrum. The TOCSY experim ents can include gradient -based 
solvent suppression schemes as Watergate (GrAdient-Tailored Excitation)6 and modified 
Watergate with double pulse field gradient spin echo called Excitation Sculpting.7 Non-
uniform sampling can be used to improve resolution in the f1 dimensi
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
rAdient-Tailored Excitation)6 and modified 
Watergate with double pulse field gradient spin echo called Excitation Sculpting.7 Non-
uniform sampling can be used to improve resolution in the f1 dimension.4 
Note! Reduction of acquired data points with NUS will also reduce the attainable signal-to-
noise ratio. 
A 13C decoupling can be implemented during acquisition period to eliminate 13C satellites of 
a strong signal if overlapping occurs with a signal of interest. A variant of TOCSY pulse 
sequence can be implemented by using band-selective excitation.8, 9 
The COSY experiment is typically processed in magnitude mode for the observation of 
J(HH) coupling pathways; acquisition of a phase sensitive COSY can be recorded to evaluate 
the J(HH) coupling constants from the anti-phase splitting of the cross peaks, if needed. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The most important quality control operations are the testing of the spectrometer 
performance and following the identification criteria. The operating procedures included in 
the Quality Manual for the laboratory should complement the Recommended Operating 
Procedures (ROP). 
Testing of the spectrometer perform

text:
identification criteria. The operating procedures included in 
the Quality Manual for the laboratory should complement the Recommended Operating 
Procedures (ROP). 
Testing of the spectrometer performance to m eet specifications requires a variety of test 
samples, usually provided by the instrument manufacturer. A set of test samples could be as 
follows: 
1. 1H resolution test sample: 5% of orthodichlorobenzene in acetone-d6. 
2. 1H lineshape and spinning sideband test sample: 0.3%–3.0% chloroform in 
acetone-d6. 
3. 1H sensitivity test sample: 0.1% ethylbenzene in chloroform-d1.

Spectrometer performance tests consist of checking lineshape, sensitivity, and resolution of 
a probe head for 1H nucleus. Other tests include checking the radio frequency field strengths 
of the observation and decoupling channels. A six - to twelve -month interval should be 
observed between extensive testing; otherwise, tests are performed whenever any 
degradation of performance is detected. Tests are performed according to procedures found 
in the spectrometer manuals or other literature (e.g. see ref. 10). Specific tests more adapted 
to laboratory application can also be implemented to more frequently evaluate the resolution 
and sensitivity of 1H nucleus. 
Note! The chemical shift is sensitive to changes of the sample temperature; therefore, the 
temperature of the sample during the NMR experiment should be known. Calibration of the 
temperature control unit can be performed with either the ethylene glycol or metha nol 
sample when operating near

temperature control unit can be performed with either the ethylene glycol or metha nol 
sample when operating near room temperature. 11, 12 
6.2 Solvents 
Deuterated solvents should have a high enrichment of deuterium, >99.5%. Chloroform -d1, 
deuterium oxide, acetone-d6, dichloromethane-d2, acetonitrile-d3, benzene-d6, and methanol-
d4 are the most common solvents for NMR spectrometry. Dichloromethane-d2 and deuterium 
oxide are considered to be the main solvents in CWC-related analysis, but some others may 
be preferred for better dissolution or to avoid overlap of resonances. The purity of the 
solvents should be checked by long-term NMR. 
6.3 Internal chemical shift references 
Tetramethylsilane [TMS, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] should be used in organic solvents as the 
chemical shift reference for proton NMR spectra. Sodium 4,4-dimethyl-4-silapentane-
1-sulfonate-d6 [DSS-d6, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm; also known as sodium3 -(trimethylsilyl)propane 
sulfonic acid -d6, TSPSA -d6], or sodium 3 -(trimethylsilyl)-3,3,2,2-tetradeuteropropionate 
[TSP-d4, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] are recommended as reference standards in water.

sulfonic acid -d6, TSPSA -d6], or sodium 3 -(trimethylsilyl)-3,3,2,2-tetradeuteropropionate

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
The NMR sample tube is first placed into the magnet. The sample temperature stabilization 
to the preset value can take up to 5 minutes depending on the temperature difference of the 
sample and the preset measurement temperature . Meanwhile, the field to the 2H resonance 
of the solvent should be locked (if no deuterated solvent is present, skip this step) and the 
appropriate experimental parameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homogeneity adjusted. The 90 
deg. proton pulse length can be calibrated if necessary ( in case of a new matrix) with the 
single scan stroboscopic nutation method.15 Once the receiver gain is adjusted, data 
acquisition may commence. After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -
transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is performed if nee
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ata 
acquisition may commence. After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -
transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is performed if needed to obtain the real spectrum in pure absorption lineshape . 
The same conditions should always be used for spectrum processing . Appropriate shift 
referencing should be used to calibrate the spectrum. These operations can be automated by 
using a sample changer and an auto-tunable gradient probe head with appropriate software. 
If non-uniform sampling is used, process the 2D experiment with appro priate algorithm 
(Compressed Sensing algorithm is recommended).4 
Compared with the sample matrix, the experimental parameters have a minor effect on the 
spectral parameters. Experimental parameters such as spectral width, flip angle, repetition 
time, number of points in the FID and in the real spectrum, number of scans, and processing 
parameters need to be comparable with those used for the acquisitio n of the database 
spectrum or spectrum of the authentic reference compound. 
Note! It is not always possible nor feasible to use the same experimental parameters, such 
as the number of

spectrum or spectrum of the authentic reference compound. 
Note! It is not always possible nor feasible to use the same experimental parameters, such 
as the number of scans for the test sample as for the reference standard, due to, e.g., different 
concentration of the compound. 
7.2 Screening 
The 2D 1H–1H correlation experiments can be used for screening solutions to reveal the 
presence of chemicals relevant to the CWC. In this case, the 2D 1H–1H correlation 
experiment may provide a high level of proof for the presence of a compound with specific 
spin system pattern or can be a powerful tool to obtain fingerprint of a complex mixture. 
7.3 Identification 
First, the spectrum is examined for resonance patterns, their positions, number of resonances, 
and their intensities or areas. This provides an idea of the subset chemical, and the structure 
of e.g. the alkyl group of the compounds of interest and the discrimination between isomers. 
An immediate identification of a compound on the basis of familiar features may also result 
with specific spin system. Information obtained from each NMR experiment is consolidated 
(one and two dimensions). C

with specific spin system. Information obtained from each NMR experiment is consolidated 
(one and two dimensions). Comparisons are made with spectra in a computer database or 
with the spectrum of an authentic compound. All av ailable information, including that 
obtained by other techniques, is used to construct a complete picture. Two examples are

To obtain a positive identification, the NMR spectral parameters for a compound must agree 
within certain limits with those of the database or the authentic compound. If the sample of 
the comp ound to be identified has been prepared so as to correspond in solvent, 
concentration, pH, and chemical shift references to t he compound in the database 
(or authentic compound), the values of δ(H) must agree with the corresponding values in the 
database (o r authentic compound) within limits of ±0.05 ppm. The values of coupling 
constants J(HH), if given in assignment, must agree within limits of ±0.2 Hz , but coupling 
constants are more easily extractable from 1H NMR spectrum. 
In addition, the resonance patterns and their intensities must match. An identification made 
by spiking a sample with the suspected chemical requires exact overlapping of the 
resonances. The amount of compound spiked should increase the peak integral of the 
compound by at least a f

text:

by spiking a sample with the suspected chemical requires exact overlapping of the 
resonances. The amount of compound spiked should increase the peak integral of the 
compound by at least a factor of 2 and a maximum factor of 4. 
Note! It is not always possible to obtain the same conditions for the reference standard as 
for the test sample (e.g. matrix effect), thus differences in the NMR spectral parameters may 
be considerable. The identification criteria may then be expanded within reasonable limits 
(e.g. doubled). In this case, identification by adding the authentic compound in the sample

7.4 Quantification 
The peak volumes in the 2D 1H–1H correlation spectra are dependent on a multitude of 
parameters. Therefore, these experiments are not recommended for routine quantification of 
sample compounds. However, the observed cross -peak volume can be regarded as linear 
with respect to the concentration of the analyte, and peak volume integration can be used in 
standard addition for identification of a particular compound. 
7.5 Trace analysis 
The detection limit for a compound depends on the magnetic field strength of the 
spe

standard addition for identification of a particular compound. 
7.5 Trace analysis 
The detection limit for a compound depends on the magnetic field strength of the 
spectrometer, the probe head, the number of scans, the flip angles, the observed nucleus and 
its relaxation time, the NMR tube diameter, the sample matrix, and the homogeneity of the 
magnetic field. With modern NMR spectrometers that have a magnetic field of ca. 12 Tesla 
and a room-temperature probe head, a limit of detection of 1 µg/ ml can be obtained. With 
special probe heads ,16, 17 the sensitivity and, hence, the detection limit can be further 
improved (e.g. 0.1 µg/ml with a cryoprobe or 50 ng of total amount with a microcoil probe 
head), and the measurement time can be reduced.

7.6 Remarks on analysis 
Non-deuterated solvents can be used if a small amount of the corresponding deuterated 
solvent is added to the sample to provide the lock conditions, if the experiment is performed 
unlocked, or if a lock nucleus other than deuterium is used. In this case, the intense solvent 
signal must be eliminated with pre-saturation, pulsed field gradients method like Watergate, 
excitation scul pting, or PURGE . For strongly salty samples, cryoprobes are 
disadvantageous, but it could be beneficial using smaller diameter tubes (e.g. 3-mm tube and 
spinner on a 5-mm probe head) or microprobes. The 90° pulse widths should be recalibrated. 
Paramagnetic salts in aqueous samples can enhance relaxation so that the resonances became 
too broad to b e observable. In this case, a pre -treatment must be performed (e.g. cation 
exchange, application of chelating agents). 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
observable. In this case, a pre -treatment must be performed (e.g. cation 
exchange, application of chelating agents). 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to all compounds that contain hydrogen atoms other than 
exchangeable, that have scalar coupling with other protons, and that dissolve to a sufficient 
degree in a solvent. The analysed liquid sample must be homogeneous and without 
paramagnetic properties. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The main advantage of the 2D 1H–1H correlation experiments in comparison to basic 1H 
NMR is to split the 1H signal in the second dimension and to reveal the proton resonances 
that belong to a specific spin system, and therefore assist to identify hydrocarbon 
substructures and finally the compounds. 
The disadvantage is the modest sensitivity compared to mass spectrometric techniques 
(several orders of magnitude compared to GC –MS if absolute amounts of compounds are 
considered). Another disadvantage is that the usability of these experiments is susceptible to 
a high level of hydrocarbon background in the samples, which may mask relevant cross 
peaks. To obtain a complete picture of a compound (with

text:

a high level of hydrocarbon background in the samples, which may mask relevant cross 
peaks. To obtain a complete picture of a compound (with all spin systems assigned), other

1. Scope

reference spectra scalable to any magnetic field to assist the identification of chemical 
warfare agents, their precursors and degradation /reaction products of chemicals related to 
the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC).

2. Summary of the method 
NMR techniques are commonly used for structural elucidation. With the 1H NMR 
spectrum interpretation, a set of information is obtained in the form of NMR parameters 
(chemical shifts and coupling constants) that converge to a chemical structure. To assist in 
the interpretation of an experimental spectrum, it is commonly compared against simulated 
spectra of tentative structures. The spectral parameters for the simulation are obtained from 
their predicted or experimentally obtained chemical shifts and scalar coupling constants . 
Based on these parameters, the simulated spectrum is calculated using quantum mechanical 
calculations, which can reproduce any features observed in experimental data (e.g. second -
order effects) with high accuracy.

using guidelines pioneered by J.A . Pople.1 Spin system definition is dependent on several 
factors, e.g. the chemica

6. Extraction of NMR parameters from experimental data 
The experimental data that is employed should be of high quality (sufficient S/N, narrow 
and symmetric lineshapes). The method of how to extract precise NMR parameters from 
experimental data depends on if the spectrum is i) first-order, or ii) second-order. 
The multiplet is first order when the chemical shift differences between the coupled nuclei 
are equal or larger than seven times the J coupling magnitude , and the J coupling is 
involved with groups that are magnetically equivalent.7 The extraction of NMR parameters 
from a first -order multiplet is , in most cases , trivial with established interpretation 
conventions.8, 9 
In case the chemical shift difference is below seven times the J coupling magnitude, and/or 
if the coupling is involved with groups that are only chemically equivalent like 
enantiotopic CH2 protons (e.g. Table 1, sulphur mustard), the r esulting second -o
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
s the J coupling magnitude, and/or 
if the coupling is involved with groups that are only chemically equivalent like 
enantiotopic CH2 protons (e.g. Table 1, sulphur mustard), the r esulting second -order 
multiplet cannot be interpreted correctly with first -order analysis. Iterative computer 
analysis is generally employed to obtain accurate NMR parameters from this kind of 
spectrum.10 In this method , the spin system is first defined for the st udied molecule, and 
the trial values for NMR para meters are given to, or predicted by, the iterator program . 
This information is used for simulation of the trial spectrum. The trial spectrum is then 
matched with the experimental spectrum, and the program uses a specific iteration 
algorithm to minimize the differences between the simulated and experimental spectra. 
When the iteration converges, the obtained simulated spectrum and NMR parameters must 
be checked by the user for their validity. An example of iterative computer analysis is 
shown in Figure 3. Table 2 lists software that provide iterative computer analysis with 
graphical interface.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the use of high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) 
spectrometry utili sing 2D 1H–13C correlation techniques , such as 2D 1H–13C HSQC-
DEPT135 1 and 2D 1H–13C HMBC 2, in both single and multiple bond 1H–13C correlation 
for the screening and identification of chemicals related to the C hemical Weapons 
Convention (CWC) . Generally,
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
DEPT135 1 and 2D 1H–13C HMBC 2, in both single and multiple bond 1H–13C correlation 
for the screening and identification of chemicals related to the C hemical Weapons 
Convention (CWC) . Generally, the procedure is suitable for identification of chemicals 
above the 10 µg/ml concentration level. NMR measurements are carried out with modern 
NMR instruments typically equipped with 5-mm NMR probe heads. 
2. Summary of the method 
NMR techniques are commonly used for structural elucidation. With the 2D 1H–13C 
correlation spectrum interpretation, a set of information is obtained in the form of NMR 
parameters (chemical shifts and coupling constants) that converge to a chemical structure. 
The information obtained from 1H-13C correlation techniques differs in relation to the 
number of bonds between the 1H and 13C nucleus. The 1H-13C HSQC-DEPT135 experiment 
shows only directly bonded 1H-13C correlations via 1J(HC) couplings. In addition, the DEPT-
135 component of the experiment results in CH2 correlations to appear antiphase (180° phase 
shift) to the CH and CH 3 environments. The 1H-13C HMBC experiment is optimised to 
observe multiple bond correlations via 2-3J(HC) couplings whil
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
in CH2 correlations to appear antiphase (180° phase 
shift) to the CH and CH 3 environments. The 1H-13C HMBC experiment is optimised to 
observe multiple bond correlations via 2-3J(HC) couplings whilst suppressing the 1J(HC) 
correlations. The main information obtained by the 2D 1H–13C correlation experiments is the 
information about hydrocarbon chemical family, in particular vesicant-related products and 
scheduled compounds that lack phosphorous nuclei. It is also possible to observe 13C-31P J-
couplings to confirm structures of organophorous compounds. Identification of a compound 
is achieved by comparison with a reference spectrum of the authentic compound. The 
number of resonances, chemical shifts, and coupling constants must be consistent.

3. Safety aspects 
The samples can potentially contain a high dosage of toxic chemicals, thus sufficient safety 
measures should be used when handling. Closing the tube with a plastic cap is usually 
sufficient if the sample is expected to be relatively dilute. If the concentration of the agent is 
high, a special screw-cap tube can be used, or the tube can be sealed by flame. 
4. Instrumentation 
4.1 General recommendations 
The requirements for spectrometers suitable for the analysis of treaty-related compounds by 
the 2D 1H–13C correlation experiments are as follows: 
1. capability to observe 1H nucleus, 
2. capability to decouple 13C nucleus, 
3. capability to apply signal suppression on selected solvent peak(s), 
4. capability for shaping rf pulses and pulsed field gradients, 
5. capability for controlling of the sample temperature to an accuracy of within ±0.5 °C, 
6. a proton resonance frequency preferably of 400 MHz or more, and 
7. a data sy
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
and pulsed field gradients, 
5. capability for controlling of the sample temperature to an accuracy of within ±0.5 °C, 
6. a proton resonance frequency preferably of 400 MHz or more, and 
7. a data system adequate for acquisition, processing, and storage of all necessary data. 
4.2 Probe head characteristics 
The 5-mm room-temperature probe heads generally used in NMR spectroscopy are suitable 
for the analysis of treaty-related compounds. The coil geometry and number of channels can 
vary depending on the type and manufacturer of the probe head. 
The 2D 1H–13C correlation experiments require a probe head with two channels tuneable to 
1H and 13C. Optimal sensitivity is achieved with so -called inverse probe heads, where the 
innermost RF coil is used for proton detection and the outer coil for 13C pulses. Using 
cryogenic and microcoil probe heads may also increase sensitivity (see section 7.5). 
5. Experimental 
5.1 Recommended conditions 
Temperature: The temperature of the NMR sample must be controlled at between 20 and 
30 °C. The boiling point of the sample solvent should be noted. 
NMR sample: The volume of sample to analyse for a 5 -mm NMR tube is 450 to 600 µl. To 
avoid c

text:

30 °C. The boiling point of the sample solvent should be noted. 
NMR sample: The volume of sample to analyse for a 5 -mm NMR tube is 450 to 600 µl. To 
avoid cross-pollution, a new tube (e.g. disposable) should be used for each sample. 
NMR solvent: To lock the frequency of the spectrometer, addition of miscible deuterated 
solvent in the liquid sample is required (50 to 150 µl). If possible, using a deuterated solvent 
similar to the protonated solvent is recommended. To determine the solvent of a liquid 
sample, first an unlocked 1H NMR experiment should be performed. If a pre -treatment is

5.3 Optional modifications 
The 2D 1H–13C HSQC-DEPT135 experiment can be conducted in a phase-sensitive mode, 
which will provide narrower peaks in the spectrum. Alternative HSQC-DEPT135 sequences 
with sensitivity enhancement are also applicable to this met hod. For instrument 
fields of >500 MHz, the 13C 180° pulses may be replaced by adiabatic pulses to improve the 
excitation efficiency over a large 13C ppm range. 
The 2D 1H–31C HMBC experiment is typically acquired in magnitude mode , however, can 
also be acquired using a phase -sensitive method. Resolution in the 13C dimension may be 
improved using forward linear prediction during processing. For instrument fields of 
> 500 MHz, the 13C 180° pulses may be replaced by adiabatic pulses to improve the 
excitation efficiency over a large 13C ppm range. 
Solvent suppression techniques like presaturation, WET,4 PURGE,5 or ROBUST6 could be 
used to achieve optimal receiver gain for the detection of
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
he 
excitation efficiency over a large 13C ppm range. 
Solvent suppression techniques like presaturation, WET,4 PURGE,5 or ROBUST6 could be 
used to achieve optimal receiver gain for the detection of target chemicals in environmental 
samples. 
6. Quality control 
6.1 Instrument performance test 
The most important quality control operations are the testing of the spectrometer 
performance and following the identification criteria. The operating procedures included in 
the Quality Manual for the laboratory should complement the Recommen ded Operating 
Procedures (ROP). 
Testing of the spectrometer performance to meet specifications r equires a variety of test 
samples, usually provided by the instrument manufacturer. A set of test samples could be as 
follows: 
1. 1H resolution test sample: 5% of orthodichlorobenzene in acetone-d6. 
2. 1H lineshape and spinning sideband test sample: 0.3–3% chloroform in acetone-d6. 
3. 1H sensitivity test sample: 0.1% ethylbenzene in chloroform-d1. 
4. 13C sensitivity test sample: 10% ethylbenzene in chloroform-d1. 
5. 13C lineshape test sample 40% dioxane in benzene-d6. 
Spectrometer performance tests consist of checking lineshape, sensitivity, an
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
13C sensitivity test sample: 10% ethylbenzene in chloroform-d1. 
5. 13C lineshape test sample 40% dioxane in benzene-d6. 
Spectrometer performance tests consist of checking lineshape, sensitivity, and resolution of 
a probe head for 1H nucleus and the sensitivity for the 13C nucleus. Other tests include 
checking the radio frequency field strengths of the observation and decoupling channels. The 
interval between extensive te sting should be six to twelve months; otherwise, tests are 
performed whenever any degradation of performance is detected. Tests are performed 
according to procedures found in the spectrometer manuals or other literature (e.g. see ref. 7). 
Note! The chemical shift is sensitive to changes of the sample temperature ; therefore, the 
temperature of the sample during the NMR experiment should be known. Calibration of the 
temperature control unit can be performed with either the ethylene glycol or methanol 
sample when operating near room temperature. 8, 9

6.2 Solvents 
Deuterated solvents should have a high enrichment of deuterium, >99.5%. Chloroform -d1, 
deuterium oxide, acetone-d6, dichloromethane-d2, acetonitrile-d3, benzene-d6, and methanol-
d4 are the most common solvents for NMR spectrometry. Dichloromethane-d2 and deuterium 
oxide are considered to be the main solvents in CWC-related analysis, but some others may 
be preferred for better dissolution or to avoid overlap of resonances. The purity of the 
solvents should be checked by long-term NMR. 
6.3 Internal chemical shift references 
The same chemical shift references as for basic 1H NMR experiment should be used for the 
corresponding dimension: 
Tetramethylsilane [TMS, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] should be used in organic solvents as the 
chemical shift reference for proton N MR spectra. Sodium 4,4 -dimethyl-4-silapentane-1-
sulfonate-d6 [DSS-d6, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm; also known as sodium3 -(trimethylsilyl)propane 
sulfonic acid -d6, TSPSA -d6], or sodiu

sulfonate-d6 [DSS-d6, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm; also known as sodium3 -(trimethylsilyl)propane 
sulfonic acid -d6, TSPSA -d6], or sodium 3 -(trimethylsilyl)-3,3,2,2-tetradeuteropropionate 
[TSP-d4, δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] are recommended as reference standards in water. 
Note! As a matter of fact DSS -d6 and TSP-d4 have a small chemical shift difference; for 
comparison of aqueous samples with different reference standards use convention DSS -d6 
δ(H) = 0.015 ppm vs. TSP-d4 δ(H) = 0.00 ppm. 
If unintentional reaction of DSS-d6 and TSP-d4 with the sample compounds is suspected in 
water, p-dioxane [δ(H) = 3.745 ppm vs. int. DSS-d6 δ(H) = 0.00 ppm] could be used instead. 
In chloroform, the shifts of p-dioxane are: δ(H) = 3.70 ppm, vs. int. TMS δ(H) = 0.00 ppm. 
The precise chemical shift of several trace level solvents with respect to TMS in selected 
sample matrices has also been reported,10, 11 which can be used as primary internal reference.

may be used as a referencing point for both dimensions [δ(C) = 0.00 ppm].

6.4 Unified scale chemical shift referencing 
The current IUPAC recommendation 12, 13 is to use a unified scale for reporting chemical 
shifts of any nuclide X other than 1H in any sample relative to a primary internal reference. 
The primary internal reference is the proton resonance of tetramethylsilane (TMS) in a dilute 
solution in CDCl 3 (volume fraction ϕ < 1 %), but other solvents can be used as the proton 
chemical shift of TMS is, by definition, in any solvent exactly zero. The precise chemical 
shift of several trace level solvents with respect to TMS in selected sample matrices has also 
been reported,10, 11 which can be used as primary internal reference.

7. Analysis of samples 
7.1. Sequence of analysis 
The NMR sample tube is first placed into the magnet. The sample temperature stabilization 
to the preset value can take up to 5 minutes depending on the temperature difference of the 
sample and the preset measurement temperature . Meanwhile, the field to the 2H resonance 
of the solvent should be locked (if no deuterated solvent is p resent, skip this step) and the 
appropriate experimental parameters are set . The observation and, if necessary, the 
decoupling channel should be tuned, and the magnetic field homogeneity adjusted. The 90 
deg. proton pulse length can be calibrated if necess ary (in case of a new matrix) with the 
single scan stroboscopic nutation method.14 Once the receiver gain is adjusted, data 
acquisition may commence . After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -
transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is p
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
is adjusted, data 
acquisition may commence . After the NMR experiment is completed, the Fourier -
transformed NMR spectrum is calculated, using appropriate window function, and phase 
correction is performed if needed to obtain the real spectrum in pure absorption lineshape . 
The same conditions should always be used for spectrum processing . Appropriate shift 
referencing should be used to calibrate the spectrum. These operations can be automated by 
using a sample changer and an auto-tunable gradient probe head with appropriate software. 
Record a 1H NMR for projection (due to the low sensitivity of 13C{1H} NMR it is not usually 
recorded) and reference the spectrum. 
Compared with the sample matrix, the experimental parameters have a minor effect on the 
spectral parameters. Experimental parameters su ch as spectral width, flip angle, repetition 
time, number of points in the FID and in the real spectrum, number of scans, and processing 
parameters need to be comparable with those used for the acquisition of the spectrum of the 
authentic reference compound.

Note! It is not always possible nor feasible to use the same experimental parameters , such 
as number of scans for the test sample as for the reference standard, due to, e.g., the different 
concentration of the compound. 
7.2 Screening 
The 2D 1H–13C correlation experiment can be used for screening solutions for the presence 
chemicals relevant to the CWC . However, it is more commonplace to use the 2D 1H-13C 
correlation experiments for structure conformation coupled with other experiments , for 
example, COSY or TOCSY. 
7.3 Identification 
First, the spectrum is examined for resonance patterns, their positions, number of resonances, 
and their intensities or areas. This provides information relating to aliphatic and/ or aromatic 
groups within a compound. Information relating to chemical functionality such as CH3, CH2, 
and CH groups can be obtained. An immediate identification of a compound on the basis of 
familiar features may also result. Inf
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ound. Information relating to chemical functionality such as CH3, CH2, 
and CH groups can be obtained. An immediate identification of a compound on the basis of 
familiar features may also result. Information obtained from each NMR experiment is 
consolidated. Compa risons are made with spectra in a computer database or with the 
spectrum of an authentic compound. All available information, including that obtained by 
other techniques, is used to construct a complete picture. 
To obtain a positive identification, the NMR spectral parameters for a compound must agree 
within certain limits with those of the database or the authentic compound. If the sample of 
the compound to be identified has been prepared to correspond in solvent, concentration, pH, 
and chemical shift references to the compound in the database (or authentic compound), the 
values of δ(H) and δ( C) must agree with the corresponding values in the database (or 
authentic compound), within limits of ±0.05 ppm and ±0.2 ppm, respectively. The values of 
coupling constants J(HH), if given in assignment, must agree within limits of ±0.2 Hz but 
coupling constants are more easily extractable from 1H NMR spectrum. In addit
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
m, respectively. The values of 
coupling constants J(HH), if given in assignment, must agree within limits of ±0.2 Hz but 
coupling constants are more easily extractable from 1H NMR spectrum. In addition, the 
resonance patterns and their intensities must match. An identification made by spiking a 
sample with the suspected chemical requires exact overlapping of the resonances. The 
amount of compound spiked should increase the peak integral of the compound by at least a 
factor of 2 and a maximum factor of 4. 
Note! It is not always possible to obtain the same conditions for the reference standard as 
for the test sample (e.g. matrix effect), thus differences in the NMR spectral parameters may 
be considerable. The identification criteria may then be expanded within reaso nable limits 
(e.g. doubled). In this case, identification by adding the authentic compound in the sample 
is recommended.

7.4 Quantification 
The peak volumes in the 2D 1H–13C correlation spectra are dependent on a multitude of 
parameters. Therefore, these experiments are not recommended for routine quantification of 
sample compounds. However, the observed cross-peak volume can be regarded as linear 
with respect to the concentration of the analyte, and peak volume integration can be used in 
standard addition for identification of particular compound. 
7.5 Trace analysis 
The detection limit for a compound depends on the magnetic field strength of the 
spectrometer, the probe head, the number of scans, the flip angles, the observed nucleus and 
its relaxation time, the NMR tube diameter, the sample matrix, and the homogeneity of the 
magnetic field. With modern NMR spectrometers that have a magnetic field of ca. ≥ 12 Tesla 
and a room-temperature probe head, a limit of detection of 10 µg/ml can be obtained. With 
cryogenically cooled NMR probe heads and preamplifiers
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
rometers that have a magnetic field of ca. ≥ 12 Tesla 
and a room-temperature probe head, a limit of detection of 10 µg/ml can be obtained. With 
cryogenically cooled NMR probe heads and preamplifiers , the sensitivity, and hence the 
detection limit, can be further improved, and the measurement time can be reduced.15 
7.6 Remarks on analysis 
Non-deuterated solvents can be used if a small amount of the corresponding deuterated 
solvent is added to the sample to provide the lock conditions, if the experiment is performed 
unlocked, or if a lock nucleus other than deuterium is used. For strongly salty samples, 
cryoprobes are disadvantageous, but it could be beneficial usi ng smaller diameter tubes 
(e.g. 3-mm tube and spinner on a 5-mm probe head) or microprobes. The 90° pulse widths 
should be recalibrated. Paramagnetic salts in aqueous samples can enhance relaxation so that 
the resonances became too broad to be observable. In this case, a pretreatment must be 
performed (e.g. cation exchange, application of chelating agents). 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to all compounds containing hydrogen atoms other than 
exchangeable with a sc
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
exchange, application of chelating agents). 
8. Evaluation of method 
8.1 Area of applicability 
The method is applicable to all compounds containing hydrogen atoms other than 
exchangeable with a scalar coupling to a carbon atom and dissolving to a sufficient degree 
in a solvent. The analy sed liquid sample must be homogeneous and without paramagnetic 
properties. 
8.2 Advantages/Disadvantages 
The main advantage of the 2D 1H–13C correlation experiment is its resolution enhancement 
of crowded 1H NMR spectra by correlation via scalar couplings with 13C chemical shifts. 
Overlapping signals from crowded 1H NMR spectra are sufficiently resolved to enable 
chemical identification (Figure 1). Additionally, the DEPT -135 component allows the 
difference of CH3 and CH verses CH 2 environments. The experiment has better sensitivity 
compared to the 13C{1H} NMR experiment with additional structural information about the 
structure of the alkyl group and partial characteri sation. The 2D 1H-13C HMBC provides 
information on 1H-13C multiple bond connectivities, and enables the detection of quaternary
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

carbon environments such as carbonyls (Figure 2). In addition, this technique works for both 
phosphorous and non -phosphorous containing chemicals. The disadvantage is the low 
sensitivity compared to mass spectrometric techniques (several orders of magnitude 
compared to GC –MS if absolute amounts of compounds are considered). Another 
disadvantage of the HSQC -DEPT135 is the lack of connectivity information between the 
proton signals of a compound. Thus, to obtain a complete picture of a compound (with all 
spin-system assigned), other NMR techniques can be recorded.

1. Scope 
This chapter focuses on the analysis of the natural toxin, saxitoxin (STX). The screening and 
the identification of STX using liquid chromatography (LC) combined with mass 
spectrometry (MS and MS/MS) is described. STX is a neurotoxin wh
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
f the natural toxin, saxitoxin (STX). The screening and 
the identification of STX using liquid chromatography (LC) combined with mass 
spectrometry (MS and MS/MS) is described. STX is a neurotoxin which belongs to the group 
of paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP) toxins. Although several structurally related PSP 
toxins exist, only STX is listed in Schedule 1 (1.A.07) of the Chemical Weapons Convention 
(CWC). The properties of STX are provided in Table 1. 
GC–MS is the most widely used technique for analysing chemical warfare agents (CWAs). 
However, it cannot be used for the analysis of STX , due to its high polarity and cationic 
nature. In contrast, t he LC–MS/MS technique allows the analysis of non -volatile or low 
volatile chemicals with very little sample preparation. Atmospheric pressure ionisation 
(API) techniques are soft ionisation methods , which allow the detection of intact STX as 
protonated molecule [M+H]+ with a low degree of fragmentation. 
2. Summary of the method 
Reversed-phase LC (RPLC) is a widely used method for screening CWAs by LC –MS/MS. 
It can also be used for initial screening of STX (Figure 1). However, the retention of highly 
polar compounds is l
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
Reversed-phase LC (RPLC) is a widely used method for screening CWAs by LC –MS/MS. 
It can also be used for initial screening of STX (Figure 1). However, the retention of highly 
polar compounds is low in RPLC , and therefore signal suppression and other 
chromatographic interferences may occur. Hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC) 
is a good choice as an efficient separation technique for identification of STX due to its polar 
characteristics. The combination with positive mode electrospray ionisation (ESI) mass 
spectrometry allows sensitive and selective detection. LC–MS/MS instruments are operated 
in either the full scan, product ion scan , or selected reaction monitoring /multiple reaction 
monitoring (SRM/MRM) mode (Table 2).

3. Safety aspects 
STX is one of the most potent natural toxins known. It is highly toxic, the LD50 of STX and 
the nerve agent VX are comparable . STX is produced by marine dinoflagellates and 
freshwater cyanobacteria. It accumulates in seafood and may contaminate drinking water. 
The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has set the regulatory values for STX in 
seafood and some drinking water health alert values have also been set by national authorities. 
Due to its high toxicity, STX must be handled with special care in a fume hood. Normal 
laboratory safety measures should be employed, such as wearing pro tective gloves and 
goggles, while handling toxic samples. STX samples may be decontaminated under alkaline 
conditions. 
Safety aspects of LC–MS analyses are discussed in Section 3 Part C: LC-based techniques.

4. Instrumentation 
4.1 LC columns 
RPLC separation technique is very robust, covers a broad range of analytes, and thus is well 
suited for the analysis of CWC-related compounds. STX can also be screened with RPLC–
MS. The high polarity of STX results in low retention and thus it elutes close to the solvent 
front at t0 (’dead volume’) of the column. In this region, chromatographic interferences such 
as signal suppression may occur. If the concentration of STX is at trace level, its ion signal 
may be difficult to detect. HILIC is an alternative option, because it is an efficient technique 
for the separation and identification of polar and hydrophilic compounds. However, HILIC 
is more sensitive to changes of the chromatographic conditions (pH, temperature, or solvent 
composition of the injected sa mple) than RPLC, and RT shifts of the analytes may occur. 
The choice of the column’s stationary phase and dimensions depends on instrumentation. 
4.2 LC–ESI/MS instrument

The choice of the column’s stationary phase and dimensions depends on instrumentation. 
4.2 LC–ESI/MS instrument 
Due to the high polarity of STX, the mass spectrometer should be operated using an ESI 
source. Single quadrupole instruments allow the detection of the protonated molecule. For a 
more sensitive and selective screening, SRM/MRM or product ion scan MS/MS mode (e.g., 
triple quadrupole, ion trap) are recommended. Additional selectivity can be obtained w ith 
high resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) instruments, such as Q-TOFs or orbitraps, where 
STX can be detected by screening for the exact molecular masses of [M+H]+ or typical in-
source decay or product ions.

6.2 Screening and identification of STX in the SRM-mode 
The SRM/MRM method on triple quadrupoles and hybrid instruments is widely used for the 
detection and quantification of toxins, metabolites, drugs, dopes , and environmental 
pollutants. As shown in Figures 1C and 2C, the MS/MS spectrum offers several fragment 
ions that can be exploited to develop a selective and sensitive SRM/MRM -method, 
independent of the instrument used. 
Based on the MS/MS spectrum, specific fragment masses for quantifier (Q) and qualifier (q) 
are chosen. Preferentially, more than one transition should be monitored for unambiguous 
identification (quantifier and qualifier). Usually the most intense fragment ion is chosen as 
a quantifier

1. Scope 
For an unambiguous identification, LC–MS/MS results have to be combined with a second 
technique, such as liquid chromatography with fluorescence detection (LC –FLD), enzyme 
linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) and lateral flow assays (LFAs) , which are briefly 
described in this chapter. Analysis of saxitoxin (STX) with LC –MS/MS is described in 
Section 3, Part F, Chapter I: Analysis of saxitoxin: LC–MS/MS. 
Mouse bioassay (MBA) was the first
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
are briefly 
described in this chapter. Analysis of saxitoxin (STX) with LC –MS/MS is described in 
Section 3, Part F, Chapter I: Analysis of saxitoxin: LC–MS/MS. 
Mouse bioassay (MBA) was the first accepted official method for the analysis of PSP toxins 
in shellfish extract.1 Due to ethical and technical reasons, this method has been replaced by 
other more sensitive and selective methods in many laboratories. MBA only measures the 
total mouse toxicity of the shellfish extract, and it is unable to distinguish between STX 
analogues or other toxic compounds. 
Two official STX methods are based on LC –FLD analysis of PSP toxins : pre -column 
oxidation method2 and post-column oxidation method.3 The post-column oxidation method 
was recently approved as an alternative FLD method for the analysis of PSP toxins in 
shellfish, whereas p re-column method has already been adopted widely as a monitoring 
method for PSP toxins, and it is also accepted as a standard method within the EU.4 
Alternatively, a receptor-binding assay (RBA)5 may be used for PSP analyses in shellfish. It 
is an option if no proper instrumentation is available for other analysis, but it is not very 
widely used.
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ternatively, a receptor-binding assay (RBA)5 may be used for PSP analyses in shellfish. It 
is an option if no proper instrumentation is available for other analysis, but it is not very 
widely used. RBA is not described in this chapter. 
The screening of STX may be performed with ELISA or LFA. There are several commercial 
immunoassay kits available for screening of PSP toxins. However, these are not accepted as 
official methods for analysis of PSP toxins in seafood. 
2. Summary of the methods 
2.1 LC–FLD method 
STX and other PSP toxins are oxidised to fluorescent aminopurine derivative s, which can 
be detected with a fluorescence detector. The oxidation is performed either before (pre -
column oxidation) or after (post-column oxidation) the chromatographic separation, and the 
analytes are separated e ither with reversed-phase LC or ion pair chromatography, 
respectively. The oxidised PSP toxin analogues are detected with FLD.

2.2 Immunoassays 
Saxitoxin ELISA is a c ompetitive enzyme immunoassay. Saxitoxin competes with 
saxitoxin-enzyme conjugate for the binding sites of STX-specific antibodies in solution. 
Saxitoxin antibodies are then bound by the second antibody immobilized on microtiter plates 
and the unbound reagents are removed by washing. The formed complex is visualised with 
a chromogenic substrate . The intensity of the obtained colour is measured with 
spectrophotometer (450 nm for tetramethylbenzidine chromogen) , and it is inversely 
proportional to the STX concentration in the sample. Typically, ELISAs are performed on 
96-well plates. 
LFA is a rapid diagnostic test for fast screening of PSP toxins in complex mixtures. The 
detection is based on a STX specific antibody, and the response is typically examined 
visually.

Prepare saxitoxin reference chemical solu tion at e.g. 1 ppm concentration and analyse the

2. Safety aspects 
The toxicity of ricin varies based on the route of entry. The least harmful route of entry is 
via ingestion : 1000–20,000 (estimated LD 50 for human) and 20,000 µg/kg (LD50 for 
mouse)1,2 When injected or inhaled, ricin is much more toxic: 2.8 –3.3 µg/kg 3,4or 1 –10 
µg/kg, 5 LD50 for mouse respectively. The estimated intranasal dose for humans is 5 –
10 µg/kg.1 
The ingested material could be e.g. ricin seeds or ricin contaminated food. The lower toxicity 
via ingestion could be due to poor absorption across the intestine. 
In a laboratory, the major risks associated with handling of ricin could be: 
1) Accidental inj

via ingestion could be due to poor absorption across the intestine. 
In a laboratory, the major risks associated with handling of ricin could be: 
1) Accidental injec tion of ricin -containing sample. When handling ricin samples, 
similar care should be taken as when handling needles possibly contaminated by 
infectious substances. 
2) Inhalation of ricin -containing powder or dust. The spreading ricin -containing 
powder or dust in to the laboratory air must be prevented in all cases. This can be 
achieved e.g. by performing all handling of ricin powder in a glove box. 
3) Splashing of ricin-containing liquid samples. When working with ricin-containing 
solutions, protection of eyes , mucosa and skin by appropriate personal protective

3. Background 
Ricin is a toxin included in both Chemical Weapons and Biological Weapons Conventions. 
It is also included international and national lists of potential risk substances. The following 
subparagraphs describe issues related to ricin and the potential risks. 
3.1 Ricinus communis plant 
Ricinus communis is a perennial flowering plant that is grown in many countries for both 
production of castor oil from its seeds or for decorative purposes. It also grows wild in many 
tropical or subtropical countries. 
Ricin is found mainly in seeds of the Ricinus communis plant. The ricin content in the seed 
increases rapidly as the seed matures and degrades quickly after germination .6 The seed 
contains a high amount – up to 50% – of its weight of castor oil, which is mostly ricinoleic 
acid7. Due to the high oil content and ease of processing of the oil , Ricinus communis is a 
promising plant for efficient production of biodiesel.8
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
weight of castor oil, which is mostly ricinoleic 
acid7. Due to the high oil content and ease of processing of the oil , Ricinus communis is a 
promising plant for efficient production of biodiesel.8 
When castor oil is removed from the seed, the remaining seed material – castor seed meal – 
is toxic due to remaining ricin and Ricinus communis agglutinin (RCA, see below). Current 
methods for production of the oil based on solvent extraction do not result in d enaturation 
of the proteins in the seed meal.9 Deactivation of ricin is required to make the seed meal non-
toxic to humans and animals. This could be achieved e.g. by denaturation of the seeds 10 or 
the seed meal.11 
3.2 Ricin protein 
The tertiary structure of ricin (62–66 kDa) is a globular, glycosylated heterodimer (PDB No. 
2AAI, released in 1991). This glycoprotein consists of two chains held together by a 
disulfide bond. Ricin A chain (30–34 kDa) is a ribosome-inactivating enzyme, which acts as 
a N-glycoside hydrolase, composed of 267 amino acids. Ricin B chain ( 32–34 kDa) is a 
galactose/N-acetyl galactosamine-binding lectin, composed of 262 amino acids. The B chain

activity.12 
Ricin belongs to the family of type-2 ribosome-inactivating proteins (RIP II). Compared to 
type 1 RIPs, which only have a single chain that functions as a ribosome-inactivating enzyme, 
only type 2 RIPs display cytotoxicity based on the lectin properties of the B-chain. 
At the cellular level, ricin B chain specifically binds to glycoproteins and glycolipids present 
on the surface of cells containing eit her terminal N -acetyl galactosamine or β -1,4-linked 
galactose residues. The mannose-type glycans of ricin B-chain can also bind to the surface 
of cells expressing mannose receptors. Upon binding and internalisation , i.e., triggering 
endocytosis of the toxi n, the whole toxin is transported through the Golgi apparatus to the 
endoplasmic reticulum, where it is cleaved into ricin A and B chains. Ricin A chain is then 
translocated into the cytosol,

text:

endoplasmic reticulum, where it is cleaved into ricin A and B chains. Ricin A chain is then 
translocated into the cytosol, where it then inactivates ribosomes by removing an adenine 
from position 4324 of the 28S eukaryotic ribosomal RNA loop in the 60S subunit . This 
prevents polypeptide chain elongation by the ribosome by inhibiting protein synthesis, which 
consequently leads to cell death. Although 106 to 108 ricin molecules can bind per cell, a 
single A-chain molecule in the cytosol is capabable of inactivating over 1500 ribosomes per 
minute.13 
It is known that a genetic recombination occurred between RCA and ricin genes. 14 Two 
isoforms, ricin D and ricin E are found in ricin isolated from different origins. Ricin E is 
considered as a gene recombination product of ricin D and Ricinus communis 
agglutinin(Araki et al., 1987). 15 Ricin E exhibited lower toxicity. Regarding the high 
sequence similiarity i.e., the A chain and the N-terminal part of the B chain of ricin D and E 
are highly alike, whereas the C-terminal part of B chain of ricin E is identical to the B chain 
of RCA120 . 16 The diffe

are highly alike, whereas the C-terminal part of B chain of ricin E is identical to the B chain 
of RCA120 . 16 The differentiation of ricin D or E is not really necessary for ricin 
identification. It is rather to provide a precise differentiation result of ricin from denatured 
ricin, and RCA120, especially in a mixture. The mixture could come from castor bean extract, 
crude ricin, or castor bean intoxicated biomedical samples. 
3.3 Ricin as warfare agent 
The first and quite well -known incident involving ricin was the murder of the Bulgarian 
dissident Georgi Markov in London in 1978. A small ricin -filled pellet was planted in his 
thigh from a modified umbrella. Markov died in hospital four days later. The actual presence 
of ricin could not be proven, but clinical and pathological evidence pointed to ricin toxin.17 
In addition to the Markov case, there have been several ricin incidents where ricin extracts 
have been injected in humans.18–23 Typical to these cases is that individual persons targeted 
individual victims who subsequently died from the exposure. Ricin’s significance as a 
potential
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
xtracts 
have been injected in humans.18–23 Typical to these cases is that individual persons targeted 
individual victims who subsequently died from the exposure. Ricin’s significance as a 
potential terror weapon relates in path to its wide availability, temperature stability (up to 
80 °C), and ability to withstand pH changes.24 
Castor beans are easily available in small quantities through companies selling plant seeds 
either in stores or via internet. As preparation of raw ricin extract from the seeds does not 
require sophisticated methods, it is possible for individual persons to produce toxic ricin 
containing powder.25 This kind of powder could be used for disruptive activities in a small 
scale, e.g. by mailing powder filled letters. 26– 28 Raw ricin extract contains many other 
components than ricin and is less t oxic but it is still toxic enough to cause poisoning if 
inhaled.

Purification of raw ricin powder into pure ricin toxin would require sophisticated equipment 
and knowledge. Also , distribution of this kind of powder would require capabilities for 
creation of aerosol from the ricin powder. The particle size of the ricin powder would have 
an effect on its inhalation toxicity.5 The control of particle size of the produced ricin powder 
would require advanced skills and technology. Based on these facts, crude ricin extract may 
be the most common threat material. 
One potential terrorist risk has been estimated to be contamination o f water supplies using 
ricin powder. Schep et al.29 estimated that in order to achieve lethal concentration in drinking 
water supply for 60,000 residents, over 7000 kg of pure ricin powder would be need ed. 
Therefore, they estimate that strategic targets wou ld be more potential targets than general 
public. A more targeted approach would be to contaminate food or drink in small scale. This

Therefore, they estimate that strategic targets wou ld be more potential targets than general 
public. A more targeted approach would be to contaminate food or drink in small scale. This 
has been estimated to require 12 mg of ricin for a 60 kg adult person.29 
Ricin is included in both Biol ogical Weapons Convention (BWC) and Chemical Weapons 
Convention (CWC). 30 , 31 The latter prohibits development, production, acquisition, 
stockpiling, retention, transfer or use of any chemical as warfare agent by any State Party. 
Only four countries are currently outside the CWC: Egypt, Israel, North Korea and South 
Sudan. The risk of military use of ricin is therefore very low in most parts of the world. 
As Ricinus communis seeds are produced and handled in large quantities and are available 
to individuals globally , authorities must be prepared to manage incidents with ricin -
containing material. Development and maintaining analytical capabilities are an essential 
part of these preparations. 
4. Aims of analysis 
The analysis strategy must be chosen based on the aims of the analysis. These aims will be 
defined both by the operating environment and the type of the incident i

4. Aims of analysis 
The analysis strategy must be chosen based on the aims of the analysis. These aims will be 
defined both by the operating environment and the type of the incident in question. Ricin 
investigations could be carried out by local, national or international authorities. 
The international organisation overseeing the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) – The 
Organisation for the Prohibition (OPCW) – could be an active authority involved in an 
internal incident. The aim of OPCW lead investigations is typically to verify unambiguously 
whether a chemical warfare agent has been used or not. This kind of verification could 
include confirming the presence of ricin toxin and evaluating its activity. Typically, OPCW 
does not require quantitation of the agent, OPCW’s role does not include identifying the 
perpetrator. 
In the past, several biological threat incidents have been documented worldwide involving 
ricin-originating powder, e.g. in a letter. A big challenge in this type of case would be the 
classification of the powder. In addition to ricin letters , 26–28 anthrax has also been sent in 
letters.32 Additionally, a multitude of hoax letters contai
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
allenge in this type of case would be the 
classification of the powder. In addition to ricin letters , 26–28 anthrax has also been sent in 
letters.32 Additionally, a multitude of hoax letters containing harmless powder materials have 
been encountered. The classification would require fast screening methods to determine 
whether the material contains ricin itself or other material related to seeds – e.g. Ricinus 
communis DNA or small molecules such as ricinine. These incident s also typically require 
the screening of surrounding areas for possible contamination. Following initial screening 
analysis, more thorough identification and verification of the ricin protein would be required. 
National and international incident s may require forensic investigation, which can provide 
evidence for subsequent legal actions. F orensic investigation could provide evidenc e on 
e.g. the identity of the responsible person(s) or origin of the material based on e.g. purity of

evidence – e.g. DNA and protein fingerprints – should be collected in a safe manner. 
As mentioned above, fast detection of ricin originating materials is often required in order 
to build a risk estimate. After the initial detection, the identification of ricin can be made 
more reliable by using more complex, accurate and, often, time consuming methods. Based 
on the scenario, the confidence level of the given result could range from detection to 
unambiguous identification. The criteria for identification of ricin are still under discussion 
internationally. 
Typically, accurate quantitation of ricin protein in the studied material would not be essential 
in incident cases. At most, estimation of the concentration level would be satisfactory for 
risk assessment purposes.

5. Analysis strategy 
When the aims of the analysis are known the strategy for the analysis can be designed. A 
schematic work flow for ricin analysis is shown in Fig. 1. There are many factors guiding 
this: e.g. type of sample, number of samples, availability of the me thods, time allowed for 
analysis. The strategy must be built so that the methods used produce all the pieces of 
evidence (see paragraph 5.1) required to reach the aim of the analysis. This could, for 
example, mean that if it is important to know if ricin t oxin in a sample could have caused 
casualties (if used in an incident), it must be tested with suitable methods if the ricin in the 
sample is enzymatically active. 
The work starts with sample preparation, which depends on both the sample matrix and the 
selected analysis methods. Typical task of the sample preparation is clean -up and/or 
enrichment. Some analytical methods require specific sample preparation (e.g. MS-based 
methods). Sample preparation is discussed in more detail in paragraph 6. 
The analysis u sually starts with a screening procedure. The
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
tical methods require specific sample preparation (e.g. MS-based 
methods). Sample preparation is discussed in more detail in paragraph 6. 
The analysis u sually starts with a screening procedure. The purpose of this is to classify 
samples and to get information on the overall sample composition. 
Screening methods can be considered as methods, which can detect a feature of the target 
substance, but cannot fully distinguish it from other similar substances. For example, 
molecular weight determination (e.g. by SDS-PAGE) can be indicative of ricin, but other 
proteins exist having a similar molecular weight. Also, all indirect detection methods 
(e.g. detection DNA or ricinine in the samples) are considered screening methods as they 
only indicate the possibility of ricin being present. Screening results need to be confirmed 
by other methods. 
Some of the screening methods are suitable for on-site use, which means that the screening 
results can guide the sampling activities. During a ricin incident, the screening results can 
also help in making operational decisions, e.g. on protective equipmen t, decontamination, 
medical treatment and evacuation. The on-site methods are often
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
a ricin incident, the screening results can 
also help in making operational decisions, e.g. on protective equipmen t, decontamination, 
medical treatment and evacuation. The on-site methods are often less sensitive and selective 
than the more sophisticated laboratory-based methods. Therefore, it must be noted that on-
site screening may produce both false negative and fa lse positive results. Thus, the on -site 
results should be confirmed using laboratory-based methods. 
The screening methods used in a laboratory can either be more sensitive (e.g. ELISA) or 
give more information on the overall sample composition (e.g. SDS-PAGE). As with the on-
site methods, the screening results should be confirmed with more selective methods,

Generally, laboratory-based immunoassays such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays 
(ELISAs) are applied for screening of multiple samples at a time, either as classical plate -
bound assays or as multiplex suspension arrays. ELISA and multiplex-ELISA belong to the 
most sensitive routine technologies with detection limits ranging from fg/ ml to ng/ml 
depending on the antibodies and the read -out system used. 36 – 44 Western Blotting is a 
classical assay format, which displays the approximate molecular weight of the analyte and 
additionally demonstrates antibody reactivity. However, Western Blots are not suitable for 
high-throughput applications and are typically less sensitive than advanced ELISA formats. 
 
Since ELISAs require several hours for analysis, fast on-site detection systems such as hand-
held lateral flow assays (LFA) 34,44– 46 and automated biosensor technologies have been 
developed33–35,47 which usually provide results within 30 min down to a few ng/ml of toxin.

(ELLA). Here, ricin is immobilized on a solid surface by bi nding with its carb

A variation of the classical ELISA approach is the enzyme -linked lectin binding assay 
(ELLA). Here, ricin is immobilized on a solid surface by bi nding with its carbohydrate -
binding B chain to asialofetuin, a glycoprotein with three asparagine -linked triantennary 
complex carbohydrate chains and terminal N-acetylgalactosamine residues. The bound toxin 
is detected by antibodies similar to conventional ELISA methods. While the method is useful 
to demonstrate the functionality of the ricin B chain, it shows limited sensitivity (low ng/ml-
range).48,49 
 
Currently, most published immunological assays are not able to distinguish ricin from the 
related RCA120, a task that might be relevant in the course of a forensic investigation. 
Interestingly, individual ELISA have been developed showing minimal cross -reactivity 
between ricin and RCA120 (crossreactivity approx. 0.1% 34,38]. In this context a recent 
development combining immunological detection wi th surface plasmon resonance (SPR) 
allowed for rapid discrimination of ricin versus RCA120 as well as recognition of mixtures 
and crude R. communis extracts based on the unique binding propertie

allowed for rapid discrimination of ricin versus RCA120 as well as recognition of mixtures 
and crude R. communis extracts based on the unique binding properties and kinetics of the

5.1.1.1 ELISA-based technologies 
Current advanced ELISA -based technologies are still among the most sensitive methods 
available to screen for ricin -containing samples in an easy to perform high -throughput 
format.33–35 ELISA are applicable to many different matrices, provided appropriate assay 
controls are performed in parallel (see below). In order to fully exploit their potency the use 
of high affinity antibodies with binding constants in t he nM/pM -range is recommended. 
Furthermore, ELISA allow for accurate quantification of toxin content provided that a highly 
pure, well characterized reference material with known protein content is used as standard.38

In sandwich-ELISA based assays, a capture antibody is immobilized onto a solid support to 
capture ricin. In the classical assay format, these are plastic microtiter plates. Other supports 
like silica microbeads, affinity columns, magnetic microbeads, glass surfaces, and biochips 
are possible as well. The bound toxin is usually detected via a secondary hapten -coupled 
detector antibody plus an enzyme conjugate to develop a measurable readout. Different assay 
variations can be performed, e.g. using indirect or direct antibody-antigen interactions, using 
different haptens (e.g. biotin, digoxigenin), using different read-out systems such as UV/VIS 
absorption of colorimetric signals, or detection of fluorescent or chemiluminescent signals. 
Additionally, signal amp lification strategies can be applied, e.g. polymeric enzyme 
conjugates or tyramide amplification. However, amplification technologies are only 
productive in those cases where the basic assay – wit
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
p lification strategies can be applied, e.g. polymeric enzyme 
conjugates or tyramide amplification. However, amplification technologies are only 
productive in those cases where the basic assay – without signal amplification – is practically 
without any measurable background, otherwise the background will be amplified to an extent 
where the signal-to-noise ratio is not improved. 
Generally, sandwich -ELISA settings detecting the holo -toxin containing both A - and B -
chain of ricin are preferable to other settings detecting one chain only. As such, ELISA for 
holo-toxin indicate the presence of the intact toxin in a given sample. This gives, however, 
no direct evidence of the biological activity of the intact toxin, requiring the performance of 
functional assays. 
ELISA-based assays are applicable to a variety of matrices and can reach sensitivities 
between 0.1 pg/ml to 1000 pg/ml depending on the antibodies and assay conditions used.33–
35,39 
The optimal working conditions for any ELISA have to be determined in a compre hensive 
validation study. Here, all antibodies used should be tested for potential cross-reactivities to 
other related lectins, especially RCA120 or the

text:

validation study. Here, all antibodies used should be tested for potential cross-reactivities to 
other related lectins, especially RCA120 or the related abrin from Abrus precatorius. Assay 
precision and accuracy should be thoroughly investigated, as well as repeatability of results 
under intra- and inter-assay conditions. A fully validated assay is characterized by its limit 
of detection, upper and lower limit of quantification, working and linear range as well as the 
known measurement uncertainty. Also, the most influencing factors on assay performance 
have to be identified including lot testing of the main tools used in the assay (e.g. antibodies, 
substrates, plastic materials). Under an accredition system according to ISO/IEC 17025 or 
DIN 15189, assay reproducibility and performance are usually reviewed and documented in 
control cards that display if results are acceptable under pre-defined performance criteria for 
each routine experiment. Helpful documents to guide a validation study are given in 
references 51–56. 
The main difficulty when using sandwich-ELISA to detect ricin from unknown samples is 
the discrimin
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
routine experiment. Helpful documents to guide a validation study are given in 
references 51–56. 
The main difficulty when using sandwich-ELISA to detect ricin from unknown samples is 
the discrimination of true -positive from false -positive signals and the exclusion of false -
negative signals. It is per se difficult to anticipate the degree of cross-reactivity between the 
antibodies used and the matrix components in an unknown sample. Since antibodies 
recognize their specific target structure in defined binding pockets or over extended surface 
areas based on electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonds, Van der Waals and hydrophobic 
forces, these noncovalent forces might be influenced by sample components (e.g. high/low 
salt conditions, lipid or carbohydrate content). Therefore, thorough validation of any ELISA 
in different matrices is indispensable. Of course, not all potential matrices can be tested in 
advance, but a comprehensive set of different matrices should be evaluated in a validation 
study.

When measuring unknown, complex samples for ricin by ELISA, parallel measurement of 
positive and negative control samples is highly recommended to ensure high quality results. 
This includes, but is not limited to: 
 Blank control (buffer only) 
 Background control (performance of an ELISA with an irrelevant capture antibody 
– this should not result in any signal; occurrence of a signal indicates a problem of 
matrix interference) 
 Matrix control (matrix tested in different dilutions; provides information on potential 
matrix components producing elevated background signals; necessary to identify the 
dilution of sample that can be reasonably measured by ELISA) 
 Spiking and recovery controls (spiking of a known amount of ricin into the unknown 
sample material to exclude inhibitory substances in the sample and to test for 
recovery; comparison of the signal obtained after spiking of the analyte in to the 
sample with the same amount of analyte spiked int
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
al to exclude inhibitory substances in the sample and to test for 
recovery; comparison of the signal obtained after spiking of the analyte in to the 
sample with the same amount of analyte spiked into buffer – the result should be 
equivalent or close to equivalent. A loss in signal indicates either a reduced recovery 
[irreversible binding and loss of ricin to matrix components] and/or a negative 
interference by matrix components on antibody-analyte interaction) 
Performance characteristics: 
 Time to result: 4–6 h 
 Detection limit: 0.1–1000 pg/ml 
 Matrix tolerance: good 
More details on the performance of an ELISA are described in Section 3, Part F, Chapter IV: 
Analysis of ricin: ELISA. 
5.1.1.2 Western Blotting 
Western Blot is a classical immunoassay format where the sample components are firstly 
separated by their molecul ar weight by SDS -PAGE, secondly the proteins are transferred 
from the protein gel onto a suitable membrane (e.g. PVDF, nitrocellulose) and thirdly the 
targeted analyte is detected on the membrane by binding to specific antibodies coupled to 
enzymatic detection and visualization (e.g. mostly chemiluminescence).57 
In Western Blot experiments, an a
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
targeted analyte is detected on the membrane by binding to specific antibodies coupled to 
enzymatic detection and visualization (e.g. mostly chemiluminescence).57 
In Western Blot experiments, an antibody that recognizes both ricin and RCA120 can be 
used, since under non-reducing separation conditions both proteins run at different molecular 
weights, so that the respective bands can be correlated to ricin or RCA120. 
Compared to ELISA-based methods, Western Blots are not applicable as screening method 
due to their limited throughput and sensitivity. The detection limit for ricin is usually in the 
range of 0.1 –10 ng/ml. As described for ELISA spiking and recovery controls should be 
implemented. However, false positive or negative signals caused by matrix components are 
difficult to examine. Since proteins are denatured by SDS for the analysis by Western 
blotting no indication of a functionally intact molecule is provided. 
Performance characteristics: 
 Time to result: 8–12 h 
 Detection limit: 0.1–10 ng/ml 
 Matrix tolerance: medium
