3.3.3 Recommended LC–ESI/Q-TOF/MS identification of digested ricin protein 
Following tryptic digestion, LC–ESI/Q-TOF/MS can also be used for un ambiguous 
identification of ricin by non-targeted and targeted peptide analysis. 
For non-targeted peptide analysis, MS/MS product ion spectra of tryptic peptides acquired 
using data dependant acquisition are matched against theoretically generated in silico tryptic 
digest using a protein database and search algorithm. Higher concentration of ricin is usually 
required for this type of identification. 
Conversely, in targeted peptide analysis, several unique peptides are selected from both the 
A and B chains for unambiguous identification of ricin using LC–ESI/Q-TOF/MS. During 
data acquisition, the mass spectrometer is run in MS/MS mode, sequentially isolating the 
desired m/z values throughout the run using optimal CID conditions. The MS/MS product 
ion spectra of these specific peptides selected are then compared with those from an 
analogous peptide from a ricin reference digest. This method has better sensitivity. The most

4. LC–MS/MS detection of N-glycosidase activity of ricin 
LC–MS/MS can also be used to detect ricin ’s N-glycosidase activity . Ricin is a type II 
ribosome-inactivating protein (RIP II) that has specific N -glycosidase enzymatic activity 
that releases free adenine from the GAGA tetraloop of 28S ribosomal RNA . This 
N-glycosidase activity can be detected by LC–MS/MS (SRM).4 The approach involves 
sample pre-treatment and subsequent incubation of the ricin enriched from the samples with 
a synthetic DNA oligonucleotide subst rate (5’ -GCGCGAGAGCGC-3’) that mimics the 
natural ribosomal RNA target contain ing the GAGA tetraloop structure. The released 
adenine from the DNA oligonucleotide substrate by ricin can then be detected by LC –
MS/MS (SRM). Increasing adenine release after incubation over negative control s can be 
attributed to the presence of active ricin or A-chain in the sample . However, the method 
cannot distinguish the activity as being solely from ricin or another RIP II proteins since all 
RIP II proteins share this N-glycosidase activity.

Sample pre-treatment is generally required to both concentrate and solvent exchange the 
sample before undertaking the depurination reaction. The pre-treatment used depends on the 
complexity of the samples. For simple aqueous samples, concentration and buffer-exchange

performed for selective extraction and enrichment of the ricin. The recommended procedures

The pre-treated sample is incubated with the DNA substrate (5’ -GCGCGAGAGCGC-3’)

of ricin’s N-glycosidase activity is achieved by detection of the free adenine released from 
the DNA substra

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the sample preparation, analysis methods as well as evaluation of the 
produced data for analysis of sediment samples related to WWII-era sea-dumped chemical 
weapons. 
The method is based on methods developed by three laboratories – Swedish Defence 
Research Agency (FOI), Military University of Technology (MUT) in Poland and Finnish 
Institute for Verification of the Chemical Weapons Convention (VERIFIN) – for the EU-
funded Chemical Munitions, Search and Assessment (CHEMSEA) project .1 The project 
methods together with analysis results have been reported in project reports.2–5 
2. Summary of the method 
A wet sediment sample is divided in to sediment and pore water portions. Aliquots of these 
portions were prepared for both gas chromatography –mass spectrometry (GC –MS), and 
liquid chromatography –mass spectrometry (LC –MS)-based analysis. Sample preparation 
methods include extractions using organic solvent as well as deri vatisation methods to 
enable the best suitable analysis methods for each target chemicals. 
The analysis is preferably performed using gas chromatography–electron ionisation tandem 
mass spectrometry (G

The analysis is preferably performed using gas chromatography–electron ionisation tandem

are based on selected reaction monitoring (SRM).

The list of target chemicals is based on the analytes studied in the CHEMSEA project. The 
starting point was to include all major chemical warfare agents (CWAs) known or suspected 
to have been dumped in Baltic Sea. Many of these target analytes are degradation products 
of those chemicals or their expected bacterial metabolites. 
3. Safety aspects 
All agents discussed in this ROP are harmful to humans and also to many other organisms. 
There are two aspects of safety which have to be paid special attention: 
1) CWAs should only be handled in an authorized laboratory. In the laborat ory, 
preparation of the reference samples has to be done according to taking all safety 
precautions, especially when working with standards containing high concentrations 
of CWAs or their degradation products or their chemical derivatives. 
2) While handling t he sediment sample, both during sampling at sea and sample 
handling in the laboratory, all se
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
concentrations 
of CWAs or their degradation products or their chemical derivatives. 
2) While handling t he sediment sample, both during sampling at sea and sample 
handling in the laboratory, all sediment samples have to be handled as if they were 
containing high amounts of CWAs. 
4. Target chemicals 
The target chemicals included in this Recommended Operating Procedure (ROP) are the 
main chemicals dumped in the Baltic Sea i.e. sulfur mustard (1), Adamsite (2), Clark I (3a), 
Clark II ( 3b), α-chloroacetophenone ( 6), Lewisite I ( 7) and Lewisite II ( 8) as well as 
components of arsine oil, which contains triphenyl arsine (4), phenyldichloroarsine (5) and 
trichloroarsine (not analysed). 
The selected target chemicals are summarised in Table 1. The intact chemicals are typically 
analysed as such (Orig). Three types of derivatisation methods have been used for the 
degradation products of the agents: 
 SR – Derivatisation using propane -1-thiol: Arsenic -containing chemicals – both 
agents and degradation products – readily react with thiols. All different forms of the 
chemical are converted into the thiol derivative. These derivatives are analysed using 
GC–MS-based methods

agents and degradation products – readily react with thiols. All different forms of the 
chemical are converted into the thiol derivative. These derivatives are analysed using 
GC–MS-based methods. 
 TMS – Derivatisation using N,O-bis(trimethylsilyl)trifluoroacetamide (BSTFA): 
Alcohols and acids can be trimethylsilylated using BSTFA. However, the reagent is 
sensitive to moisture in the samples. These derivatives are analysed using GC –MS-
based methods. 
 Ox – Oxidation using hydrogen peroxide (H 2O2): Both arsenic and sulphur -
containing chemicals can be oxidised in aqueous samples. All different forms of the 
chemical were converted into the oxidised for m. The same oxidation reactions can 
occur in the sample also naturally – probably after sampling and exposure to 
atmospheric oxygen. These derivatives are analysed using LC –MS-based methods. 
Often, the oxidation enhanced ionisation of the chemical and, the refore, the 
sensitivity.

4.1 Categorisation of chemicals 
All chemicals in the Table 1 are fully conformed to be potential target chemicals. During the 
CHEMSEA project, one of the goals was to find suitable target chemicals for further studies. 
The chemicals listed in Table 1 can be categorised based on their relevance to the analysis: 
1a –Agent which is known to have been dumped in Baltic Sea6 
1b –Agent which may have been dumped in Baltic Sea6 
2a –Degradation product, which has been found in Baltic Sea by at least two 
laboratories2 
2b –Degradation product, which has been found in Baltic Sea by at least two 
laboratories. However, this is a relatively poor analyte and should not be used if 
another analyte (e.g. another derivative) for the same chemical is available2 
3a –Known degradation product for an agent (categories 1a/b), which has been found in 
Baltic Sea by only one laboratory2 
3b –Known degradation product for an agent (categories 1a/b), which has not been found 
in Baltic Sea2

During the project CHEMSEA some chemical warfare agents were excluded from the target 
list based on the combination of rapid degradation in water with degradation product with 
common origin from industrial activity and dumped in relative small quantities. Tabun 
degrades rapidly with phosphate as end product and according to literature only dumped in 
the part of Danish water not covered by this study. 
Based on the results of CHEMSEA project, it was decide d that thiodiglycolic acid 
(CAS 123-93-3) will not be included in further lists of target chemicals

text:
5. Sample preparation 
In most carried out projects, the sediment samples have been sent from the sampling team at 
sea to the analysis laboratory frozen on dry ice. Blank sediment samples were taken at sea 
at a distance from the dumping area. During work up procedures the sediment should not be 
dried and reconstituted in water. Dried sediment oxidises the sample rapidly. 
The basic principle of the sample preparation is to separate a sediment sample into two 
components: solid material (later called sediment portion) and water (later called pore water 
portion). The separation is done by centrifugation as shown in Figure 1. Both of the portions 
are separately treated before instrumental analysis as shown in Figures 2 and 3. 
The results for the sediment portion are given in µg/kg, where the weight of sediment is dry 
weight, dw. The dry weight of each sediment portion has to be determined separately as the 
water contents of each sediment sample is different. The results for the pore water sample 
are given in µg/l of pore water.

The received frozen sediment samples are registered at the analysing lab and labelled 
according the receiving laboratory quality system. The samples are kept frozen until time for

dry weight determination 5 g of sediment. Both blank sediment samples and the sediment 
samples should be prepared u

dry weight determination 5 g of sediment. Both blank sediment samples and the sediment 
samples should be prepared using the same procedure. 
Sediment dry weight. For calculation of dry fraction in sediments, known amounts of moist 
sediments (approximately 5 g) is placed in pre-weighted beakers. The sediment samples is 
dried at approximately 100 °C in an oven until the constant weight was reached. In this way, 
the percentage of water content in the sediment can be determined. 
Separation of sediment and pore water. The sample is thawed and homogenised by mixing 
with a plastic spoon. A sample of 50 g is taken to centrifugation. The centrifugation should 
sediment particles to a pellet and leaving a particle free supernatant (e.g. 1000 RCF 10 min 
has proven to be suffic ient for Baltic Sea sediment). Filter paper might be required during 
decanting the liquid pore water from the sediment pellet. The centrifuged sediment pellet is

5.1.1 Sample preparation of sediment samples-organic extraction 
This extraction will isolate compounds as annotated in Figure 3. Ca. 10 g (exact weight 
should be determined) of the sediment pellet is extracted twice with 10 ml of 
dichloromethane with agitation in 30 minutes. The organic dichloromethane layer is 
combined and the removal of water is done by adding 1 g anhydrous Na 2SO4 for drying. 
Prior to analysis, the extract was then evaporated to approximately 1 ml and internal standard 
is added (HCB or 13C-labelled HCB) to a final concentration of 100 µg/l. The extracts is 
divided in two fractions prior GC–MS/MS analysis: 
 The first portion, preparation A1, is analysed by GC–MS/MS for intact chemicals 
 The second portion, preparation A2, is derivatised by adding 10 µl of propane-1-thiol 
and incubating the sample at 60 °C for 10 min. This portion is analysed by GC –
MS/MS for derivatised arsenic based chemicals.

6. Instrumentation 
The analysis of the samples A1–A6 and B1–B6 described in chapter 5 is done by two basic 
instrument types: GC –MS and LC –MS. The instrumentation used by the laboratories 
performing the analysis in CHEMSEA and therefore listed in this ROP is totally based on 
the availability of the instruments during the CHEMSEA project. 
It was noted by the CHEMSEA project partners that the tandem mass spectro
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
CHEMSEA and therefore listed in this ROP is totally based on 
the availability of the instruments during the CHEMSEA project. 
It was noted by the CHEMSEA project partners that the tandem mass spectrometric method 
(MS/MS) gave superior results analysing complex sediment samples in the regard of both 
selectivity and sensitivity as compared to the single stage mass spectrometric methods (MS). 
Therefore, it is recommended to use GC–MS/MS and LC–MS/MS. 
In the CHEMSEA project, all tandem mass spectrometry instruments – both GC–MS/MS 
and LC–MS/MS – were based on triple quadrupole technology (QqQ). The measurements 
were done using selected reaction monitoring (SRM). Based on current information, it is 
very probable that similar detection limit and selectivity could be obtained also by using high 
resolution tandem mass spectrometers such as quadrupole-time-of-flight (Q-TOF) or hybrid-
orbitrap (available only for LC–MS/MS) instruments. The advantage of the high resolution 
instruments is that instead of SRM measurement, which gives signal only of the selected 
reaction(s), they can produce full spectrum data. 
When taking analysis methods in use, it is essential to have reference s
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
is that instead of SRM measurement, which gives signal only of the selected 
reaction(s), they can produce full spectrum data. 
When taking analysis methods in use, it is essential to have reference standards available to 
be able to properly tune the mass spectrometer for the analysis of the chemicals with the 
particular instrument in use. One also has to test and optimise the SIM ions or SRM transition 
for best possible sensitivity. 
The goal of the method development was to reach limits of quantitation (LOQ) of 10 µg/kg 
dw for each of the chemicals. In practice for some chemicals, the obtainable LOQ could be 
in the range of 30 to 50 µg/kg dw.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the analysis of Central Nervous System (CNS) acting chemicals that 
have the potential to be misused as weapons to cause permanent harm, or death, to humans. 
It describes the testing and ev
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
describes the analysis of Central Nervous System (CNS) acting chemicals that 
have the potential to be misused as weapons to cause permanent harm, or death, to humans. 
It describes the testing and evaluation of current Recommended Operating Procedure s 
(ROPs) for sample preparation, analysis, screening and identification of selected CNS acting 
chemicals from environmental samples. These ROPs include those for: 
 sample preparation from wipes (see Section 2, Part B, Chapter V.C: Wipe samples), 
 screening and identification using gas chromatography -electron ionization/mass 
spectrometry (GC–EI/MS) (see Section 3, Part B, Chapter II: Gas-chromatography–
electron ionisation/mass spectrometry (GC–EI/MS)), and 
 liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) (see Section 3, Part 
C, Chapter III: Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS)), 
These ROPs were evaluated for two CNS active chemicals, fentanyl and amphetamine. 
2. Background 
The Scientific Advisory Board (SAB) of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical 
Weapons (OPCW) has, since its Fifteenth Session in April 2010, considered the history of 
the development of incapacitating chemical
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ry Board (SAB) of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical 
Weapons (OPCW) has, since its Fifteenth Session in April 2010, considered the history of 
the development of incapacitating chemicals since the 1950s. 1 This consideration has 
included the fact that no chemical has been discovered or developed that satisfies the 
requirements of being able to produce almost instantaneous incapacitating effects which will 
last for some hours with no health risks to the exposed individuals. 
The SAB recognised that chemicals such as fentanyl, which are considered to be safe when 
used under controlled medical conditions, can have a very low safety margin when delivered 
as an aerosol, based on factors including uneven dissemination, variability in human
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:

response, and a need for rapid onset of action.1 The SAB noted that some fentanyl analogues 
have lethality comparable to the organophosphorus nerve agent VX.1 In view of these factors, 
the SAB has most recently discussed them as “CNS acting chemicals” rather than as 
“incapacitants”. The SAB also recommended that the Technical Secretariat of the OPCW 
commence preparations for verification activities that could be required during an 
investigation of alleged use, including sample collection and the use of analytical data.2 
With the exception of 3 -quinuclidinyl benzilate (BZ) (Sch edule 2.A.3), CNS acting 
chemicals are not included in the Schedules of the Annex on Chemicals of the Chemical 
Weapons Convention (CWC, hereinafter the “Convention”). Their use as toxic chemicals 
for warfare purposes is prohibited by Article II.2 of the CW C, which defines a “toxic 
chemical” as: 
‘Any chemical which through its chemical action on life processes can
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ir use as toxic chemicals 
for warfare purposes is prohibited by Article II.2 of the CW C, which defines a “toxic 
chemical” as: 
‘Any chemical which through its chemical action on life processes can cause death, 
temporary incapacitation or permanent harm to humans or animals. This includes all 
such chemicals, regardless of their origin or of their method of production, and 
regardless of whether they are produced in facilities, in munitions or elsewhere.’ 
This is widely termed the “General Purpose Criterion” and prohibits all toxic chemicals as a 
method of warfare. The CWC distinguishes between a “Toxic Chemical”, as defined above, 
and a “Riot Control Agent” (RCA), which is defined by Article II.7, as: 
‘Any chemical not listed in a Schedule, which can produce rapidly in human sensory 
irritation or disabling physical effects which disappe ar within a short time fo llowing 
termination of exposure.' 
The use of RCAs for “law enforcement including domestic riot control purposes”, according 
to the Article II.9(d), is not prohibited under the CWC, but their use in warfare is prohibited 
under the General Purpose Criterion. 
At its Twentieth Session, the SAB was requested by the
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
according 
to the Article II.9(d), is not prohibited under the CWC, but their use in warfare is prohibited 
under the General Purpose Criterion. 
At its Twentieth Session, the SAB was requested by the OPCW Director-General to provide 
technical advice on an initial list of RCAs that had been declared by States Parties, 
researched, or were available commercially. The SAB advised the Director-General that 17 
chemicals correspond to the CWC definition of a RCA.3 The list of 17 RCAs was provided 
to CWC States Parties as a point of reference in support of their declarations. (Chemical 
structures for these RCAs appear in Section 1, Part A, Chapter III. Chemicals.) The list of 
RCAs does not include fentanyl or amphetamine, or any of their analogues. 
Subsequently, the OPCW Director-General requested the SAB to re -examine the RCA 
question,3 taking into account all available scientific literature up to March 2017. The list of 
17 RCAs remained unchanged, but 43 additional chemicals considered by the SAB at its 
Twenty-Fifth Session were provided as a reference list of substances 4 that do not meet the 
criteria of an RCA (and should not be declared as such) but have historically been
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
dered by the SAB at its 
Twenty-Fifth Session were provided as a reference list of substances 4 that do not meet the 
criteria of an RCA (and should not be declared as such) but have historically been considered 
for use as an RCA. 
RCAs cause an immediate disabling effect on personnel. They act mostly on the sensory 
nerves of the peripheral nervous system in the eyes, nose, an d respiratory tract, and skin; 
they have little or no effect on the CNS. Their effects are usually confined to sensory 
irritation of a temporary and harmless nature where those personnel exposed can process 
information normally and run away. The situation differs for CNS active compounds, whose 
action on the central nervous system can lead to incapacitation including cognitive 
impairment, loss of motor function and ultimately unconsciousness. There will be a delay in

time to their pe ak effectiveness after exposure and t heir action may prevent humans from 
escaping or protecting themselves. 
CNS active compounds include anaesthetics, sedatives and analgesics that have been 
developed for medical purposes .5 Such compounds are designed to be delivered 
intravenously only under strict medical supervision with concurrent monitoring of the health 
of the patient. As such chemicals might be aerosolised and misused, verification methods 
could be usefully developed and tested,1 and such methods are described herein. 
3. Examples of CNS acting chemicals 
3.1 Moscow Theatre Siege 
The most prominent use of CNS acting compounds for counter-terrorist purposes was in the 
Dubrovka Theatre in Moscow during the hostage crisis in 2002. The crisis began when 
Chechen militants, equipped with explosives, s eized the Dubrovka Theatre in Moscow 
taking over 800 hostages during a sell-out musical performance. The Russian Special
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
n 2002. The crisis began when 
Chechen militants, equipped with explosives, s eized the Dubrovka Theatre in Moscow 
taking over 800 hostages during a sell-out musical performance. The Russian Special Forces 
surrounded the theatre. After a siege lasting two-and-a-half days, they pumped a chemical 
aerosol into the building’s ventilatio n system and then raided the theatre. The aerosol 
disseminated into the theatre rendered most of the hostages and terrorists unconscious. Over 
120 hostages died through a combination of the aerosol and inadequate medical care.6 
The medical personnel were not informed about the composition of the aerosol and were 
unable to adequately treat the casualties. Afterwards the Russian Health Minister stated that 
the chemical used in the raid had been a “fentanyl-based substance”.7 Traces of remifentanil 
and carfentanil (derivatives of fentanyl) were found on the clothing of British hostages.6,8 
3.2 Fentanyl 
Fentanyl (Figure 1) N -phenyl-N-(1-(2-phenylethyl)-4-piperidinyl)propanamide, is a 
synthetic opioid, related to meperidine. The chemical and physical properties of fentanyl are 
listed in Table 1. Fentanyl was first synthesized by Dr. Paul Jansse
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
yl)-4-piperidinyl)propanamide, is a 
synthetic opioid, related to meperidine. The chemical and physical properties of fentanyl are 
listed in Table 1. Fentanyl was first synthesized by Dr. Paul Janssen in 1960.9 It is a highly 
potent narcotic that is commonly used as a surgical anaesthetic and for pain treatment 
(a therapeutic plasma concentration for analgesia is usually 1–2 ng/ml and for anaesthesia it 
is 10–20 ng/ml).10 Fentanyl has been reported to be 80-100 times more potent an analgesic 
than morphine.

3.3 Amphetamine 
Amphetamine ( Figure 2 ), 1-phenylpropan-2-amine, is a synthetic substance that acts as

In the human body, amphetamine mainly acts by releasing noradrenaline and dopamine. The

With large doses, stereotyped behaviour occurs. The duration of action is several hours.11

Analysis of amphetamines by GC usually requires their prior derivatization. Analyses that 
involve silylation of amphetamine with N,O-bis(trimethylsilyl)trifluoroacetamide (BSTFA) 
and N-methyl-N-(tert-butyldimethylsilyl)trifluoroacetamide (MTBSTFA) have been 
described.18,19 Several methods for detecting amphetamine and related compounds by 
LC−MS/MS have also been developed, including in wipe samples .20,21 Amphetamine free 
base is a volatile liquid at room temperature. This should be taken into account during sample 
preparation; evaporating the sample to dryness can cause significant loss of the analyte.18 
4. Summary of the method 
ROPs for sample preparation of wipe samples (see Section 2, Part B, Chapter V.C ), and 
screening and identification of CNS acting chemicals in wipe samples using GC-EI/MS (see 
Section 3, Part B, Chapter II) and LC–ESI–MS/MS (see Section 3, Part C, Chapter III), were 
tested. GC–MS full scan and LC–MS/MS multiple r
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
of CNS acting chemicals in wipe samples using GC-EI/MS (see 
Section 3, Part B, Chapter II) and LC–ESI–MS/MS (see Section 3, Part C, Chapter III), were 
tested. GC–MS full scan and LC–MS/MS multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) were 
applied. Sample preparation was based on successive extraction of analytes from spiked 
wipe samples with organic solvent and aqueous solvent. Two solvents (dichloromethane and 
acetone) and three wipe materia ls (cotton swab, Whatman filter paper, and cotton wipe ) 
were used. Samples were then analysed using GC–MS and LC–MS/MS techniques. 
5. Safety aspects 
Normal laboratory safety procedures when working with hazardous chemicals were 
followed. Due to the high potency and chemical stability of fentanyl and amphetamine, extra 
attention was paid when handling the substances. In this experimental all the equipment that 
had been in contact with the analytes was rinsed with 10% KOH in ethanol decontamination 
solution (VERIFIN), or in the case of fentanyl, left to stand overnight in a solution of 10% 
Fichlor (sodium dichloroisocyanurate) in 1:1 (v/v) ethanol:water (Dstl) . Decontamination 
solution waste was then collected in a plastic container and sen
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
eft to stand overnight in a solution of 10% 
Fichlor (sodium dichloroisocyanurate) in 1:1 (v/v) ethanol:water (Dstl) . Decontamination 
solution waste was then collected in a plastic container and sent to the local waste disposal 
company for further processing (VERIFIN) or incinerated on-site (Dstl). The waste should 
be assumed physiologically active and handled accordingly. 
6. Instrumentation 
6.1 GC-EI/MS instrument 
Any modern GC –EI/MS instrument capable of a scanning speed of at least 1 scan/s and 
covering a mass range of at least m/z 40-600 can be used. Electron energy used is 70eV. In 
adjusting ion source temperature and electron multiplier voltage refer to instrument manual. 
It is recommended to use solvent delay time 3 min and >3 min for silylated samples. 
6.2 GC columns 
A 30 m-long DB-5MS-fused silica capillary column (0.25 mm i.d. and film thickness 
0.25 µm), preferably the low-bleed MS column, is used.

6.3 LC–API/MS instrument 
Any modern LC–API–MS/MS instrument can be used. It should have a scanning speed of 
at least 1 scan/s and cover a mass range of at least m/z 50–600. Mass resolution ≤1 amu 
(preferred 0.75 amu). Recommended collision gas is argon. 
6.4 LC–ESI/MS instrument 
Any modern LC-ESI-MS/MS instrument can be used. It should have a scan -speed capacity 
of at least 1 scan/s and cover a mass range of at least m/z 50-500. Mass resolution ≤1 amu 
(preferred 0.75 amu). Recommended collision gas is argon. 
6.5. LC columns 
A 100 mm-long UPLC C18 column (2.1 mm i.d.) packed with 1.7 µm particles (VERIFIN), 
or a 50 mm UPLC C8 column (2.1 mm i.d.) packed with 2.7 µm particles (Dstl), is used.

11. Screening and identification 
The ROPs that describe the methods for screening and identifying CWC -related chemicals 
were tested for the candidate chemicals. For the study, a cotton wipe containing fentanyl and 
amphetamine (10 µg each) was extracted with acetone. Acetone was selected as the 
extraction solvent due to its high extraction efficiency (Table 12). The cotton wipe used in 
this experiment is the same as the one the OPCW uses for on-site sampling. Two aliquots of 
acetone extr
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
extraction solvent due to its high extraction efficiency (Table 12). The cotton wipe used in 
this experiment is the same as the one the OPCW uses for on-site sampling. Two aliquots of 
acetone extract were prepared, one for LC–MS/MS analysis and one for GC–MS analysis. 
The aliquot prepared for GC–MS analysis was silylated with BSTFA. 
11.1 GC–MS screening and identification 
GC-EI/MS analysis produces two kinds of analytical data that can be used in screening and 
identification of the chemical: the mass spectrum and the retention time. The identification 
is performed by comparing the exp erimental mass spectrum and retention time of an 
unknown chemical to the library mass spectra and retention times of known chemicals. The 
retention time is usually converted into the retention index (RI). The degree that describes 
how closely the experimental unknown spectrum matches the library spectrum is expressed 
as the net match factor (NMF). Reference mass spectra were recorded and a spectral library 
was built for the test analytes before the screening experiment. 
The silylated wipe extract was analysed with GC–MS in full scan mode (Appendix 3, Figures 
12-13). The produced data w
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ectral library 
was built for the test analytes before the screening experiment. 
The silylated wipe extract was analysed with GC–MS in full scan mode (Appendix 3, Figures 
12-13). The produced data was then analysed using AMDIS (the Automated Mass Spectral 
Deconvolution and Identification System) software. The software performed spectral 
cleaning, gave NMF for the found m ass spectra and calculated the RIs. Each analyte of 
interest was found by AMDIS. The mass spectra extracted by AMDIS were also searched 
against the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) database which includes 
a large variety of mass spectra produced by different laboratories. The determined RIs 
(retention indices) and match factors were 1303 and 2770, and 95 and 93 for amphetamine-
TMS and fentanyl, respectively. 
11.2 LC–MS/MS screening and identification 
The first step in LC–MS/MS screening was to analy se the wipe sample extract in LC–MS 
full scan mode. The [M+H]+ ions of the analytes were then extracted from the TIC according 
to their m/z. The extracted precursor ion chromatograms are given in Figure 4. Fentanyl and 
amphetamine could be clearly detected from the background.

12. Evaluation of methods 
The CNS active chemicals were screened and identified from an acetone extract of a spiked 
cotton wipe. The extract was screened using the LC–MS/MS and GC–MS methods described 
in the ROPs in: 
 Section 1, Part B, Chapter I: Screening, 
 Section 3, Part B, Chapter II: Gas-chromatography–electron ionisation/mass 
spectrometry (GC-EI/MS), and 
 Section 3, Part C, Chapter III: Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry 
(LC–MS/MS). 
GC–MS analysis required derivatization of amphetamine with BSTFA. The GC–MS 
screening and identification were based on analysis of the produced full scan data by AMDIS 
software. In the LC–MS/MS screening and identification, the precursor ions were extracted 
from the LC–MS full scan TIC. After that, the transitions characteristic to the target 
chemicals were detec ted using MRM. Both GC–MS and LC–MS/MS techniques and the 
tested ROPs were valid for screening and identification of the CNS
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
r that, the transitions characteristic to the target 
chemicals were detec ted using MRM. Both GC–MS and LC–MS/MS techniques and the 
tested ROPs were valid for screening and identification of the CNS active chemicals at parts-
per-million (ppm, µg/g) concentration s. Of the two techniques, LC–MS/MS was the most 
appropriate for analysis of the chemicals in question. 
13. Conclusions 
CNS acting chemicals pose a risk to society if used by terrorists or state actors. Since ROPs 
are lacking, there are no tested methods to detect or identify these chemicals in case of 
allegations of use. Collaboration is needed to develop verification methods for them and 
their precursors. The analytical methods developed might be tested in Confidence Building 
Exercises. In this regard, the OPCW SAB in 2016 encouraged ‘collaboration between 
laboratories in OPCW Member States, with a view to supplying spectra and other data on 
CNS acting compounds to the [OPCW] Validation Group for evaluation.’1

1. Scope 
This chapter describes methods used for the identification of urinary biomarkers resulting 
from human exposure to chemical warfare agents (CWA s). Biomarkers addressed include 
hydrolysis metabolites of nerve agents and hydrolysis, glutathione conjugated, and -lyase 
metabolites and DNA adducts of sulfur mustard , as presented in Figure 1 . The methods 
include solid phase extraction (SPE) sample preparations, separation by gas chromatography 
(GC) or liquid chromatography (LC), and detection by mass spectrometry (MS). 
Biomedical samples collected following suspected CWA use are evaluated for biomarkers 
of exposure. Ideally, the biomarkers selected should occur solely from exposure to a CWA 
and should not be present in samples collected from unexposed persons. Alternatively, the 
selected biomarker(s) may be present at concentration
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
rs selected should occur solely from exposure to a CWA 
and should not be present in samples collected from unexposed persons. Alternatively, the 
selected biomarker(s) may be present at concentrations relevant to CWA exposure which are 
substantially differentiated from those present in an unexposed population. Given the high 
toxicity, anticipated low doses, and variability of time of sample collection, low 
concentrations of these biomarkers are expected (ng/ml).

2. Safety aspects and clinical sample considerations 
Specific safety concerns for CWAs are presented in Section 2, Part A, 
Chapter I: Introduction. Since unreacted CWA concentrations are typically low in 
biomedical samples, the primary safety concern is the biohazard potential of the clinical 
sample itself. Follow universal precautions , and treat all urine samples as if infectious, 
particularly if blood is visibly present. After use, all residual biomedical samples, solutions, 
and lab ware that have been in contact with biomedical samples should be decontaminated 
in designated decontamination containers with an appropriate disinfectant (e.g. bleach) 
before disposal. 
Maintain urine samples frozen ( -20 °C or colder) to minimize biomarker degradation, 
prevent mold growth, and reduce potential spillage during sample transport. 
3. Summary of nerve agent urinary biomarkers 
Nerve agents readily hydrolyze in the human body, forming the alkyl phosphonic acid s 
(Appendix 1). Due to high polarity, the se metab

3. Summary of nerve agent urinary biomarkers 
Nerve agents readily hydrolyze in the human body, forming the alkyl phosphonic acid s 
(Appendix 1). Due to high polarity, the se metabolites are rapidly excreted in urine without 
further transformation . Human exposures to sarin ha ve been confirmed through the 
identification of the hydrolysis product, isopropyl methyl phosphonic acid, in urine .1 The 
urinary nerve agent alkyl phosphonic acids have not been detected in the general population; 
however, direct exposure to the alkyl phosphonic acids themselves could result in the 
presence of these compounds. Control samples from unexposed persons within the same 
geographical area can be used to rule out this possibility. 
3.1 Nerve agent hydrolysis metabolites 
Various methods can be applied to separate and detect alkyl phosphonic acids in urine. Solid 
phase extraction has been used for sample preparation and concentration. Separation by LC 
has been well documented, using either hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC) or 
reversed phase chromatography. Separation by GC has also been used, but requires 
derivatization. Both tandem and high resolution mass
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
using either hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC) or 
reversed phase chromatography. Separation by GC has also been used, but requires 
derivatization. Both tandem and high resolution mass spectrometry have successfully 
detected these compounds from urine samples to concentrations of 1 ng/ml or less. 
The following alkyl phosphonic acids have been evaluated using the methods described 
below: ethyl methylphosphonic acid (EMPA, CAS 1832 -53-7), the metabolite o f VX 
(O-ethyl S-2-diisopropylaminoethyl methylphosphonothiolate, CAS 50782-69-9); isopropyl 
methylphosphonic acid (iPr MPA, CAS 1832 -54-8), the metab olite of GB ( O-isopropyl 
methylphosphonofluoridate CAS 107 -44-8); pinacolyl m ethylphosphonic acid (PMPA, 
CAS 616-52-4), the metabolite of GD (O-pinacolyl methylphosphonofluoridate, CAS 96 -
64-0); cyclohexyl methylphosphonic acid (CMPA, CAS 1932 -60-1), the metabolite of GF 
(cyclohexyl methylphosphonofluoridate, CAS 329-99-7); and 2 -(methyl)propyl 
methylphosphonic acid (iBuMPA, CAS 1604-38-2), the metabolite of VR (O-isobutyl S-2-
diethylaminoethyl methylphosphonothiolate, CAS 159939-87-4).

3.1.1 Sample preparation 
Sample preparation of alkyl phosphonic acids can be performed using SPE. A normal phase 
approach is suitable because of the high polarity of these compounds, but a high acetonitrile 
concentration is required to allow interaction of the compounds with the sor bent. 
Alternatively, a reversed phase mechanism can also be used if the sample has been acidified 
to promote binding of the neutralized alkyl phosphonic acids to the sorbent. Typically a silica 
sorbent has been used for aqueous normal phase separations, and a polymeric sorbent 
designed for enhanced retention of polar compounds has been used for reversed phase 
separations.

3.1.2 LC–MS 
Chromatographic separation of alkyl phosphonic acids can be performed using HILIC or 
reversed phase HPLC. The reagents and chemicals needed for HP LC–MS vary according 
to the approach selected; however, a minimum of HPLC grade reagents , ideally LC–MS 
grade when available, should be used. Note that for HILIC separations high purity 
ammonium acetate (>98%) is necessary, as a significant background response has been noted 
for low purity ammonium acetate. The chemicals needed for HPLC-ESI-MS/MS are given 
in Table 2.

Analytical HPLC columns used for HILIC separation of alkyl phosphonic acids include Si-
HILIC or Amide -HILIC. A minimum length of 50 mm with a 2.1 mm i.d. or less and a 
particle size of 1.7-3 µm have successfully been applied to the extracted urine samples. The 
pressure for this i socratic separation, which is high in acetonitrile falls within the pressure 
ranges of a typical HPLC and does not necessitate the use of a UHPLC system. 
Analytical HPLC columns used for reversed phase separation of alkyl phosphonic acids

4. Summary of sulfur mustard urinary biomarkers 
Sulfur mustard is metabolized through an interactio n with glutathione to form 
1,1’-sulfonylbis[2-S-(N-acetylcysteinyl)ethane] (SBSNAE) and further reacts with -lyase 
enzymes to form 1,1’-sulfonylbis[2-(methylsulfinyl)ethane] (SBMSE), 1-methylsulfinyl-2-
[2-(methylthio) ethylsulfonyl]ethane (MSMTESE) , and 1,1’ -sulfonylbis[2-
(methylthio)ethane] (SBMTE) (Appendix 2). Additionally, DNA adducts are formed 
following a reaction with the sulfonium ion, excised, and excreted into urine. The four major 
DNA adducts from sulfur mustard exposure are N7 -(2-hydroxyethylthioethyl)-2’-guanine 
(N7-HETEG), bis(2-ethyl-N7-guanine)thioether (Bis-G), N3-(2-hydroxyethylthioethyl)-2’-
adenine (N3
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
e four major 
DNA adducts from sulfur mustard exposure are N7 -(2-hydroxyethylthioethyl)-2’-guanine 
(N7-HETEG), bis(2-ethyl-N7-guanine)thioether (Bis-G), N3-(2-hydroxyethylthioethyl)-2’-
adenine (N3 -HETEA) and O6 -(2-hydroxyethylthioethyl)-2’-guanine (O6 -HETEG) 
(Appendix 3) . These compounds are excreted into urine and serve as unique, short and 
medium term biomarkers of exposure. Sulfur mustard also hydrolyzes to form thiodiglycol 
(TDG) which is excreted into urine ; however, TDG is not a unique biomarker of sulfur 
mustard exposure as it is present in populations not exposed to sulfur mustard.6 Collectively, 
the presence of these biomarkers in urine can be used to confirm exposure to sulfur mustard.

4.1 Sulfur mustard metabolite detection 
Urine samples containing sulfur mustard metabolites are prepared for analysis using SPE or 
supported liquid-liquid extraction (SLE). Multiple methods have been developed to measure 
the individual biomarkers using LC – and GC–MS analysis. Conversion of the  -lyase 
metabolites into a single analyt e, SBMTE or SBMSE, has been used to simplify detection 
and increase sensitivity. Alternatively, two of the -lyase metabolites, the glutathione 
conjugate, and TDG can be measured simultaneously in a single SPE–LC–MS method. 
4.1.1 Sample preparation 
Sample preparation of the sulfur mustard biomarkers can be performed using reversed phase 
SPE or SLE. A single SPE method was developed to extract TDG, SBMSE, MSMTESE, 
and SBSNAE from urine. The individual biomarkers can also be isolated from urine for 
detection with LC–MS or GC–MS. In lieu of analyzing all -lyase metabolites, the 
metabolites can be either reduced or oxidized to form SBMTE or SBMSE, respectively. This

4.2 Sulfur mustard DNA adducts 
Urine samples containing sulfur mustard DNA (SM -DNA) adducts are prepared for 
analysis using SPE with detection by LC–MS analysis. According to animal exposure 
studies, N7-HETEG is the most abundant of these four adducts, Bis-G and N3-HETEA 
are less abundant, while O6 -HETEG is the least prevalent.12 SM-DNA adducts can be 
detected up to 29 days after SM exposure with higher dosages; however, for lower doses, 
the concentration of these SM-DNA adducts in vivo is anticipated to be quite low (pg/ml–
ng/ml level).13 
Note! Reference materials necessary for this assay must be synthesized in-house as they 
are not commercially available.

The C18 cartridge (commercial or self-loaded; 1 g of C18 packing material and

4.2.1 Sample preparation 
The C18 cartridge (commercial or self-loaded; 1 g of C18 packing material and 13 mm 
bed depth in a 6 ml cartridge), is ﬁrst conditioned with 2 ml methanol and 4 ml water, 
then the urine sample is passed through the conditioned cartridge without suction. The 
cartridge is washed with 3 ml water and 2 ml of 20% methanol (v/v). Four SM –DNA 
adducts are eluted by 2 ml of 20% methanol (v/v) in 5% formic acid (v/v) solution and 
1.5 ml of 50% methanol (v/v) in 5% formic acid (v/v) solution, which are collected 
together and evaporated to dryness. The residue is resolved in 50 µl of 50% methanol in 
water and centrifuged at about 10, 000 x g for 10 min. The supernatant is ready for UP 
LC–MS/MS (+ESI) SRM analysis. 
For the choice of elution solution for SPE, considering the pH of urine is ca. 8, and that 
the pKa values are pKa,1 = 3.2–3.2 for guanine and adenine, pKa,2 = 9.2–9.6 for guanine, 
and pKa = 4.1 for adenine, the analytes should be transformed to ionic forms with low 
pH and then eluted. It is found that the extraction recovery is noticeably improved wit

and pKa = 4.1 for adenine, the analytes should be transformed to ionic forms with low 
pH and then eluted. It is found that the extraction recovery is noticeably improved with 
the addition of an acidic modifier (e.g. formic acid) in the elution solution.

1. Scope 
This chapter describes methods used for the identification of blood biomarkers resulting 
from human exposure to chemical warfare agents (CWA s). Biomarkers addressed include 
hydrolysis metabolites and protein adducts of nerve agents (Figure 1) and hydrolysis, 
glutathione conjugated, and -lyase metabolites, protein adducts, and DNA adducts of sulfur 
mustard (Figure 2). The methods presented includ e release of protein bound nerve agents 
through fluor idation, enzymatic digests, solid phase extraction (SPE) or affinity capture 
sample preparation, separation by gas chromatography (GC) or liquid chromatography (LC), 
and detection by mass spectrometry (MS). 
Biomedical samples collected following suspected CWA use are evaluated for biomarkers 
of exposure. Ideally, the
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
tography (GC) or liquid chromatography (LC), 
and detection by mass spectrometry (MS). 
Biomedical samples collected following suspected CWA use are evaluated for biomarkers 
of exposure. Ideally, the biomarkers selected should occur solely from exposure to a CWA 
and should not be present in samples collected from unexposed persons. Alternativ ely, the 
selected biomarker(s) may be present at concentrations relevant to CWA exposure which are 
substantially differentiated from those present in an unexposed population. Given the high 
toxicity, anticipated low doses, and variability of time of sample collection, low 
concentrations of these biomarkers are expected (ng/ml).

2. Safety aspects and clinical sample considerations 
Specific safety concerns for CWAs are presented in Section 2, Part A, Chapter I: 
Introduction. Since unreacted CWA concentrations are typically low in biomedical samples, 
the primary safety concern is the biohazard potential of the clinical sample itself. Follow 
universal precautions, and treat all blood samples as if infectious. After use, all resi dual 
biomedical samples , solutions, and lab ware that have been in contact with biomedical 
samples should be decontaminated in designated decontamination containers with an 
appropriate disinfectant (e.g. bleach) before disposal. 
Maintain whole blood samples at +4 °C to minimize biomarker degradation. Freezing whole 
blood samples will lyse red blood cells and may impact measurement of CWA exposure 
biomarkers; any biomarkers selected should be validated for compatibility if lysed whole 
blood samples are to be used. Maintain plasma or serum samples frozen (-20 °C or colder) 
to minimize biomarker degradati
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
any biomarkers selected should be validated for compatibility if lysed whole 
blood samples are to be used. Maintain plasma or serum samples frozen (-20 °C or colder) 
to minimize biomarker degradation, prevent mold growth, and reduce potential spillage 
during sample transport. 
3. Summary of nerve agent blood biomarkers 
Nerve agents form protein adducts in the human body after loss of the leaving group , and 
these adducts are the primary biomarker s of nerve agent exposure in blood samples 
(Appendices 1 and 2). The main nerve agent targets in blood are the cholinesterases and 
albumin. Nerve agents react with the same active site in red blood cell acetylcholinesterase 
(AChE) and neuronal AChE; however, AChE is not typically used as a biomarker due to its 
relatively low concentration in blood (~0.5 µg/ml)1 and difficulty to access . 
Butyrylcholinesterase (BChE) has the same active site and forms the same nerve agent 
specific adducts as AChE. BChE is freely available in serum/plasma samples and is found 
in ~10× higher concentrations (~5 µg/ml) than AChE 1, making BChE a more ideal 
cholinesterase biomarker. While the typical plasma concentration of albumin (40 mg/ml) is 
~
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
lasma samples and is found 
in ~10× higher concentrations (~5 µg/ml) than AChE 1, making BChE a more ideal 
cholinesterase biomarker. While the typical plasma concentration of albumin (40 mg/ml) is 
~10,000× higher than BChE and albumin has a relatively long half -life (20 days), nerve 
agents react 500× slower with albumin than with cholinesterases.2 Additionally, V-series 
agents are significantly less reactive with albumin than are G-series agents.3,4 
Nerve agent BChE adducts undergo degradation through a hydrolysis commonly referred to 
as aging while nerve agent adducts to albumin do not. During aging on BChE, the agent 
specific O-alkyl group is replaced by a hydrogen (Appendix 1) , leaving behind a generic 
marker of nerve agent exposure. The rate of this degradation process varies significantly 
between nerve agents with faster degradation rates fo und in the G -series agents versus the 
V-series agents . While the unaged, nerve agent specific protein adducts have not been 
detected in blood samples from the general population, some of the Schedule 1 nerve agents 
potentially share common aged protein adducts with other non-schedule organophosphorus 
compounds. Control sam
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
tected in blood samples from the general population, some of the Schedule 1 nerve agents 
potentially share common aged protein adducts with other non-schedule organophosphorus 
compounds. Control samples of unexposed persons within the same geographical area can 
be used to rule out the possibility that measurement of a non-specific BChE adduct is due to 
exposure to a non-schedule cholinesterase inhibitor. 
Nerve agents also readily hydrolyze in the human body, forming the alkyl phosphonic acids 
(see Section 4, Chapter I, Appendix 1). While these polar compounds are rapidly excreted 
in the urine, they can also be found in the blood. See Section 4, Chapter I, Chapter part 3 for 
a more complete description of the nerve agent hydrolysis products and their analysis .

The nerve agent metabolites have not been detected in blood samples from the general 
population; however, exposure to the p hosphonic acids them selves may result in the 
presence of these compounds. Control samples from unexposed persons within the same 
geographical area can be used to rule out this possibility. 
A concise overview on all these different methods applied to the diverse tissue samples of a 
female victim fatally poisoned with sarin during the Syrian Arab Republic conflict in 2013 
has been presented recently.5 
3.1 Nerve agent hydrolysis metabolites 
Analysis of nerve agent hydrolysis metabolites has been addressed previously (see Section 
4, Chapter I, Chapter part 3.1). Nerve agent hydrolysis metabolites in plasma or serum can 
be prepared and analyzed similarly to the metabolites in urine; however , initial sample 
volumes may need to be adjusted depending on the specific protocols being followed.6 
3.2 Nerve agent protein adducts 
Protein-based methods for confirming nerve agent exposure ha
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
er , initial sample 
volumes may need to be adjusted depending on the specific protocols being followed.6 
3.2 Nerve agent protein adducts 
Protein-based methods for confirming nerve agent exposure have been developed with 
varying levels of specificity and include the Ellman activity assay , fluoride reactivation, 
albumin adducts, and BChE adducts. BChE is a convenient and reliable biomarker because 
it is easily extracted from blood products, has a high reaction rate with nerve agents, and has 
a relatively long half-life (12 days7); BChE adducts have been measured up to 16 days post-
exposure.8 Nerve agent adducts to BChE do undergo aging, so information on specific agent 
used can be lost over time. Nerve agent adducts to albumin do not undergo the aging process, 
but the reactivity of albumin at Tyr-411 is reduced for the V -series agents as compared to 
the G -series agents .9 Fluoride reactivation will release the phosphonofluoridate forms of 
adducted nerve agents from all proteins in a sample, but this process does not work once 
aging has occurred. The Ellman activity assay is not considered specific enough for 
confirming nerve agent exposure and is not included further
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
teins in a sample, but this process does not work once 
aging has occurred. The Ellman activity assay is not considered specific enough for 
confirming nerve agent exposure and is not included further in this discussion. 
3.2.1 Phosphonofluoridates 
Fluoride reactivation has proven to be a highly sensitive method for detecting nerve agent 
exposure. Protein bound nerve agents can be released as the phosphonofluoridate form if the 
adduct has not aged. However, the loss of the agent defining O-alkyl group through aging 
eliminates the possibility of refluoridation and makes the detection of rapidly aging nerve 
agent adducts unlikely in low dose exposures. Likewise, displacement of the OP adduct from 
BChE and AChE after oxime therapy reduces the effectiveness of this diagnostic approach.

have been reported for tabun (GA) [O -ethy

3.2.2 Nerve agent adducts to butyrylcholinesterase 
GB, GD, GF, VX, and VR [O-isobutyl S-2-diethylaminoethyl methylphosphonothio late, 
CAS 159939-87-4] are nerve agents that share a common methyl -phosphorus bond that is 
preserved after reaction with the active site serine (Ser -198) of BChE. The agent -specific 
methyl nerve agent adducts to BChE can lose their corresponding O-alkyl group resulting in 
an aged product known as the m ethyl phosphonate (MeP) adduct . Methyl nerve agent 
adducts to BChE form the common MeP adduct at different
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
ChE can lose their corresponding O-alkyl group resulting in 
an aged product known as the m ethyl phosphonate (MeP) adduct . Methyl nerve agent 
adducts to BChE form the common MeP adduct at different rates, and the reaction to form 
the aged adduct continues to occur after a clinical specimen is collected. Measurement of the 
nerve agent-specific adducts and their common ag ed adduct in blood samples is therefore 
critical to confirm exposure to nerve agents (Appendix 1). 
3.2.2.1 Sample preparation 
Preconcentration of BChE can be performed using affinity capture with either procainamide 
gel or BChE specific antibodies. Both approaches isolate BChE in blood samples that can 
then be digested with pepsin to produce the nonapeptide FGE (S*)AGAAS which contains 
the active site Ser-198 (S*) targeted by nerve agents. Nerve agent specific and aged adducts 
to BChE (as well as the unadducted form) can be measured as the nonapeptide using LC–
MS/MS. While other enzymes can be used, the pepsin produced adducted nonapeptide is 
generally considered the primary biomarker of nerve agent exposure. 8 The method s 
described are suitable for retrospective detection of nerve agent exposure by

generally considered the primary biomarker of nerve agent exposure. 8 The method s 
described are suitable for retrospective detection of nerve agent exposure by measurement 
of adducts to the Ser-198 residue of human BChE in plasma. Detailed descriptions of the 
methods included have been published.12-14

Prior to sample processing, conjugate procainamide to CNBr-active Sepharose 4B gel as 
previously described12 remove particulates from plasma by centrifugation at 13,000 × g for 
5 min and then filtration using 0.45 μm microporous membranes. Dilute 100 μl of the filtered 
plasma sample with 4.5 ml Buffer B (15 mM Na2HPO4, 5 mM NaH2PO4, pH 6.7) in a 20 ml 
screw-capped bottle. Mix together with 2.5 ml of prepared procainamide-gel which has been 
preconditioned with 15 ml of Buffer B. Incubate the gel mixture at room temperature with 
shaking at a speed of 60 r/min for 1.0 h. Load the reaction gel solution onto an empty 6.0 ml 
SPE column, and wash with 10 ml of Buffer B. Elute the bound BChE with 4.5 ml of Buffer 
C (15 mM Na 2HPO4, 5 mM NaH2PO4, 2 M NaCl, pH 6.7). Collect the 4.5 ml eluate, and 
concentrate it to ~100 μl using a 4.0 ml 100-kDa cut -off filter by ultrafiltration with 
centrifugation at 12,000 × g.

3.2.3 Nerve agent adducts to tyrosine 
The method described is suitable for retrospective detection of exposure to the nerve agents 
GA, GB, GD, GF, VR, VX , and VM [O-ethyl S -2-diethylaminoethyl 
methylphosphonothiolate, CAS 21770-86-5] by simultaneous measurement of their adducts 
to tyrosine (Tyr) (Appendix 2). The most likely source of nerve agent adducted Tyr in plasma 
samples is albumin although any protein bound nerve agent adducted Tyr present in the 
sample should be detectable. 
A simple approach was established using SPE combined with UHPLC–MS/MS for the 
measurement of OPNA–Tyr adducts in plasma.4 Plasma proteins are enriched by acetone 
precipitation and then digested with pronase which allows any specific adducted OPNA-Tyr 
biomarkers to be measured . The resulting OPNA-Tyr adducts are detected by UHP LC–
MS/MS.

4. Summary of sulfur mustard blood biomarkers 
Sulfur mustard , bis(2-chloroethyl)sulfide, metabolizes in the human body through 
hydrolysis, interaction with glutathione, or reaction with -lyase enzymes. While these 
compounds are excreted in the urine, they can also be found in the blood.16, 17 See Section 4, 
Chapter I, Chapter part 4 for a more complete description of these sulfur mustard metabolites 
and their analysis. While the glutathione and -lyase metabolites have not been detected in 
blood samples from the general population , the hydrolysis product thiodiglycol (TDG) is 
present in populations not exposed to sulfur mustard.18, 19 Measurement of TDG alone is not 
indicative of sulfur mustard exposure. Additionally, measurement of reactive sulfur mustard 
and its oxidation products bis--chloroethyl sulfoxide (SMO) and bis--chloroethyl sulfone 
(SMO2) in plasma have been reported in the literature 20; however, these species are 
especially short-lived and require use of the selective derivatizing agent 2 -(3,5-
bis(mercaptomethyl)phenoxy) acetic acid for observation. 
Sulfur mustard is a highly reactive alkylating agent that will form addu
title: Recommended Operating Procedures for Analysis in the Verification of Chemical Disarmament

text:
rt-lived and require use of the selective derivatizing agent 2 -(3,5-
bis(mercaptomethyl)phenoxy) acetic acid for observation. 
Sulfur mustard is a highly reactive alkylating agent that will form adducts with proteins 
through an episulfonium ion intermedia te. Sulfur mustard can form stable adducts with a 
variety of amino acids including valine (Val), glutamic acid (Glu), histidine (His), and 
cysteine (Cys). Typically, it is the stable adduct (S-2-hydroxyethylthioethyl; S -HETE) 
formed on Cys-34 of human serum albumin which has been the primary biomarker in blood 
for confirming exposure to sulfur mustard (Appendix 3). 
As a highly reactive electrophile, sulfur mustard can also readily react with DNA via its 
episulfonium ion. DNA alkylation and damage is believed to be the crucial factor in initiating 
sulfur mustard induced toxicity. Alkylation by sulfur mustard mainly occurs at the N7 or O6 
positions of guanine (G) and the N3 position of adenine (A) to form various DNA adducts. 
There are four major DNA adducts from sulfur mustard exposure: 
N7-(2-hydroxyethylthioethyl)-2’-guanine (N7-HETE-G); bis(2-ethyl-N7-guanine)thioether

mustard adducts are approximately 61%, 16%, 15 %, and 0.1 %, respectively 21. Their 
chemical structures are shown in Appendix 4. 
4.1 Sulfur mustard metabolites 
Analysis of sulfur mustard metabolites is covered in Section 4, Chapter I, Chapter part 4.1. 
Sulfur mustard metabolites in blood can be prep ared and analyzed similarly to the 
metabolites in urine; however, initial sample volumes may need to be adjusted depending on 
the specific protocols being followed.16, 17 A single SPE method for simultaneous detection 
of four sulfur mustard biomarkers (TDG, SBMSE, MSMTESE and SBSNAE) in urine22 can 
also be used in plasma samples while total proteins in plasma are removed using the acetone 
or acetonitrile precipitation method.

4.2 Sulfur mustard protein adducts 
As stated above, the stable adduct S-HETE formed on Cys-34 of human serum albumin has 
become the primary blood biomarker for confirming exposure to sulfur mustard, and there 
are multiple methods available in the literature that describe different ways of assessing this 
biomarker. Albumin can be isolated using either Cibacro n Blue s epharose23 or 
immunoaffinity columns24. Recently, less selective sample preparation approaches such as 
protein precipitation have been shown to be equally effective .25, 2 6 Additionally, two 
different enzymes have been used to digest sulfur mustard adducted albumin to make 
analysis by LC–MS/MS simpler: 1) pronase to produce the [S-HETE]-Cys-Pro adduct and 
2) proteinase K to produce the [S-HETE]-Cys-Pro-Phe adduct. The methods described are 
suitable for retrospective detection of sulfur mustard exposure by measurement of the sulfur 
mustard adduct to the Cys-34 residue of human serum albumin in plasma , and the two 
different peptides represent different biomarkers applicable to verification analysis. Detailed

Following reaction with sulfur mustard, part of the alkylated DNA can be repaired in vivo. 
These sulfur mustard DNA base adducts are excised from damaged DNA. While primarily 
excreted in the urine, they can also be found in the blood. However, not all of the alkylated

1. Scope 
This chapter describes the role, the purpose and the history of Proficiency Tests (PT) 
organised by the Technical Secretariat of the Organisation for Prohibition of Chemical 
Weapons (OPCW), as well as general provisions of sampling and analysis under the 
Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). 
2. Sampling and Analysis under the CWC 
The CWC calls for using Sampling and Analysis (S&A) as one of the tools to support 
verification activities. Samples can be analysed on -site by the inspection team (IT) or 
transferred off-site to Designated Laboratories (DL). The objective of S&A can be different 
depending on the type of the particular inspection. At chemical weapons related facilities, 
the objective of S&A is to confirm the type of agent being destroyed (inspections under 
article IV and V of the CWC), and at industrial facilities the objective is to confirm the 
absence of Schedule 1 chemicals or any other undeclared Scheduled chemicals (inspections 
under Article VI o

text:
article IV and V of the CWC), and at industrial facilities the objective is to confirm the 
absence of Schedule 1 chemicals or any other undeclared Scheduled chemicals (inspections 
under Article VI of the CWC). See Section 1, Part A, Chapter III: Chemicals for the 
discussion on the Schedules of chemicals.

Both of them have not been officially invoked up to now (December 2017). In the first case,

The provisions for S&A under the CWC can be summarised as follows: 
 Samples are generally collected by Inspected State Party (ISP) site representatives, 
or alternatively, by the inspection IT, if agreed upon in advance. 
 Where possible, the analysis will be done on-site. Samples can be analysed by the IT 
using its approved equipment, or alternatively, by the ISP in the presence of the IT, 
if so requested by the IT. 
 If the IT deems it necessary , it shall transfer samples for analysis off -site to 
laboratories designated by the OPCW. However, during Schedule 3 and Other 
Chemical Production Facilities (OCPF) inspections, it can do so only in case of 
unresolved ambiguities, and also only subject to ISP agreement.

3. OPCW Proficiency Tests and Designated Laboratories 
3.1 Introduction 
The first international interlaboratory comparison (round -robin) test for the verification of 
chemical disarmament took place in 1989 on Finnish initiative. This test and three 
subsequent tests were coordinated by Finland. 1–4 The Provisional Technical Secretariat 
(PTS) of the Preparatory Commission of the OPCW coordinated the first international 
OPCW/PTS interlaboratory comparison test in 1994. 5 Two further tests —so called ‘trial 
proficiency tests’—were arranged by the PTS in 1995. 
The OPCW has been conducting Official PTs since 1996 to designate laboratories for the 
analysis of authentic samples. In 1996 and 1997 one test was conducted each year, and since

1998 two annual tests are conducted . The OPCW Designated Laboratory network is an 
important element of the verification regime of the CWC. The existence of laboratories with 
proven expertise in off -site analysis of CWC -related samples provides a high degree of 
confidence that chemical analyses yield unambiguous results, thus rendering a significant 
element of deterrence against breaches of the CWC. 
The tests are part of a mechanism that ensures laboratory competence in the analysis of 
chemicals related to the Convention. Unlike many other proficiency test schemes, the OPCW 
PT is qualitative, i.e. the laboratories must determine if out of a very large set –essentially 
infinite – of chemicals relevant to the CWC, any are present in the samples. 
3.2 Conduct of OPCW Proficiency Tests 
The OPCW PT scheme is accredited by the Dutch Accreditation Council (Raad voor 
Accreditatie; RvA) since 2001. The OPCW Official PT s are conducted in compliance with 
ISO 1 7043:2010,7 with the assistance of two designated

ccredited by the Dutch Accreditation Council (Raad voor 
Accreditatie; RvA) since 2001. The OPCW Official PT s are conducted in compliance with 
ISO 1 7043:2010,7 with the assistance of two designated laboratories that respectively 
prepare the samples and assist in the evaluation of results based on OPCW requirements. 
When a laboratory wants to participate for the first time, it has to be nominated and notified 
by its National Authority. Then, the Secretariat informs the participants of the test plan and 
the scenario before a sample is dispatched. The sample preparation laboratory dispatches the 
samples to the participating laboratories at no cost and the participating laboratories have to 
report the identified chemicals relevant to the test within 15 days after receipt . Any 
laboratory that fails to submit the PT report will fail the test unless it informs the Secretariat 
of its intention to withdraw before the end of the test and provides a satisfactory explanation. 
Once all participants complete the test , or the time period ends, the OPCW Laboratory and 
the assisting evaluating laboratory evaluate the results independently and concurrently in 
accordance with the rele

the assisting evaluating laboratory evaluate the results independently and concurrently in

The draft report is then discussed by the evaluating laboratory and the OPCW Laboratory. 
Prior to drawing any conclusions on the performance of individual laboratories, t he 
Secretariat prepares: 
(a) an assessment of the stability, quality and validity of samples to determine the 
applicability of the test; and 
(b) an assessment of the evaluation of the test results. 
The Secretariat prepares a preliminary evaluation report based on all above-mentioned data, 
and thereafter informs the participants of their performance and requests comments. The 
Secretariat organises a one -day meeting of all participants at the OPCW head quarters to 
discuss the preliminary results of the PT. After a general session, the participants are given 
the opportunity to meet individually with the representatives of the OPCW Laboratory, the 
evaluating laboratory and the sample preparation laboratory. The participants are given two 
week

3.3 Samples and reporting 
Unlike most PTs aiming for quantitative analyses of known compounds in pre-determined 
matrices, the OPCW PT is primarily based on the qualitative analysis of samples of unknown 
sample composition in order to determine the presence of an essentially infinite number of 
possible chemicals relevant to the CWC. The participants receive two sets of three samples 
each (test sample , control, blank).ii There is no indication for the type of the sample ; thus 
each sample has to be analysed like a test sample. The laboratory creates its own solvent 
blank to prove the absence of the reported chemicals in the instrument before introducing 
the sample. The salient features of the test are as follows: 
 Diverse nature of chemicals: The OPCW PT is primarily based on qualitative analysis 
and aims to confirm the presence of CWC -related chemica ls, which are scheduled 
chemicals and/or precursors/degradation products of scheduled chemicals spiked at 1–
10 ppm level. The nature of chemicals may

chemicals and/or precursors/degradation products of scheduled chemicals spiked at 1–
10 ppm level. The nature of chemicals may vary from highly volatile early -eluting 
chemicals (e.g. pinacolyl alcohol: 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol) to non-volatile late-eluting 
chemicals (e.g. BZ: 3-quinuclidinyl benzilate). 
 Blind testing for an almost infinite number of chemicals in complex matrices: 
Participants receive samples of unknown composition to be analysed for the presence 
of a large number of pos sible chemicals in various matrices ( e.g. soil, water, organic 
waste, wipe), often with a high background compris ed of polyethylene glycol (PEG), 
diesel, etc. 
 No prescription of methods : Laboratories have no restrictions regarding sample 
preparation or analytical methods. Sample preparation procedures often require clean-
up, extraction, derivatisation and concentration steps. All i dentifications must be

one technique must be spectrometric.

one technique must be spectrometric. 
 Detailed reporting of results: Participants’ reports must contain names, structures and 
CAS numbers (if available) of the identified chemicals, a detailed description of the 
employed sample preparation methods, a description of the employed analytical 
methods, the analytical data (chromatographic and/or spectrometric) , and the 
analytical conditions. There must be an unbroken chain of evidence linking each 
sample to the corresponding reported chemicals throughout the entire report. 
 Short timeline: Participants have only 15 calendar days after receipt of the samples to 
perform the analyses and dispatch the report. 
 Zero tolerance for false positive : Any reported chemical that is not contained in the 
sample matrix or that cannot be formed in the sample matrix constitutes a false positive 
result. Only chemicals relevant to the aim of the test should be reported. In addition, 
reporting a chemical that is present in the sample , even as a minor constituent of the

3.4 Chemicals 
Over the course of the past 41 OPCW PTs, all major classes of scheduled chemic als have 
appeared as spiking chemicals, with the exception of chemicals in schedules 1.A.07 and 
1.A.08 toxins (saxitoxin and ricin, respectively), 2.A.02 (perfluoroisobutylene; PFIB), 
1.B.09–12 and some highly reactive and/or volatile Schedule 3 chemicals. In the initial phase 
of PTs, the concept behind sample composition included at least one spiking chemical that 
was either completely unknown, or whose analytical data, chemical properties or analytical 
behaviour were different from already known chemicals. Participating laboratories had to 
make a significant effort to identify the structure of spiking chemicals, with particular 
consideration of assignment of certain atoms or functional groups. Over time and partially 
as a response to new requirements of OPCW inspections, the focus of OPCW PTs has shifted 
from the testing of participants’ capabilities to identif y unknown chemicals to the 
improvement of samp

as a response to new requirements of OPCW inspections, the focus of OPCW PTs has shifted 
from the testing of participants’ capabilities to identif y unknown chemicals to the 
improvement of sample preparation procedures and reporting skills. As a result, there has 
been an increase in the complexi ty of sample matrices , including more challenging sets of 
background chemicals and a more challenging selection of chemicals to be reported, and a 
decrease of complexity of the structures of the spiking chemicals, which caused less 
chemical identification ambiguity. 
An overview of the classes of chemicals used as spiking chemicals in the 41 PTs is shown 
in Fig. 1. The most frequent schedule is 2.B.04, as this is the group with the largest number 
of chemicals covered by the CWC (there is in fact an unlimited number of potential 2.B.04 
chemicals). Another reason for the predominance of 2.B.04 chemicals is that even though 
some of them seem to be simple in structure (e.g. methylphosphonic acid) , they present an 
analytical challenge for both sample preparation and instrumental analysis. The vast majority 
of 2.B.04 chemicals need to be carefully extracted from samples and the

analytical challenge for both sample preparation and instrumental analysis. The vast majority 
of 2.B.04 chemicals need to be carefully extracted from samples and then derivatised for use 
with the most popular technique used by PT participants , gas chromatography –electron 
ionisation mass spectrometry (GC–EI/MS), before they are analysed. Both processes have 
an impact on the overall performance of analysis and the correctness of reporting. 
Furthermore, many 2.B.04 chemicals are direct degradation products or precursors of 
schedule 1.A chemicals , and thus their presence is almost always expected in samples 
containing schedule 1.A chemicals. 
The second most frequent group of chemicals are non-scheduled chemicals (N.S.), of which 
those related to the sulphur mustard family (1.A.04), including thiodiglycol (2.B.13; the only 
scheduled degradation product for sulphur mustard) were most often used as spiking 
chemicals (43 times). Next are the VX family (1.A.03) related chemicals ( 9 times) and the 
tabun and triethanolamine-related chemicals (4 times, respectively). 
The reason for including such chemicals in PT samples is that they are known

3.5 Criteria for performance evaluation 
The performance scoring is done as follows:9-10 
(a) Each correct identification is positively scored (+1 point). 
(b) Identification of a degradation product(s) instead of the spiking chemical is positively 
scored (+1 point) if the original spiking chemical is no longer present in the sample.

3.6 Designation of laboratories 
In order to achieve designation, the laboratories must participate in at least one PT per year 
and have performed successfully in the last three consecutive tests with a minimum rating 
of three As, or two As and one B. This effectively means that only one spiking chemical can 
be missed in three consecutive tests. Additionally, the laboratory must be accredited for the 
analysis of CWC-related chemicals by an internationally recognised accreditation body. The 
most common international standard DLs are following

are temporarily suspended or may lose the d esignation status (e.g. scores F due to false

A relative new rule allows laboratories that have analysed authentic samples to be awarded 
an A grade under the condition that the analysis was satisfactorily, the analytical task was at 
lease as difficult as a Proficiency Test and that the amount of work to analyse such samples 
is not less than the duration of a Proficiency Test.

.6 Common errors in laboratories’ reports 
Reporting of irrelevant chemicals, mistakes in identification of spiking chemicals and 
breaches in the chain of evidence are the most c ommon e rrors observed in PT reports. 
A compound has to be confirmed by at least two analytical techniques, one of which has to 
be spectrometric. Incomplete confirmation of identification leads to non-scoring. 
Only chemicals related to the CWC that are relevant to the aim of the test scenario should 
be reported. An understanding of the definition of scheduled chemicals is essential to avoid 
reporting irrelevant chemicals. Care should be taken to report name, structure, CAS number 
of the identified chemicals, as all of these must be correct to qualify the chemical for scoring. 
The chain of evidence with respect to the sample identity must be maintained throughout the 
report. For example, incorrect aliquot name in sample tracking leads to breach of the chain 
of evidence and, as a consequence, the corresponding chemical is not scored. 
Reasons for not reporting a chemical that has been spiked are inadequate sample clean -up, 
poor extraction and missed derivatisation steps during sample preparation.

4. Global strategy for an OPCW Proficiency Test in a participating laboratory 
A PT report must be sent to the OPCW within 15 calendar days after sample arrival at the 
laboratory. Thus, it is critical to plan the general conduct of sample preparation and analysis 
(see Fig. 2) . Due to the large amount of relevant chemicals of different nature s, sample 
preparation procedures cannot be very specific. It is therefore necessary to design general 
methods that allow recovery of the spiking chemicals from different matrices. These 
methods may then be modified to help identification or to improve reporting data depending 
on the specific characteristics of a sample. 
Another aspect to take into account before sample arrival is the clean-up of lab equipment 
and the set-up of analytical instruments. The supplies used for sample preparation should be 
new or pre -cleaned ensuring deactivation of glassware active sites. All analytical 
instrumentation should be calibrated and their performance tested in order to avoid false 
positives due to equipment contamination or other operational problems.
